exp.8:9:
David tells Ziba, Saul's former servant, to work the land of Mephibosheth along with his sons and his servants, and to bring in the harvest. In this way Saul's grandson will have something to live on. Furthermore, Mephibosheth will always eat at the king's table. The text adds that Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.

David speaks with Ziba after speaking with Mephibosheth, who was crippled and called himself a "dead dog." David had promised kindness to Saul's family because of his covenant with Jonathan, and for that reason he returns the land and gives him a place at his table.

For today: God's grace reminds us that we should treat with kindness those who cannot provide for themselves, and faithfully keep the promises we make, even when we receive nothing in return.
exp.17:27:
Ahimaaz runs up to King David and greets him with the word "All is well," which was a common greeting and also a way of saying that he brought good news. He falls down to the ground in respect and praises the Lord because he delivered up, that is, gave the victory over, those who had risen up against the king.

Ahimaaz, the son of the priest Zadok, runs to report the outcome of the battle against Absalom, David's son, who had rebelled. He speaks of the victory but avoids saying the most painful thing: that Absalom had died. Then David asks about his son, and Ahimaaz answers evasively. He perhaps wanted to give only the happy part of the news.

For today: let us give thanks to God for his victories, but let us be honest and sensitive when we share difficult news. Telling the whole truth, with love and care, is better than showing only what is pleasant.
exp.10:16:
This verse says that the men of the besieged city (Rabbah) came out to fight against Joab. In the battle several of David's soldiers died, and among them was Uriah the Hittite.

The narrator reports the result of the plan David had ordered in secret. David had committed adultery with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and wanted to hide his sin. Joab, the commander of the army, placed Uriah where the fighting was most dangerous. Other men died as well, so the maneuver cost more lives than Uriah's alone.

For today: a hidden sin often leads to worse ones and harms more people. Instead of covering up our failures, it is better to confess them to God promptly and seek repentance, as David did afterward (Psalm 51).
exp.6:24:
David asks God to carry out the promise he made about him and his family. The word "despiértala," an old way of saying "make it come true" or "keep it alive," is not used here, so that comment is left out. The phrase "for ever" shows that David wants the promise to last. He also asks God to do "as thou hast said," that is, just as he said it.

David, the king of Israel, is the one speaking. God had just promised him through the prophet Nathan that he would build a "house," meaning a lasting line of descendants and a firm kingdom for him. David answers with humility, remembering how God redeemed Israel from Egypt. He demands nothing; he relies on what God has already said. Many Christians see in this promise a foreshadowing of Jesus, a descendant of David.

When we pray, we can rely on the promises of the Bible. Praying with God's Word gives us confidence and reminds us that God is faithful.
exp.19:12:
It says that when they had removed Amasa's body from the road, all the people who had stopped beside him went on after Joab to pursue Sheba, son of Bichri. The verse then notes that the wording in the old text, which was written for readers of a different translation, is handled here: the source's own quoted words are not part of the verse you see, so no comment on them is carried over.

This is a narrative, not a speech. Sheba had led a rebellion against David. Joab, the commander of the army, had just killed Amasa, another commander, and the people stood still looking at the body. One of Joab's soldiers moved the corpse aside and covered it, and so the people resumed the march. The text does not approve of the crime; it only tells what happened.

For today: let us not be swept along by whoever leads with force or cunning without asking whether what they do is right. Before following anyone, let us consider their actions in the light of God's Word.
exp.12:22:
It says that two years passed after what Amnon did to Tamar. Absalom held a sheep-shearing festival at Baal-hazor, near Ephraim, and invited all the king's sons. The shearers are the men who cut the wool from the sheep, a time of year that was usually marked with food and joy.

This is part of the story of David's family. Amnon had abused Tamar, Absalom's sister, and David was angry, but the Bible does not say that he did anything about it. Absalom said nothing, but he kept his hatred. The text does not explain his whole plan here, but the invitation seems to be an opportunity carefully prepared. Later we will see that he had a dark purpose.

For today: silent resentment does not disappear with time; it can grow. If something has hurt you, bring it to God and seek healthy help, before bitterness makes the decisions for you (Hebrews 12:15).
exp.6:1:
Here the king David speaks with the prophet Nathan. He says that he dwells in a house made of cedar, a fine and costly wood, while the ark of God still remains in a tent, "within curtains."

David was already settled in his palace, because God had given him rest from his enemies. The ark was the symbol of God's presence among his people. David feels uneasy about that difference and thinks of building a house for God. Nathan encourages him at first, but that same night God speaks to him and gives him a different message, as seen in what follows.

When God gives us rest and blessing, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are giving him first place. Even so, it is wise to seek God before acting, even when our desire is good.
exp.5:13:
The verse says that David danced or leaped with all his strength before God, holding nothing back. He was wearing a "linen ephod," a simple garment like an apron or short tunic that the priests used. He was not dressed as a king, but as an ordinary worshiper.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Samuel. David is bringing the ark of God, the symbol of the divine presence, to Jerusalem, the city of David. Earlier, the ark had been in the house of Obed-edom, and there God blessed him. Now all Israel celebrates with sacrifices, trumpets, and shouts of joy. Later, Michal, his wife, despises him for this.

Today we can worship God with sincerity and devotion, without worrying too much about what others think. Our gratitude to God deserves to be expressed from the heart, even if someone does not understand it.
exp.18:20:
Abishai, son of Zeruiah, asks whether Shimei should not be put to death for what he did. Shimei had cursed the Lord's anointed, that is, King David, whom God had chosen and set apart to rule. Abishai takes it for granted that the offense deserves the death penalty.

Shimei, of the tribe of Benjamin, had insulted and cursed David when the king was fleeing from his son Absalom (2 Samuel 16). Now Absalom is dead, David is returning, and Shimei is the first to come and ask for forgiveness. Abishai, a loyal soldier of a hard temper, wants to punish him. David restrains him and spares his life.

Today we can learn that justice and mercy must go together. When someone offends us and then repents, we do not always have to demand what they deserve. Let us ask God for a heart that knows how to forgive, as He forgives us.
exp.12:13:
He says that Amnon did not listen to Tamar. She begged him not to do her harm, but he, being stronger, forced her and abused her. "Being stronger than she" means he had greater physical strength. "Lay with her" is an old way of saying that he sexually abused her. It is an act of violence, not of love.

Context: Amnon was the son of King David, and Tamar was his half-sister. He pretended to be sick so that he could be alone with her. Tamar pleaded with him using reasons: she spoke of her shame, of what is right in Israel, and of a lawful way out. He would not listen. The Bible presents this act as a serious wrong, and it shows that she was the innocent victim.

For today: The Bible takes seriously the pain of those who suffer abuse and does not blame them. If someone tells you that they were hurt, listen to them with respect, believe them, and help them seek protection and support. And if you have lived through something like this, it is not your fault; seek help from people you trust.
exp.20:2:
Here David asks the Gibeonites what he can do to make right the harm that was done to them. "Atonement" means doing something to repair an offense and remove the guilt. "The inheritance of the Lord" refers to the people of Israel and their land. David wants the Gibeonites to bless Israel again, that is, to ask for the good of the nation.

Here King David is speaking. There had been famine for three years, and God told him that the cause was the blood Saul had shed when he killed the Gibeonites. Israel had made a covenant of peace with them, and Saul broke it. David seeks justice for those who were wronged.

For today: when we have hurt someone, it is not enough to hope they will forget. We can follow David's example: approach with humility, listen to the one we have wronged, and ask how to repair the damage, without excuses.
exp.6:19:
This verse says that David is left without words before God. He asks what more he could say, because God already knows him completely. The word "servant" refers to someone who serves his lord, and "Lord God" is a way of addressing God with respect and reverence.

David speaks in prayer, sitting before the ark, after God promised him, through the prophet Nathan, a lasting descendant and an enduring house. David wanted to build a temple, but God answered that He would make a "house" for David, that is, a royal family. David responds with wonder and humility before such kindness, which he had not earned.

For today: sometimes, instead of saying much, it is enough to rest in the fact that God truly knows us, with our struggles and desires. You can pray simply, give thanks, and trust that He understands what you cannot put into words.
exp.0:17:
This verse is a short note before David's song. It says David ordered the people of Judah to be taught "the use of the bow," and that this is written in the "book of the upright." In Hebrew this book is called "the book of Jashar," which means "the upright" or "the just." It was an ancient collection of songs that we no longer have. The word "bow" may be the name of the song, or it may mean that the song was to be learned with a bow in hand. It is not certain.

The narrator explains why David composed this lament, a funeral song, after the deaths of Saul and Jonathan. David wanted Judah to learn it and remember it.

Today we too can honor those who have passed away, even those who hurt us, by remembering what was good with respect. Turning grief into prayer or into a song helps us heal and not forget.
exp.11:29:
David took the crown from the king of Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites. It weighed a talent of gold (about 30 kilograms) and had precious stones in it. They set it on David's head. David brought out a great quantity of riches from the city.

The narrator tells what happened after Joab, the commander of the army, attacked Rabbah. Joab asked David to come and complete the victory, so that the honor would belong to the king. Some translate "their king," and others understand "Milcom," the Ammonite god; the Hebrew allows both readings.

For today: triumphs and honors can puff up the heart. David received a crown right after his serious sin, and he still needed humility. May our successes lead us to thank God and to acknowledge our faults, not to feel superior.
exp.5:2:
This verse tells that David and his people brought the ark of God up on a new cart and carried it out of the house of Abinadab, in Gibeah. The sons of Abinadab, Uzzah and Ahio, were driving the new cart. "Drave" means that they were driving it.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David wanted to bring the ark, the symbol of God's presence, to Jerusalem. They were doing it with celebration and great enthusiasm. But the law said that the ark was to be carried with poles on the shoulders of the Levites, not on a cart. The text of this verse does not point this out, but the account that follows shows that something went wrong.

For today: good intentions and great enthusiasm in serving God are not enough. It is also important to seek how He wants to be honored, by knowing His Word and obeying it with humility.
exp.22:3:
This verse compares the just ruler to the light of a clear morning, when the sun rises and there are no clouds. It also compares him to the grass that springs up from the ground, made to shine by the sun after the rain. The word "ruler" here means the one who governs or has authority. The idea is that a leader who fears God brings clarity, freshness, and life to his people.

David speaks in what the Bible calls his final words. He says that God himself gave him this message by his Spirit. He describes what someone who governs should be like. In the verses that follow, he admits that his own house is not perfect, but he trusts in the covenant God made with him. Some also see here a look forward to the Messiah, the perfect King.

For today: if you have any authority, in your home, your work, or your church, try to exercise it with justice and respect for God. In this way your conduct can be like a clean morning that brings encouragement and helps others to grow.
exp.2:1:
This verse begins a list of the sons who were born to David while he was living in Hebron. The word "firstborn" means the eldest son, the first one born.

The narrator presents this list in the middle of the account of the long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. While David ruled over Judah alone, his family was growing and his position was becoming secure. The list also prepares the reader for the painful family conflicts that would come later, since Amnon and Absalom will be the main figures in them.

For today: God can bless a life and yet wounds still remain within a family. Let us care for our homes with prayer, a good example, and attentiveness, for the fruits of our decisions are seen over time.
exp.18:8:
This verse tells us that throughout all the tribes of Israel the people were arguing with one another. They remembered that David had saved them from their enemies, including the Philistines. But now the king had been forced to flee the land because of Absalom.

The people of Israel had followed Absalom in his rebellion, and Absalom died in battle. Then the people were confused and ashamed, not knowing what to do. That is why they began to remember the good that David had done and to ask why no one was bringing the king back. In this way David's return to Jerusalem is prepared.

Today we can learn to remember with gratitude the good that others have done for us, before we let ourselves be carried away by confusion or the fashion of the moment. And if we are wrong to follow someone, we can always set things right with humility.
exp.12:17:
This verse says that Tamar was wearing a robe of many colors, which was the clothing of the king's unmarried daughters. A servant of Amnon took her out into the street and locked the door behind her. The phrase "she had been thrown out" means she was sent away, and "servant" refers to someone who serves in a household.

The narrator tells what follows Amnon's rape of his half-brother's sister Tamar. She had begged him not to send her away like that, because it would add to her shame. He despised her and ordered his servant to take her out. The robe shows her position and her purity, which Amnon destroyed. Shutting the door shows his coldness and his rejection.

God sees the pain of those who have been wounded and rejected. Today we can stand with someone who suffers abuse, believe them, listen to them, and help them seek protection, without staying silent or minimizing what happened.
exp.16:28:
This verse ends the list of what was brought to David and his people. Besides beds, wheat and beans, they brought honey, butter (here meaning cream from milk), sheep, and cheese made from cow's milk. All of it was so they could eat. Those who helped thought: "These people are hungry, tired, and thirsty in the wilderness."

The one telling the story is the author of the book. David was fleeing from his son Absalom and had arrived at Mahanaim, on the other side of the Jordan. Three men, Shobi, Machir, and Barzillai, provided supplies for him. The text does not explain all their reasons, but it does show that they saw the need and acted.

Today we can notice who is exhausted or going without, and help them with something concrete. A meal, a visit, or a little money can be the way God cares for someone through us.
exp.3:2:
The verse explains a detail about the people of Beeroth. "Fled" means they escaped, and "sojourners" means they lived as foreigners there, not being from that place. Gittaim was the place where they took refuge, and they stayed there until this day, the time when this is being written.

The narrator tells the story of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, and of Baanah and Rechab, two of his captains. He clarifies that they were from Beeroth, a town assigned to Benjamin. The Bible does not explain here why the Beerothites fled; some think it was because of some war or violence, but that is only a guess. This detail prepares the account of the betrayal by these two men.

For today: God sees those who have been displaced and those who live as strangers. We can treat with respect and help those who have had to leave their land. Also, being a captain or holding a good position does not guarantee a good heart; let us guard our loyalty and our decisions.
exp.14:27:
Here David tells Zadok and Abiathar that he will wait in the open country of the wilderness, that is, in the plains near the fords of the Jordan, until word comes from them. "You" and "your" refer to the priests and to their sons. The phrase "to certify me" means to let him know or to inform him.

David speaks as he flees from Jerusalem, because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. He had asked that the ark of God be returned to the city, and he places his future in God's hands. The priests and their sons would serve as his messengers and would inform him of what happened. Some see here also a prudent strategy, not only faith.

For today: in times of crisis, trust God, but act with wisdom. Wait with patience and seek the counsel of faithful people, without rushing ahead.
exp.1:21:
Abner, commander of Saul's army, warns Asahel once more to stop chasing him. He tells him that if he does not turn aside, he will have to strike him down and kill him. And he asks how he could ever face Joab, Asahel's brother, with his head held high. The phrase about lifting one's face (looking someone in the eye, with honor) is left out here, and the other source-language remarks are removed since they do not appear in the verse your readers see.

After a battle between the men of Saul and the men of David, Asahel, who was very swift, was pursuing Abner. Abner did not want to kill him, since he knew that would bring revenge from Joab. But Asahel paid no attention, and the account shows how pride and stubbornness can end in tragedy.

For today: when someone warns you wisely, listen in time. Sometimes the insistence on getting our own way costs us more than we expect. Humility keeps us from dangerous paths.
exp.0:4:
Here David asks a direct question of a young man who arrived with news from the battle. He does not simply accept what he hears; he wants to know how he can be sure that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead.

David is in Ziklag, where he has returned after defeating the Amalekites. The young man arrives running from the Israelite camp, and his report brings the hardest blow: the king is dead, and Jonathan, David's friend, as well. David's question does not come from coldness but from a wish to verify the facts. Later, the young man will tell a story that the Bible does not confirm, and for that reason people debate whether he was telling the truth.

For today: when you receive serious news, do not let yourself be carried away by emotion or by rumors. Ask calmly, seek clarity, and trust God while you wait.
exp.9:10:
Joab speaks to his brother Abishai. He tells him that if the Syrians prove stronger than he is, Abishai will come to help him; and if the Ammonites prove stronger than Abishai, Joab will come to help him.

Joab is the commander of Israel's army. The Ammonites and the Syrians had surrounded them, with enemies in front and behind. Joab divided the troops: he faced the Syrians with the best soldiers, and Abishai faced the Ammonites. This agreement to help one another gave them security in the midst of great danger.

For today: no one should face difficult struggles alone. In the family, the church, or at work, we can agree to support one another, and also ask for help without shame when we feel weak. Joab, moreover, entrusted the outcome to God.
exp.13:18:
David asks the woman from Tekoa whether Joab is behind everything she has told him. She swears by his life, saying that none can turn to the right hand or to the left from anything the king has said, meaning there is no way to avoid his question. She admits that Joab sent her and put all these words in her mouth.

Joab, the commander of the army, wanted David to bring back his son Absalom, who had been banished for killing his brother Amnon. Joab used this woman to tell an invented story and lead the king to see his own situation. David realized the plan.

For today: when someone shows us a truth through a story or advice, let us listen with humility and honesty. And before deciding something important, let us ask ourselves whether we are seeking justice and reconciliation with wisdom.
exp.13:27:
This verse says that Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without being able to see the face of King David, his father. The phrase "see the king's face" means to be received by him, to stand in his presence. So Absalom was close by, in the same city, yet he remained kept apart from his father.

The account has no one speaking. Instead, the narrator tells what happened. Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and fled. Later Joab arranged for him to return to Jerusalem, but David would not receive him. The reconciliation was left unfinished. The Bible does not fully explain David's reasons, and the silence between the two prepared tensions that would come later.

For today: a broken relationship is not healed simply by being near. If there is a wound in your family, seek sincere dialogue, forgiveness, and honesty in time, before silence and resentment grow.
exp.10:17:
This verse says that Joab sent a messenger to David to tell him everything that had happened in the battle. The phrase about the affairs of the war means the matters or news of the fighting.

Joab was the commander of David's army. He was besieging the city of Rabbah. David had ordered him, in writing, to place Uriah in the most dangerous position so that he would die and thus cover up his sin with Bathsheba. Now Joab gives his report, but he had already arranged how he would deliver the news of Uriah's death.

For today: a report can be true in its facts yet be used in the service of something wrong. Let us ask God for courage not to take part in cover-ups, and to live with integrity even when someone in authority pressures us.
exp.0:25:
David says he feels deep grief over the death of Jonathan, whom he calls "my brother." He says their friendship was very sweet, that is, very dear and pleasant. He affirms that Jonathan's love was "wonderful," extraordinary, greater than the love of women. "I am distressed" simply means "I am deeply grieved."

David sings this lament after learning of the deaths of Saul and Jonathan in the battle against the Philistines. Although Saul had pursued him, David honors him publicly. Jonathan, Saul's son, had made a covenant of loyalty with David and defended him. Some see here a comparison with faithfulness and sacrifice; the text says no more than that, and it is not fitting to add details it does not mention.

Today we can value faithful friends, tell them how much they mean to us while they are alive, and be that kind of friend to others.
exp.13:3:
The woman of Tekoa came before King David. She bowed low, with her face to the ground, as a sign of respect, and asked him for help, saying, "Help, O king," that is, "Majesty, help me!"

Joab, the commander of the army, wanted David to be reconciled with his son Absalom, who had been banished for killing his brother Amnon. Joab taught this woman what she should say, and she pretended to be a widow in mourning with a story similar to David's own. In this way, the king would see his own situation from the outside. Interpreters debate whether Joab acted with good intentions or for convenience, and the Bible does not fully make this clear.

For today: Before asking for help or advice, approach with humility and sincerity. And when someone speaks to you the truth, even indirectly, listen with an open heart, without becoming defensive.
exp.8:8:
Here King David sends for Ziba, who had been Saul's servant. He tells him that everything that belonged to Saul and his family is now given to the son of his master, that is, to Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson. The sentence that explains the old wording is removed, since the reader's verse uses different words.

David speaks as king, and he does so because of the promise of kindness he had made to Jonathan, the friend who had shown him loyalty. Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, was in a fragile situation. David returns the lands to him and invites him to always eat at his table. Ziba and his family are to work those lands to support him.

For today: keeping a promise and helping someone who is at a disadvantage is a concrete way of showing God's love. Think of someone to whom you owe support or remembrance, and do something simple for that person today.
exp.9:0:
This verse tells us that the king of the Ammonites, the people living next to Israel, died, and that his son Hanun became the new king. The phrase "it came to pass" simply means "it happened." The phrase "after this" points to a time after the events that came before in David's reign.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book, who presents the change of rule in Ammon. The verses that follow say that David wanted to show kindness to Hanun, because Hanun's father had shown kindness to him earlier. The Bible does not spell out here what that kindness was. But the Ammonite leaders became suspicious of David and misread his gesture, which set the stage for a conflict.

Today we can learn not to draw hasty conclusions about other people's intentions. Before distrusting a kind gesture, it is wise to ask, to listen, and to seek wisdom from God, so that we do not damage a relationship over mere suspicion.
exp.21:42:
Here David says he crushed his enemies like dust and trampled them like the mud of the streets. "Trampled" means stamping down hard, and "scattered" means spreading them out until nothing is left. These are strong images of a complete victory.

David sings this song of thanksgiving when God rescued him from Saul and other enemies. He speaks in poetic, war-filled language. But notice that he credits the victory to God: "You gave me." The enemies called on the LORD for help, and He did not answer them. After this, the text shows David as the head of nations.

For today: do not use this verse to justify violence or revenge against people. Instead, trust that God is the one who delivers and sustains. When you face a struggle, pray, act with justice, and give God the glory for every victory.
exp.15:6:
Shimei shouts at David to leave. He calls him "thou bloody man", that is, a violent man guilty of killing. "Man of Belial" means a worthless man, one with no regard for God.

Shimei was of the family of King Saul. David was fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled. Shimei takes advantage of this moment of weakness to accuse him, throwing stones at him and cursing him. He was convinced that God was punishing David for the fall of Saul's house. The Bible does not show that David had killed Saul or his family, so the accusation was very doubtful. Even so, David did not respond with violence.

For today: when someone attacks us with injustice, we can keep silent, examine our hearts, and trust that God is the righteous judge, instead of responding with revenge.
exp.14:32:
David answers Husai: if you go with me, you will be a burden to me. The verse reads, "Unto whom David said, If thou passest on with me, then thou shalt be a burden unto me."

David speaks while he is fleeing from Jerusalem, because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Husai, his faithful friend, arrives with torn clothes and dust on his head, signs of mourning. David has just prayed that God would make the counsel of Ahithophel fail. Then, instead of accepting Husai's company, he asks him to return and serve Absalom in order to help him from within. In this way David does not reject Husai; he gives him a different task that is more useful.

For today: serving God and others does not always mean doing what we most desire or what seems closest to us. Sometimes loyal love shows itself by accepting the place where God puts us, even when it is difficult or not easily seen.
exp.19:1:
This verse tells how nearly all the people of Israel stopped following David and began following Sheba, son of Bichri. By contrast, the men of Judah stayed close to their king, accompanying him from the Jordan River all the way to Jerusalem. "Clave" means cling to, stay loyal.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Sheba, a man from Benjamin, blew a trumpet and cried out that they had no portion in David. This happens shortly after Absalom's rebellion, when the tribes were still divided and resentful over how David would return to the throne. Sheba took advantage of that discontent to stir up another rebellion.

For today: when there is division and shouts that sweep the crowd along, it is easy to be carried away. Let us ask God for firmness to be loyal to what is just and true, even when most people take another path.
exp.22:6:
It says that whoever wants to touch the thorns, that is, wicked people, must protect himself with iron and with the shaft of a spear. In the end, those thorns are burned right there on the spot.

Those are part of David's last words. He compares a righteous king to the morning light (earlier verses) and the wicked to dangerous thorns. Although his family is not perfect, God made an everlasting covenant with him. Some understand that God himself judges the wicked; others, that the king must confront them firmly.

For today: do not approach evil carelessly, nor trust in your own strength. Trust in God's covenant and justice, and let Him judge what you cannot put right.
exp.21:23:
He says that David was blameless before God, meaning sincere and whole in his loyalty, without living a double life. It also says that he kept himself from his wrongdoing, which means his tendency to do what is evil. The verse adds nothing else about those words.

David speaks, at the end of his life, in a song of thanksgiving because God rescued him from Saul and from all his enemies. He does not say that he never sinned, since the Bible records his serious falls. Many understand that he is speaking of his general faithfulness to God, of not having abandoned him to follow other gods. Some think he is referring to his innocence in the face of the accusations of his enemies.

Today, we can ask God to help us be the same in public and in private. It is also wise to recognize what our most frequent weakness is and to set practical limits to guard against it, trusting in the grace of God.
exp.22:30:
This verse names two of David's men: Abi-albon, who came from Arbath, and Azmaveth, from Barhum. The place names "from Arbath" and "from Barhum" tell us where they came from. They were probably towns near Judah and Benjamin, although some of the names are spelled differently in other texts, such as 1 Chronicles 11.

The author of the book, who is not identified, gives a list of David's mighty men. They were soldiers who supported him in his battles. After mentioning the deeds of the most famous ones, the text goes on with individual names without saying what they did. Even so, they were recorded.

God notices faithful people, even when no one applauds them. Today you can serve steadily in your family, your work, or your church, without seeking fame. What you do together with others, with loyalty, has value before God.
exp.15:21:
This verse tells that they set up a tent for Absalom on the roof of the palace. There Absalom went in to his father David's concubines, and he did it in the sight of all Israel. The verse of the roof is that it was the flat top of the house, and the phrase "went in" means that he had sexual relations with them.

Absalom had rebelled against his father David, who fled from Jerusalem and left ten concubines behind to look after the palace. Following the advice of Ahithophel, Absalom did this public act to show that the break with David was final. It also fulfilled what God had announced through Nathan (2 Samuel 12:11-12), although that does not make Absalom's action good.

Good advice can sometimes lead to a destructive path. Before following an opinion, even one that comes from someone very respected, let us compare it with the Word of God and with a humble heart.
exp.21:43:
It says that God rescued David from the strivings of his own people and kept him safe to be "head of the heathen," that is, leader of nations. Even peoples David did not know came to serve him. "Strivings" means conflicts or struggles.

David sings this song of thanksgiving near the end of his life, after being delivered from his enemies and from Saul. Before he became king over all Israel, he faced internal divisions, and later his victories extended his influence over other peoples. David attributes all of this to God, not to his own strength. Some also see in these words a look ahead to the reign of the Messiah, but this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: when you look back and see conflicts overcome and doors that opened, give thanks to God out loud. Recognizing that He sustained you keeps you humble and confident for what lies ahead.
exp.21:24:
This verse says that God rewarded David according to his righteousness and the cleanness of his hands before Him. The word "recompensed" is rendered in the verse you read as "recompensed," and the phrase "according to" matches "according to" in your verse. "Cleanness" speaks of a life without guilt in the eyes of God. It does not say that David was perfect, but that he sought to obey God with sincerity.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, when God delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. Earlier, he says that he kept God's laws in mind and guarded himself from wickedness. This same song also appears in Psalm 18. Some understand that David is speaking of his general faithfulness to the Lord, not of being without sin, since the Bible also records his serious failures.

Today, we can live with sincerity before God, without pretense. When we fail, let us confess and return to Him. God sees the heart and cares for those who seek Him with integrity.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that David was now settled in his palace. God had given him rest from all the enemies who surrounded him. The word "came to pass" means that it happened. The word "sat" means that he was established and secure. The phrase "round about" means on every side. "Rest" means peace and quiet.

The narrator of the book tells how David's life stood after many wars. With that peace, David begins to think about God and notices that he lives in a house of cedar, while the ark of the covenant still stays in a tent. For this reason he speaks with the prophet Nathan. Nathan opens a very important moment: God will respond with a promise about David's descendants.

For today: when God gives you a time of calm, do not use it only to rest or to get comfortable. Ask yourself how you can thank him and serve him better, with your time, your possessions, or your attention to others.
exp.14:14:
The servants of David answer him that they are ready to do whatever the king decides. What remains is a promise of total loyalty, with no conditions attached.

David has just received word that his son Absalom has won the hearts of the people and is coming against him. David decides to flee from Jerusalem to avoid a massacre in the city. The ones speaking are the servants who were with him, and their answer shows that they remain faithful just when the king is weak and the situation seems lost.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are loyal only when everything goes well or also in difficult times. In the same way, our willingness toward Christ, our King, is tested when following him costs something. Let us ask God for a firm and faithful heart in hardship.
exp.12:32:
Jonadab tells King David not to be overwhelmed by believing the false report that all his sons have been killed. According to him, only Amnon died. The words "let not my lord the king take the thing to his heart" mean "don't dwell on it" or "don't take it as true." "Voice" here refers to the rumor that was circulating.

News reached David that Absalom had killed his sons, and the king tore his clothes in grief. Jonadab, David's nephew and the adviser of Amnon, speaks calmly. He says Absalom had planned this since Amnon violated Tamar. The text does not explain how Jonadab knew this, and there is no way to know for certain.

For today: when faced with bad news, it is wise to wait and verify before reacting. But we also see that grief without justice or forgiveness can end in violence. Let us place our wounds in God's hands.
exp.9:3:
This verse tells how Hanun, king of the Ammonites, seized David's messengers, shaved off half of each man's beard, cut their clothing in half up to the buttocks, and sent them away. The verse of the words "shaved" and "sent away" is given in the wording above: to shave means to remove the beard with a razor, and to send away means to dismiss them back to where they came from.

The narrator describes what happened when King Nahash died. David wanted to show kindness and sent comforters. But the Ammonite princes planted suspicion, and Hanun believed the worst. In that culture, the beard was a sign of dignity, so this was a public humiliation. It ended in war.

For today: before judging someone's intentions, ask and listen. Suspicion without evidence, fed by bad advice, can turn a kind gesture into an offense and destroy relationships. Ask God for wisdom and humility.
exp.2:8:
Abner makes a strong oath: "May God punish me severely if I do not do for David what the Lord promised him." The phrase "So do God" was a formula calling for punishment on oneself if one failed to keep one's word. The word "Á" is an old form of "to," and the sentence that explained it is removed here because the reader's verse does not contain it.

Abner was the commander of Saul's army and was supporting Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, as king. Ish-bosheth accused him of sleeping with Rizpah, one of Saul's concubines, and Abner became extremely angry. So he decided to switch sides to David and transfer the kingdom. His motive seems more anger and wounded pride than obedience to God, although the promise to David was real.

Today, God can carry out his plans even when people act from mixed motives. Let us ask him to cleanse our intentions, so that we obey by faith and not out of pride or resentment.
exp.18:9:
It says that Absalom, whom the people had anointed as king, died in battle. So those who are speaking ask why they remain quiet and inactive, doing nothing to bring David back. "Anointed" means they had set him apart as king by pouring oil on him.

The speakers are the people of the tribes of Israel, who were divided and confused after the rebellion. They had followed Absalom, but he was no longer there. They remembered that David had rescued them from their enemies. So they urge one another to restore him. Soon David also speaks to the elders of Judah.

For today: when we recognize that we have been following a wrong path, it is not enough to lament or to stay still. God invites us to take concrete steps back, to ask forgiveness, and to restore what we have damaged.
exp.2:21:
This verse tells how David's men and Joab returned from a raid carrying a large amount of plunder. But Abner was no longer in Hebron, because David had sent him away and he had gone off in peace.

The narrator is describing what happened while Joab, the commander of David's army, was away. Abner, who had earlier been commander of Saul's army, had come to offer that all Israel would join David. David welcomed him with a feast and let him go safely. The text sets up Joab's reaction, which will come in anger. The Bible later says that Joab killed Abner, and here we can see that David acted in good faith.

For today: when someone seeks peace, let us receive them with honesty and without deceit. We should also be careful that resentment does not lead us to destroy what God may be healing.
exp.4:10:
This verse tells that Hiram, king of Tyre, sent David messengers, cedar wood, carpenters, and stonemasons (workers who shape stone). They built David's palace.

The narrator describes how David was becoming established in Jerusalem, his new capital. That a foreign king supported him shows that his kingdom was recognized. The next verse explains the meaning: David understood that God had confirmed him as king for the sake of his people. Some see here the hand of God using a non-believer to help.

For today: God can give us help through unexpected means, even through people who do not share our faith. Let us receive with gratitude whatever comes, and, like David, remember that every achievement comes from God and should serve others, not only ourselves.
exp.18:18:
Here Shimei asks King David not to hold his wrongdoing against him. "Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me" means not to treat him as guilty, and "do not remember" means not to recall it or hold a grudge over what he did when David fled from Jerusalem.

Shimei belongs to Saul's family. When David was escaping from his son Absalom, Shimei cursed him and threw stones at him (2 Samuel 16). Now Absalom is dead, David is returning as king, and Shimei, fearing for his life, immediately humbles himself and admits his sin. Abishai asks that he be put to death for cursing the Lord's anointed. Some think his repentance was more fear than a true change of heart; the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when you have failed, do not make excuses or hide. Acknowledge your mistake with humility and ask forgiveness from the person you offended. And when it falls to you to forgive, remember the mercy you have received.
exp.12:6:
This verse tells how King David sends his daughter Tamar to the house of her brother Amnon to prepare food for him. The phrase "prepare food for him" means cooking something for him. The small fried cakes mentioned earlier were little flat breads fried in oil. David does this believing that his son is truly sick.

Amnon pretended to be ill following the advice of his cousin Jonadab, and so he deceived his father. His real purpose was to be alone with Tamar, and what follows in the account is a terrible assault against her. David acts with trust and good intentions, but without realizing the deception.

For today: It is wise to be attentive and not to trust blindly, even within the family. Those who care for others, such as parents or leaders, should ask, observe, and protect the most vulnerable. And if someone suffers abuse, they deserve to be heard and protected.
exp.19:5:
Here David tells Abishai, his nephew and military commander, that Sheba, the son of Bichri, will do more harm than Absalom did. He orders him to take the king's servants, that is, the loyal soldiers, and go after him quickly. The fear is that Sheba will reach cities with walls and escape. The word "fenced" in the verse means protected by walls.

Sheba had just stirred up a rebellion against David, right after Absalom's revolt. David had asked Amasa to gather Judah within three days, but Amasa was slow. That is why David acts with urgency, before the problem grows. The Bible does not explain all his reasons, but his concern is clear.

For today: it is not wise to let a small problem grow through neglect. With prayer and wisdom, it is good to face it in time, before it causes more harm.
exp.2:33:
This verse is part of David's lament for Abner. It tells us that Abner did not die like a prisoner, with his hands tied and his feet in chains. He died the way a man falls at the hands of wicked people, that is, betrayed and murdered. When the people heard this, they all wept again.

David speaks at Abner's funeral. Abner was the commander of Saul's army. Joab had killed him treacherously in Hebron, partly out of personal revenge. David wanted everyone to know that he had taken no part in that death. That is why he mourns him publicly, and the people recognize his sincerity.

For today: when someone suffers injustice, it is not enough to stay silent or look the other way. We can honor the victims with clear and truthful words and with compassion, and live in a way that shows our actions reject violence.
exp.12:5:
This verse tells how Amnon lay down and pretended to be sick. When King David came to see him, Amnon asked that his sister Tamar come to his house and prepare two cakes, small loaves or flat cakes, so that he could eat them from her hand.

Amnon is speaking with his father, King David. He is following the advice of his cousin Jonadab. His real desire was to be alone with Tamar, his half-sister, whom he wanted in an unjust way. The sickness was a deception, and David, suspecting nothing, agreed. What follows in the account is a painful tragedy.

For today: lies often dress themselves up as necessity or affection. If something has to be hidden through deception, that is a warning sign. Let us strive to live with honesty, and to watch carefully over those who are under our responsibility.
exp.15:4:
It says that King David came to a place called Bahurim, which was near Jerusalem. There a man from the family of Saul, named Shimei, son of Gera, came out to meet him. This man was cursing David, that is, speaking words of hatred and ill fortune toward him.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who recounts how David was fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled. David was hurt, tired, and humiliated. Shimei took advantage of that moment of weakness to vent his resentment, since he belonged to the family of the previous king, Saul. Because the text gives no further details here, we only see his anger and his attack.

When we are going through a trial, sometimes people come along who criticize us or wound us even more. This passage invites us to keep our calm, not to answer with anger, and to place our situation in God's hands, who sees everything with justice.
exp.14:15:
This verse tells us that David left Jerusalem together with all his household. He left only ten of his concubines, secondary wives of the king, to look after the palace. The phrase "after him" means "behind him."

David flees because his son Absalom had rebelled and was coming to take the throne. The king wants to avoid a battle inside the city that would harm the people. The text does not explain why he chose to leave those women behind. Later in the story, they suffer the consequences of that rebellion (2 Samuel 16:21-22).

Today we can learn that the decisions of those who hold authority affect others, sometimes in painful ways. Before deciding, let us think about those who will be left exposed or vulnerable, and ask God for wisdom to care for others.
exp.17:13:
Joab replies that he will not waste time arguing with that man. He takes three darts (small spears or short arrows) and drives them into Absalom's heart while Absalom is still alive, hanging in the middle of an oak tree (a large kind of oak).

Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David, and had tried to take the throne from him. His hair had become tangled in the tree during the battle. Joab, the commander of David's army, is speaking here. A soldier had refused to kill Absalom because David had ordered that he be looked after. Joab openly disobeys that order from the king.

Today this reminds us that acting on our own, even with good reasons or justified anger, can break trust and hurt others. It is better to obey, to seek wisdom, and to trust God before making drastic decisions.
exp.5:8:
This verse says that David was afraid of God that day. The word "afraid" here means he had fear, a respect mixed with alarm. So he asked, "How shall the ark of the Lord come to me?" That is, he wondered how something so holy could come near him.

David speaks after Uzza died when he touched the ark while it was being carried to Jerusalem. The law said the ark was to be carried by the Levites with poles, not on a cart (Numbers 4:15). David was saddened and frightened, and so he left the ark at the house of Obed-edom, where it became a blessing. Some believe David also felt anger, but the text only says he was saddened.

For today: God is loving, but He is also holy. Let us come to Him with reverence and obedience, seeking to do things as He directs, not only as seems good to us.
exp.15:3:
Here King David tells Ziba that everything that belonged to Mephibosheth will now be his. Ziba bows down and asks that he may continue to find favor in the king's sight.

David is fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled. Ziba, a servant of the house of Saul, arrives with provisions and accuses Mephibosheth of wanting the throne. David decides quickly, without hearing Mephibosheth. Later, in chapter 19, Mephibosheth gives a different account, and the Bible does not make everything that happened fully clear. For this reason, this story shows a hasty decision.

For today: before judging or making an important decision, especially in moments of pain or pressure, it is wise to listen to all sides. Asking God for wisdom helps us not to act only on what we are told.
exp.12:27:
Absalom ordered his servants to wait for the moment when Amnon is cheerful from the wine. When he gives the signal, they are to kill him. He tells them not to be afraid, because he takes the responsibility upon himself.

Absalom speaks at the feast of his sheep-shearing. Two years earlier, Amnon had abused Tamar, Absalom's sister, and David did not punish him. Absalom held a grudge and planned this revenge through deception, inviting the king and then Amnon.

For today: pain and injustice, if we keep them locked inside, can turn into revenge and bring about more death. Let us bring our wound before God, seek justice by honest ways, and not let resentment grow in secret.
exp.16:22:
He says that Ahithophel, when he saw that Absalom had not followed his counsel, saddled his donkey (the word he used means putting the saddle on it), and went back home to his house in his city. There he put his household affairs in order, then hanged himself and died. They buried him in the tomb of his father.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Ahithophel had been David's counselor and joined Absalom's rebellion. His advice was to attack David immediately, but Hushai, sent by David, succeeded in persuading Absalom to reject it. Ahithophel probably understood that the rebellion was lost and that he would be remembered as a traitor. The Bible only reports the event, without approving it.

For today: when wounded pride or fear crushes us, let us not make final decisions alone. Let us seek help, talk with someone we trust, and bring our pain before God, who gives hope.
exp.3:0:
He says that when Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, learned that Abner had died in Hebron, he lost all his strength. "His hands became limp" is an old-fashioned way of saying that his hands went weak and slack, like someone who has lost all courage. "Terrified" means that all Israel was filled with fear and dismay.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Abner was the general who held up Ish-bosheth's kingdom against David. He had been killed by Joab, the commander of David's army. Without Abner, Ish-bosheth was left without support, and the people, who depended on that leadership, felt that everything was falling apart. The text says nothing more about how each person felt; it only shows the great shock.

When we lose the thing on which all our security rested, fear paralyzes us. It is wise to place our trust not only in people or positions, but in God, who does not die or change. He holds our weary hands.
exp.17:17:
This verse tells that Absalom, while he was still alive, had a pillar set up for himself in the King's Valley. He said he had no son to keep his name in remembrance, so he gave the monument his own name. The phrase "to this day" means that when this was written, the place was still called "Absalom's place."

The narrator tells this right after Absalom's death, since he rebelled against his father David. He was buried in a pit under a heap of stones, without honor. The contrast is strong: he wanted a monument, and he ended up with a heap of stones. The Bible also says that Absalom had three sons (2 Samuel 14:27), so perhaps they died young; the text does not explain this.

For today: seeking fame or being remembered can be empty. It is better to live with humility and faithfulness to God, because He is the one who gives a remembrance that lasts.
exp.16:19:
It says that Absalom's men came to the woman's house in Bahurim and asked about Ahimaaz and Jonathan. She answered that they had already crossed the ford of the waters, that is, the shallow place in the stream or river. The soldiers searched and did not find them, so they returned to Jerusalem empty-handed.

The two young men were carrying a secret message for David, who was fleeing from Absalom. They were hiding in a well, and the woman protected them with her answer. The text does not judge her or explain her decision; it only shows that her action saved the message and, with it, the lives of David and his people.

God often works through ordinary people who never appear in the headlines. Today we can ask ourselves what opportunity we have to protect someone vulnerable or to help with courage. Still, let us pray for wisdom to act with integrity, for this account does not teach that lying is always right.
exp.16:5:
This verse tells of Hushai coming to Absalom. Absalom repeated to him what Ahithophel had advised and asked whether they should follow that advice or not. He asked for his opinion, saying, "Now you speak."

Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David, and Ahithophel was his chief counselor. Hushai, on the other hand, was a friend of David and pretended to support Absalom in order to hold back Ahithophel's plan. The Bible says afterward that the Lord determined to defeat the good advice of Ahithophel (17:14).

For today: before making an important decision, do not rely on just one voice. Seek advice, but pray and examine who is giving it and with what intention. God can guide you even through people who act with wisdom.
exp.7:9:
Toi, king of Hamath, sent his son Joram to visit King David. He sent him to greet David in peace and to congratulate him, because David had defeated Hadadezer, Toi's enemy. Joram brought gifts of silver, gold and bronze. The word "vessels" here most likely refers to bronze objects. In another passage (1 Chronicles 18:10), the son is called Hadoram; it is either the same person under another name, or a different person, and this is not known for certain.

The narrator describes how David's kingdom grew. By defeating Hadadezer, David gained great fame, and other kings sought his friendship. Toi was glad, because he now had one fewer enemy. Then David dedicated these gifts to the LORD.

For today: when God gives us a victory or a blessing, we can receive it with gratitude and hand it back to Him. What we have is not only for our own pride, but to honor God and to serve others.
exp.21:41:
They looked around, but there was no one to save them. Even when they cried out to the Lord, he did not answer them. David speaks at the end of his life, in a song of thanksgiving because God rescued him from Saul and from his enemies. Here he describes the defeat of those who opposed him. The text does not explain why God did not answer those enemies; the context suggests they had risen up against the king whom God had anointed, though the passage does not spell this out.

For today: it is not healthy to seek God only when we are in trouble while living far from him. We can draw near to God sincerely every day, and not only in crises, trusting that he hears the heart that is humble and repentant.
exp.6:28:
David asks God to bless his family, that is, his descendants, so that they may continue always before Him. The phrase "let it please thee" is rendered in plain modern English as "please accept this with pleasure," which is how David asks God to receive his request. David leans on what God has already promised: if God has spoken it, then His blessing will make his house blessed forever.

David, the king, speaks after the prophet Nathan brought him God's promise: that God would build him a house, that is, a lasting dynasty. David had wanted to build a temple, but God promised him something greater. This prayer is his humble and grateful response. Christians see in this promise a foreshadowing of the Messiah, a descendant of David.

For today: when you pray, rest on what God has already promised in His Word. Ask Him with humility and confidence, knowing that He is faithful to fulfill what He says.
exp.17:4:
King David gave an order to his three military commanders: Joab, Abishai, and Ittai. He asked them to deal gently with Absalom, the young man, that is, the young man himself. Gently here means with kindness and gentleness. The whole army heard that order.

David was about to send his troops out to fight against the followers of his son Absalom, who had rebelled and wanted to take the throne from him. The soldiers would not let him go into battle, so he stayed by the city gate. Even so, as a father, he publicly asked that his rebellious son be cared for. The text does not explain all his reasons, but it shows his love, and also his difficulty in separating his role as a father from his role as king.

Today it reminds us that love can remain alive even when someone has hurt us. But it also teaches us to ask for wisdom, so that affection does not keep us from acting with justice and clarity.
exp.15:20:
Here Ahithophel advises Absalom to have relations with the concubines whom David left behind to look after the palace. The word rendered "go in unto" in the verse refers to intimate relations with them. The word "abhorred" means that Absalom would become a declared enemy of his father, with no possibility of reconciliation. In this way, Absalom's followers would be encouraged, because they would see that there was no turning back.

Ahithophel was a highly respected counselor who had previously served David and now supported the rebellion. His plan was a public act of rupture and of seizing power. Years earlier, the prophet Nathan had announced that disgrace would come upon David's house (2 Samuel 12:11-12), although the Bible does not make this wickedness right.

For today: a counsel that is much admired can still be evil. Before following an idea, test it against the Word of God and with a humble heart, not only by who says it.
exp.0:21:
They say that the weapons of Jonathan and of Saul never returned without having struck their enemies. "Blood of the slain" and "fat of the mighty" speak of enemies fallen in battle; the "fat" is a poetic image for the strength of the warriors. Jonathan's bow did not turn back, and Saul's sword did not return "empty," that is, without achieving its purpose.

David sings this lament after the deaths of Saul and Jonathan on Mount Gilboa. Although Saul had pursued him, David does not mock him. He honors the good that was in both of them and mourns the defeat of Israel, without letting the Philistines rejoice.

Today we can learn to remember with respect the good that was in others, even in those who wounded us. In grief, gratitude and honesty heal more than resentment.
exp.1:23:
This verse tells us that Joab and his brother Abishai did not stop and kept pursuing Abner. When they came to a hill called Ammah, near Giah and along the road through the wilderness of Gibeon, the sun was already going down. The word "hill" here means a small rise or knoll. The exact location of that place is not known.

Here the narrator speaks. Asahel, brother of Joab, had been killed by Abner after ignoring his warnings. Now Joab wants revenge. This happens during the war between the followers of Saul and the followers of David.

For today: the desire for revenge can keep us going after someone without thinking about the consequences. Before reacting in anger, it is wise to stop, pray, and seek peace, as Abner later asked.
exp.14:9:
Absalom sends secret messengers to all the tribes of Israel.

The narrator describes how Absalom organizes a rebellion against his father, King David. He had asked permission to go to Hebron on the pretext of fulfilling a vow to God, but in reality he was preparing a coup d'état. Hebron was an important city in Judah, where David himself had been proclaimed king. Many followed him without knowing what was really happening.

Today we learn that religious appearances can hide crooked motives. Before following anyone, it is wise to examine their intentions. And when we use God's name, let us do so with sincerity, not to achieve our own ends.
exp.4:22:
It says that David asked God what to do in the face of the new Philistine attack. God answered him that he should not go up straight at them, but should go around and confront them from the side of the trees, which were mulberry trees or poplars (scholars are not sure which).

The Philistines had already been defeated once, but they came back to the valley of Rephaim. David did not assume he would repeat the same tactic. The one speaking is God, who answers David, now king of Israel, when David seeks his direction before fighting.

For today: even though God has helped us before in a similar situation, it is wise to ask him again. He does not always guide us the same way. Praying and waiting for his direction at each new stage keeps us from relying only on habit or on our own experience.
exp.16:4:
Absalom asks that Hushai the Archite also be called, so that they may hear what he has to say. The phrase "the Archite" indicates that he was from the region of the Archites.

Absalom had rebelled against his father David and had already received the counsel of Ahithophel, which seemed good to him. Hushai, on the other hand, was a friend of David and pretended to support Absalom. The Bible shows that God allowed Hushai's counsel to prevail (2 Samuel 17:14). Absalom did not know that he was listening to someone with another purpose.

Asking for another opinion can be wise, but we also need discernment. Before deciding, let us seek sincere counsel, pray, and compare everything with the Word of God, not only with what sounds good.
exp.12:18:
Tamar puts ashes on her head, tears the robe of many colors she was wearing, and, with her hands on her head, goes away crying out. The ashes and the torn clothing were signs of mourning and deep grief.

Here the storyteller speaks. Tamar has just been assaulted by her half-brother Amnon, who then threw her out of his house with contempt. Her robe was the garment proper to the king's unmarried daughters, so in tearing it she shows that something very precious has been taken from her. Her cry is a public complaint about the wrong she has suffered, not an expression of shame on her own part.

Today, this passage teaches us to take seriously the pain of someone who has suffered abuse. Let us listen without hurrying to silence the person, as happened to Tamar, and accompany her in seeking help and justice. God sees the wounded.
exp.12:30:
This verse tells how David, on hearing the report that all his sons had been killed, got up, tore his clothes, and threw himself to the ground. His servants also tore their clothes and stood beside him. The word for these attendants can be understood as servants or aides, and tearing one's clothes was a visible way of showing deep grief.

The narrator describes the king's reaction to a false rumor. Absalom had ordered the killing of his brother Amnon because of what Amnon had done to their sister Tamar. In the middle of that turmoil came the exaggerated news that all the king's sons had died. Shortly afterward, Jonadab makes clear that only Amnon had been killed.

Today we can learn not to be carried away by rumors. Before reacting with fear or despair, it is wise to confirm the facts and bring our anguish to God calmly, seeking sensible counsel.
exp.11:19:
David got up from the ground, where he had been lying face down, and he washed, put oil on himself, and changed his clothes. Then he went to the house of the Lord, that is, to the place of worship, and he worshipped. After that he went back to his own house, asked for food, they served it to him, and he ate. Putting oil on oneself was a sign of cleanliness and joy, and changing clothes is simply putting on different ones.

This is part of the story of David after his sin with Bathsheba. God had announced that the child of the two of them would die. David fasted and pleaded for seven days so that God would have mercy. When he learned that the child had died, he stopped his extreme mourning. The narrator shows his faith: he accepted God's decision and first worshipped him.

For today: when a loss comes, we can weep and pray sincerely, but we can also draw near to God, accept what we cannot change, and take care of our bodies and our lives again.
exp.11:6:
Nathan says to David, "Thou art the man." That is, you are the rich, unjust man in the story. Then Nathan speaks on behalf of God and reminds David of what God had done for him: he anointed him (chose him and set him apart with oil) as king over Israel, and delivered him out of the hand of Saul, who was hunting him down.

Nathan is a prophet sent by God. David had taken Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah put to death. Nathan told the parable of a rich man who took the only little ewe lamb from a poor man, and David, outraged, condemned himself without realizing it.

It is easy to see the sins of others and excuse our own. Today we can ask God to show us our hearts with honesty, and to remember his goodness before we harden ourselves. His correction seeks to lead us to repentance and to his forgiveness.
exp.20:18:
This tells of another battle against the Philistines, in a place called Gob. Elhanan of Bethlehem struck down (that is, defeated and killed) a warrior named Goliath of Gath. The shaft was the wooden pole of his spear, as thick as a weaver's beam, the great beam of a loom.

It is part of a list of victories over Philistine giants, at the end of David's reign. His men had just stopped him from fighting, to protect his life. This verse is difficult: 1 Chronicles 20:5 says that Elhanan killed the brother of Goliath. Some think there was an error in copying the text, and others that there was another warrior with that name. It is not known for certain.

God uses many people, not only the famous. Serve faithfully where you are, even when no one notices.
exp.4:1:
Here the leaders of Israel's tribes tell David that even earlier, while Saul was king, it was he who led the army out to battle and brought it back home. They also remember that God promised he would be the shepherd of his people and their ruler, that is, their governor and leader.

The tribes of Israel speak here, gathered in Hebron. Saul had already died, and David was ruling over Judah alone. Now they acknowledge his leadership and ask that he reign over all of them. They base their decision on two things: what they saw in him and what God had said.

For today: God often prepares people in hidden places before giving them greater responsibility. Be faithful where you are, serve with humility, and trust that God opens doors in his time. And if you lead, remember that caring for others is part of your calling.
exp.14:2:
Absalom tells each person who arrives with a legal problem: "What you claim is good and right, but the king has no one to hear you." The phrase "for the king" means "on behalf of the king," that is, that there is no representative of the king to attend to their case.

Absalom, David's son, speaks at the city gate, where legal cases were settled. Little by little he wins the hearts of the people, criticizing his father's administration without evidence. Then he offers himself as the ideal judge. His goal was to prepare a rebellion against David.

Today, beware of the one who agrees with you only to win your trust. Sweet words can hide personal interests. Let us ask for wisdom to tell sincere care apart from manipulation, and let us seek out those who serve with integrity.
exp.2:28:
This verse says that David asks that the punishment for the death of Abner fall on Joab and his family. It mentions five hardships: an illness with a discharge (a bodily discharge that left the person unclean), leprosy (a skin disease), a person who leans on a staff (perhaps from disability or weakness), death by the sword, and lacking bread (poverty).

It speaks of David, now king in Hebron. Joab treacherously killed Abner, who had come in peace to unite the people under David. Joab said he was avenging his brother Asahel, but he did it through deceit. David publicly distances himself and asks that the guilt rest on Joab. It is a curse, not a certain prophecy; the Bible does not say it was fulfilled to the letter.

For today: personal revenge destroys, and peace is kept through honesty. When we are wronged, let us leave justice in God's hands and not use deception to settle accounts.
exp.23:13:
Here David says that he is in great distress. Among three possible punishments, he prefers to fall into the hand of God, because God's mercies are many, rather than into the hands of people. That is, he trusts in God's goodness more than in human cruelty.

David speaks with the prophet Gad. He had taken a census of the people, and this displeased God. The text does not detail all the reasons, and it has been interpreted in several ways, perhaps out of pride or from trusting in his military strength. God offers him three options: famine, flight, or plague. David chooses to put himself in God's hands.

For today: when you face the consequences of a mistake, do not run away from God. Come to Him with humility, because His mercy is greater than any human judgment.
exp.21:26:
This verse says that God acts according to the heart of each person. With the one who is clean, that is, sincere and pure, God shows himself pure and trustworthy. With the crooked, the one who twists the path on purpose, God shows himself opposed and unyielding toward his wickedness.

David speaks in this song of thanksgiving, toward the end of his life, after God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He recounts how the Lord sustained him. He says that God was faithful to him, since David sought to walk with integrity, though he was not perfect. Some see here a general principle of how God deals with people.

For today: if you want to experience more of God's nearness, live with sincerity before him. Confess your faults, leave deception behind, and walk honestly, trusting in his mercy.
exp.23:16:
Here David sees the angel who was striking the people, and he speaks to God. He acknowledges his guilt: "I have sinned, and I have done wickedly." He calls the people "these sheep," meaning innocent people whom he, like a shepherd, was supposed to care for. He asks that the punishment fall on him and on his father's house.

David speaks after having ordered a census of the people, something God regarded as a serious sin. The Bible does not fully explain why it was wrong; some think it was pride or trust in his military strength. A plague had already killed thousands. David, as king, takes responsibility and shows the heart of a shepherd.

For today: when we fail, let us not look for excuses or blame others. Honestly acknowledging our mistake, and caring for those who suffer because of it, is the first step toward asking forgiveness and beginning to repair the harm.
exp.22:12:
Three of David's thirty chief warriors went down to meet him at the cave of Adullam. It was harvest time. Meanwhile, the Philistine army had camped in the valley of Rephaim.

The author of the book is listing David's bravest men. Here it is the narrator speaking, not David. David was fleeing from Saul or hiding from the Philistines, and the cave was a refuge. Scholars debate exactly when this episode took place, and the text does not make it clear. What it does show is the loyalty of these men, who risked passing close to the enemy.

For today: loyalty is tested in difficult times. We can ask ourselves whom we stand with when there is risk, and how we can be faithful to God and to the people he has placed in our path, even when it costs us.
exp.0:11:
This verse says that David and his men wept, mourned, and did not eat until evening. They did this for Saul, for his son Jonathan, for the people of the Lord, and for the house of Israel. The phrase "by the sword" means in battle, as the verse itself says they had fallen in war. To fast means to go without food as a sign of grief.

Here the narrator speaks. A young Amalekite came saying that he had killed Saul, and he brought Saul's crown and his armband. His account does not fully agree with 1 Samuel 31, so he probably lied to win David's favor. David did not rejoice at the death of his pursuer; instead he was filled with sorrow.

For today: let us learn to mourn with honesty, even for those who have wronged us. Grief over a loss does not have to be mixed with resentment or celebration. We can ask God for a compassionate heart, one that suffers with his people and does not rejoice in the downfall of others.
exp.2:4:
This verse ends the list of the six sons born to David in Hebron. The sixth was Ithream, the son of Eglah, one of his wives.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of the book who presents a family summary. David was reigning in Hebron over Judah, while the house of Saul was still in dispute with him. The list shows that his household was growing, though it also reveals a family with several wives, something that would later bring conflict. Very little is known about Eglah.

For today: God works through real and sometimes imperfect stories. Care for your home with prayer and wisdom, and trust that God can guide even what is full of weakness.
exp.21:0:
This verse says that David sang a hymn of thanksgiving to God. He sang it when God rescued him from all his enemies and from Saul. The phrase "spake unto the Lord" means that he directed these words to God himself, as a sung prayer. "The Lord" is the name of God.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who presents David's song. David was pursued for years by King Saul and also faced other wars. This song appears almost word for word in Psalm 18. It is not known with certainty when exactly he wrote it, since the text only says it was the day that the Lord had delivered him. Looking back, David recognizes that his victory came from God.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, don't wait until you have forgotten it. Take a moment to thank God, either in writing or aloud, remembering how he sustained you.
exp.4:6:
David conquered the stronghold of Zion, a well-defended place in Jerusalem, and from then on that site was called "the city of David." The word "Nevertheless" would be rendered as "but" or "however" in today's English, and with it the text emphasizes that, even though the Jebusites felt secure, David managed to take the place.

The narrator tells how David, already king over all Israel, went to Jerusalem, which was inhabited by the Jebusites. They mocked him, saying that even the blind and the lame could defend the city. Scholars debate the exact meaning of that taunt, but clearly it expressed great confidence in their walls. David took the city and made it his capital.

For today: sometimes we face obstacles that seem impossible and voices that mock our faith. This passage encourages us to keep moving forward with confidence in God, who gives strength and direction to accomplish what He has entrusted to us.
exp.5:21:
Here David says he is willing to humble himself even further to honor God. "Vile" means of little value or despicable in the eyes of others. The "maidservants" are the female servants. David states that he does not mind being low in his own sight, and that these same servants, the ones Michal mocked, will respect him.

David speaks with Michal, Saul's daughter and his wife. He had just brought the ark of God to Jerusalem, dancing with joy before the Lord. Michal despised him in her heart and criticized him with sarcasm. David answers that his praise was for God, who chose him as king. The text does not clearly say whether Michal's lack of children was a punishment or a circumstance; it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: do not let the opinion of others hinder your sincere worship. Praising God with humility is worth more than guarding your image.
exp.12:34:
Jonadab says to King David: "Look, the king's sons are coming, just as I told you." That is, the princes arrive alive, and their arrival confirms what Jonadab had announced: that only Amnon had died.

Jonadab was David's nephew and a friend of Amnon. Absalom had ordered Amnon killed for having dishonored his sister Tamar. First came the rumor that all the king's sons had died, and Jonadab calmed David. When the sons appear, it is shown that he was right, but the king's grief does not go away, and Absalom flees.

For today: before reacting to a rumor, wait for the facts. And remember that being right does not remove the pain of the consequences. We can avoid much anguish if we seek the truth with calm and wisdom.
exp.21:17:
It says that God rescued the speaker from powerful enemies, people who hated him and who were stronger than he was.

David is speaking, in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul, as the text at the beginning of the chapter indicates. He uses grand images, such as seas and deep waters, to show that God intervened with power. He tells it as a testimony of gratitude.

Today, when you face something bigger than yourself, there is no need to pretend you are strong. You can admit your limit, ask God for help, and afterward remember and tell how he sustained you.
exp.6:4:
God tells the prophet Nathan to go to David, his servant, and ask him a question: "Shalt thou build me an house for me to dwell in?" The words "go and tell" are a command, and "Thus saith the Lord" shows that this is a message from God. "House" here means a temple.
