David was already living in his palace and wanted to build a worthy place for God. Nathan, without consulting God, had told him to do what was in his heart. That same night God corrects Nathan and speaks. The question is not a simple refusal; God shows that he had never asked for a house, since he had walked with his people in a tent. Later, God promises David that he himself will build David a house, that is, a dynasty.

We may have good desires to serve God, but it is wise to ask him first and listen to his answer. God does not need our works to be great; he invites us to obey him with humility.
exp.1:28:
This verse tells us that Abner and his men fled all through the night. They crossed the plain (the flat valley land along the Jordan), crossed the Jordan River, and went through the region called Bithron. In the end they reached Mahanaim, on the other side of the river. It is not known for certain where Bithron was; we only understand that it was a part of the route.

Here the narrator is speaking. There had been a battle between David's men and those of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul. Abner had asked Joab to stop pursuing them, and Joab sounded the horn to halt the fighting. Abner used the chance to escape during the night.

For today: conflicts that drag on leave death and wounds behind. Knowing when to stop in time, listening to a call for peace, and not continuing to fight out of pride can prevent much pain in family, work, or church.
exp.19:24:
This verse closes a list of King David's main officials. Sheva was the scribe, that is, the secretary who put the affairs of the kingdom in writing. Zadok and Abiathar were priests, in charge of religious service. Ira the Jairite was the chief minister near David; the phrase "chief minister" is old-fashioned and can be understood as an adviser or a high assistant. Some versions call him a priest, and it is not entirely clear what his exact role was.

Here no character is speaking; it is the narrator's account. After the rebellion of Sheva son of Bichri, the story shows that the kingdom was once again put in order. The list reveals an organized government, with military leaders, administrators, scribes and priests.

For today: God values order and steady service. Every task, even one that goes unnoticed, like that of the scribe, helps the community function. Serve faithfully wherever you are.
exp.18:0:
This verse tells that someone brought word to Joab, the commander of the army, that King David was weeping and mourning for his son Absalom. The phrase "brought word" means "informed him," and "mourning" refers to his grief over a loss.

David's army had just won a battle against Absalom, who had rebelled against his father. Absalom died in that fight. The narrator is speaking here, describing how the news reached Joab. The verses that follow show that the king's weeping dampened the joy of the soldiers, and they entered the city ashamed, as though they had lost.

For today: grief and duty can clash. David loved his son even though Absalom had betrayed him. We can learn to mourn honestly, but also to consider how our sorrow affects those around us who have served us faithfully.
exp.5:4:
David and all the house of Israel celebrated with joy before God as they brought the ark. They played many instruments: harps and psalteries (stringed instruments), timbrels (tambourines), flutes and cymbals (metal plates). The phrase "fir wood" is uncertain; some scholars believe it refers to another kind of wood, such as cypress or pine.

The writer tells how David moves the ark of God toward Jerusalem. It was a time of festivity and honor to God. However, the account goes on to the death of Uzzah, because the ark was not being transported as God had commanded. This shows us that sincere joy must be accompanied by obedience and reverence.

For today: worshiping God with gladness is good, but we must also seek to do so with respect and according to his Word. May your joy and your obedience walk together.
exp.5:10:
The ark of God stayed for three months in the house of Obed-edom, a man described as the Gittite, which is usually understood to mean he came from Gath. During that time, the Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his family. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "blessed" means that he gave him his favor.

The account is told by the author of the book. David had been frightened because Uzzah died when he touched the ark, so he did not dare to bring it to Jerusalem and left it in that house. The text does not explain what the blessing consisted of, but the report to David shows that it was evident.

For today: the presence of God is not something we should fear, but something to receive with respect and reverence. When we give him an honest place in our home and in our lives, we can expect his care, even if it does not always come in the way we imagine.
exp.22:36:
It says that Zelek, a man of Ammon, and Naharai, from the city of Beeroth, were among David's mighty men. Of Naharai it adds that he was armourbearer to Joab, that is, the one who carried his weapons and accompanied him in battle. Joab was the son of Zeruiah, David's sister. That Zelek was an Ammonite shows that there were also foreigners among these warriors.

The author of the book presents a list of David's mighty men, the most outstanding soldiers of his army. There is no speech here, but a record. Its purpose is to honour each one for his service to the king. The list ends with 37 names.

For today: God notices those who serve, even when their task is quiet or supportive, like that of an armourbearer. Serve faithfully where you are; your work does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.6:17:
It says that King David went in before God and presented himself before Him. Humbly he asked: "Who am I, and what is my house?" That is, "What am I worth, and what value does my family have?" He wanted to know why God had brought him to that place of honor. The phrase about presenting himself before the Lord means that he came before God; many understand that he sat down or remained there in prayer, and the Hebrew text allows for that idea.

David speaks as king now. He has just heard, through the prophet Nathan, God's promise that his family and his kingdom would be established forever. David does not answer with pride but with wonder and gratitude, acknowledging that everything he has is a gift from God.

For today: when you receive blessings or achievements, follow David's example. Before taking credit, pause to give thanks, recognize that God has brought you this far, and pray with a humble heart.
exp.4:14:
This verse is part of a list of sons born to David in Jerusalem. Three names appear here: Ibhar, Elishua, and Nepheg. The words "and" in the verse only join the names in the list. The list continues in the next verse.

The author of the book, whom Jewish tradition associates with Samuel and other writers, tells how David established himself as king in Jerusalem. After mentioning that he took more wives, the account lists his children. This shows that his kingdom was growing and becoming secure. Nothing more is said about these three sons here. Moreover, the Bible does not hide the fact that this practice of having many wives would bring trouble to his household.

For today: God pays attention to every person, even to names that are barely mentioned. Remember that your life matters to Him, even when others do not notice it. Also think about how our decisions at home leave a mark on our children.
exp.11:22:
This verse says that when David's little son died, he stopped fasting and weeping. He asks sincerely: "Why should I fast now that he is dead? Can I bring him back?" And he concludes: "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me."

David, the king of Israel, speaks here. His son with Bathsheba was sick as a consequence of David's sin, and he pleaded with God for the child's life with fasting and weeping. When the child died, he accepted God's will, worshiped, and went back to eating. Some think "I shall go to him" expresses hope of being reunited; others think it only says that he too will die. The text does not fully settle the question.

For today: cry out to God with your whole heart while there is hope, and when He has already answered, rest in His care, grieve honestly, and keep going forward in faith.
exp.1:20:
Abner, who is fleeing in the middle of the battle, tells Asahel to turn aside and take the armour of another young soldier instead of pursuing him. The young men are the young soldiers, the armour is what is taken from a defeated enemy, and "following after him" means following behind him. But Asahel refused to give up the pursuit.

This happens after the battle between the men of David and those of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul. Abner was the commander of Saul's army, and Asahel, brother of Joab, was a very swift warrior. Abner did not want to kill him, because he knew that this would bring enmity with Joab. The verses that follow show that Asahel ended up dead.

For today: when someone wise warns us and offers a way out, it is wise to listen. Stubbornness or pride can lead us to fight battles that are not ours and to pay a very high price.
exp.9:15:
This verse says that King Hadadezer of Syria sent for the Syrian soldiers who lived across the Euphrates River. They came to a place called Helam, led by Shobach, the captain of his army. The word "Syrians" appears in the verse, so no comment is needed on it; the sentences explaining the old form of a word and the title "general" are removed, since those words do not appear in the verse you read.

This is part of the historical account of the war between Israel and the Ammonites, who had allied themselves with the Syrians. The Syrians had been defeated by Joab and Abishai, but they did not accept the defeat and gathered more troops. Here no character is speaking; the narrator tells what Hadadezer did to fight against Israel again.

For today: stubbornness and pride can lead us to insist on a path that has already failed. Instead, we can stop, acknowledge our mistakes, and seek God's guidance before moving forward.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that Paltiel, Michal's husband at that time, went with his wife weeping along the way to a place called Bahurim. There Abner, commander of the army of Ish-bosheth, told him to return, and he obeyed. The old word forms in the verse are simply forms of the everyday words for "went" and "following her," and the way it reads "told him" is the same as "said to him."

Abner is the one speaking. He was taking Michal to David, who claimed her as his first wife. Abner was seeking an agreement with David, and returning Michal to him was part of that deal. The text does not explain everything Paltiel felt, but his weeping shows real grief. The Bible tells us nothing more about him.

For today: God asks us to see the pain of people, even when decisions made by those in power affect them. If you are in a position of authority, treat with compassion those who lose something. And if you suffer a loss you cannot control, remember that God sees your tears.
exp.18:12:
David tells Amasa to say that he is a close relative: the phrase "my bone and my flesh" means blood kin. Then he makes a solemn oath: the words "God do so to me, and more also" are a way of saying "may God punish me if I do not keep my word." He promises that Amasa will be captain of the army in place of Joab.

David speaks after the death of Absalom, when he wants to return to Jerusalem. Amasa had commanded Absalom's army, and Joab, David's general, had killed Absalom. With this offer, David seeks to reconcile Judah and win Amasa over. Many also see here a political desire to set Joab aside.

Today we can learn to seek reconciliation and to extend a hand to those who have failed us. But it is wise to do so without letting pride or convenience direct our decisions.
exp.22:4:
It says that David's family is not so with God, yet God still made with him an everlasting covenant, well ordered and sure. "Salvation" here means salvation or well-being, and "make it grow" means to make it grow or bring it to fulfillment. David trusts that God will complete what he promised.

These are part of David's "last words," near the end of his life. He speaks of the righteous ruler who fears God, and acknowledges that his own house has not been entirely like this. He thinks of the promise in 2 Samuel 7 about his dynasty. Many Christians see in this a sign pointing to Jesus, the perfect King.

For today: you do not have to be perfect to trust God. He keeps his promises because of his faithfulness, not because of our merit. Rest in his grace and keep obeying him with humility.
exp.19:11:
It says that Amasa lay in the middle of the road, covered in his own blood. A man saw that all the people were stopping to stare, so he moved the body from the road into the field and covered it with a cloak (a cape or garment), because everyone who came near him stood still beside it. The phrase "wallowed in blood" in the verse above describes a wounded body lying in its own blood.

The narrator tells what happened after Joab, David's commander, treacherously killed Amasa while they were pursuing Sheba, who had rebelled against David. The people kept stopping, and this slowed the pursuit. Removing the body from the road allowed the army to move on. The account does not justify Joab; it only describes the events.

For today: violence and betrayal leave wounds that stop others and make us pause to look. This invites us to seek justice with integrity, without deceit, and to treat others' pain with respect.
exp.17:9:
This verse tells of a soldier who saw Absalom hanging from a holm oak, a kind of large evergreen oak, and went at once to inform Joab, the commander of David's army.

The setting is the battle between David's army and the followers of Absalom, his rebellious son. Absalom was riding a mule, which passed under a thick tree, and his head became caught. The soldier speaks with Joab, but he does not attack Absalom, because David had ordered that he be looked after. Later, Joab did act against that order.

For today: God sees what we do and the trouble we cause. This passage invites us to reflect on rebellion, and also to value obedience and respect for a given word, even when others pressure us to act differently.
exp.12:38:
It says that King David was already longing to see his son Absalom. Over time, the pain over Amnon's death had faded. "Longed to go forth unto" means "was eager to see". "Comforted" means he had already found peace after the loss.

The narrator tells this after Absalom killed Amnon, his half-brother, and fled to Geshur. He stayed there three years. David was a king and also a wounded father. Some scholars point out that the Hebrew can be understood in more than one way, but the most common idea is that David missed Absalom.

Today, time can ease pain, but it does not always mend broken relationships. If there is a family member who has become distant, it is not enough to miss them in silence. Ask God for wisdom and humility, and take a concrete step toward reconciliation, with truth and with love.
exp.9:8:
This verse tells how Joab, the commander of David's army, saw that the enemy was closing in on him from two sides: there were troops in front of him and behind him. Then he chose the best soldiers of Israel and arranged them in battle formation against the Syrians. The "companies" are groups of soldiers organized together.

The passage is narrative; it is not a character speaking, but the narrator. David had sent Joab because the Ammonites had humiliated his messengers, and they hired Syrian soldiers to fight. Joab found himself between two fronts, and so he divided his forces. Then he put his brother Abishai against the Ammonites, and he himself faced the Syrians, who were the greater threat.

For today: when you feel pressed from several sides, do not freeze. Think calmly, put your priorities in order, and ask for help from those who are with you. Joab planned with wisdom and, as you will see in the following verses, he also trusted in God.
exp.22:17:
Abishai, brother of Joab and son of Zeruiah, was the leader of a group of three mighty men. "He lifted up his spear" means that he fought with it, and "had the name" means that he became famous. It is said that he defeated three hundred men in one battle.

The author of the book lists David's most outstanding warriors. This comes right after the account of three brave men who risked their lives for water from Bethlehem. Abishai appears as another example of loyalty and courage. Some scholars note that the text distinguishes between "the three" and "the thirty," and the details are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God can use our courage and our strength to serve others with loyalty. Ask yourself what ability you have and how you could put it at the service of someone this week, without seeking fame.
exp.12:14:
It says that after abusing his half-sister Tamar, Amnon felt a hatred for her stronger than the "love" he had claimed to have. The phrase about him hating her right away means that he hated her immediately.

Amnon, David's son, speaks. He had pretended to be sick so he could be alone with Tamar, and he forced her, even though she begged him not to. What he felt was not true love but selfish desire. Once he had satisfied it, his sin and shame were exposed, and he blamed her with his contempt. Tamar protests that sending her away is an even greater wrong.

For today: true love cares for and respects people; it does not use them and then discard them. If someone has suffered abuse, the fault is not theirs, and seeking help and protection is right. And if we feel desires that harm others, we must stop and ask God and wise people for help.
exp.19:20:
Joab says that he does not want to destroy the city. His only demand is that they hand over Sheba, son of Bichri, a man from the region of Ephraim who lifted up his hand against David, that is, he rebelled. If they hand him over, Joab will leave. The woman answers that they will throw his head to him over the wall.

Joab, David's general, was pursuing Sheba in the city of Abel. A wise woman challenged him for wanting to destroy a peaceful city. Joab clarifies that he is only seeking the rebel, and she commits to resolving the matter.

For today: when there is a conflict, a wise person can keep many from paying for the guilt of one. Before reacting with violence, let us seek dialogue, the truth, and solutions that protect the innocent.
exp.2:26:
He says that when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside, into the middle of the city gate, as if to speak in private. He spoke to him "smoothly," that is, with gentleness and apparent kindness. There, on the spot, he struck him in the belly, under the fifth rib (the phrase is old, and it is understood as a deadly blow to that area). Abner died. The reason given is the death of Asahel, Joab's brother.

The narrator tells this after Abner made a peace agreement with David. Joab distrusted him, and had him return without David knowing. Earlier, Abner had killed Asahel in battle. Interpreters see in Joab revenge and perhaps also fear of losing his position.

For today: revenge hides its resentment behind kind words. Ask God to heal your wounds and to free you from repaying evil with evil.
exp.2:7:
Abner becomes very angry at Ish-bosheth's question. He asks with irony, "Am I a dog's head, a worthless man working for the enemy?" He says he has been loyal to Saul's family and did not hand Ish-bosheth over to David. Yet now Ish-bosheth accuses him of this woman's offense.

Abner, the commander of the army, speaks to King Ish-bosheth, son of Saul. Ish-bosheth had accused him of taking Rizpah, one of Saul's concubines, which could be seen as a claim to the throne. The text does not say whether Abner did so; he is offended by the accusation and breaks with Ish-bosheth.

For today: when you are corrected or accused, examine your heart before reacting in anger. A wounded pride can lead us to decisions that cause great harm. Ask God for humility and calm.
exp.15:12:
This verse tells how David and his men continued on their way while Shimei followed them along the side of the hill, keeping some distance from them. He walked alongside, hurling curses at them, throwing stones at them, and kicking up dust. Scattering dust was a gesture of contempt and mockery.

Here the narrator describes David's flight from Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled against him. Shimei, a man from the family of Saul, takes the moment to insult him. Abishai wanted to punish him, but David stopped him. He said that perhaps God was permitting that curse and that perhaps God would look upon his affliction and repay him with good. The Bible does not fully explain what David was thinking; it only shows his humility.

For today: when someone attacks us with unjust words, we do not have to respond at once in anger. We can keep silent, examine our hearts, and trust that God sees our affliction.
exp.17:24:
The watchman, who was standing high on the wall, cried out and told King David that someone was running toward the city. David reasoned that if only one man was coming and not a group, he probably brought good news. The watchman is the one who looks out from the wall; the verse says he cried and told the king.

David was waiting for news about the battle against his son Absalom. He was sitting between the two gates of the city, waiting anxiously. His reasoning made sense: soldiers fleeing a defeat usually came in a group, not as a lone messenger. But the news would be more painful than he expected, for Absalom had died.

For today: when we wait for important news, it is natural to feel anxious and to draw hasty conclusions. It is better to hand the waiting over to God in prayer, for He sustains our hearts whatever the news may be.
exp.17:28:
This verse says that King David, anxious, does not ask about the battle but about his son: "Is the young man Absalom safe?", that is, whether he is well. Ahimaaz answers that he saw a great tumult when Joab sent them, but that he did not know what it was.

After Absalom's rebellion, his army was defeated. Ahimaaz ran with the news of the victory, but Joab knew that Absalom had died. Many understand that Ahimaaz avoids telling the hard truth, perhaps because he did not know it well or because he did not dare. David, as a father, still loves his rebellious son.

Today we can learn to speak the truth with love and honesty, without hiding it out of fear. And also to remember that, even when someone fails us, a father's or mother's love can continue to ache and ask for prayer and God's comfort.
exp.6:22:
This verse says that no nation on earth is like Israel. God himself went to redeem them so they would be his own people, gave them a name, and did great and awe-inspiring deeds for them. The word "terrible" in the King James Version here means impressive, the kind of thing that causes awe. He freed them from Egypt, from the other nations, and from their gods.

The one speaking is King David, in prayer. God had just promised him, through the prophet Nathan, that his family would have an enduring kingdom. David responds with humility and gratitude, remembering how God had acted before in the history of his people. That gives him confidence that God will keep what he has promised.

For today: when you doubt the future, remember what God has already done for you and for his people. Thanking him for the past strengthens confidence that he will remain faithful.
exp.22:9:
This verse speaks of Eleazar, one of David's mighty men. He rose up and fought against the Philistines until he was exhausted; his hand stuck to the sword, as if it had cramped. The word "salvation" in this passage means deliverance or victory. That day God gave a great victory, and the people came back behind Eleazar only to gather the plunder, that is, what was left on the field.

These are among the last words of David, in which his bravest men are remembered. The account highlights Eleazar's courage, but it credits the victory to the LORD. The Bible does not explain why the people had fled earlier; it only shows that Eleazar stayed firm when others withdrew.

For today: God can use our perseverance, even when we feel alone or tired. Keep doing what is right with faithfulness, and remember that the final result comes from God.
exp.0:20:
David speaks to the mountains of Gilboa as though they were people. He wishes that no dew or rain would fall on them, and that they would not yield fields for offerings. The shield lay cast down on the ground there, and the final phrase can be understood in two ways: as if Saul had never been anointed king, or as if his shield had never been anointed with oil.

David sings this lament after the death of Saul and Jonathan in battle against the Philistines. Although Saul had pursued him, David does not celebrate his death. He mourns the fallen king and his friend, and he wants Israel to remember them with respect.

For today: when someone who wronged us fails or dies, we can avoid mockery and resentment. It is possible to grieve sincerely, to acknowledge the good that was there, and to leave the final judgment in God's hands.
exp.9:4:
This verse tells how David heard about what Hanun had done to his messengers. They were deeply ashamed, so David sent word for them to stay at Jericho until their beards had grown back, and then to return. The phrase "to meet them" in the verse means that he sent someone to receive them, or to go out to meet them.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and then David, who was king of Israel. He had sent messengers to comfort Hanun over the death of his father, but the Ammonite leaders suspected them. Hanun humiliated them by shaving off half of their beards and cutting away part of their clothing. In that culture, the beard was a sign of dignity, and this was a serious insult.

For today: when someone is hurt or humiliated, we can approach them with compassion, care for their dignity, and give them time to recover, without demanding that they act as if nothing had happened.
exp.8:2:
Here King David asks whether anyone is left of Saul's family to whom he can show "the kindness of God," that is, a generous goodness like the goodness God shows. Ziba answers that there is still a son of Jonathan, who is "lame on his feet," meaning he has difficulty walking.

David speaks as king, but he does so remembering the promise of friendship he made with Jonathan. Ziba, a former servant of Saul, is the one who knows where the young man is. Later the text tells us his name is Mephibosheth. In that time, new kings usually eliminated the descendants of the previous king, so David's intention is surprising.

Today we can ask ourselves: to whom can I show kindness without expecting anything in return? Think of someone weak or forgotten, and generously keep a promise or a debt of affection.
exp.7:6:
It says that David took the shields of gold that were carried by the officers of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, and brought them to Jerusalem. "Servants" here means officers or soldiers serving the king. Some translators understand that they were gold shields, while others think they could be quivers or weapons decorated with gold; the Hebrew allows for that uncertainty.

The account is from the biblical narrator, who summarizes David's victories. Hadadezer and his Syrian allies were defeated, and David took the spoils, as was the custom in the wars of that time. The text says that the LORD preserved David wherever he went, and so it presents these victories as part of God's care over the kingdom.

For today: what God gives us or entrusts to us is not only for our own benefit. David brought the shields to Jerusalem, the center of the kingdom. We can ask ourselves how to use our resources, talents, and achievements with gratitude, serving others and recognizing that God is the one who sustains us.
exp.23:15:
It says that the angel of the Lord was already stretching out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, but God changed his mind about the evil and had compassion, deciding to hold back the punishment. He told the angel: "It is enough; stay now your hand." The word for the threshing ground is the flat place where wheat was beaten out to separate the grain. The angel stopped at the threshing place of Araunah, a Jebusite (an inhabitant of Jerusalem before Israel).

David had taken a census of the people, and this brought a plague upon Israel. He chose to fall into the hand of God and not into the hand of men, trusting in his great mercy. The narrator tells here of the moment when the punishment is stopped. Some understand that "repented" speaks of God's compassion, not of any mistake on his part.

When we fail, we can come to God with humility, because his mercy is greater than our error and he knows how to stop judgment in time.
exp.9:18:
The allied kings who served Hadadezer saw that they had lost to Israel. So they made peace with David and came under his rule. After this, the Syrians no longer wanted to help the Ammonites.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Ammonites had insulted David's messengers, and they looked for Aramean allies to fight. David went out with his army and defeated them. The text shows how that alliance ended: it was broken by the defeat. Some scholars see here the fulfillment of God's promises to protect Israel, although the passage does not say it in those words.

For today: alliances built on pride or on doing harm fall apart when difficulty comes. It is wise to seek peace and to lean on what is just and firm, trusting God more than human strength.
exp.13:2:
Joab tells the woman from Tekoa to come before King David and speak to him in a certain way. In other words, he gives her the script: Joab put the words in her mouth, meaning he told her exactly what to say.

The narrator explains that Joab, the commander of David's army, noticed that the king missed his son Absalom, who had been banished for killing his brother Amnon. Joab prepared this woman to tell a made-up story and so lead the king to accept Absalom's return. Interpreters disagree about whether Joab acted for the good of the kingdom, out of compassion, or for his own advantage.

For today: before we speak to influence others, let us examine our intentions. Seeking reconciliation is good, but we must pursue it with sincerity and truth, without manipulating anyone.
exp.19:23:
This verse is part of a list of the chief officials of David's kingdom. Adoram was in charge of the tribute, which was the forced labor or the payments the people gave to the government. Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was the recorder, an old word for someone who kept track of the affairs of the kingdom and reminded the king of them; some understand him as a chronicler or secretary of state.

The narrator of the book presents this list after the rebellion of Sheba, which Joab brought to an end. With order restored, it shows who helped David govern. The list seems to come from a later period in his reign. About Adoram's work the text says nothing more, so it is best not to assume details.

For today: God uses unglamorous tasks, such as managing, recording, and organizing. If your work is of that kind, do it with honesty and order, because it also serves others and God.
exp.10:2:
This verse tells how David sent to ask who the woman he had seen was. He was given her name, her father's name, and her husband's name: Bath-sheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite. The people who answered him made it clear that she was a married woman.

The narrator describes David in Jerusalem while his army was at war. He is the king and gives the orders; his servants only report. The answer works as a warning, because David already knew she had a husband. Even so, he went ahead. The text does not justify this, and later God confronts him for it.

For today: when a temptation appears before us, the first step matters. If we already know something is wrong, we should not keep investigating or drawing closer; better to stop, flee, and ask God or someone we trust for help.
exp.18:26:
He says that Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant, "slandered" him, that is, he spoke falsely about him and spoke ill of him before King David. Mephibosheth adds that the king is "as an angel of God," meaning someone wise and able to judge rightly. For that reason he leaves the decision to him: "do therefore what is good in thine eyes."

Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, is speaking when David returns to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Ziba had made David believe that Mephibosheth stayed behind to take advantage of the situation. Mephibosheth says that Ziba deceived him and left him behind. His neglected appearance and humble attitude support his account, though the text does not fully settle who was telling the truth.

For today: when you are falsely accused, do not despair or seek revenge. Speak the truth with humility and entrust the outcome to God, who sees the heart.
exp.20:8:
It says that David handed seven of Saul's descendants over to the Gibeonites, and they hanged them "before the Lord" on a hill. "Hanged" here may mean hanging the bodies up or displaying them after death; the text gives no further detail. Everything happened at the beginning of the barley harvest, that is, the spring harvest.

The narrator tells what happened after a three-year famine in Israel. According to the chapter, God said that Saul had wronged the Gibeonites, with whom Israel had a covenant. David asked them what restitution they wanted, and they requested this. The passage is difficult, and readers understand it in different ways, since the Bible does not explain everything.

For today: promises and injustices matter to God, and their effects can last for years. If we have harmed someone, it is good to acknowledge it with humility and seek to make right what can be made right.
exp.0:18:
This verse opens David's funeral song. It says that the glory of Israel, that is, its honor and its pride, has been slain on the high places. The word "slain" stands for what the verse calls the fallen, and the "mighty" are the warriors who have fallen, especially Saul and Jonathan. The song itself is a lament, a mourning song.

David speaks after learning of the deaths of Saul and Jonathan in the battle against the Philistines, on the mountains of Gilboa. Although Saul had pursued him in order to kill him, David does not celebrate his death but mourns. He also orders that this song be taught to the people of Judah. Some understand "the bow" to name the song itself; others, a military training exercise. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: learn to grieve sincerely, even the loss of someone who harmed you. Honoring the good that was in a person keeps the heart healthy and keeps bitterness away.
exp.13:10:
In this passage the woman asks King David to remember the Lord and not allow the relatives of the dead man, who are seeking to avenge his blood, to do more harm by killing her other son. "Those close to the blood" were the family members who were expected to take revenge for a death. David swears by the Lord that not even one hair of her son will fall to the ground, meaning that he will be completely protected.

A woman from Tekoa, sent by Joab, speaks here while pretending to be a widow whose son is in danger. It is an invented story meant to lead David to reflect on his own son Absalom, who was banished for having killed his brother Amnon. David does not yet see that he himself is at the center of the matter.

For today: sometimes we judge other people's situations easily, but we find it hard to show the same mercy at home. Let us ask God for humility to recognize our own need for forgiveness and reconciliation.
exp.2:13:
David sends messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, who was ruling over Israel, and demands that he return his wife Michal to him. David recalls that he won her by paying a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, the proof Saul asked for as the price of marrying her.

David speaks from a position of strength: Abner, the commander of Ish-bosheth's army, has just offered him an alliance to unite all of Israel under his command. David makes the return of Michal, his first wife, whom Saul had given to another man, the condition for this.

Interpreters debate whether David acted out of love, out of legitimate right, or out of political advantage, since he was Saul's son-in-law. The Bible does not make this clear, and the text also shows the grief of Paltiel, who followed her weeping.

For today: claiming what is rightfully ours does not excuse us from seeing the pain of others. As we pursue what belongs to us, let us take care in how we treat those who are affected.
exp.11:25:
This verse tells us that Joab, the commander of David's army, kept up the war against Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites. There he managed to capture the royal city, which was probably the fortified part where the palace stood. Some believe it is the same as the "city of waters" mentioned later.

The narrator tells this while David was in Jerusalem, after his sin with Bathsheba and the birth of Solomon. Joab did the hard work on the battlefield. Then, with humility and loyalty, he asks David to come and complete the victory, so that the honor belongs to the king.

For today: Joab did not keep the recognition for himself, but gave it to his leader. We can learn to work with honesty and not always seek applause, but to serve with humility wherever God places us.
exp.13:1:
Joab sends to Tekoa and brings back a clever woman, that is, a woman skilled and wise in speaking. He asks her to pretend to be in mourning: to put on mourning clothes, not to perfume herself with oil, and to look like a woman who has been grieving a dead person for a long time. Putting on mourning means dressing and behaving like someone who is in mourning. Anointing with oil was a way of using oil as a cosmetic.

Joab sees that King David misses his son Absalom, who had been sent away into exile for killing his brother Amnon. Joab prepares a made-up story to move the king's heart. The Bible does not clearly state all of his reasons; some think he wanted to help David, and others think he was also looking out for his own advantage.

Today, this passage invites us to seek reconciliation, but with honesty. A good goal does not justify deception. Let us work to restore relationships with truth and love.
exp.9:5:
What it says: The Ammonites realized they had gravely offended David. Instead of seeking peace, they hired soldiers from other Aramean peoples (the "Syrians"): twenty thousand from Beth-rehob and Zoba, a thousand from the king of Maacah, and twelve thousand from Ish-tob.

Context: The narrator of the book tells the story. David had sent messengers to comfort Hanun over the death of his father, but Hanun's advisers saw them as spies and humiliated them. The Ammonites knew this would bring war, so they prepared to fight.

For today: When we have done wrong, it is better to acknowledge it and seek reconciliation than to reinforce our pride. Asking forgiveness in time can prevent greater conflicts.
exp.16:9:
This verse says that if Absalom attacks David and his men, even the bravest soldier, with a heart like a lion's, will lose his courage. The phrase "as the heart of a lion" describes a man of great courage, and "will melt" means his courage will drain away from fear. And the men "who are with him" are strong and brave warriors. All Israel knows that David and his people are real fighters.

The speaker is Hushai, David's friend, who pretends to be loyal to Absalom. Absalom had rebelled, and David was fleeing. Hushai gives advice different from Ahithophel's, in order to buy time so that David could prepare. He praises David's bravery to instill fear and hold back an immediate attack. It is a strategy, and the Bible later shows that God was at work in this.

For today: do not let yourself be carried away by hasty decisions or by fear. Ask God for wisdom, listen calmly to counsel, and remember that He can work even in the middle of difficult situations.
exp.19:8:
Joab approaches Amasa and asks him, "Art thou in health, my brother?", which was a common greeting. With his right hand he takes Amasa by the beard to kiss him, as was done among relatives and friends. The word "right" refers to the right hand, as the verse says. But his left hand already held the dagger.

Joab was David's general. David had appointed Amasa in place of Joab, and Joab and Amasa were cousins. The Bible does not say in detail everything Joab was thinking, but the account shows that he used a friendly greeting to kill Amasa by surprise. The narrator speaks, and Joab speaks.

For today: let us be careful not to use kind words or gestures of affection to hide bad intentions. May our greeting and our heart say the same thing, and may we be sincere with those we deal with.
exp.18:14:
This verse tells how David, after Absalom's rebellion, returns toward Jerusalem and reaches the Jordan River. There, at a place called Gilgal, the people of Judah come out to meet him and help him cross the river. The phrase about helping him cross means bringing him over to the other side.

The one telling the story is the author of the book. David had fled because of his son's rebellion, and Absalom had already died. Then David sought to win back the loyalty of Judah, his own tribe, and sent them a message through the priests. Judah answered by calling him to return. Some scholars also see here a political move by David to unite the people again.

For today: when there are wounds or divisions, restoring a relationship calls for concrete steps from both sides. Take the first step yourself with humility, and receive with grace the one who wants to return.
exp.14:29:
David went up weeping along the slope of the Mount of Olives. He walked with his head covered and his feet bare, signs of mourning and humiliation. All the people who were with him did the same: they covered their heads and went up weeping.

The account is told by the narrator of Samuel. David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled and took away the support of many people. David leaves the ark in the city, trusting that God will decide his fate. His weeping shows grief over his son's betrayal. Some believe it also reflects repentance for his own past failures, but the text does not state this directly.

For today: when pain comes, there is no need to pretend to be strong. David wept, humbled himself, and kept going toward the place of worship, trusting God. We can weep before God and support one another through trials.
exp.18:6:
Joab tells King David to get up, leave the place where he has shut himself away, and speak kindly to his servants, that is, to his soldiers and attendants. "Comfort" here means speaking to their hearts, encouraging them, and acknowledging them. Joab warns that if David does not come out tonight, all of them will abandon him, and that will hurt him more than any misfortune he has suffered in his life.

Joab, the commander of the army, speaks harshly. Absalom, David's son, had rebelled and died in the battle. David was grieving inconsolably, and the people, who had risked their lives for him, felt ashamed and scorned. Joab does not speak tenderly, but his warning was urgent.

For today: the pain is real, but it must not blind us to those who stand beside us. Even in mourning, we can be thankful for and care for those who sustain us.
exp.16:11:
It says that Israel's army will fall upon David wherever he is found, gently but completely, like the dew that covers the whole ground. "We will come upon him" means to attack, and "not so much as one left" means that no one will be left alive, neither David nor his men.

The speaker is Hushai, David's friend, who pretends to be loyal to Absalom. His real purpose is to give David time to flee and regroup. With grand and stirring words, he persuades Absalom not to follow Ahithophel's advice. The verses that follow say that God allowed Ahithophel's good counsel to fail.

For today: even when other people's plans seem convincing and powerful, God remains in control. We can trust that he knows how to guide events, and we should be wary of speeches that flatter our pride.
exp.13:12:
Here the woman turns the king's argument back on him. She says to him: "Why do you think something like this against the people of God?" She says that the king, by promising protection to her son, condemns himself, because he does not bring home his own banished one. The word "guilty" means he is found at fault; the one who has fled or been driven out is the banished one.

The speaker is a wise woman from Tekoa, sent by Joab. She tells an invented story about her son so that David will see his own situation with Absalom, who fled after killing Amnon. David had forgiven her son, but not Absalom.

For today: we are quick to show grace to others, but slow to extend it to those who hurt us most. Let us ask God for humility to examine whether our mercy is even-handed, and to seek reconciliation wherever it is possible.
exp.5:12:
It says that when the men carrying the ark of God had gone six steps, David offered an ox and a well-fed ram as a sacrifice. The verse does not make clear whether the sacrifice was made every six steps or only at the beginning; it has been understood both ways.

The narrator tells of David's second attempt to bring the ark to Jerusalem. Earlier, a man named Uzzah died when he touched it, and the ark stayed for three months at the house of Obed-edom, where God blessed the household. Now David moves it with more care and with joy, beginning with offerings.

For today: before we move forward in something important, we put God first with humility and gratitude. We can pray and acknowledge his place before taking each step, not only once we are already on our way.
exp.8:5:
It says that Mephibosheth, grandson of King Saul and son of Jonathan, came before David and fell down with his face to the ground, in a sign of respect. David called him by name, and he answered, "Behold thy servant," meaning, "Here I am, at your command." The phrase "did reverence" refers to a bow of honor, and "fell on his face" means that he knelt or lay down on the ground.

David had promised his friend Jonathan to show kindness to his family. Ziba, a servant of Saul's household, told him where Mephibosheth was, and David sent for him. Mephibosheth probably feared David, since many kings of that time eliminated the descendants of the previous king.

For today: David's kindness reminds us that we can keep our promises and treat with grace those who have no way to repay us. Think of someone to whom you can show that kindness this week.
exp.13:19:
It was Joab, the king's servant, who changed the way the matter was presented. "To fetch about this form of speech" means giving the matter a new turn, telling it in a different way in order to reach an end. The woman adds that King David is wise like an angel of God, and that he knows what happens on the earth.

The woman of Tekoa is speaking. Joab had asked her to tell David an invented story about a son who had been banished. In this way he wanted to lead the king to forgive his son Absalom. David discovers that Joab is behind it, and she acknowledges the plan. Her praise may be sincere, but it also sounds like flattery meant to soften the moment.

We may seek reconciliation, but with honesty. If we speak with truth and humility, we avoid manipulating others, even when our intentions are good.
exp.12:25:
Absalom asks his father David that, if he cannot go to the sheep-shearing feast, at least let his brother Amnon go with them. David answers with a question: "Why should he go with thee?", that is, "why him in particular?" Shearers are the men who cut the wool from the sheep.

Absalom speaks with deceit. Two years earlier Amnon had abused Tamar, Absalom's sister, and Absalom had held onto his hatred. David's question shows that he may have suspected something, but the Bible does not say what he was thinking. In the end he gives way under the pressure, and Absalom uses the feast for his revenge.

For today: let us be wary of kindness that hides resentment, and let us not allow an unhealed wound to lead us into wrongdoing. Let us bring our pain before God and seek justice and forgiveness, not revenge.
exp.5:20:
David answered Michal that everything he did was "before the Lord," meaning to honor God and not to impress people. He reminds her that God chose him, and not Saul or his family, to be prince, or leader, over Israel. That is why he says he will keep dancing with joy before the Lord.

David speaks after bringing the ark of the Lord to Jerusalem amid festivities and praise. Michal, Saul's daughter, criticized him with contempt because he showed himself without his royal dignity, dressed simply. Interpreters debate how much was exposed, but the point is his humility. David defends his worship and his calling.

Today, do not let criticism or what people will say keep you from worshiping God with sincerity. If your heart is directed toward Him, His approval is worth more than that of others.
exp.15:7:
Shimei tells David that God is repaying him for all the blood spilled from Saul's family. In his view, David ruled in Saul's place, and now the kingdom is passing to Absalom. He says David has been "taken in his mischief" (caught in his guilt) and calls him "a bloody man" (a violent man, guilty of killings).

Shimei, a relative of Saul, speaks while David is fleeing Jerusalem because of Absalom's rebellion. He insults David and throws stones at him. His accusation is doubtful, because the Bible does not say that David killed Saul's family in order to reign. Even so, David does not respond with revenge; he considers that God may be using this insult.

When someone criticizes us harshly, even if the criticism is unfair or ill-intentioned, we can pause our reaction and ask ourselves with humility: Is there something here that God wants to teach me?
exp.23:7:
This verse says that Joab and the commanders traveled through all the land of Israel and returned to Jerusalem after nine months and twenty days. The word "Jerusalem" refers to Jerusalem, and the phrase about having gone through the land means that they had covered the whole territory from one end to the other. It was a long and thorough journey.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David had ordered a census of the people, although Joab tried to talk him out of it. This verse sums up how long the task took. The verses that follow show the result and David's remorse. The Bible does not fully explain why the census was a sin; it has been interpreted as pride or as trust in human strength rather than in God.

For today: be careful about measuring your security only by numbers, possessions, or achievements. God wants you to trust in Him. And if you make a mistake, do as David did: acknowledge it quickly and ask forgiveness sincerely.
exp.10:25:
This verse tells that Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, learned that her husband had died and mourned for him. Mourned here means she expressed her grief and lived through the period of mourning, which was a custom of the time. The phrase about her husband having died is simply the verse's statement that he was already dead when she heard the news.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Uriah died in the war, but David had ordered that he be left without support in the battle to hide his sin with Bathsheba. The text shows her grief and then makes clear that God saw what David had done and was not pleased.

For today: our hidden decisions can cause real pain to other people. If we have failed, let us not hide the wrong; let us go to God with sincerity, ask for forgiveness, and try to correct whatever harm we can.
exp.12:28:
It says that Absalom's servants killed Amnon, just as their master had ordered them. Seeing this, the other sons of the king got up, each one climbed onto his mule, and fled. "Servants" are the attendants or helpers; "mules" are riding animals, widely used by the king's sons.

The narrator tells the outcome of a plan of revenge. Two years earlier, Amnon had violated Tamar, Absalom's sister, and David did not punish him. Absalom held on to his resentment, arranged a feast, waited until Amnon was merry with wine, and ordered him killed. The brothers fled out of fear, not knowing what would happen next.

For today: unaddressed pain and injustice can turn into resentment and end in violence. Instead of keeping the wound hidden, let us seek justice, counsel, and healing, and leave vengeance in God's hands.
exp.2:2:
This verse continues the list of the sons born to David in Hebron. The second was Chileab, son of Abigail, who had been the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. The third was Absalom, son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur.

The writer of the book presents details about David's family while his household grows stronger and Saul's house declines. Many believe that marrying the daughter of a foreign king was a political alliance, though the text does not explain this. The Bible records these marriages without approving of them, and later Absalom will cause great trouble.

For today: God fulfills his plans even through imperfect people, but our family decisions leave lasting marks. Care for your home with prayer, wisdom, and faithfulness.
exp.21:14:
It says that God sent out arrows, that is, darts, and with them scattered and confused the enemies. He also made lightning flash, and the lightning overwhelmed them. The phrase "scattered them" means that God dispersed them, that is, broke them up and threw them into disorder. "Consumed them" means that the lightning destroyed them and brought them to an end.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, near the end of his life, after the LORD had delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He uses poetic images of storm, thunder, and trembling to describe how God intervened on his behalf. These are not details of a literal weather event but language that expresses the power of God.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems bigger than you are, remember that God sees and is able to act. Cry out to Him with confidence, and then give thanks, as David did, for every deliverance.
exp.0:26:
This verse closes a song of mourning. It repeats the lament: the mighty have fallen, and even their weapons have been lost. "Perished" means that they came to an end or were destroyed. The "weapons of war" stand for the strength and the glory of those warriors, who are no longer here.

David is the speaker, and he composes this elegy, known as "the song of the bow," after the death of King Saul and his friend Jonathan in battle against the Philistines. Although Saul had pursued him, David does not celebrate Saul's death; he mourns him with respect. Some understand that "weapons of war" also refers to the warriors themselves, as a poetic way of speaking about them.

For today: learn to grieve honestly and to honor what is good in others, even in those who hurt you. Do not be in a hurry to skip past sorrow; God receives your sincere sadness.
exp.7:4:
The Syrians of Damascus (also called Arameans) came to help Hadadezer, king of Zobah, a kingdom north of Israel. David struck them, that is, defeated them in battle, and twenty-two thousand men died. The figure points to a very great victory.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, whose author is not known for certain. He tells how David was expanding his kingdom and how God sustained him. The Syrians entered the war to defend their ally, but they were defeated. Afterward they were made subject to David and paid him tribute. The next passage summarizes it this way: "The LORD preserved David wherever he went."

For today: when you face pressures that seem greater than you are, remember that God cares for those He calls. Trust in Him and do your part with courage, without using this passage to justify violence.
exp.13:6:
This woman tells the king that her whole family has turned against her. They demand that she hand over the son who killed his brother, so that they can kill him too and take the inheritance. She says that would put out the one spark left to her, that is, her last hope. Her husband would have no name or remnant, meaning no family name and no descendants on the earth.

She is a woman from Tekoa, sent by Joab, the commander of David's army. She tells a story, perhaps invented, to move the king's heart. The purpose was for David to reconsider his attitude toward his son Absalom, who had killed his brother Amnon and was in exile.

For today: justice matters, but so does mercy. Before judging someone harshly, let us ask whether we can act with compassion, seeking to restore and not only to punish.
exp.1:0:
It says that David, after Saul's death, asked God what to do. First he wanted to know whether he should go up into any of the cities of Judah, and God told him to go. Then he asked which one, and God answered: to Hebron. Old words: the phrase "enquired" means he asked for direction; "said again" means he asked once more; and "go up" is used because that region lies in higher ground.

The account follows the death of Saul, which appears in the book before. David had lived running away from him, and now the way was open. Yet he did not act on his own or take advantage of the moment. The text presents him seeking the voice of God first, and then Hebron becomes the place where his reign over Judah begins.

Before taking an important step, it is wise to pray and ask God humbly. Even when a door seems open, it is wise to ask for direction and not rush ahead. God can guide step by step, as here: first a general direction and then a more specific one.
exp.17:21:
He says that Ahimaaz, son of the priest Zadok, insists on running after Cushi to bring the news to the king, no matter what happens. Joab asks him what good it does to run if he will get no reward for that news. "Yet again" means "said once more," and "news" is what the message is about.

Joab is the commander of David's army. He has just killed Absalom, the king's rebellious son, and he sends Cushi, a Cushite, to tell the king. Joab wants to protect Ahimaaz, because the news is painful and the king might react badly. Ahimaaz, however, is very determined. The Bible does not fully explain his reasons, so we do not know what moved him.

For today: before carrying a message, it is wise to examine our motives and listen to wise advice. Eagerness to be first is not enough; the timing, the manner, and the love with which we speak also matter.
exp.14:19:
Here David asks Ittai whether it makes sense that, having arrived only yesterday, he should now be made to wander about with them. David says, "I go wherever I may go," meaning without knowing where he is going. He asks Ittai to return with his brothers and wishes him "mercy and truth," that is, kindness and faithfulness from God. The phrase about making him go up and down means "I am going to make you go up and down."

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled against him. Ittai was a foreigner from Gath, and David, with generosity, offers him the freedom to stay in safety. He does not want to drag him into an uncertain and dangerous situation.

For today: true generosity thinks of the good of the other, even in the midst of our own pain. And Ittai's loyalty reminds us that accompanying someone in their difficult moment is worth more than staying comfortable.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that the soldiers of the tribe of Benjamin gathered together as one group around Abner and took their stand on the top of a hill. The word "troop" refers to an organized group of soldiers, and the hill is a small rise of ground.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. After the death of Saul, there is war between the followers of Ish-bosheth, who are from Israel, and the followers of David. Abner, commander of Ish-bosheth's army, had killed Asahel, brother of Joab, and Joab and Abishai were pursuing him. The Benjamites, the tribe of Saul and of Abner, gathered to defend themselves from a high place.

Today we can see how much harm violence between brothers causes. When there is conflict, seeking peace in time prevents more pain. Let us ask God for humility to speak and to forgive before the wound grows.
exp.7:0:
It says that David defeated the Philistines, an enemy people of Israel, and subdued them. He also took a place called Metheg-ammah. "Smote" means that he beat them in battle, and "subdued" means that he brought them under his control. It is not known for certain what Metheg-ammah is. Many think it refers to Gath and its villages, according to a parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 18:1.

The author of the book tells the story of Israel. This comes right after God promised David a house and a lasting kingdom (chapter 7). The account shows how David strengthened his kingdom and gave security to the people.

For today: God keeps what He promises, though sometimes He does it step by step. Trust Him in your struggles, and do not lose heart if progress is slow.
exp.18:7:
He says David obeyed the advice he received: he got up and sat at the city gate, which was the public place where important matters were handled. There they told all the people that the king was sitting at the gate, and the people went to see him. On the other hand, "Israel" (those who had followed Absalom) had fled, each one to his own home.

Joab spoke harshly to David, because the king was mourning the death of his son Absalom, and this discouraged the soldiers who had saved his life. Joab warned him that if he did not go out to encourage them, he would lose all support. David responded and showed himself publicly before his people.

For today: grief is real and deserves to be felt, but we also have responsibilities toward those around us. With God's help, and sometimes with honest counsel, we can get up and serve.
exp.4:18:
He says that David, before fighting against the Philistines, asked God whether he should go and whether God would give him the victory. God answered yes: "Go up," because He would surely deliver them into his hand. The phrase "asked" means he sought direction from God, and "deliver them into his hand" means giving him victory over them.

The Philistines learned that David was already king over all Israel, and they went out to attack him, spreading across the valley of Rephaim. David did not act on impulse. He himself is the one speaking here, and he does so because he knew the war depended on God and not only on his own strength or experience, though he was a skilled warrior.

Before making important decisions, seek God's guidance in prayer and in His Word. Even if you already have experience or feel capable, ask Him first. Then act with confidence in what He shows you.
exp.14:1:
Verse 2 tells how Absalom would get up early and stand beside the road that led to the city gate. When anyone came with a lawsuit (a legal problem) to be judged by the king, Absalom would call him over and ask what city he was from. The man would answer that he was from one of the tribes of Israel.

The narrator of the book tells us this. Absalom, the son of King David, was building up his image with chariots, horses, and guards. The city gate was the place where cases were heard. The verses that follow show his purpose: to win the affection of the people so that he could take the throne from his father.

For today: let us make sure our kindness is sincere. Let us be wary of anyone who flatters to gain power, and let us also examine our own motives when we serve.
exp.18:30:
It says that Barzillai, a man from the region of Gilead, came down from Rogelim and crossed the Jordan River together with King David. He wanted to accompany him to the river's edge, on the other side. The Gileadite in the verse means that he came from Gilead, and Rogelim was his town.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David was returning to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. Barzillai had been loyal, since, as the following verse says, he provided food when David fled to Mahanaim. Now he was going along with him to see him off with respect and to honor him on his return.

For today: loyalty shows itself in difficult moments and also in moments of celebration. We can ask ourselves to whom we owe thanks, support, or companionship, and do so with generosity and without expecting anything in return, as Barzillai did.
exp.6:7:
God tells the prophet Nathan to say this to David: "I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to make you ruler over my people Israel." The word "sheepcote" in the verse refers to the pen or place where the flock rests, and "ruler" here means a chosen leader or governor.

David wanted to build a house for God, a temple. God speaks through Nathan and, before talking about plans, reminds David who raised him up. God had never asked for a house of cedar; he had walked with his people in a tent. The point is that God is the one who gives and sustains, not the one who needs to be given things.

For today: remember where God took you from. Everything you have, your opportunities and your place, comes from his goodness and not only from your own effort. That keeps us humble and grateful, and it helps us serve God without thinking we are doing him a favor.
exp.7:12:
It says that David made a name for himself when he came back from defeating the Syrians, since he struck down eighteen thousand men in the Valley of Salt. The word "smiting" here means that he defeated them in battle and killed many of them.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who sums up David's victories. The verses around it show that David dedicated what he won to God, and that "the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went." Other passages (1 Chronicles 18:12 and the heading of Psalm 60) mention Edom and other army commanders, so scholars explain that difference in several ways.

For today: if God gives you success or recognition, do not keep it to show off. Give thanks for it, use it justly, and offer God the best of what you have received.
exp.18:2:
This verse says that David's soldiers, who had just won the battle, entered the city of Mahanaim quietly and as if hiding, just as an army that fled defeated does, feeling ashamed. The soldiers' secrecy means entering without being noticed.

The narrator tells what happened after the death of Absalom, David's son who had rebelled against him. Joab told the army that the king was mourning his son without comfort. Thus the victory celebration turned into mourning, because the soldiers felt as if they had done something wrong by defending the king.

Our emotions and words, though understandable, affect those around us. If we lead or care for others, let us make room both for pain and for recognizing those who have fought beside us.
exp.4:23:
It says that David was to wait for a sign: a loud sound, like footsteps or wind, in the tops of the mulberry trees (a kind of tree). When he heard it, he was to move, because the Lord would go out ahead of him to defeat the Philistine army. A loud sound means a very powerful noise. Here, to strike means to attack or to win in battle.

The one speaking is God, who answers David after David asked him for guidance. The Philistines had attacked again in the valley of Rephaim. This time God did not give him the same instruction as before: he told him to go around the enemy and wait for the sign. Some think the sound was a divine intervention; the text does not explain exactly what it was.

For today: before acting, ask God and wait for his direction, even if you have already lived through a similar situation. What worked yesterday may not be today's plan. Trusting means obeying at the moment he indicates.
exp.20:1:
This verse tells us that King David sent for the Gibeonites to speak with them. The text clarifies who they were: they were not Israelites, but a remnant of the Amorites, a people who lived in Canaan. Israel had made a binding oath of peace with them (Joshua 9). Saul, however, tried to kill them, and the Bible says he did it out of zeal for Israel and Judah. The word "remnant" here means "survivors."

After three years of famine, God explained to David that the trouble came from Saul's offense against the Gibeonites. David acts as a responsible king and seeks to make things right by listening directly to those who were harmed.

Today we learn that a promise made, even to those who are different from us, matters greatly to God. When there is injustice, the way forward is to acknowledge it, listen to the one who was wronged, and seek to repair it.
exp.6:26:
For thou, O Lord of hosts, God of Israel, hast revealed to thy servant, saying, I will build thee an house: therefore hath thy servant found in his heart to pray this prayer unto thee.

This verse says that God himself made David aware of a promise: "I will build thee an house." The phrase "hast revealed to thy servant" means that God told him this personally. "House" here means family and descendants, not a building. "Hath thy servant found in his heart" means that David took courage to pray in this way. A prayer like this is a humble plea in which someone asks for something.

David speaks in prayer after the prophet Nathan brought him God's message. David wanted to build a temple, but God promised instead to establish a dynasty of kings from his family. David does not ask for something new: he rests on what God has already said. Many Christians see in this promise an announcement of Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when we pray, we can rest on the promises God has already given in his Word. Praying with confidence is not demanding, but responding in faith to what God has said.
exp.21:16:
It says that God stretched out his hand from heaven, took hold of David with force, and drew him out of "many waters," that is, out of many deep waters. The phrase "took me" is the same as "he took hold of me," and "drew me out" means "he pulled me out." The waters are an image of danger, like a flood that drowns.

David, now an old man, speaks in a song of thanksgiving for having delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. The verses before this describe God as a power that shakes creation to help him. Here the water is not literal; it is poetic language for speaking about troubles that overwhelmed him. What follows explains that his enemies were stronger than he was.

For today: when you feel that problems are pulling you under, cry out to God with confidence. He can help you, sometimes in unexpected ways. Afterward, do not forget to give thanks, as David did.
exp.6:12:
God says that a son of David will build a temple to honor his name. In return, God himself will make the throne of that kingdom firm forever. The word "for ever" is part of the verse's wording, so its meaning is simply that the throne will last without end. The temple is the house in this passage, though the word "house" can also mean a family or a royal line.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan to David. David wanted to build a house for God, but God answers that he will build a house for David, meaning a royal line of descendants. Many understand that the first fulfillment was Solomon, who built the temple. Christians also see a fuller fulfillment in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: God keeps his promises even when we do not see the full result. We can serve him faithfully and trust that he keeps working beyond our lifetime.
exp.18:39:
David crossed the Jordan River and arrived at Gilgal. Chimham, the man Barzilai had entrusted to him, went with him. All the people of Judah also escorted the king, along with half the people of Israel, that is, a part of the northern tribes.

Here the narrator speaks. David was returning to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. He had promised to look after Chimham as a gesture of gratitude toward Barzilai, who had supported him during his flight. But the verse ends by showing a tension: Judah and the other tribes were beginning to dispute who had more right to accompany the king.

For today: gratitude is shown through concrete actions. And when peace returns, care must be taken that pride or rivalry does not divide those who ought to celebrate together.
exp.5:5:
It says that when they came to the threshing floor of Nachon (a flat place where grain was threshed), the oxen pulling the cart stumbled or shook it. Uzzah, one of those driving the cart, reached out his hand and took hold of the ark of God so that it would not fall.

It is part of the account in the book of Samuel. David was bringing the ark to Jerusalem with music and joy. But the law said the ark was to be carried by the Levites with poles, and that it was not to be touched (Numbers 4:15). Here it was riding on a new cart, as the Philistines had done. The text that follows speaks of rashness. Some see in this a lack of care in the way God was being honored.

For today: God deserves to be honored with sincerity and also according to his Word. Good intentions do not replace obedience. Let us ask him for humility to learn how he wants to be worshipped.
exp.10:0:
It says that a year passed and the time came when kings went out to fight. David sent Joab, his servants, and all of Israel's army. They defeated the Ammonites and surrounded the city of Rabbah to lay siege to it. But David did not go with them: he stayed in Jerusalem. The old spelling "Á" is the earlier form of "a," and "Ammonitas" is simply the Ammonites.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling David's story without embellishment. The Ammonites had insulted David's messengers, and that is why there was war. The detail that the king stayed at home prepares what follows: his fall with Bathsheba. The text does not say why he stayed, so it is best not to invent reasons.

For today: when we stop doing what we are responsible for, we become more exposed to temptation. Ask yourself whether there is some responsibility you are avoiding, and ask God for the strength to carry it out faithfully.
exp.12:23:
Absalom approaches King David and tells him that he now has his sheepshearers, that is, the workers who cut the wool from the sheep. It was a time of work and celebration. Absalom invites the king and his servants to go with him.

The phrase "thy servant" in the verse is a respectful way of speaking about oneself.

Absalom speaks with courtesy, but the text has already told us that he had been holding a grudge against Amnon for two years because of what Amnon did to Tamar, his sister. The invitation seems generous, though it hides a plan. David refuses to go, and then Absalom manages to get Amnon to go. We will see the consequences later.

For today: resentment kept silently can grow and lead us to act with deceit. Bring your pain to God and seek justice and healing without revenge, before bitterness takes control of you.
exp.7:10:
This verse says that David set apart for God the vessels of silver, gold, and bronze that Toi had sent him. He also set apart the silver and gold he had taken from the nations he had conquered. To "dedicate" means to set something apart for sacred use. The LORD, the name of God, is the one to whom these things were given. "Subdued" means brought under control or defeated.

The account comes from the narrator of Samuel. It tells how Toi, king of Hamath, was glad that David had defeated Hadadezer, his enemy, and sent gifts to him through his son. David did not keep this wealth for himself but dedicated it to God. The text does not explain the exact use of these things, though many think they were kept for worship and for the future temple.

For today: what we achieve or receive is not only for ourselves. We can recognize God as the source of everything and ask him how to use our possessions, successes, and talents to honor him and help others.
exp.12:26:
It says that Absalom pressed his father, King David, so hard that he finally let Amnon and all the king's other sons go with him. Absalom asked for this with a hidden plan.

Absalom was holding the sheep-shearing feast. Two years earlier, Amnon had dishonored Tamar, Absalom's sister, and Absalom had been holding a grudge. David suspected nothing and gave in to the pressure. The verses that follow show that the whole thing was a trap to kill Amnon. The text does not say why David gave in; it only shows him trusting his son.

For today: kind insistence is not always sincere. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern intentions. And if we feel resentment, let us hand it over to God in time, before it leads us to do harm.
exp.14:11:
Absalom sends for Ahithophel from his city, Giloh, one of David's counsellors. He does this while he is offering sacrifices. The conspiracy was strong, because more and more people kept joining Absalom.

The narrator describes how Absalom prepares his rebellion against his father David. He uses the sacrifices to appear devout, and he draws in a highly respected counsellor. Some understand that Ahithophel had personal motives, since the Bible links him with a family from Giloh, but the text does not explain this with certainty. The two hundred guests went along without knowing anything.

Today we can learn not to be impressed by a religious appearance. Before supporting someone, it is wise to ask about their motives and their fruit. And if we have been hurt or deceived, God remains our refuge.
exp.6:13:
God says that he will be like a father to David's son, and that this son will be like a son to Him. If he does wrong, God will correct him "with the rod of men" and "with the stripes of the children of men," that is, with human punishments, measured and real, like those a father would use to correct a child.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan to David. David wanted to build a temple, but God promises him that his descendants will reign and that his son will build the house. Many understand that this refers first to Solomon, and the New Testament also applies this promise to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5). The correction in this verse fits the kings who failed.

For today: God corrects us because He loves us as a Father, not to destroy us. When you feel correction, do not run away; listen, acknowledge your mistake, and return to Him, knowing that His mercy remains with you.
exp.16:25:
This verse says that the army of Israel, together with Absalom, camped in the region of Gilead. The phrase "pitched in" describes setting up a military camp. Gilead was an area east of the Jordan River.

Here no character speaks; this is the narrator's account. Absalom had rebelled against his father David, and David had fled to Mahanaim, also in that area. Absalom crossed the Jordan with his troops and prepared for battle. The text also mentions that he placed Amasa, a relative of Joab, in command of the army. In this way we see that the family and the kingdom were divided.

For today: when there are family conflicts, pride and anger can grow until they become opposing sides. We should not wait for everything to explode; let us seek reconciliation and wise counsel in time, before the wounds grow deeper.
exp.5:3:
This verse tells us that the ark of God was brought out of the house of Abinadab, in Gibeah (a high place, a hill). While they were carrying it, Ahio, the son of Abinadab, walked in front of the ark, and his brother Uzzah went with him, guiding the cart.

The text does not say who is speaking; it is the narrator of the book, who tells how David wanted to bring the ark to Jerusalem.
