The ark represented God's presence among his people, and David wanted it at the center of Israel's life. However, the law said that the ark was to be carried on the shoulders of the Levites, not on a cart. The account thus prepares the way for what happens next.

For today: wanting to honor God is good, but it is also wise to ask how he wants to be honored. Seek his Word, not only your good intention.
exp.23:22:
This verse says that Araunah gave everything to King David, and he did so with the generosity of a king. Then he wished him well: "The Lord thy God accept thee," that is, that God would receive you with favor and show you his kindness. The phrase "all these things did Araunah, as a king, give" can be understood in two ways: that Araunah gave as a king would give, or that he himself was of royal descent. Scholars do not agree.

David had sinned by counting the people, and a plague was striking Israel. A prophet told him to build an altar on Araunah's threshing floor. Araunah, with good will, wanted to give him the land, the oxen, and the wood for the sacrifice.

Araunah was generous, but David replied that he would not offer to God something that cost him nothing. Today we can ask ourselves: does my service to God cost me anything, or do I give only what I have left over? Sincere devotion has value before Him.
exp.22:5:
This verse says that wicked people, whom it calls here "the sons of Belial," will be like thorns that are pulled up and thrown away. No one takes them up with the hand, because they wound. "Belial" means something like "worthless" or "wickedness," and it is used to describe corrupt and rebellious people.

These are part of the final words of David, a poem he spoke at the end of his life. Before that, it speaks of the righteous ruler who governs in the fear of God and is like the light of the morning. Then it contrasts that rule with the ungodly, who are dangerous and end up burned. David also trusts that God made an everlasting covenant with him.

For today: do not lose heart in the face of evil that seems to be advancing. God sees it and has the last word. Try to live with justice, and trust God's promises, which are firm even when you do not yet see everything.
exp.0:6:
In this verse, Saul, wounded and leaning on his spear, looked back, saw the young man, and called to him. The young man answered, "Here am I."

The speaker is a young Amalekite who comes to David with news of the deaths of Saul and Jonathan. David asks him how he knows, and he tells his version of what happened on Mount Gilboa. We do not know whether he is telling the truth: the account in 1 Samuel 31 is different, and many think he embellished the story to win David's favor.

Today we can learn to be honest, especially when we believe a lie would benefit us. It also invites us to say "Here am I" with willingness when someone needs us, but always with sincerity and good intentions.
exp.22:15:
These three mighty men of David broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate, took it, and brought it to David. David would not drink it, but poured it out before the Lord. The word "broke" here means they forced their way through by strength, and "well" refers to a pit where water is kept.

The narrator describes a moment in David's life, when he was in the stronghold and the Philistines were occupying Bethlehem, his hometown. David expressed a longing for home, and his brave men took him seriously and risked themselves to fulfill it. Then David, seeing the cost, declared that the water was like the blood of those men.

Today we can learn to value the sacrifice of others and not treat lightly what cost someone so much. We can also offer to God, with humility, what others give us with such love.
exp.17:15:
This verse tells us that Joab sounded the trumpet, a horn used to give orders in battle. At that signal, David's army stopped chasing the soldiers of Israel who had followed Absalom. The phrase "held back the people" means that Joab stopped the pursuit.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David, and had just died. Joab, the commander of David's army, brought the fighting to an end. Some understand that he did this to prevent more deaths among brothers; the text does not explain his reasons in detail.

For today: knowing when to stop is wisdom. When a conflict has reached its end, continuing to strike only adds pain. Let us ask God for self-control to seek peace and not prolong the fighting.
exp.17:31:
This verse says that King David asks Cushi whether the young man Absalom is well. The word "safe" here means in good health or unharmed. Cushi does not say directly that Absalom died, but he suggests it: he wishes that all the enemies of the king would end up the same way as that young man.

Cushi is speaking, a messenger who brings news from the battle against Absalom's army, since Absalom had rebelled against his father. Cushi announces the victory, but David thinks only of his son. So when he understands the answer, he breaks down and weeps, as the following text shows.

For today: sometimes a victory brings pain, especially when family is involved. We can be honest with God in our weeping and also be careful when we bring bad news, with respect and compassion.
exp.16:15:
He says that an urgent message must be sent to David: that he must not spend the night in the plains of the wilderness, but must cross the Jordan right away. If he does not, the king and all his people could be "swallowed up," that is, destroyed or wiped out. "Send quickly" means to send word without delay.

It is Hushai, David's friend, who speaks, pretending to be an adviser to Absalom. After Absalom preferred his counsel over that of Ahithophel, Hushai passes the report on to the priests Zadok and Abiathar so that they can warn David. He feared that Ahithophel might still manage to attack David, even though his counsel had been rejected.

For today: when God gives you an opportunity or a warning, act promptly. Obedience and prudence should not be left for tomorrow. Moreover, God can care for us by using ordinary people who faithfully do their part.
exp.21:3:
David says that he will ask help from the LORD, who deserves to be praised, and that in this way he will be saved from his enemies. "Call on" means to call out with trust. "Worthy to be praised" means he deserves to be praised. "Saved" means rescued or kept safe.

David speaks at the end of his life, in a song of thanks because God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul (2 Samuel 22:1). Before this, he called God his rock, shield, and refuge. Then he describes the mortal danger he faced. This song appears almost word for word in Psalm 18.

For today: when you are afraid or under pressure, do not wait for the storm to pass before you pray. Call on God now, and praise him while you do, remembering how he has cared for you before. Praise strengthens trust, even when you do not yet know how he will help you.
exp.22:32:
It says that Shammah, who came from Harar (Arar in this version), was one of David's brave men. It also mentions Ahiam, son of Sharar, likewise from Arar. These are names in a list, and no account is given of their deeds. In 1 Chronicles 11:34-35 similar names appear with some variations, and it is not certain whether they are the same people or differences that arose in copying.

The text is part of the last words of David, followed by a list of his most outstanding warriors, called "the thirty." The writer of the book names them so that those who supported David in his battles and in his reign are remembered. That even men with no known story are named shows that their service was valuable.

For today: God sees and remembers faithful service even when it goes unnoticed. You do not need to be famous or stand out to be important in his work. Serve steadily where you are, trusting that God values what you do.
exp.10:15:
Joab, the commander of David's army, was besieging the enemy city. There he placed Uriah in the spot where he knew the strongest men of the enemy were fighting. The word "besieged" in the verse means that he surrounded the city in order to attack it.

The narrator describes how David's plan is carried out. David had committed adultery with Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, and he wanted to cover it up. When that failed, he sent an order by letter that Uriah should be killed in battle. Joab obeyed, even though it was an unjust command. Later, God sends the prophet Nathan to rebuke David.

A hidden sin often leads to another, worse one. If we have failed, the best thing is to confess it quickly to God and repair the harm, without concealing it. Moreover, obeying an authority does not free us from responsibility when we are asked to do wrong.
exp.9:14:
It says that the Syrians, when they saw that Israel had defeated them, did not give up but gathered their forces together again. The word "Syrians" here refers to the Arameans. The phrase about gathering again means they came together once more. The phrase about being defeated before Israel means they were beaten.

This is the account of the writer of Samuel, not a speech. It tells of the war between David and the Ammonites, who had humiliated David's messengers and then allied themselves with the Syrians. Joab had won the first battle, but the Syrians did not accept their defeat and called on Hadadezer to fight again.

A victory does not always end the struggle. What seemed settled yesterday, whether a temptation, a problem, or a tension, can return with force. For this reason it is wise to stay alert, to pray, and not to become overconfident, like David, who mobilized all of Israel and continued to depend on God.
exp.18:38:
All the people crossed the Jordan River, and then King David crossed as well. When he reached the other side, David kissed Barzillai, an elderly man who had helped him, and blessed him. Then Barzillai went back to his home.

After Absalom's rebellion, David returns to Jerusalem. Barzillai had supported him with provisions when David fled, and he went with him as far as the Jordan. David offered to have him live with him at the court, but Barzillai, already very old, preferred to die in his own city and suggested that Chimham go in his place. The text does not make clear who Chimham is; many think he was Barzillai's son.

Today we can honor with affection those who have helped us in difficult times. A hug, a word of blessing, or a sincere thank you are worth a great deal, and it is also wise to recognize our own limits, as Barzillai did.
exp.12:12:
Tamar tells Amnón that if he abuses her, her shame will follow her everywhere, and he would be left as one of the fools, that is, people without sense and without respect for God. Then she asks him to speak with the king, since the king would not refuse him.

Tamar, the daughter of King David, speaks to her half-brother Amnón, who already has her cornered. She tries to stop him with reasons. Her remark about asking the king's permission can be understood in several ways: some think she only wanted to buy time, since the Law forbade that marriage. The Bible does not make this clear.

Today: when someone says "no," that "no" must always be respected. If someone confides that they have suffered abuse, listen to them, believe them, and help them seek protection. Staying silent is never neutral.
exp.22:14:
This verse shows David expressing a wish out loud: he longed to drink fresh water from the well of his hometown, Bethlehem, by the gate. A "well" is a pit or reservoir that holds water, and the phrase "Oh that one would give me" is an old way of saying "I wish someone would give me."

David speaks in a difficult moment. He is hiding in a stronghold while the Philistines occupy Bethlehem, his town. It was probably a sigh of homesickness rather than a command. Even so, three of his mighty men risked their lives to bring him the water, and David, moved by it, did not drink it but poured it out before God.

For today: value the sacrifices others make for you and respond with humility and gratitude. Also, be careful with your words, because a simple wish can lead others to take risks. Honor God above your own desires.
exp.10:3:
David sent messengers to fetch Bathsheba, and she was brought to him. She came to him, and he lay with her. The phrase "took her" means he took her by his royal power. Then she purified herself from her uncleanness, that is, from her ritual impurity caused by menstruation (Leviticus 15), and went back to her house.

This is part of the historical account in Samuel. David was supposed to be at war, but he stayed in Jerusalem. He saw Bathsheba, learned that she was married, and still acted. The text does not tell us what she felt, and it does not say she freely agreed; before a king, her room to refuse was minimal. That is why many read it as an abuse of power. The pregnancy that follows leads to the cover-up and the death of Uriah.

For today: sin usually advances step by step: a look, a question, an order. Stop early, recognize your limit, and never use your authority to take what does not belong to you.
exp.23:18:
David got up and went to the place the prophet Gad had pointed out to him. He did this because it was a command from God and not his own idea. The word for going up here means going to a higher place, and the word for the message means a spoken word or message.

Background: David had taken a census of the people and recognized that this was a sin. A plague was striking Israel. David asked that the punishment fall on him and his family, not on the people. Then God sent Gad with clear instructions: build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah. There David would offer sacrifices, and the dying would stop.

For today: when we acknowledge our failures with humility, God shows us the next step. Obeying Him promptly, even when it costs us, is part of returning to Him with a whole heart.
exp.9:7:
This verse says that the men of Ammon came out of their city and drew up in battle formation at the entrance of the gate. The Syrians they had hired, from Zoba, Rehob, Ish-tob, and Maacah, did not join them but stayed apart, out in the open field. The word "companies" in the verse refers to groups of soldiers, and "by themselves" means separately.

The narrator tells of the war between Israel and Ammon. The Ammonites had shamed David's messengers and knew that this would bring consequences. That is why they paid foreign armies. With the Ammonites facing the gate and the Syrians in the field, Joab was surrounded on two fronts, as the following context shows.

For today: when we act wrongly, it is tempting to look for support from any side before admitting the mistake. That kind of security is often fragile. It is better to make things right with humility and trust in God, not in compromised alliances.
exp.1:7:
This verse tells that Abner, the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, and brought him over to Mahanaim. The word "host" here does not mean a royal court, but an army camp, and "captain of Saul's host" means the military commander. The original text names Mahanaim, although the verse as you see it simply says the place by its name.

Saul had died, and David had already been anointed king by the house of Judah. The one acting here is Abner, who would not accept David and sought to keep the kingship within Saul's family. Scholars agree that Abner held much power and that Ish-bosheth depended on him, although the text does not spell out all of his reasons.

For today: God carries out his purposes even when others resist with their own decisions. We can ask ourselves whether we are seeking God's will or only defending our comfort or our power.
exp.14:7:
Absalom tells King David that, while he was living at Geshur in Syria, he made a promise to God: if God brought him back to Jerusalem, he would serve Him. Now he says he wants to go and fulfill it. A "vow" is a solemn promise made to God. "Geshur" was a neighboring region where Absalom took refuge after fleeing for having killed his brother Amnon.

Absalom, David's son, is the one speaking. It seems like a pious request, but the following text shows it was a pretext: Hebron would serve him as a starting point to proclaim himself king and rebel. Some commentators doubt that the vow really existed; the text does not make this clear. The "forty years" found in some older versions is probably a copying error, and many believe it was four.

Using religious words to cover selfish intentions is dangerous. Let us examine our motives: may our devotion to God be sincere and not a facade to get what we want.
exp.21:20:
David says here that God dealt with him according to his righteousness, and that the cleanness of his hands was the basis of his reward. The phrase "hath he recompensed me" in the verse above means God paid him back, and "according to the cleanness of my hands" describes the honest conduct on which that repayment rested. "Clean hands" speak of conduct that was honest, without violence or deceit.

David sings this psalm of thanksgiving after God delivered him from his enemies, among them Saul. The nearby verses say that God brought him out into a large place, a place of freedom, because God delighted in him. David does not claim to be perfect, since the Bible also records his serious sins. He speaks of his general faithfulness to God, and some understand it to refer mainly to his innocence before those who were pursuing him.

For today: live with integrity, even when no one sees you or recognizes you. And trust that God sees your faithfulness and knows how to care for you and to respond in his time.
exp.8:3:
Here David asks where Jonathan's son is, and Ziba, a servant of Saul's household, tells him that he is staying in the house of Machir, son of Ammiel, in a place called Lo-debar. "That one" refers to the son who was lame in his feet, whom Ziba had just mentioned.

David wanted to show kindness, a goodness that reflects the faithful love of God, because of the promise he had made to his friend Jonathan. Ziba is the one who provides the information. Little is known about Lo-debar; it is located east of the Jordan. The text does not explain why Mephibosheth was there, though it may have been a place of refuge and little visibility.

For today: God and his people seek out those who have been forgotten or hidden away. Think of someone who is alone or set aside, and look for a concrete way to show them kindness this week, with a visit, a phone call, or some help.
exp.9:6:
This verse says that David, when he heard that the Ammonites were preparing for war with the help of Syrian soldiers, sent Joab, his military commander, together with the whole army of the mighty men. "Sent" means that he gave the order to go out; "the mighty men" were the strongest and best-prepared warriors of Israel.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Samuel. David's messengers had been humiliated by the Ammonites, and they, knowing that they had made themselves hateful to David, hired foreign armies. David did not wait to be attacked, but responded with his whole army under the command of Joab.

For today: when we face a serious problem, it is good to act with responsibility and preparation, without ignoring it. Even so, we do well to trust God while we do what is ours to do.
exp.23:24:
It says that David built an altar to God in that place and offered two kinds of sacrifices: burnt offerings, which were burned completely as a full surrender, and peace offerings, which expressed gratitude and fellowship with God. The phrase "was intreated" means that God was moved to mercy and held back his anger. Then the plague that was punishing Israel was stopped.

The narrator is the author of the book. David had taken a census of the people, and a plague came as a consequence. David bought the threshing floor of Araunah, where the angel had stopped, and he did not want to receive it for free. He wanted his offering to cost him something. Many believe that this place was later connected with the temple, although the text of this verse does not say so.

For today: our worship should not be cheap or only words. Think of something concrete, such as your time, your money, or your forgiveness, and give it to God with humility, grateful for his mercy.
exp.2:17:
Abner urges Israel's leaders to act now: "Now then do it," that is, to make David king. He reminds them that the Lord had spoken of David, his servant, saying that by David's hand he would save Israel from the Philistines and from all their enemies.

Abner, commander of Saul's army, had quarreled with Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, and now he switches sides. He speaks with the elders of Israel and with the tribe of Benjamin to persuade them to recognize David. The Bible does not detail in this passage where the Lord made that promise; it presents it only as a word already known. Abner may also have had interests of his own, and the text does not hide this.

For today: God keeps his promises, but he sometimes expects us to act with obedience. Let us not put off until tomorrow what God has already shown us clearly.
exp.9:2:
This verse shows the officials of Ammon speaking to their new king, Hanun. They tell him not to think that David is honoring his father by sending "comforters," meaning people who come alongside those who are grieving. In their view, David has really sent these men to search out the city, that is, to spy on it and then destroy it.

It is the Ammonite princes who speak, as counselors to the king. Hanun had just lost his father and was new to the throne. David wanted to return a kindness that Hanun's father had shown him earlier. The Bible does not say whether the princes were sincere or had other interests, but their suspicion led Hanun to humiliate the messengers.

For today: before assuming bad intentions in someone who shows kindness, it is wise to ask questions and listen calmly. Suspicion without evidence can damage relationships and bring painful consequences.
exp.21:2:
This verse says that David trusts in God as his rock, that is, a firm and secure place. He calls him a shield, who protects him from danger. He speaks of the horn of his salvation, meaning a power that saves, since the horn was a symbol of strength. He also calls him his stronghold, his refuge, and his savior. The word "violence" refers to the attacks and the wickedness of his enemies.

David sings this song on the day God delivered him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, who pursued him to kill him. He speaks from gratitude, looking back and recognizing that God was his defense in very difficult years.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, do not look first to your own strength. Tell God in prayer, "You are my refuge." Remembering how he helped you before strengthens your trust for what comes next.
exp.22:21:
This verse sums up what Benaiah did: he killed lions, defeated a giant Egyptian, and took away his spear. "Had the name" means that he became famous, that his reputation was great among David's brave warriors. "Among three mighty men" refers to a group of outstanding fighters.

The passage is a list of the bravest men in David's army. The narrator remembers them to honor their loyalty and courage. The next verse makes clear that Benaiah did not become one of the first three, although he was highly respected. Some think that "among the three" means his fame brought him close to them.

For today: God notices those who act with courage and faithfulness, even if they are not the first. Do what is right today with firmness, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.13:8:
She says that the woman from Tekoa asks King David to rule in her favor, and she is willing to take on any blame. Here "the iniquity" means the guilt or the punishment for not keeping the law as it was expected. She says: if there is guilt, let it fall on me and my family; the king and his throne are without guilt.

The woman speaks as someone sent by Joab, according to the chapter, with an invented story about two sons and a killing. She wanted David, as he decided to forgive her supposed son, to understand that he should also bring back Absalom, his son who had been sent away. She makes sure the king is not left exposed by his decision.

For today: sometimes helping others means taking on risk and responsibility, instead of placing it on someone else. But we also learn to be sincere, without manipulating others, even for good causes.
exp.2:11:
Abner sent messengers to David with a message on his behalf. First he asks: "Whose is the land?", a question meant to make David think about who should rule. Then he proposes: "Make your league with me, and I will help you bring all Israel under your command."

Abner was the commander of Saul's army and had supported Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, as king. But he had become angry with him and decided to switch sides. Interpreters debate whether he was thinking of the good of the people or of his own advantage; the Bible does not fully make this clear.

Today, when we seek peace or unity, let us examine our motives. Even good results can come from mixed intentions, and God invites us to pursue what is good with a sincere heart.
exp.14:18:
Here King David asks Ittai, a man from Gath: "Why are you also coming with us?" He tells him to turn back and stay with the king, because he is a foreigner and is also far from his homeland. The word "exile" means a person who lives outside the place where he is from. "Return" means go back.

David is fleeing Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. In that hard moment, David speaks with kindness. He does not want Ittai, who has only recently arrived, to suffer for a problem that is not his own. He offers to release him from the duty of accompanying him. Some understand that the "king" Ittai was to return to is Absalom, although the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: true loyalty does not depend on comfort. Ittai reminds us that we can stand beside those we love in difficult times. And David teaches us to care for others, even when we ourselves are suffering.
exp.15:5:
It says that Shimei, while cursing, threw stones at David and at all of King David's servants. Even so, the people and the mighty men were walking beside the king, on his right hand and on his left. "Right hand" is the hand on the right side, and "left" is the hand on the left side. That is, David was surrounded and protected.

The narrator tells this moment while David is fleeing from Jerusalem because of the rebellion of his son Absalom. Shimei, of the family of Saul, takes advantage of the king's fall to insult him and blame him for the blood of Saul's house. The Bible does not say here that David was guilty of that, and interpreters see it in different ways.

For today: when we are attacked or humiliated, we do not always need to respond with anger. David bore the insult calmly and left his case in God's hands. We can ask God for self-control and humility.
exp.3:1:
This verse introduces two men: Baanah and Rechab, brothers, sons of Rimmon, from the town of Beeroth. They were captains of companies, that is, leaders of groups of soldiers who served Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul. It is clarified that Beeroth was counted as part of the tribe of Benjamin, the same tribe as Saul.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, preparing the account. Israel was very weak: Abner, the commander of the army, had died, and Saul's son had lost heart. These two captains appear just before they do something serious, which the text will recount immediately. Why they acted as they did, the passage does not explain here.

For today: holding a position or being close to someone does not guarantee a faithful heart. Let us ask God for integrity, especially when we see others growing weak and the temptation to take advantage appears.
exp.0:16:
This verse says that David composed and sang a lament for the death of Saul and of his son Jonathan. The word "lamented" means that he mourned, weeping and expressing his grief. A lament is a sad song sung when someone dies.

The account tells that a young man from the Amalekites came before David saying that he had killed Saul, hoping for a reward. David did not celebrate; instead he condemned him for daring to lay hands on the anointed of the LORD. After that, David expressed his sorrow in the form of a song. It is remarkable that he mourned even Saul, who had hunted him to kill him. The text does not say that David hid his suffering, but that he turned it into poetry.

For today: when someone who wronged us suffers a loss, we can choose respect and compassion instead of gladness or resentment. Weeping honestly before God is also healthy.
exp.7:17:
Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, was in charge of the Cherethites and the Pelethites, who were David's personal guard. Their exact origin is not certain; some think they were foreign soldiers. David's sons are called "princes," that is, they held important positions close to the king. The verse uses a word that usually means "priests" here, so it is understood in several ways.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. After recounting David's victories, he presents the list of his main helpers. In this way he shows that his kingdom was already well organized and firm.

For today: no one serves well alone. David had helpers with clear tasks. In your family, your church, or your work, share responsibilities and recognize the service of others. Order and teamwork can also honor God.
exp.20:12:
This verse says that David ordered the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan to be gathered up, and that the bones of those who were hanged were also collected. The word "hanged" refers to the seven descendants of Saul who had been executed shortly before and left hanging on the mountain.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. There was famine in the land because of an injustice Saul had committed against the Gibeonites. Rizpah, the mother of two of those executed, guarded the bodies with great devotion. When David learned of this, he acted to give all of them a proper burial. Afterward, the text says that God was moved to show favor to the land.

For today: honor those who have passed away, and humbly make amends for the wrongs of the past. If there is something we can correct or care for with love, we should not leave it for later.
exp.13:26:
It says that Absalom had three sons and one daughter named Tamar, who was very beautiful. Where the verse would note an older wording, the sentence is removed here, since that wording does not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of the book, who continues describing Absalom. Earlier he highlighted his beauty and his hair. Now he mentions his family. Some think Tamar received her name from her aunt, Absalom's sister, who had been dishonored (2 Samuel 13). That is a possibility, but the text does not say so. Then it is told that Absalom remained away from the king.

For today: beauty and fame attract attention, but they do not replace a humble heart. Let us ask God to care for our character more than our image.
exp.19:7:
It says that when Joab's troops reached the great stone at Gibeon, Amasa came out to meet them. Joab was wearing his fitted battle garment, and over it a belt with a dagger in its sheath, at waist height. As he went forward, the dagger fell out. The verse of the old wording is removed here because the reader's verse does not contain those words.

This is part of the account of Sheba's rebellion. David had appointed Amasa commander of the army in place of Joab. The narrator describes the dagger here because Joab is about to kill Amasa through deceit. It is not made clear whether the dagger fell by accident or whether Joab let it fall on purpose; many read it as a move meant to make him appear unarmed.

For today: violence is sometimes hidden behind friendly gestures. Let us distrust the ambition and jealousy in our hearts, and seek sincere relationships, without duplicity.
exp.9:13:
This verse tells how the Ammonites saw the Syrians fleeing, their hired allies, and then they too fled from Abishai, the brother of Joab, and shut themselves up in their city. The "Syrians" are the Arameans, and the phrase "shut themselves up" is rendered here simply as they went inside the city, as the verse itself reads.

The account continues the war between Israel and the Ammonites, who had humiliated David's messengers. Earlier, Joab divided his army into two fronts and encouraged his brother with words of courage and confidence that God would decide the outcome. When the Syrians fled, the Ammonites lost their support and their courage. The text does not say the war ended completely, since the Syrians gathered again later.

For today: do faithfully what is your part, with courage and unity, and leave the outcome in God's hands. Also, do not place your security only in human support, because it can fail.
exp.11:30:
The verse tells that David brought out the people of Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and put them to work under saws, harrows of iron, and axes of iron. The phrase "made them pass through the brickkiln" refers to the brickkilns, the furnaces where bricks were made. He did the same to all the other Ammonite cities, and then he returned to Jerusalem.

It is a scene from the account of the war against Ammon. The narrator speaks without commenting on whether God approved of this. Scholars debate whether it was forced labor or torture and death; the Hebrew text allows both readings.

For today: the Bible sometimes reports deeds without approving them, and the violence of power leaves its marks. May power never make us forget the dignity of the people who are under our authority. Let us treat them with justice and mercy.
exp.18:11:
Here David tells the elders of Judah: "You are my brothers, my own family." He asks them why they would be the last to bring the king back. The phrase "my bones and my flesh" means that they are close relatives. "The last" means those who come at the end.

David speaks after the death of Absalom, who had rebelled against him. The other tribes of Israel already wanted David to return, but Judah, his own tribe, had stayed silent. David sends the priests Zadok and Abiathar to speak to them. He seeks reconciliation and appeals to family ties, not to force. The text shows that the heart of Judah turned toward him.

For today: when a relationship is broken, it is sometimes wise to take the first step with humility and to remember what unites us. A kind gesture can open the door to reconciliation.
exp.2:14:
This verse tells how Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, sent for Michal and took her away from her husband Paltiel, son of Laish. Paltiel was her husband at that time.

The narrator describes one step in the political agreement between David and Abner, commander of Ish-bosheth's army. David demanded that his first wife, Michal, be returned to him before he would negotiate. Ish-bosheth, weak before Abner, complied. Saul had given Michal to Paltiel earlier (1 Samuel 25:44). The text does not explain her feelings, but it shows Paltiel's grief, since he followed her weeping.

The decisions of the powerful, even political ones, can wound ordinary people. Today we can ask God for sensitivity to treat with compassion those who suffer the consequences of decisions made by others, and to comfort them.
exp.12:21:
It says that Absalom did not say a single word to Amnon, neither good nor bad. But inwardly he hated him, that is, he despised him with hatred, because Amnon had raped Tamar, his sister. The word "forced" here means raped.

The account tells what happened after Amnon assaulted Tamar. Absalom told his sister to keep quiet and took her into his house. David was very angry, but the text does not say that he punished Amnon. Absalom's silence was not peace: the verse that follows shows that he waited two years and planned his revenge.

For today: silent resentment does not disappear; it grows and can lead to more pain. If someone has hurt you or has hurt someone you love, seek justice and help in healthy ways, and ask God to heal your heart before hatred makes the decisions for you.
exp.0:9:
A young Amalekite tells David that he killed Saul, the king who was wounded in battle. He says he did it because Saul was not going to survive his fall. As proof, he brings the crown and the armlet, which is a bracelet the king used to wear. He hands them to David, whom he calls "my lord."

This messenger is the one speaking, and he hopes to receive a reward from David. His account differs from chapter 31 of 1 Samuel, where Saul takes his own life. Many think the young man invented or embellished the story to win David's favor. Others believe that Saul, already wounded, may indeed have asked him for help. The Bible does not make this clear. David, however, does not celebrate: he weeps.

Today we can learn not to take advantage of another person's misfortune for our own benefit. And, like David, we can respect and grieve the fall of others, even of those who have wronged us.
exp.5:16:
It says that the Israelites brought the ark of the Lord and set it in the prepared place, inside a tent that David had put up for it. Then David offered sacrifices: the "burnt offerings" were offerings that were burned whole for God, and the "peace offerings" were offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving, from which the meal was also shared.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The ark represented God's presence with his people. Earlier, an attempt to bring it had ended in tragedy (2 Samuel 6:1-11). Now David brings it with joy and worship. The texts do not say that this tent was the tabernacle of Moses, so it is better not to claim that.

For today: before making plans or celebrating, we put God at the center. David gave him a place and thanked him with offerings. We can begin the day, the week, or a project by giving thanks and seeking his presence with reverence and joy.
exp.12:15:
She says that Tamar answers Amnon: "It is not right. To send me away now is a greater wrong than the one you already did to me." The phrase "there is no cause" means "there is no justification." And "he would not hearken unto her" means that Amnon refused to listen to her.

It is Tamar, daughter of King David and half-sister of Amnon, who speaks. He had just abused her with violence, and then, filled with hatred, he sent her out. Tamar, already wounded, defends her dignity: to be cast out in this way, in shame and without protection, made the injustice worse. The Bible does not present her as guilty.

For today: when someone suffers abuse, we should listen to her seriously, believe her, and protect her, not silence her or rush to hide the problem. God sees the pain of the wounded, and we can be instruments of his care and of justice.
exp.14:12:
This verse tells us that someone came with news for King David. He told him that most of the people of Israel were supporting Absalom, his son. The phrase "the hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom" means that the loyalty and affection of the people had turned toward Absalom.

The one speaking is an unnamed messenger. Absalom had prepared a rebellion with great patience, winning the people over, and now the conspiracy was growing. David, on hearing this, decides to leave Jerusalem to protect the city and his people.

For today: popularity can change very quickly, so let us not place our security in the approval of people. When we face losses or betrayals, let us seek God with humility and act with wisdom, without clinging to pride.
exp.0:19:
He says that the news of the deaths of Saul and Jonathan should not be told in Gath or announced in the streets of Ashkelon, two Philistine cities. That way the Philistine women would not rejoice or celebrate.

David speaks in a lament, a funeral song, after Israel's defeat on Mount Gilboa, where Saul and his son Jonathan died. David feels grief and does not want Israel's enemies to mock. Although Saul had hunted him, David mourns him with respect.

For today: when someone who hurt us falls or suffers, we are not called to rejoice or to speak of their fall with mockery. We can honor the good that was in that person, mourn with sincerity, and guard the good name of others.
exp.7:15:
This verse names two officials of King David. Joab, son of Zeruiah, was the commander of the army, that is, the head of the soldiers. Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was the recorder, who kept the records and handled the affairs of the kingdom. Some understand him as the king's chronicler or spokesman; the Hebrew allows for several translations.

The narrator of the book lists the main people responsible for David's government. It comes after the king's victories and after the statement that he reigned with right and justice. It shows that the kingdom did not depend on a single man, but on an orderly structure.

For today: doing things well almost always requires teamwork. Recognize and value those who serve alongside you in your family, church, or work, and faithfully carry out the task God has given you.
exp.0:1:
It says that on the third day after David returned to Ziklag, a man came from Saul's camp. He had his clothes torn and dirt on his head, signs of mourning and grief in that time. When he came before David, he bowed down to the ground and paid him homage, as one would before someone in authority.

The narrator is the one telling this. David had just defeated the Amalekites and did not yet know what had happened in Israel's battle against the Philistines. This man arrives with news of Saul's death. His gesture of reverence suggests that he already saw David as the future king. Later in the chapter, his account will have important consequences, and the Bible does not make clear whether everything he said was true.

Today we can learn to receive hard news calmly, asking questions and listening before we react. It is also wise to examine carefully what we are told, especially when the person speaking might have interests of their own.
exp.14:34:
Here David tells Hushai that he will not be alone in Jerusalem. The priests Zadok and Abiathar will be there too. Whatever Hushai hears in the king's house, he must report to them.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled and took the support of the people from him. Hushai, his faithful friend, wants to go with him, but David asks him to return and pretend to serve Absalom. In this way he will be able to undo the counsel of Ahithophel, who had gone over to Absalom's side. The priests and their sons would be the secret channel for sending news to David.

Today we see that God often works through loyal people who serve where they are, even when the place is not comfortable. Ask yourself: where has God placed me to be faithful, and how can I support, with wisdom and honesty, those who need help?
exp.16:14:
Hushai tells the priests Zadok and Abiathar what happened at Absalom's council. He explains that Ahithophel gave one piece of advice, and that he himself gave a different one. The word "counsel" in the verse means that he gave his opinion or plan. "The elders of Israel" were the leaders of the people.

Hushai was a friend of David, and he had presented himself to Absalom as if he were his counselor. His mission was to make Ahithophel's plan fail. Now he informs the priests, who were David's secret allies, so that they can warn David to cross the Jordan. The text says that the LORD allowed the good counsel of Ahithophel to be defeated.

For today: God can work in the middle of confusing or unjust situations, even through people who act with wisdom and courage. When you face a difficult situation, pray, act with prudence, and trust that God is still in control, even when you cannot yet see it.
exp.5:18:
Here it is said that David, after bringing the ark to Jerusalem, gave every Israelite, men and women alike, a loaf of bread, a piece of meat, and a flask of wine. Then everyone returned to their homes. "Gave out" means that he handed each person their share. Some translations render the phrase about the meat differently, and the exact sense of that Hebrew term is not entirely certain.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Samuel. David rejoices that the ark of God, the sign of his presence, has at last arrived at its place. After offering sacrifices and blessing the people, he holds a shared feast. Everyone receives the same, regardless of rank. Right after this comes the clash with Michal, who scorns David's joy.

For today: when God blesses us, our joy grows when we share it. Think of someone you could invite to your table or help generously this week.
exp.5:17:
It says that David, after finishing offering the sacrifices, blessed the people. The "burnt offerings" were offerings that were completely burned in honor of God. The "peace offerings" were offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving, of which a portion was shared in a meal.

The "Lord of hosts" is a name for God that emphasizes his power and his authority over all things.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David had just brought the ark of God to Jerusalem with great joy. As king, he also played the role of spiritual guide: he worshiped God and then blessed the people in God's name, not in his own. Right after this, it is told that he gave food to everyone.

For today: when God blesses us, it is not meant to be kept only for ourselves. We can thank him from the heart and then share what we have received with others, through kind words, help, and generosity.
exp.18:10:
Here King David sends the priests Zadok and Abiathar with a message for the elders of Judah, his own tribe. He asks them why they would be the last to bring the king back to his house, since all Israel had already spoken of his return.

David speaks after the death of Absalom, who had rebelled against him. The other tribes were already talking about bringing him back, but Judah, where David came from, had remained silent. David wants his return to be peaceful and wants his own people not to feel left out. Some think he also seeks to win their political support.

For today: when there is a break in a relationship, do not wait to be the last to take the step toward reconciliation. Sometimes those closest to us are the slowest to draw near, and a kind word spoken in time can open the way.
exp.21:39:
It says that God gave David strength to fight, like someone who fastens a belt of power around him before battle. It also says that God brought down under his feet those who rose up against him. The phrase about fastening and the phrase about bringing down are the two images in the verse, and each is simply rendered here in ordinary words.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, when God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul (2 Samuel 22:1). The words about pursuing and destroying reflect the warfare of his time as king of Israel. What matters is that David acknowledges that the victory did not come from his own strength, but from God.

For today: we do not take this text as permission to harm others. We can apply it this way: when facing a difficult trial, ask God for strength, and after coming through it, thank him instead of boasting.
exp.21:47:
It is God who defends David and brings about justice for him. "He has avenged me" means that God vindicated him against his enemies and acted on his behalf. "Subdues the peoples under me" means that God placed the nations under his authority.

David, now an old man, speaks in a song of thanksgiving that recalls how God delivered him from Saul and from other enemies (2 Samuel 22:1). He does not claim the victory for himself; he praises it as the work of God, whom he calls his rock, that is, his firm refuge. Some understand this as a song that also carries a prophetic tone about the Messiah, although the text speaks first of David.

For today: when you are wounded or treated unfairly, avoid taking revenge on your own. Hand the situation over to God in prayer, trust that He does justice in his own time, and give thanks for every help received.
exp.13:9:
In this verse, King David promises to protect the woman. He tells her that if anyone accuses her or threatens her over what she asked for, she should bring that person to him, and that person will no longer trouble her. "Touch" here means harm or bother.

David, the king, is speaking with a woman from Tekoa. She tells a story about her son, who had killed his brother, and her relatives want to kill him. Many understand that Joab sent her so that David would reflect on his own son Absalom, who had been banished for a similar crime. David does not yet see the comparison, and he promises to protect her.

For today: Those who hold authority can use it to protect the vulnerable. But we also need humility to listen, and to see whether what we advise others we should also apply in our own lives.
exp.18:41:
The men of Judah replied to the men of Israel that they had accompanied the king because he is one of their own tribe, their close relative. They ask why the Israelites are angry, since they themselves have not lived at the king's expense and have received no gifts from him. The phrase "eaten something of the king" means having been supported by his provisions.

David returns to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Judah was the first tribe to receive him and escorted him when he crossed the Jordan. The other tribes of Israel felt ignored and make their complaint. Judah defends itself by pointing to its family bond. The argument becomes so tense that soon another rebellion breaks out, although the text shows that both sides spoke with pride and with wounds.

When someone feels set aside, it is easy to respond defensively. Before arguing, let us listen with humility and seek peace, remembering that we are brothers.
exp.12:16:
Amnon calls his servant, the young man who attended him, and orders him: "Take this woman out of here, throw her out into the street, and lock the door behind her." In the verse, the word "Put" is the command to remove her, and "this woman" is Tamar, his half-sister.

Amnon is the speaker, the son of King David. He had just abused Tamar, and suddenly his supposed love had turned into hatred. She begged him not to send her away, because that would be one more wrong added to the first, but he would not listen. He treats her like an object he no longer wants, taking no responsibility at all. The Bible tells this plainly and does not approve of it.

For today: when someone suffers an injustice, let us not leave them alone. Let us listen, protect, and stand with them in compassion, instead of staying silent or looking the other way.
exp.17:16:
This verse says that Joab's men took Absalom's body and threw it into a large pit in the forest. On top of it they piled a huge heap of stones. Then all Israel, that is, those who had followed Absalom, fled, each man to his own home.

This is part of the account of Absalom's rebellion against his father David. Joab had killed Absalom and stopped the pursuit. The narrator tells the ending without any honor: a pit in the forest and a heap of stones. Many understand that the heap of stones was a sign of shame, as happens in other cases in the Bible. The following text speaks of the pillar Absalom had set up for himself so that he would be remembered.

For today: seeking fame or recognition can leave us empty. It is better to live with humility, honoring God and our family, for only what we do in obedience to Him endures.
exp.21:25:
This verse says that God deals with each person according to their heart. "Merciful" means kind, gentle and compassionate. "Upright" means sincere, whole, without deceit. In other words, the one who seeks what is good finds God's kindness, and the one who walks righteously finds Him faithful and open.

David speaks this, near the end of his life, in a song of thanksgiving because the LORD delivered him from Saul and from all his enemies. He does not claim to have been perfect, but says that he sought to follow God with sincerity and turned away from wickedness. He acknowledges that God is faithful to those who are faithful to Him.

For today: if you want to experience God's kindness up close, come to Him with sincerity. Today, without pretending, confess to Him what weighs on you and ask Him for help to live honestly at home and at work.
exp.13:29:
Absalom speaks to his servants and reminds them that Joab's field of barley is next to his. He orders them to set it on fire, and they do it. "Set fire" means to burn; "fields" are the cultivated land.

Absalom had been in Jerusalem for two years without being able to see King David. He had asked Joab, a leader close to the king, to speak on his behalf, but Joab ignored him twice. So Absalom turns to violence to get his attention. Afterward, Joab comes, and Absalom explains that he wants to see the king. The Bible does not approve of his act here; it only shows his impulsive character.

When someone ignores us, we may feel tempted to force a response through anger or pressure. It is better to speak with clarity and patience, seeking reconciliation without harming others or letting resentment take control of us.
exp.13:11:
This verse says the woman asks King David for permission to say something more. Her request is phrased as "I pray thee," and she calls herself "thine handmaid," speaking with humility. David grants her the freedom to speak with the word "Say on."

This woman is from Tekoa, and Joab sent her to persuade David with an invented story about a son in danger. David has just promised her that her supposed son will be safe. Now she uses that promise to show him that he himself has a banished son, Absalom, and that he should bring him back.

For today: when we have to say a hard truth, let us do it with humility and respect, asking for the chance to speak. And listening with patience, as David did, helps us see what we did not want to see.
exp.12:10:
Here the account tells that Tamar brings Amnon the food she prepared, and he seizes her forcefully and asks her to lie with him. "Took hold of her" means that he restrained her by force. Calling her "my sister" makes the act more serious, because she was his half-sister, a daughter of the same father, David.

Amnon pretended to be sick and sent all the servants out so he could be alone with her. Tamar had come at the command of King David, suspecting nothing, only to care for her brother. She protests, asks him not to dishonor her, and proposes speaking with the king. Amnon acts with deceit and abuse of power.

For today: the Bible does not stay silent about abuse; it calls it by its name. If someone pressures you or isolates you to harm you, it is not your fault. Seek help and trusted people. If you are a leader or a family member, protect the vulnerable.
exp.1:9:
Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. The verse also says that only the tribe of Judah followed David, that is, it supported him as king.

The narrator of the book describes how the people were divided after Saul's death. Abner, the commander of the army, set Ish-bosheth up as king to keep power in Saul's family. David's seven years and a half in Hebron suggest there was a period of waiting before he reigned over all Israel. Scholars explain the difference from Ish-bosheth's two years in several ways, and it is not certain which explanation is best.

Today we can learn to trust God's timing. Sometimes promises take a long time to arrive, and others rush ahead with human plans. To wait with faith and integrity, without forcing our way, is also a way of obeying.
exp.17:25:
He says that the watchman saw another man running alone and called out to the gatekeeper. King David replied that this one was also a messenger. The verse's two source-language words, the watchman who keeps guard from a high place and the gatekeeper at the door, are simply the watchman and the gatekeeper of the verse, so no separate note is needed.

We are in the war between David and his son Absalom. David waits for news of the battle, sitting between the two gates of the city. The watchman speaks, reporting what he sees, and David speaks, interpreting it: if someone runs alone, he brings news, and David thinks it will be good news. Soon two messengers arrive: Ahimaaz and another man. Ahimaaz brings word of the victory, but David also wants to know whether his son is alive.

For today: when we are waiting for hard news, we can give our anxiety to God in prayer, while remaining watchful and patient. Sometimes the answer comes in parts, and we need to trust while the whole of it arrives.
exp.1:31:
It says that Joab and his men marched through the whole night and came to Hebron when the day was already breaking.

The account has no character who speaks; it is the narrator who tells the story. The battle between David's men and Abner's men had just taken place, in which Asahel, Joab's brother, died. After burying him in Bethlehem, the group continued on their way to Hebron, where David was. Perhaps Joab and his men were tired and in mourning, but they did not stop.

There are days when we carry losses and weariness, and still we must go on with our responsibilities. When you walk through a difficult night, take the next step in faith, trusting that God is with you and that the dawn will come.
exp.2:0:
This verse says there was a long war between the followers of Saul and those of David. Over time, David grew stronger, while Saul's family grew weaker. "House" here means family and supporters, not just a building. The phrase "grew stronger and stronger" means he gained strength and support.

The author of the book is not identified; it is a historical account. Saul had died, and David was reigning only over Judah from Hebron, while Saul's son Ish-bosheth had the support of the other tribes. This verse summarizes years of conflict before David was accepted as king over all Israel. The verses that follow list the sons born to him in Hebron.

For today: sometimes God's promises are not fulfilled overnight. David had to wait and go through conflicts. If you are in a long season of waiting or difficulty, remain faithful and trust that God is working slowly, even if you don't notice it every day.
exp.23:4:
They crossed the Jordan and camped at Aroer, on the right side (the south) of the city that lies in the middle of the valley of Gad, near Jazer. The verse of the source words is removed here because the verse reads "pitched in Aroer" and "the midst of the river of Gad," and the meaning of "river" as a valley with a stream is already reflected in the verse's own wording.

This is the narrator speaking. David had ordered the census, and Joab, although he warned him it was not a good idea, obeyed. The places mentioned mark the route through the territory of Israel. The text does not explain all of David's reasons here, but the account shows that the census displeased God.

For today: when a decision troubles us, obeying out of habit is not enough. It is wise to stop, pray, and listen to sound counsel before moving forward.
exp.11:2:
This verse describes the poor man in the story. He had only one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and raised himself. The lamb grew up alongside his children, ate from his own food, drank from his own cup, and lay in his arms. He treated her as a daughter.

Here the prophet Nathan, sent by God to David, speaks. David had taken Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah killed. Nathan does not accuse him to his face, but tells this parable so that David will recognize the seriousness of his sin for himself.

For today: God sees what is precious to others, even when it seems small in our eyes. We can ask ourselves whether we are abusing our position or power, and take tender care of what others love.
exp.8:10:
Ziba tells King David that he will do everything the king has commanded. Then it is made clear that Mephibosheth will eat at the king's table, treated as if he were one of the king's own sons.

David speaks with Ziba, a former servant of Saul. David had promised his friend Jonathan that he would look after Jonathan's family. For that reason he gave back Saul's lands to Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, who was lame in both feet. David not only provides for him materially, but gives him a place at his own table, which was a great honor and a sign of acceptance.

God treats us with that same grace: he gives us a place at his table even though we do not deserve it. Today we can imitate David by keeping our promises and welcoming with dignity those who feel weak, forgotten, or without a place.
exp.12:11:
Tamar tells Amnón not to force her. "Force" here means abusing someone against her will. She explains that such a thing "must not be done in Israel," meaning that God's people do not act that way. "Folly" here is a mild word for a serious evil, a wickedness.

Tamar, daughter of King David and half-sister of Amnón, speaks. He pretended to be sick so that he could be alone with her. Tamar resists with courage, appeals to what is right in Israel, and tries to stop him with her words. Even so, Amnón abuses her. The guilt is his alone.

Today, this text teaches us to take every person's "no" seriously and to believe those who report abuse. If anyone is in danger, let us seek help and protection without delay. God has compassion on victims and does not blame them.
exp.19:21:
What the text says: A woman of the city spoke wisely to all her neighbors. They cut off the head of Sheba, the rebel, and threw it out to Joab. Then Joab blew a trumpet, the army withdrew, and each man went back to his tent. Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.

Context: Sheba had led a rebellion against David. Joab, the commander of the army, besieged the city of Abel. A wise woman negotiated with him: if they handed over only the guilty man, the city would be spared. In this way the conflict ended without destroying all the inhabitants.

For today: Wisdom and dialogue can prevent greater tragedies. Before reacting with anger in a conflict, look for solutions that protect the innocent and resolve the problem at its root.
exp.11:4:
It says that David became very angry when he heard the story of the rich man who took the poor man's only little ewe lamb. The phrase "his anger was greatly kindled" means his anger burned strongly. David swears "As the Lord liveth", a solemn way of affirming something, and declares that the man who did this "shall surely die", meaning he deserves a severe punishment.

The prophet Nathan tells this story to David at God's direction. David had taken Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah put to death. Nathan does not accuse him directly, but with a parable. David, without realizing it, condemns himself. A few words later Nathan will say to him: "Thou art the man." It is worth noting that the law did not call for death for stealing a sheep; David's reaction shows his indignation, and also how blind he was to his own sin.

We often see the wrongs of others clearly and find it hard to see our own. Let us ask God for humility to examine ourselves with the same justice with which we judge others, and to receive correction without excuses.
exp.22:31:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Eliahba, from Shaalbon (a town or place), and Jonathan, described as "of the sons of Jashen." No one knows for certain who Jashen was; some scholars believe the original text has a small variation, and the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11 reads differently.

The writer is the narrator of the book, who presents David's mighty men, called "the thirty." He does not want only to recount battles, but to acknowledge the men who supported the king with loyalty and courage. They come from different places, united by a single purpose.

For today: God notices people whom sometimes no one remembers. Serve faithfully wherever you are, even if your name is not famous; God does not forget your work.
exp.19:2:
David returned to Jerusalem and set apart the ten concubines (secondary wives) whom he had left to look after the palace. He placed them under guard in a house, provided them with food, but never had relations with them again. They lived shut away, like widows, until their death.

The narrator tells this after Absalom's rebellion, in which Absalom had publicly shamed them (2 Samuel 16:21-22). Meanwhile, another revolt arises, that of Sheba. The text does not explain David's motives: it may have been protection, shame, or a legal measure. They were victims, and their lives were marked by the sins of others.

Today we see that sin wounds innocent people too. We can look on those who suffer because of others' mistakes with compassion, and help them receive care, dignity, and hope.
exp.13:7:
What the verse says: The king answers the woman that she should go home in peace. He promises that he himself will give an order or decision in her favor. The phrase "I will give charge concerning you" means "I will give orders about your case."

Context: King David is speaking. A woman from Tekoa comes before him with a story about two sons who fought, and one killed the other. Now her family wants to kill the surviving son. Most scholars understand that Joab sent her with this story to lead David to think about his son Absalom, who was banished for killing his brother. David does not yet know this; he responds with compassion, but still without giving a full decision.

For today: Those who have authority should listen carefully to those who suffer. But it is also wise to act with justice and wisdom, not only with kind words.
exp.2:29:
This verse explains why Abner died. Joab and his brother Abishai killed him in revenge, because Abner had killed their brother Asahel during the battle at Gibeon. The word "and" here only joins the sentence to what came before.

The narrator of the book gives us the reason behind the crime. Abner had made peace with David, and Joab murdered him treacherously in Hebron (v. 27). Earlier, Abner had killed Asahel, though he did it while defending himself from Asahel's pursuit (2 Samuel 2:18-23). For this reason David distances himself from the deed, curses the house of Joab, and publicly mourns Abner.

Today, resentment can lead us to harm others and to justify ourselves with excuses. If someone has wounded us, let us ask God for help to forgive and to leave justice in his hands, instead of taking revenge.
exp.18:1:
This verse says that the day of victory turned into sorrow for the whole army. The soldiers heard that the king was deeply grieved over the death of his son. Mourning is deep sorrow for someone who has died. Here the word "grieved" means sorrow and anguish.

The account tells what happened after David's troops defeated the rebels led by Absalom, the king's son. Absalom died in the battle. David, as a father, wept inconsolably, and this discouraged those who had risked their lives for him. Joab, his commander, learned of it and soon afterward rebuked the king.

For today: grief is real and deserves to be mourned, but our emotions also affect those around us. We can ask God for comfort and wisdom to suffer without forgetting to give thanks and to care for those who stand beside us.
exp.15:16:
Absalom asks Hushai whether this is the loyalty he shows to his friend David. The word "kindness" in the verse means loyalty or faithful affection. Absalom is surprised that Hushai did not go with David when David fled from Jerusalem.

Absalom had rebelled against his father David and had just entered Jerusalem. Hushai, David's friend, came and greeted him as king. Absalom suspects him and tests him. Many understand that Hushai was acting in secret to help David, although the text does not say so in this verse; the account that follows shows it.

For today: when someone questions your loyalty, act with wisdom and sincerity before God. Ask Him to guide you to be faithful to people and to what is right, without being carried away by the pressure of the moment.
exp.1:17:
It says that the three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Zeruiah was David's sister, so they were his nephews. Of Asahel it is said that he was "light of foot," that is, very swift, "as light of foot as a wild roe," an animal like a small deer, quick and nimble.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. After the battle at Gibeon, where David's men defeated Abner's men, he introduces those who take part in the pursuit. He highlights Asahel's speed because it explains why he runs after Abner, the commander of Israel's army. What follows shows that speed alone was not enough to make his decision wise.

For today: the gifts God gives us, such as talent, strength, or speed, need good judgment. Before we rush after something, let us ask for wisdom.
exp.21:48:
This verse says that God brought David out from among his enemies and set him in a safe, high place, far from those who rose up against him. The phrase "lifted me up on high" means that he put him in a place of safety. The verse's "delivered me" is the same idea as "brought me out." The "violent man" is a violent or wicked man.

David speaks here, near the end of his life, in a song of thanks to God for rescuing him from many dangers. Many think the "violent man" refers to Saul, although the text does not give the name, and it could also speak of other enemies in general. David acknowledges that his victory came from God, not from his own strength.

For today: when you go through an unjust or difficult situation, tell God what you feel and trust that he can take care of you. And when you come through it, do not forget to thank him sincerely.
exp.13:4:
Here King David asks the woman, "What aileth thee?", that is, "What is wrong with you?" She answers that she is a widow and that her husband is dead. With those words she begins to present her case.

The woman is from Tekoa, and she comes before David. Joab, the commander of the army, put these words in her mouth so that she would tell a story to the king. According to the account, Joab wanted David to reconsider his position toward his son Absalom. She pretends to be a widow in trouble, and the text does not say that everything she tells is true.

Today we can learn to listen with compassion, but also with wisdom. Before judging a case, it is good to ask God for discernment and to look at everything with humility.
exp.23:2:
Joab answers King David with respect but with concern. He tells him that God could multiply the people a hundredfold, and that he hopes the king will see it with his own eyes. But right away he asks: why does my lord the king want this? That is, he does not understand the reason for counting the people.

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. The king had just ordered a census of all Israel. The text says God's anger was against Israel, and it does not explain the reason in detail. Joab suspects the motive is not good, perhaps pride or trust in the number of soldiers. Even so, David insists and does not listen to him.

For today: before making a decision, examine your motives. If a wise person questions you sincerely, listen to them, and do not place your security in your numbers or achievements, but in God.
exp.14:30:
Someone tells David that Ahithophel, his trusted counselor, is among those who have joined Absalom's rebellion. David answers with a short prayer: he asks the Lord (the name of God in the Old Testament) to turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness, that is, to make it senseless and useless.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. He goes weeping, with his head covered and barefoot, signs of mourning and humility. Ahithophel was known for giving very wise advice, so his betrayal was a heavy blow. David does not make a plan for revenge; first he prays. Shortly afterward Hushai appears, who will help counter that advice. The Bible does not say exactly how the prayer and Hushai's arrival are connected, but the account puts them together.

When a betrayal or a problem that overwhelms you comes, first bring your concern to God in a simple and sincere prayer, and then act with confidence that he can guide things.
exp.15:11:
This verse says that David hopes God will see his suffering, that is, his pain and humiliation. With the word "perhaps" he does not affirm with certainty, but leaves the door open to God's mercy. He hopes that God will give him something good in return for the curses he is receiving today.

David speaks while fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled against him. Along the way, Shimei, a man from the family of Saul, insults him and throws stones at him. Abishai wants to kill him, but David stops him. We do not know whether God really sent Shimei; David interprets it this way and responds with humility, without seeking revenge.

When someone offends us or life hurts us, we can avoid revenge and place our pain before God. He sees what we suffer, and we can wait on his goodness without demanding how or when he will respond.
exp.23:19:
This verse tells how Araunah, when he looked up, saw King David coming toward him with his servants. He went out to meet them and bowed down with his face to the ground. Bowing down to the earth was a sign of respect before someone in authority.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David went up to Araunah's threshing floor, Araunah being a Jebusite, because the prophet Gad had told him to build an altar there to the LORD. This happens after a plague had fallen on the people, and David was seeking to have the deadly sickness stopped. Araunah did not know why the king had come, and that is why he received the king with humility.

For today: when God guides us to do something, we can obey with humility, and also treat with respect and kindness those we meet along the way. Araunah honored David, and David would later honor God with an offering that truly cost him something.
exp.14:33:
Husai is told to go back to Jerusalem and present himself to Absalom as his new servant. Just as he served David before, he will now say that he will serve the new king. "Defeat" means to undo or make fail. "Ahithophel" is the counselor of Absalom.

David speaks with his friend Husai as he flees from Jerusalem, because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. David is climbing the mountain, worshiping God in the midst of his pain. Ahithophel, formerly David's counselor, has joined Absalom. David does not want Husai to come with him as a burden, but to help him from within, pretending loyalty to Absalom in order to frustrate Ahithophel's advice.

For today: in times of crisis, David prays, worships, and also acts wisely. We can trust God and, at the same time, take prudent steps, asking for help from faithful and honest people.
exp.4:0:
It says that all the tribes of Israel went to Hebron to meet with David. They said to him, "we are thy bone and thy flesh," a way of saying that they were part of the same family and people as him. Hebron was a city in Judah, where David was already reigning.

The speakers are the representatives of the northern tribes. Saul and his son had died, and David had been reigning alone over Judah for about seven years. Now they acknowledge his leadership, remembering that he had already led them in battle and that God had chosen him as shepherd of the people. For that reason they make a covenant with him and anoint him king.

For today: to recognize and respect those whom God has placed as guides, and to seek unity, especially when we go through times of change. Unity grows when we remember that we are one people under God.
exp.1:14:
Then twelve men from the tribe of Benjamin stood up on the side of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, and twelve of David's servants. They were two equal groups, ready to face each other. "Went over" means they moved forward toward the middle, between the two sides.

The narrator describes the moment after Abner, commander of Ish-bosheth's army, proposed to Joab, David's commander, that some young men should "play" a contest, meaning they should stage a kind of combat. Israel was divided: some followed the house of Saul and others followed David. What seemed like a game ended in a slaughter, and the text does not say that God commanded it.

Today, this account warns us that pride and division turn a "test of strength" into tragedy. Before accepting a challenge or an argument, it is wise to ask where it may lead us and to seek peace.
exp.2:25:
He says that Joab left David's presence and, on his own, sent messengers after Abner. They caught up with him at the well of Sirah and brought him back. David knew nothing about it. "Without David knowing it" means the king gave no permission and did not know what was happening.

Joab was the commander of David's army. Abner, formerly commander of Saul's army, had come to make a peace agreement with David, and David let him go in peace. Joab, who wanted to avenge the death of his brother Asahel, accused Abner of spying and acted in secret. His plan ended in murder.

For today: when we feel resentment, it is easy to justify decisions made in secret. If we cannot do something openly, or with the knowledge of those who lead us, it is better to place it in God's hands before we act.
exp.21:34:
It is God who trains David for war. "Teaches my hands" means that he gives him skill in fighting. "Gives me strength so that my arms break a bow of steel" speaks of a power greater than natural strength. Some versions translate "bronze" or "copper" instead of "steel," because the exact metal of the Hebrew is understood in several ways. In any case, it was a very hard bow to bend.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and recognizes that his victories were not due to his skill alone. Everything he knew how to do and the strength he had came from God.

For today: what you can do in your work, your family, or your studies is also a gift. Thank God for your abilities and ask him to help you use them with humility and to face your struggles with confidence in him.
exp.16:10:
This verse says that Hushai advises Absalom to gather all Israel, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, an army as numerous as the sand. He also asks that Absalom himself go out to battle. The word "counsel" in the verse corresponds to "recommend" in the source, and "by the sea" corresponds to "by the shore of the sea."

Hushai, David's friend, speaks before Absalom and his advisers during the rebellion. Ahithophel had proposed attacking David at once. Hushai, who had presented himself as loyal to Absalom, seeks to gain time so that David can organize. His counsel appeals to Absalom's pride. The Bible later shows that the Lord allowed this advice to be accepted (2 Samuel 17:14).

For today: a piece of advice can sound very convincing and still have a hidden purpose. Before deciding, let us ask God for wisdom, examine the motives of the one advising us, and take care that our pride does not make us listen only to what flatters us.
exp.2:3:
This verse continues the list of the sons born to David in Hebron. Here appear the fourth, Adonijah, son of Haggith, and the fifth, Shephatiah, son of Abital. The names of the mothers are given because David had several wives, and each son is identified by his mother.
