The author of the book recounts, as in a family record, what happened while David reigned alone over Judah, in Hebron. Meanwhile, the house of Saul and the house of David were at war. This list shows that David's family was growing and becoming stronger. It also reveals that having many wives would bring conflicts, as the Bible tells later on. Adonijah, for example, later tried to make himself king.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to names that seem unimportant. Care for your home with prayer and wisdom, because the decisions you make today affect the family for years.
exp.17:32:
This verse says that King David, on learning that his son Absalom had died, was filled with grief. He went up to the room over the gate of the city and wept. He kept calling out his son's name and wished he had died in his place. "Was much moved" means that he was deeply stirred and shaken within. "Chamber over the gate" was a room above the entrance of the city.

Here David speaks. Absalom had rebelled against him and tried to take away his kingdom. Joab and the soldiers defeated the rebellion, and Absalom died in the battle. Cushi brought the news as a victory, but David only asked about his son. His response shows a father's love that remains in place despite the betrayal.

For today: grief over someone we love, even if they hurt us, is real and should not be hidden. Bring it honestly to God, and ask him to give you comfort and mercy.
exp.21:38:
This verse says that David finished off his enemies completely: he "consumed" them (destroyed them entirely), he "wounded" them, and they could no longer rise. The phrase about being fallen under his feet is an image of total victory, like someone who treads on the defeated.

It is David the king speaking, in a song of gratitude to God, written when the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He does not claim the victory for himself: in the verses that follow he says that God clothed him with strength and gave him the triumph. The language of war was typical of his time and of his role as king of Israel.

For today: we do not use this verse against people, but to trust that God gives us strength in the struggles, sin, and fear we face. In the face of whatever threatens you now, ask God to sustain you, and thank him afterward.
exp.12:19:
Absalom asks Tamar whether Amnon was with her, meaning whether he abused her. He tells her to keep quiet, that he is her brother, and not to take this so much to heart.

Absalom, Tamar's brother, is the one speaking. She has just been violated by her half-brother Amnon and sent away with contempt, and she left weeping with the signs of mourning. Absalom seems to want to handle the matter in silence. Later it becomes clear that he did not forget it: he kept hatred against Amnon. The Bible does not explain in detail his reasons for telling her to be quiet.

For today: when someone suffers abuse, they should be listened to, believed, and accompanied, not asked to keep quiet. Silence protects the guilty and leaves the victim more wounded. God is near to those who are broken in heart.
exp.22:33:
This verse names two more of David's warriors. Eliphelet was the son of Ahasbai, and his family came from Maacah, a small region north of Israel. Eliam was the son of Ahithophel, from the town of Giloh (also called Gilo), in the hill country of Judah.

The narrator of the book lists the brave men who accompanied David. They came from different places, and some had foreign origins. Ahithophel, Eliam's father, was David's counselor and later joined Absalom's rebellion. Some think this Eliam is the same one who appears in 2 Samuel 11:3, but this is not certain.

God uses people from all kinds of families and places to carry out his work. Even if no one remembers them, their names matter. Today you can serve faithfully where you are, without seeking applause. God sees and remembers your work.
exp.22:34:
This verse mentions two more of David's brave warriors: Hesrai, who was from the area of Carmel, and Pharai, who was from Arbi. In the Reina-Valera 1909 the names appear with a different spelling; today many write Hezrai and Paarai. They are places in the territory of Judah.

The text is not a speech but a list that forms part of the end of the book. Here the "thirty" warriors who accompanied and defended David are named. About these two men we know nothing more from this chapter: only their names and their origin. Some scholars think the list honors their loyalty, although the text gives no further details.

God notices those who serve faithfully, even when almost no one remembers their story. If your work goes unnoticed in your family, your church, or your job, keep going with perseverance. What is done faithfully is not lost before God.
exp.21:4:
It says that David felt surrounded by deadly dangers, like waves that rise up and give no way of escape. The phrase "torrents of wickedness" refers to floods of evil or of wicked people. The word "made me afraid" here means that they terrified him or filled him with fear. Some translations say "torrents of destruction" or "of Belial," and the sense is similar.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving to God, which the text places at the time when the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and remembers how close he came to death. He does not hide his fear, and he tells it to show that God rescued him.

Today, when you feel that problems are sweeping you away like a current, do not pretend you have no fear. Tell God honestly, as David did, and cry out to Him. Then, when the trial has passed, remember with gratitude how He held you up.
exp.23:9:
David felt remorse after receiving the result of the count. "His heart struck him" means his conscience hit him, like a thorn. Then he acknowledged before God that he had sinned greatly, asked him to take away his guilt, and called himself a fool, meaning someone who acted without wisdom.

David speaks with God after Joab handed him the count of the people. The text does not explain here in detail why the census was a sin. The chapter begins by saying that God had been angry with Israel, and Joab had tried to stop David. Many think David trusted in the power of his army more than in God, but the passage does not say this clearly.

When our conscience troubles us, we should not silence it or make excuses. We can be honest with God, say "I have done very foolishly," and ask for his forgiveness. He welcomes whoever humbles themselves sincerely.
exp.6:9:
God promises that he will give Israel a secure place. He says he will "plant" them, like someone who plants a tree so that it takes root and cannot be pulled up. The "wicked" are the evil people, and "afflict" means to make them suffer. He promises that there will no longer be oppression as there was in the past.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan and gives a message to David. David wanted to build a temple, but God answers by reminding him of what he has already done for him: he took him from tending sheep and made him king. He then promises peace for the people and a lasting house for David. Some believe this promise was partly fulfilled in Solomon and also points to Jesus, a descendant of David.

God is the one who gives stability and rest. When you feel that your life is unsteady, remember that he can plant you and give you roots. Trust in his faithfulness and seek to put down roots in him each day.
exp.2:38:
Here David says that he is still a "tender" king, that is, weak or newly placed in the office, though he has already been anointed. He recognizes that the sons of Zeruiah, Joab and Abishai, are too hard for him, that is, hard to control. For that reason he does not carry out justice himself, but asks the Lord to repay the doer of evil according to his wickedness.

David speaks after Joab killed Abner treacherously. Abner was going to help him unite all Israel under his reign. David wants to make clear that he did not order that death, and he shows this through public mourning. Some think he also admits that he did not have enough strength to punish Joab at that time.

For today: when you come across an injustice that you cannot correct, do not fold your arms or take revenge. Act with honesty, do what is within your reach, and leave the rest to God, who judges with justice.
exp.15:9:
David answers Abishai, who wanted to kill Shimei for cursing the king. "Sons of Zeruiah" refers to Abishai and his brother Joab. The words "What have I to do with you?" mean something like "we don't agree, don't pressure me." David says that Shimei curses because God allows it, and that no one can call him to account.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled. On the way, Shimei, a man from the family of Saul, curses him and accuses him of being violent. David does not know whether there is any truth in the accusation, and he decides not to take revenge. Commentators debate whether God really "commanded" Shimei or whether David only recognizes that God permits it.

For today: when you are criticized or treated badly, before responding in anger, stop and ask yourself whether God wants to teach you something. Trusting God helps us respond with humility.
exp.19:9:
This verse tells us that Amasa did not pay attention to the sword that Joab held in his hand. Joab struck him in the belly (the "fifth rib" refers to the area of the stomach), and Amasa died right there. Afterward, Joab and his brother Abishai continued pursuing Sheba, the son of Bichri. The "bowels" are the internal organs.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David had appointed Amasa as commander of the army in place of Joab, and Sheba had led a rebellion. Joab, perhaps moved by jealousy and ambition, greeted Amasa as a friend and killed him by treachery. The Bible recounts the event without approving of it.

For today: violence disguised as affection is deception. Let us guard our hearts so that we do not hide resentment behind kind words, and let us seek peace with sincerity.
exp.15:15:
This verse says that Hushai, David's friend, came before Absalom and cried out, "God save the king, God save the king." The word "came to pass" means "happened," and "Archite" indicates that he was from a clan called the Archites. Hushai greets Absalom as king, although he was David's friend.

Context: Absalom had rebelled against his father David, who fled from Jerusalem. David had asked Hushai to return and frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel (2 Samuel 15:32-34). That is why Hushai speaks in words that Absalom takes as loyalty, but which can carry a double meaning. Scholars debate how much of this was cunning and how much a careful response.

For today: when you have to act in confusing situations, ask God for wisdom and prudence, and be faithful to what is right, even when you cannot say everything.
exp.6:11:
When David dies (the phrase "he will sleep with his fathers" is an old way of speaking of death), God will raise up one of his descendants. The word "seed" means offspring, and "from your own body" means that this will be a son of his own. God promises that he "will establish his kingdom," that is, he will make it firm and secure.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple for God, but God answers that he himself will make David a "house," meaning a dynasty. The promise was first fulfilled in Solomon, and many Christians see its full fulfillment in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: God keeps his promises even when we do not see the result. David would not see everything that was promised, but he trusted. We can do the same and trust that God continues to work beyond our lives.
exp.15:18:
Husai says: "Whom should I serve? Should I not serve the son of the king? As I have served your father, so will I be in your presence." Here "should I serve" means "ought I to serve." Husai implies that his loyalty is to the king's family.

Husai is speaking with Absalom, who rebelled against his father David and took Jerusalem. Earlier, David had asked Husai, his friend, to return to the city and pretend to support Absalom in order to frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel (2 Samuel 15:32-37). For this reason his words are clever and have a double meaning. The text does not comment on whether that was right, so it is best not to claim more than it says.

For today: loyalty and wisdom matter, but not everything is what it seems. Ask God for discernment to act with integrity in complicated situations.
exp.4:4:
This verse sums up how long David ruled. First he reigned seven years and six months in Hebron, and over the tribe of Judah only. Then he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem, already over all Israel and Judah. Together they add up to the forty years of the verse before. The name Jerusalem refers to the city of Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book gives a brief summary before telling of the capture of Jerusalem. The elders of Israel had just anointed David as king in Hebron. This closed a time of division and began a united kingdom. The text shows that this process was long and not immediate.

For today: God keeps his promises, but often with patience. David waited years before reigning over the whole people. If you are waiting for something from God today, be faithful in the place where you are now, as David was in Hebron.
exp.12:0:
This verse introduces three sons of David. Absalom has a very beautiful sister named Tamar, and Amnon, another son of David, became infatuated with her. Here the word "loved" sounds like affection, but what follows in the account shows that it was a selfish and harmful desire. Tamar and Absalom were full brother and sister, both children of the same mother and father; Amnon was a half-brother to both, from a different mother.

This is the beginning of a very painful episode. The narrator is the author of the book of Samuel, who recounts without embellishment the troubles within David's family. This happens after David sinned with Bathsheba, and many readers see a connection with the consequences God had announced for his household, although the text does not say so directly here.

Today it reminds us that not every strong feeling is true love. It is wise to examine our desires in the light of God and set boundaries in time, before they hurt others.
exp.17:2:
Here the men of David tell him not to go with them into the battle. "You shall not go out" means "you will not go." "We flee" means "let us flee." "They will not care for us" means that the enemy would not be concerned about them. They say David is worth about ten thousand soldiers, and they ask him instead to support them from the city.

David is fleeing from his son Absalom, who rebelled against him. He has organized his army into three groups and wants to go with them. The people speak out of love and out of reason: if the king is killed, everything is lost. David accepts their advice and stays at the gate.

For today: sometimes loving means accepting the advice of wise people who care for us, even when we want to do everything ourselves. Knowing how to listen is a form of humility and wisdom.
exp.2:30:
Here David orders Joab and all the people who were with him to tear their clothes, put on rough mourning clothes, and weep openly before Abner's body. The "sackcloth" is the coarse cloth worn as a sign of grief. The "bier" is the stretcher or coffin on which the dead man was carried. David himself walked behind it, showing respect.

David speaks as king of Judah. Abner, commander of Saul's army, had come to offer him peace, and Joab killed him out of revenge. By having Joab take part in the mourning, David makes it clear before all the people that he did not agree with that crime. Many understand that he also wanted to prevent further division and violence in the nation.

For today: when there is injustice, silence is not enough. We must reject evil clearly and humbly, and seek peace and truth without letting ourselves be carried away by revenge.
exp.16:27:
This verse lists what three men brought to David and his people: beds, bowls, clay vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched corn, beans, lentils, and parched pulse. The word "basons" refers to bowls for drinking, and "parched corn" was grain ready to eat without much cooking. The phrase "brought beds" simply means they brought beds to David.

The speaker here is not a character but the narrator of the book. David was fleeing his son Absalom, who had rebelled, and he arrived weary at Mahanaim. There Shobi, Machir, and Barzilai, three men of good standing, brought him provisions. The next verse explains why: they knew the people were hungry, tired, and thirsty.

For today: concrete help is a form of love. Notice who is going through a hard time and offer something practical, such as food, rest, or company, without waiting to be asked.
exp.5:22:
This verse says that Michal, the daughter of King Saul, never had children, and that this lasted until the day she died. The name appears here as "Michal" in the KJV, and the verse below refers to her by that name.

Here the narrator closes the scene of 2 Samuel 6. Michal had scornfully criticized David because he danced with joy before God when the ark was brought to Jerusalem. David answered that he was doing it for the Lord. The text does not explain the reason she had no children. Some think it was a punishment from God for her attitude; others say the fact is simply recorded, perhaps because of the distance between her and David. There is no certainty.

For today: let us guard our hearts so that we do not despise the sincere worship of others. A proud or critical attitude can draw us away from joy and from the relationships God wants to give us.
exp.4:11:
David realized something important: God himself had established him as king over Israel. The idea of being established means that God had firmly set him in his place. God had also raised up his kingdom, and David understood that this was not only for his own sake, but for the sake of his people Israel.

Here the narrator of the book is telling us what David came to understand. David had just conquered Jerusalem and was growing in power. Hiram, king of Tyre, sent him materials and workers to build his house. The text stresses that all this success came from God, not only from David's own effort.

For today: if God gives you a place of influence, at work, in your family, or in your church, remember that it is not meant only for your own benefit. Ask him to help you use it to serve and bless others.
exp.2:37:
Here David speaks to his servants about the death of Abner. He asks them whether they do not realize that a man of importance and great worth had fallen that day in Israel. The word "prince" here means a leader or chief, and "fallen" in this verse means that he died.

David is the one speaking. Abner, commander of Saul's army, had come to help him unite the tribes under his reign, but Joab, commander of David's army, killed him out of revenge. David grieves publicly and wants everyone to know that he had no part in that crime. The people understood it this way. Moreover, David acknowledges that his power is still fragile and that Joab and his brother are hard to control.

For today: let us learn to recognize the worth of people and to lament injustice, even when it is uncomfortable. Also, when something wrong happens near us, let us act with honesty and allow God to be the final judge.
exp.20:17:
And it came to pass after this that there was another battle with the Philistines at Gob. There, a warrior of David named Sibbechai, from the Hushathite clan, struck down Saph, one of the descendants of the giants. Here "struck down" means that he killed him. Some translate "giants" as "Rephaim," a people of great stature.

The narrator of the book recounts several wars against the Philistines at the end of David's reign. After David nearly died at the hands of another giant, his men protect him and point out that other brave men were also fighting. The account shows that the victory did not depend on a single hero.

Today we can learn that God often carries out his work through a team. Some people are not very well known, like Sibbechai, but their faithfulness matters. Serve wherever you are, without waiting for applause, and rejoice when others also contribute.
exp.23:0:
It says the anger of God was kindled again against Israel, and that David was moved to give an order: to count the people of Israel and Judah.

The narrator of 2 Samuel introduces the start of a difficult episode. He does not explain here why God was angry. The text does not fully clarify who moved David: this passage attributes it to God, while 1 Chronicles 21:1 mentions Satan. Scholars explain this in several ways. Joab, the general, is surprised by the order and asks why the king wants it.

Today we can ask ourselves what lies behind our plans. Counting can be normal, but doing it to trust in our numbers and not in God is dangerous. Let us ask for a humble heart that rests in Him.
exp.19:14:
They came and laid siege to Seba in Abel of Beth-maacah, where he had taken refuge. They surrounded the city, built a ramp of earth up against the wall (this is the "rampart"), and all the soldiers working alongside the wall were trying to pull it down. "Besieged" means surrounded.

The narrator tells how Joab pursued Seba, who had started a revolt against David. Seba fled through the tribes of Israel and shut himself up in this city. Joab wanted to end the uprising quickly. What follows shows that a wise woman intervened before the city was destroyed.

When there is conflict, force may seem like the only way forward, but sometimes a calm and wise voice prevents greater harm. Before acting harshly, it is good to stop, listen, and look for a solution that preserves life and peace.
exp.4:2:
This verse tells how the leaders of Israel went to see David in Hebron. There David made an agreement with them, in the presence of God, and they anointed him as king over all Israel. The "elders" are the heads and representatives of the tribes. A "covenant" is a formal commitment between both parties. "Anointed" means they poured oil on his head, a sign that he was set apart to rule.

The one acting here is the people, through their leaders. After Saul's death, David already reigned alone over Judah. Now the other tribes recognize that he is one of their own, that he had already led them in battle, and that God had chosen him to shepherd his people.

For today: whoever leads should take up their role with clear commitments and with humility before God, knowing that their authority is a service and not a privilege.
exp.13:14:
She says that the woman came to speak with the king because the people had made her afraid. With "the people have made me afraid" she refers to the threat from her relatives, who wanted to take away her son. She tells that she was encouraged to speak, thinking: "It may be that the king will perform the request of his handmaid." "Handmaid" is a humble way of calling herself before the king.

The one speaking is the woman of Tekoa, sent by Joab. She tells a made-up story about her son in order to move David's heart and lead him to think about his son Absalom, who was banished. Many understand that the whole thing was a strategy. Here she explains her courage in coming before the king.

For today: when something frightens us, we can take a step of courage and speak with humility. It is also good to ask for wisdom to tell the truth honestly and not with deception.
exp.23:20:
Araunah asks King David why he has come to visit his servant. David answers plainly: he wants to buy the threshing floor, that is, the flat place where grain was beaten out, in order to build an altar to the Lord there. His purpose is that the plague, the death that was killing the people, may be stopped.

David had sinned by taking a census of the people, and God sent a plague upon Israel. The prophet Gad told him to set up an altar on Araunah's threshing floor. Araunah, a respectful and generous man, is surprised to see the king arrive, and David explains his reason with sincerity.

For today: when we recognize our wrongs, it is good to respond with humility and concrete action. David does not stop at repentance; he seeks to worship God and to help others, and he is willing to pay a price for it.
exp.20:10:
This verse says that David was told what Rizpah was doing. She was the daughter of Aiah, and she had been a woman of Saul's household. "Was told" in the verse means "was informed." A "concubine" was a woman who lived with a man as a secondary wife, which was common in that time.

The narrator tells that there was a famine in Israel and that David sought God. Then seven of Saul's descendants were handed over to the Gibeonites and hanged. Rizpah, who had lost two sons among them, watched over the bodies for months and kept away the birds and the wild animals. When David was told about it, he wanted to honor the dead, and he also buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan.

For today: faithful, steady love does not go unnoticed. Caring tenderly for those who suffer, even when no one else does, can move other hearts to act with compassion.
exp.22:35:
This verse names two more warriors from David's list of mighty men. Igal was the son of Nathan and came from Zobah, a region to the north of Israel. Bani was from Gad, one of the tribes. Notice that some of these heroes came from different places, and even from outside Israel.

The author of the book records here the elite men who accompanied David, known as the thirty. It is a kind of honor roll at the end of David's reign. About Igal, other ancient versions of the text give a slightly different name, and it cannot be known for certain which is the original.

God takes note of people whom almost no one remembers. Though only their names remain of these men, their faithfulness was written down. Serve wherever you are, without seeking applause; what you do with steadiness and loyalty does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.23:10:
This verse says that in the morning, after David had already confessed his sin, God spoke to the prophet Gad.

The narrator is speaking here. David had ordered the people to be counted, and his conscience accused him. He had asked for forgiveness, yet God still sent Gad with a message about the consequences. Some think David trusted in his military strength instead of trusting in God, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: when we fail, God forgives us if we repent from the heart, but sometimes he allows us to face the consequences. We can accept them with humility, trusting that his mercy remains with us.
exp.16:3:
This verse says that the plan Ahitofel had just proposed pleased Absalom and all the leaders of Israel. The word "elders" refers to the respected heads and authorities of the people. "Saying" here means the proposal or advice.

Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David, and Ahitofel was a highly respected counselor who was now supporting him. His plan was to attack David at night, when he would be exhausted, and to kill only him. Although everyone agreed, Absalom also wanted to hear Hushai, who in reality was loyal to David. In this way God was going to frustrate the counsel of Ahitofel.

That something seems good to many does not mean it is right. Before following advice, it is wise to pray, to listen to other wise voices, and to ask ourselves whether it honors God.
exp.21:9:
It says that God bowed down the heavens and came down to the earth, and that thick darkness was under his feet. The word "bowed" is an older way of saying "bowed down," and the phrase is poetic: it describes God coming with great power, like a huge storm, to act on behalf of his servant.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. The images of trembling, smoke, fire, and dark clouds show that God is not distant: he intervenes. Many understand these images as poetic figures, not as a literal event that was seen in this way.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems, remember that God sees, draws near, and acts. Before asking for help, you can give thanks for the times he has already sustained you.
exp.5:15:
It says that when the ark of God was entering the city of David, Michal, the daughter of Saul, looked out through a window. She saw the king leaping with all his might before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "despised" means looking down on someone with scorn.

The narrator tells how the ark returns to Jerusalem amid celebration, trumpets and worship. David, wearing a linen ephod (a simple linen garment), joins in with joy. Michal was the daughter of Saul, the previous king, and her gaze from the window shows that she watches from a distance, without taking part. The text does not explain all her reasons; it only says that she despised him in her heart.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we look at the worship of others with criticism or whether we join in with humility. God looks at the heart, and sincere joy toward Him should not embarrass us.
exp.10:8:
Here it says that Uriah, instead of going home, spent the night at the entrance of the king's palace, alongside the guards and attendants of David. The phrase "lay at the door" means that he lay down at the entrance; "servants of his lord" refers to the king's officials; and "went down" means that he went off, or went, to his house.

David had sent for Uriah from the front line of battle. He had already slept with Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, and she was pregnant. David hoped that Uriah would go home and sleep with her, in order to cover up his sin. The narrator tells us that Uriah did not do this. Later he will explain that it did not seem right to him to enjoy comforts while the ark and his companions were in the field.

Today, Uriah's integrity challenges us not to seek comfort when others are suffering. It also reminds us that hiding a sin almost never works; the better course is to acknowledge it before God with sincerity.
exp.16:21:
This verse tells how David and all his people got up during the night and crossed the Jordan River before the sun rose. No one was left behind; everyone managed to get across. The phrase "by the morning light" refers to the time just before daybreak.

The account is narrated by the writer of Samuel. David was fleeing from his son Absalom, who had rebelled. Ahimaaz and Jonathan, hiding in a well, had warned him of the plan of Ahithophel, the counselor who wanted to attack him quickly. David acted on the warning without delay and crossed the river. In this way he gained time and moved away from danger.

For today: when God gives us a clear warning, it is wise to act promptly and not put off until tomorrow what we can do today. Also, let us take care of all who depend on us, so that no one is left behind.
exp.12:35:
This verse tells us that, as soon as the watchman finished speaking, the sons of King David arrived and wept aloud. David and all his servants also wept with great sorrow. The word "weeping" in the verse refers to strong expressions of grief, and "servants" means the people who served the king.

Amnon, David's son, had been killed on the orders of his brother Absalom, who did it to avenge their sister Tamar. At first a false report spread that all the king's sons had been killed. Jonadab, a cousin, calmed David by saying that only Amnon had died. When the sons arrived, the truth was confirmed and everyone wept. Absalom fled.

God allows us to weep when sin and violence break apart a family. If you are living through a wound like this, do not hide it: bring it honestly before God, seek comfort from trusted people, and ask for wisdom to act with justice and mercy.
exp.10:18:
Joab gives an order to the messenger he will send to David. He tells him that, once he has finished telling the king everything that happened in the battle, he must be ready for what comes next.

The one speaking is Joab, the commander of David's army. He was besieging the city of Rabbah. David had ordered him to place Uriah in a dangerous spot so that he would die, and Joab carried it out. Now Joab carefully prepares the report, thinking about how the king will react. The Bible shows a hidden plan here, and it does not approve of it: later the text says that what was done displeased the Lord.

For today: when someone arranges words to hide an injustice, the sin grows. It is better to speak with truth and not help cover up evil, even when it costs us.
exp.2:32:
Here David composes a lament for Abner and asks a question: "Did Abner die as a fool dies?" The word "lamenting" means singing or speaking a mourning song for the dead. "Fool" here refers to a foolish or wicked man, someone who dies because of his own guilt or as a criminal.

David speaks in public during Abner's funeral. Abner was the commander of Saul's army, and Joab had killed him treacherously in Hebron. David wants everyone to see that he took no part in that crime. For this reason he orders mourning, walks behind the coffin, and weeps. The verses that follow explain that Abner fell in an ambush, not through a fair trial.

Today, this passage invites us to reject violence and injustice, and to weep sincerely when someone suffers harm. It also encourages us to act with integrity, so that our actions and our grief show what is truly in the heart.
exp.16:12:
It says that, if David takes refuge in a walled city, all Israel will bring ropes and drag that city to the stream (or valley), until not one stone is left. Where the verse quoted the word for "appear," the rewrite is "seems better": the text says God allowed Husai's advice to seem better. This is an exaggeration meant to show an overwhelming force.

The speaker is Hushai, David's friend, who pretends to be an advisor to Absalom. His real purpose is to counter Ahithophel's plan, which called for attacking David at once. Hushai wants to buy time so that David can organize. The text says that God allowed his advice to seem better.

For today: sometimes words full of grandeur and confidence sound convincing, but they are not wise. Before following a piece of advice, it is good to ask whether it is true and whether it pleases God. And we can trust that He works even when we do not see how.
exp.23:12:
Gad comes before David and presents him with three possible punishments from God: seven years of famine, three months of fleeing from his enemies, or three days of plague in the land. Gad asks David to think carefully about his answer, since he must bring it back to God.

Gad is the prophet who served alongside David. He speaks on behalf of the LORD, after David had taken a census of the people, something his own conscience later rebuked him for as sin. The text does not detail all the reasons here, but it shows that the king's sin had consequences for the whole nation.

Today we can learn that our decisions affect others, and that when we fail, it is best to place ourselves in the hands of God, who is merciful, as David later acknowledged.
exp.14:23:
Zadok was also there, going along with David, together with the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant, which was the symbol of God's presence. They set the ark down on the ground. Abiathar, another priest, went up there while all the people finished leaving the city. The sentence about "set down" meaning they left it on the ground can stay as is, but "went up" is uncertain: some understand that Abiathar stood in a high place or presided, though the text does not fully clarify this.

The narrator tells of David's flight from Jerusalem because of the rebellion of his son Absalom. The priests want to accompany him and bring the ark, believing that this way God would be with the king. David will answer that the ark must return to the city.

Today we can learn that the presence of God is not controlled or carried along as a guarantee. In moments of crisis, let us trust in his will and leave the outcome to him, as David did.
exp.4:15:
This verse finishes a list of sons born to David in Jerusalem. Four more names appear here: Japhia, Elisama, Eliada, and Eliphelet. They are all men's names, and the list continues the one begun in the previous verse, with Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon.

The account is by the author of the book, who is not identified. It tells how David, now king over all Israel, settled in Jerusalem. The list shows that his reign was becoming established and that his family was growing. It has also been noted that, in that period, having many wives was common among kings, though the Bible does not present this as an ideal. Immediately after, the attacks of the Philistines follow.

For today: God pays attention to people, even to those who are hardly mentioned. Remember that your life and your name matter to Him, and serve faithfully even when no one applauds you.
exp.20:19:
It says there was another battle against the Philistines in the city of Gath. There was a very tall man there, with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. He was also a descendant of the "giant," which here probably refers to a family or race of men of great stature.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who is not identified with certainty. He is summarizing the last wars of David's reign against the Philistines. The next verse tells that this man challenged Israel, and Jonathan, David's nephew, killed him. The passage shows that the fearsome enemies fell before David and his servants.

For today: problems that seem enormous are not bigger than God. David did not fight alone; his team also had a part. Face your "giants" by trusting in God and leaning on other believers.
exp.5:14:
This verse tells how David and all the people of Israel brought up the ark of the Lord to Jerusalem, with shouts of joy and the blast of the trumpet. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence with his people. The shouting, meaning very great joy expressed aloud, is what the verse describes.

It is the narrator of the book who describes the scene. Before this, the ark had been far from the center of Israel's life for many years, and an earlier attempt to bring it up ended badly, with the death of Uzzah. Now David moves it with sacrifices and reverence. Soon after, Michal despises him for the way he celebrates, which shows that not everyone understood that joy.

For today: worshiping God can include sincere and visible joy. We do not need to measure our worship by what others think, but offer it with a grateful and reverent heart.
exp.2:22:
This verse tells how Joab returned with his army and, when he arrived, was informed that Abner, the son of Ner, had visited King David. He was told that David had sent Abner away and that Abner had gone "in peace," that is, without being held or harmed. The phrase "was given word" means that someone let him know.

The one speaking here is the narrator, who reports the news that Joab receives. Abner had been commander of Saul's army and came to make an agreement with David to unite Israel under his rule. Joab, David's general, was not present when everything happened. The text that follows shows that Joab distrusted Abner and confronted David for having let him go.

For today: when we do not know the whole story, it is easy to react with suspicion or anger. Before judging, it is wise to listen, seek the truth, and seek peace.
exp.16:23:
This verse tells of two movements at the same time. David arrives at Mahanaim, a city east of the Jordan, and there he finds a place to take refuge. Absalom, his son, also crosses the Jordan, but with the whole army of Israel to pursue him.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, without speaking in the first person. David flees because Absalom rebelled and wanted to take the throne from him. A counselor of David, Hushai, had given Absalom a plan that gave David time to escape. That is why David arrived safely.

For today: when you feel pursued or surrounded by problems, remember that God can give you a refuge and time to catch your breath, even when everything seems against you. Trust, and seek that safe place.
exp.22:25:
This verse continues the list of David's mighty warriors. It names Helez the Paltite (or "Paltite") and Ira, son of Ikkesh the Tekoite. Tekoa was a town in Judah, south of Bethlehem. The names appear with almost no details.

The author of the book records the final events of David's reign and honors his "thirty" trusted men. Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator. Each one is named because his loyalty helped David and Israel. No deed is told of Helez or Ira; the Bible gives no further information, and it is not right to invent any.

For today: God sees and remembers those who serve without anyone applauding them. If your work is quiet, do it faithfully. Your name may be little known among people, but God knows it.
exp.18:5:
Joab speaks harshly to King David. He tells him that he is loving those who hate him (Absalom, who rebelled) and hating those who love him (his loyal servants).

Joab, the commander of the army, speaks after the victory over Absalom's rebellion. The army returned in shame, as if it had done something wrong, because the king kept weeping over his dead son. Joab fears that the people will lose heart and abandon David. His words are harsh, but the text shows that David listened to them and went out.

For today: grief is real and deserves to be mourned, but we should not forget those beside us who need us. Even in sorrow, let us give them gratitude and attention.
exp.18:33:
Barzillai answers the king with a question: "How long do I have left to live, that I should go up with you to Jerusalem?" He writes "Jerusalem" in the older spelling, and "go up" because Jerusalem sits on high ground. With this he means that he has little time left and that the journey is not worth making.

Barzillai, a wealthy man of eighty years, had supplied David with food in Mahanaim during his flight. David, grateful, offers to let him live with him at court. Barzillai, humbly, turns down the honor and acknowledges his limits because of his age.

For today: know how to be thankful for what you receive, but also to recognize with humility your seasons and your limits. Not every honor must be accepted; sometimes serving well and stepping aside is the wisest course.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that King Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, daughter of Aiah. Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, confronts Abner: "Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?" A concubine was a secondary wife, and "going in to her" means having relations with her.

Ish-bosheth, who ruled over Israel with Abner's support, was speaking, and Abner was the commander of his army. At that time, taking the wives of the previous king was seen as a claim to the throne. Ish-bosheth suspects that Abner wants power. The Bible does not say whether the accusation was true, and Abner becomes angry and does not respond directly to it.

For today: before accusing someone, let us look for evidence and speak with respect. An accusation made lightly can break a relationship of trust and bring serious consequences, as happened here.
exp.7:14:
This verse says that David was king over all the tribes of Israel and that he acted with righteousness and justice toward all his people. "Judgment" refers to applying the laws correctly, and "justice" to treating each person fairly.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, summarizing David's reign after recounting his military victories. Just before this, it says that the LORD preserved him wherever he went. Then his chief officials are listed. In this way, the text shows that his kingdom had not only strength but also order and good government. Even so, the book will later show that David also failed.

For today: if you have some authority, whether in your home, your work, or your church, try to treat everyone with fairness, without favoritism. Ask God to help you be just and honest in everyday life.
exp.16:16:
It says that Jonathan and Ahimaaz, the sons of the priests, were waiting by the spring of Rogel. They could not go into the city without being seen. So a servant girl would carry the messages to them, and they would go and report to King David. The verse "told" them, and "went and told" King David, so the reports were passed along in that way.

David was fleeing from his son Absalom, who had rebelled. Hushai, David's friend, had given advice to buy time, and he wanted David to know the danger quickly. The priests Zadok and Abiathar could not leave without drawing attention, so they used their sons and a girl as secret messengers. The Bible does not give her name.

God can use ordinary people who go unnoticed to carry out an important role. Today, a timely message, a prayer, or a quiet act of service can help others a great deal. Let us faithfully do what is ours to do.
exp.12:29:
This verse tells that, while the king's sons were still fleeing along the road, a false report reached David: that Absalom had killed all his sons and that not one of them was left.

The narrator describes what happened after Absalom had Amnon killed at a feast, a deed he ordered as an act of revenge. In the panic, people brought David an exaggerated account. Later, Jonadab makes clear that only Amnon had died. The cause went back years earlier: Amnon had abused Tamar, Absalom's sister.

For today: when we receive bad news, it is wise to pause and confirm the facts before reacting. Fear tends to make things seem larger than they are. We can bring our distress to God and ask him for calm so that we may act with wisdom.
exp.15:22:
In those days, the counsel of Ahithophel was held in such high regard that it was as if someone had asked God directly. Ahithophel's name appears here in its KJV form, and the phrase "inquire of God" means to ask God for an answer. This was true both when he advised David and when he advised Absalom.

The narrator of the book makes this comment right after Ahithophel's terrible advice. Absalom had rebelled against his father David, and Ahithophel, who had formerly advised the king, switched sides to the son's cause. His counsel was highly respected, but here it was used for evil and to shame David publicly.

For today: a person can be very wise and have great standing, but that does not guarantee that their advice is right. Before following any advice, let us compare it with the Word of God, and ask God to give us wisdom with humility and a good heart.
exp.18:13:
This verse says that the hearts of all the men of Judah were turned, all together and as one person, toward David. Then they sent him a message: "Return, you and all your servants." The verse's word "bowed" means that something moved them to change their attitude, and "servants" refers to his followers.

David, already king, had fled from Jerusalem when his son Absalom rebelled, and Absalom died. Now the people hesitated to bring him back. David sent messengers to the elders of Judah, reminding them that they were his own family, and offered Amasa, Absalom's former commander, the command of the army. The text says that something "bowed" the hearts, and it does not make clear whether this refers to David, to his message, or to God at work.

Today, after a conflict, humility and kind words can open the way to reconciliation. We can take the first step, even when others hesitate.
exp.8:4:
This verse says that King David sent people to fetch Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, and he was brought out of the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, from Lo-debar. The word "fetched" means "he took him," that is, he had him brought. Lo-debar was a remote place, and the text gives no further details about it.

The one acting here is the narrator, telling what David does. Shortly before, David had asked whether anyone was left of Saul's house to whom he could show kindness. He was doing this because of the covenant of friendship he had made with Jonathan. Ziba, a servant from Saul's household, told him about this son who was lame in his feet, and David did not stop at words: he sent for him.

For today: true kindness moves and seeks people out. God sought us out when we were far away. We can think of someone who has been forgotten, alone or cut off, and do something concrete for them this week, such as a visit or a phone call.
exp.20:21:
This verse closes the account of the battles against the descendants of the Philistine giants. It says that four enormous warriors, born to a giant from Gath, died at the hands of David and his servants, that is, his soldiers. The word "giant" here stands for a term that can also be a family or clan name.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who summarizes Israel's wars against the Philistines in the last years of David's reign. Earlier, it is told how Jonathan killed a man who had twelve fingers on his hands and twelve toes on his feet. It is not known with certainty who the "giant" was or how these four are related to him. What is clear is that the victory came through the effort of the whole group.

For today: great challenges are rarely overcome alone. God often works through the unity of his people. Value the work of others and serve alongside them.
exp.1:26:
Joab swears by God: "As God liveth." He says that if Abner had not spoken, his men would have kept pursuing their Israelite brothers from the morning on. The words are difficult, and they can be understood in two ways: that the fight would have ended sooner if Abner had not stirred up the battle, or that the pursuit would have continued until the next day.

Joab, the commander of David's army, is speaking. Abner, the commander of Saul's army, has just asked him to stop the pursuit and prevent more deaths among brothers. Joab answers firmly, but he agrees to stop and blows the trumpet.

For today: when a conflict harms people who should be united, it is wise to stop in time. You do not need to win the argument; sometimes the bravest thing is to seek peace before bitterness grows.
exp.11:14:
This verse tells that Nathan the prophet went back to his house after delivering God's message. Then the Lord struck the child, that is, made him fall sick, and the baby became very ill. The verse says the child was born to Uriah's wife, who is Bathsheba.

Nathan had just confronted David about his adultery with Bathsheba and about having Uriah killed. David acknowledged his sin and God forgave him, but the consequences followed. Interpreters explain in different ways why the child died; the Bible does not go into more detail beyond what it says here.

For today: God truly forgives when we repent, but some consequences of our decisions can remain. This invites us to take sin seriously, to come to God quickly with humility, and to trust in his mercy even in pain.
exp.8:1:
It says there was a servant from Saul's family named Ziba. He was called to appear before David, and the king asked him if he was Ziba. Ziba answered, "Thy servant is he," a humble way of saying "at your service."

David has just asked whether anyone is left from the house of Saul to show kindness to, remembering his promise of friendship with Jonathan. Since Saul had been his enemy, searching for his descendants was not the usual thing to do in that time. Ziba, who knew that family well, will be the one to give him the lead about Mephibosheth.

Today: David's kindness grew out of a fulfilled promise. Think of someone to whom you owe gratitude or a word you gave, and look today for a concrete way to show them care, even if a long time has passed.
exp.23:8:
This verse says that Joab, the commander of the army, handed King David the result of the census. Israel had eight hundred thousand strong men, ready to fight with the sword, and Judah had five hundred thousand. Gave up the sum means that he reported the total. Drew the sword means that they were soldiers.

The narrator tells us that David ordered this census, and Joab, though he questioned it, carried out the order. The text then shows that David felt guilty and acknowledged his sin. The Bible does not explain this in detail, but it seems that David trusted the size of his army more than God. The figures in 1 Chronicles 21 are different, and scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, strength, or plans. Trust God first, and if you fail, confess with humility as David did.
exp.17:12:
This soldier tells Joab that if he had killed Absalom in secret, he would have put his own life at risk. He thinks King David would find out about everything, because nothing is hidden from the king. He adds that Joab himself would not defend him but would turn against him. Doing something that would cost him his life is what he means by acting against his own life.

A man from David's army is speaking. Joab, the military commander, reproaches him for not having killed Absalom, who was caught in a tree. The soldier defends himself: he heard the king's command not to harm the young man. Joab disregarded that command shortly afterward.

For today: doing what is right does not always feel easy, but it gives firmness. This soldier acted with integrity, even though others pressed him. Before acting, ask yourself whether your decision would hold up in the light, for nothing is hidden from God.
exp.16:20:
It says that when Absalom's servants had left, Ahimaaz and Jonathan climbed out of the well where they had been hiding. They went at once to tell King David. They urged him to get up and cross the river quickly, because Ahithophel had advised an attack on him.

The writer then explains how David was saved. Absalom had rebelled, and David was fleeing. Ahimaaz and Jonathan were David's secret messengers. A woman hid them in a well and tricked the pursuers. Now they carry out their mission of warning the king.

Today we can learn that God often takes care of his people through ordinary people who act with courage and speed. If God puts it on your heart to help or warn someone, do it promptly, and trust that he can use your small obedience.
exp.18:31:
This verse says that Barzillai was an old man, eighty years old. He had supplied King David with food and necessities while David stayed in Mahanaim. He was able to do this because he was very wealthy. The word "provided" in the verse means food and the things needed to live.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David was fleeing from his son Absalom, and Barzillai had helped him in that difficult time. Now the king returns to Jerusalem after the rebellion, and Barzillai accompanies him as far as the Jordan. This detail explains why David wants to honor him and offers him a place to live at the court.

For today: Barzillai used his wealth to serve in a time of need, without expecting anything in return. We can ask ourselves what we have, whether money, time, a home or help, and who needs that today. God often remembers and honors humble generosity.
exp.2:19:
This verse tells that Abner came to David at Hebron, accompanied by twenty men. David held a feast for him and the men with him. The word "feast" means a special meal of welcome, and the old-fashioned spelling "a" is written here as the usual "to."

Abner was the commander of Saul's army and had supported Saul's house against David. Now, after a falling-out with Ish-bosheth, he decides to approach David and help unite all Israel under his rule. David receives him with hospitality, which opens the door to an agreement. The text does not say everything David was thinking, so it is best not to assume too much.

For today: when there is a broken relationship or a disagreement, sharing a meal and receiving someone kindly can open the way to peace. A simple gesture of hospitality can help people listen to one another.
exp.12:9:
Amnon asks Tamar to bring the food into the chamber, that is, into his private room, so that he can eat from her hand. Tamar takes the cakes, which were small fried loaves she had prepared, and brings them to her brother.

It is Amnon, the son of King David, who is pretending to be sick. Tamar was his half-sister, and she obeys, thinking she is helping someone who is ill. But Amnon had already sent everyone out of the house, and what follows shows that his plan was to harm her. Thus a request that seems simple hid a cruel deception.

For today: not everyone who asks for a favor has good intentions. Let us learn to be prudent, to listen to our inner unease, and to seek help from trusted people. And if anyone has suffered abuse, the blame is never theirs; it is good to seek support and justice.
exp.5:0:
This verse says that David gathered together the best men of Israel, thirty thousand in all. The phrase "gathered together again" is the meaning of the verse's wording. "Chosen" refers to select men, probably warriors or representatives of the people. The text does not make clear whether they were soldiers or a broader assembly.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David was already king over all Israel and had taken Jerusalem. Now he wants to bring the ark of God, a symbol of the Lord's presence, to his new capital. Gathering so many people shows that he wanted to do this as a matter for the whole nation. The verses that follow tell how the move went wrong, because they did not carefully follow what God had commanded.

For today: good intentions and great enthusiasm are valuable, but they are not enough. Before we undertake anything to honor God, let us look in his Word for how he wants it done, and not only for how it seems best to us.
exp.22:2:
This verse says that God himself spoke to David, and what he said is this: the one who rules over people must be just, and must rule with respect and reverence toward God. The word "ruleth" in the verse is an older word meaning the one who rules or governs. "The God of Israel" and "the Rock of Israel" are other names for God, emphasizing his power and his protection.

Here David speaks, now an old man, in what the Bible calls his "last words," that is, his final words. He says that the Spirit of God spoke through him. David, who was a king, leaves a teaching about what a good ruler should be like. Then he compares such a ruler to the light of the morning, and he also acknowledges that his own family was not perfect.

For today: if you have authority over others, at home, at work, or in the church, try to act with justice and remember that you are accountable to God.
exp.21:19:
He spoke of how God brought David out of a narrow, cramped place into a wide one, that is, into freedom and safety. He rescued him because God took pleasure in him. The phrases "brought me forth" and "delivered me" are the verse's own wording, and "a large place" describes an open space free of pressure. "He delighted in me" means that God was pleased with him and wanted to show him favor.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving he composed when God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and acknowledges that enemies stronger than he was attacked him in his day of distress, but God was his support. The verses that follow speak of his faithfulness, and some understand this as his sincerity toward God rather than perfection.

For today: when you feel trapped, remember that God can open a way for you. Thank him for the times he has already done so, and trust that he cares for you because he loves you.
exp.21:6:
David says that in great distress he called upon God and cried out to him, and God heard him. "Called upon" means calling out to ask for help. "His temple" here probably refers to God's heavenly dwelling, since in David's time the temple in Jerusalem did not yet exist. "My cry came into his ears" expresses that God attended to his plea closely and truly.

He speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. Earlier he describes feeling surrounded by death and danger. Afterward, the song shows God acting with power, with the trembling of the earth and fire, in response to his cry.

For today: when you feel distress, you don't need to have the perfect words. Cry out to God with sincerity, trusting that he listens to you. Then remember and give thanks each time he helps you.
exp.17:29:
What it says: King David orders Ahimaaz to step aside and wait. "Turn aside" means "step to the side," and "stood still" means "stopped." Ahimaaz obeys and stays still, waiting.

Context: David was waiting for news of the battle against his son Absalom. Ahimaaz arrived first and gave a report of victory, but when David asked about Absalom, he avoided answering clearly. So David made him wait until Cushi arrived. It is likely that Ahimaaz did not want to give the painful news of Absalom's death, although the text does not say this in so many words.

For today: Sometimes we have to wait to receive the full truth. And when it falls to us to speak, let us not hide what is hard; let us tell the truth with respect and compassion.
exp.15:13:
King David and all the people who were with him arrived very tired at their destination, and there they stopped to rest. Some scholars believe the Hebrew word could also be the name of a place, but the general sense is the same.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator who tells the story. David was fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled against him. On the way, Shimei cursed him and threw stones at him, but David endured the insult and hoped that God would see his affliction.

After sorrows and humiliations, the body and the heart need rest. If you are worn out, do not blame yourself for stopping. Resting is a way of trusting that God cares for you and can give you new strength.
exp.10:21:
The messenger went out, arrived where David was, and reported to him everything Joab had instructed him to say. The word "shewed" is an older form of "showed," and "reported" here means he gave a detailed account.

Here the narrator of the story is speaking. Joab, the commander of the army, was besieging the city of Rabbah. He had sent Uriah to the most dangerous part of the battle, just as David had ordered, and Uriah died. Joab expected the king to be angry about the defeat, so he prepared the message to soften the blow with the news of Uriah's death. The text does not say what Joab really thought deep down, but it does show that he knew what David wanted to hear.

For today: a hidden sin often drags other people into silence, manipulation, or cover-up. If we have done wrong, it is better to confess it soon, as David later did, and not keep covering it up.
exp.22:37:
This verse continues the list of David's mighty men. It names two men, Ira and Gareb, and says that both were "an Ithrite." That probably means they came from the family of the Ithrites, a clan that lived in Kiriath-jearim, though some think it may have been a different group or place. The Bible tells us nothing more about them.

The text has no direct speaker. It is the narrator of Samuel who keeps the record of the warriors who helped David in his reign. The list ends with "thirty-seven," since it includes the famous "thirty" and other leaders. These names are mentioned to acknowledge their service, even though they did no deeds that are recounted.

For today: God sees and remembers those who serve faithfully, even when no one else notices. You do not need to be famous to be valuable in his work. Do your work with steadiness, because the Lord does not forget what you do out of love and loyalty (Hebrews 6:10).
exp.11:21:
Here David explains why he was fasting and weeping while his son was sick. He said, "Who knows whether God will be gracious to me?" That is, he had no certainty, but he had hope that God would change the outcome and the child would live.

David speaks with his servants, who did not understand his change after the child's death. This son was born from his sin with Bathsheba, and God had announced it through the prophet Nathan. David pleaded for as long as there was hope. When the child died, he accepted God's will, worshiped, and went on.

For today: we can pray with persistence and sincerity, even though we do not know how God will respond. And when an answer comes that is different from what we asked for, we can worship, trust God, and receive strength to keep living.
exp.1:16:
That day there was a very fierce battle, and Abner and the men of Israel lost to the servants of David. The narrator of the book tells of the war between two sides after the death of Saul. Abner supported Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, while David was recognized as king in Judah. Before the general battle, twelve men from each side fought and died together, which was very tragic. Then the fighting spread. David's men won, and soon Joab, Abishai, and Asahel appear, whose actions will bring further consequences.

For today: conflicts between brothers or families leave deep wounds, even when someone "wins." Seek peace and resolve disagreements in time, before they grow and cost lives, relationships, or trust.
exp.11:8:
Here God asks David why he despised his word and did what is evil. The phrase "despised" in the verse above means to look down on something and treat it as unimportant, so David treated the Lord's commandment as if it did not matter. He had Uriah the Hittite killed with the sword, and the verse's point that he was put to death in battle, at the hand of the enemy, is shown in the verse by the words "with the sword of the children of Ammon." David also took Uriah's wife to be his own wife.

The prophet Nathan speaks in God's name. He has just told David a parable, and he says to him, "Thou art the man." David had taken Bathsheba and arranged the death of her husband, Uriah. God reminds him of everything he had given him and shows him the seriousness of his sin.

For today: do not minimize your faults or hide them. God sees everything and has given us much; instead of justifying ourselves, we can acknowledge the wrong honestly and ask him for forgiveness.
exp.14:28:
What it says: Zadok and Abiathar, the two priests, returned to Jerusalem carrying the ark of God, and they stayed there. "Returned" means they carried it back, and "stayed there" means they remained in the city.

Context: The author of the book is the one telling the story. David was fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled against him. The priests had brought out the ark to accompany him, but David asked them to take it back and to send him news of what happened. He did not want to use the ark as a charm to secure his victory, but to leave his future in God's hands. Besides this, the priests and their sons could help him as informants.

For today: When we go through a crisis, let us not try to manipulate God or secure a result in our own way. We can act with wisdom and at the same time humbly trust that He will decide what is best.
exp.6:20:
Here David tells God that all the great things he has done and promised came from his own word and from his own heart. "Great things" here means wonderful works and promises. "Servant" is David himself. God also made them known to him so that he would understand them.

David is praying after the prophet Nathan brought him God's promise: his family and his kingdom would be established forever. David sits before the Lord, amazed. He understands that he did not receive this on his own merit, but because God chose to give it out of pure goodness.

For today: when you see God's goodness in your life, do not think first about what you deserve, but about who God is. Give thanks with humility, remembering that his favors come from his love and his faithful word.
exp.23:14:
It says that God sent a deadly sickness on Israel, from that morning until "the appointed time," which was probably the limit God set, and which some understand to mean three days. A "pestilence" is a plague or epidemic. Seventy thousand men died, from Dan in the north to Beer-sheba in the south; that is, across the whole nation.

The narrator tells the consequences of David taking a census of the people, something the text presents as a sin. Gad, God's prophet, gave him three possible punishments. David chose to fall into the hands of God, trusting in his mercy. Afterward, God stopped the angel, and David confessed his guilt and prayed for the people.

Today we see that our decisions, especially those of people who lead, affect others. When we fail, the best thing is to acknowledge it honestly and turn to God's mercy, not to excuses.
exp.19:0:
This verse tells us that there was a wicked man named Sheba, from the tribe of Benjamin. He blew a trumpet (the "horn" was a ram's horn sounded to call the people together) and shouted that Israel had no share or inheritance in David, the son of Jesse. Then he told them to go back, each man to his tents, that is, to their homes or tents.

The narrator describes Sheba as a "man of Belial," since he took advantage of a moment of tension. David had just returned after the rebellion of Absalom, and the tribes of the north and Judah were arguing over who had done more for the king (2 Samuel 19). Sheba used that anger to divide Israel.

Today, when there are conflicts between people, it is easy for someone to stir up anger with words that drive people apart. We can choose to be peacemakers: to think before we speak, not to repeat complaints that divide, and to seek reconciliation.
exp.14:21:
Here David agrees that Ittai the Gittite should cross over with him. "Go and pass over" means "all right, come with us." Ittai crosses over together with all his men and their households, including the little ones. "Gittite" means that he was from Gath, a Philistine city.

David is fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Ittai was a foreigner who had arrived only recently. David had offered to let him return to a safe place, but Ittai swore his loyalty to the king, whatever might happen. So David answers him with these words. The crossing of the brook Kidron marks the beginning of the road toward the wilderness.

Today we can learn from Ittai's loyalty: remaining faithful to someone in difficult times, not only when everything is going well. It also invites us to value those who stand with us in trials and to be that kind of support for others.
exp.2:18:
This verse tells how Abner, the commander of Saul's army, also spoke with the tribe of Benjamin. Then he went to Hebron to report to David what the elders of Israel and the whole house of Benjamin had decided.

Abner was switching sides. After Saul's death, he had supported Saul's son Ish-bosheth, but now he wanted to bring Israel together under David. Benjamin was Saul's tribe, so its support was very important. Abner said that God had promised that David would deliver Israel. His personal motives are not spelled out here, and the text shows a mix of reasons.

For today: when God has already shown the way, it is wise to listen patiently to others and to seek unity, without forcing our own will on them.
exp.14:20:
Ittai answers the king with an oath: "As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives". He says that, whether it means death or life, he will be wherever the king is. "Servant" here means someone who puts himself at the king's service.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Ittai is from Gath, a foreigner who had arrived not long before with his men. David, out of kindness, offers to let him stay so as not to expose him to danger. But Ittai speaks with total loyalty, even when the future is uncertain and everything seems lost.

Today it teaches us what loyalty is when it does not depend on circumstances. We may ask ourselves whether we follow Christ only when things go well, or also in difficult moments. Whoever remains faithful in trial shows a true love.
exp.1:12:
It says that Joab, David's nephew and commander of his army, went out with David's men and met Abner and the men of Ish-bosheth by the pool of Gibeon. They sat down, or stopped facing each other, some on one side of the pool and the others on the other side.

The narrator describes how the conflict between the two sides began. Judah was following David in Hebron, and the rest of Israel was following Ish-bosheth, Saul's son. Abner, commander of Ish-bosheth's army, came to Gibeon, and Joab went out to meet him. Here there is still no fighting, only two groups separated by a pool and a growing tension.

For today: many great quarrels begin with situations that seem small. Before we take our places on opposite sides, let us ask God for wisdom to seek peace and not to feed pride.
exp.1:30:
It says that David's men defeated the men of Benjamin and Abner's soldiers, and that three hundred and sixty of the enemy died. They also picked up the body of Asahel, Joab's brother who had died earlier, and buried him in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. "Smitten" means they defeated them in battle, and "buried him" means they laid him to rest.

Here the narrator of the book is summarizing the outcome of a battle. Israel was divided: David ruled over Judah, and Abner supported the house of Saul. The Benjamites were Saul's tribe. This struggle between brothers of the same people left many dead, and the account sadly records the cost of that division.

For today: conflicts among those who should be united leave deep wounds. Before letting a quarrel grow within the family, the church, or the workplace, seek peace and reconciliation while it is still possible.
exp.20:3:
The Gibeonites tell David that they do not want money or gold from Saul or from his family. They also do not want any Israelite to be put to death. David answers them that he will do whatever they ask.

There is a famine in the land, and David seeks God, who points to a bloodguilt that Saul brought upon the Gibeonites. They were a people with whom Israel had made an oath (Joshua 9), but Saul tried to wipe them out. David wants to repair the harm. What they ask for afterward is hard to understand, and readers interpret it in different ways.

For today: when we have hurt someone, repairing the harm begins by listening humbly to what the injured person needs, not to what is comfortable for us. Promises and agreements matter to God.
exp.4:5:
David and his men went to Jerusalem to attack the Jebusites, the people who lived there. They mocked David and told him he would not enter, saying that even the blind and the lame would be enough to stop him. "Dwelt" means lived, and "take away" means remove or drive out.

The ones speaking are the Jebusites, confident that their fortified city was impossible to take. David had just been acknowledged as king over all Israel and was seeking a central capital. Scholars explain the reference to "the blind and the lame" in several ways: it may be a taunt, or a reference to defenders or symbolic figures. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: do not lose heart when others mock what God has placed in your heart. What seems impossible is not impossible for one who trusts in the Lord. Act with faith and with perseverance.
exp.6:15:
God promises David that his family and his kingdom will remain firm forever. "House" means his descendants, his dynasty. "Before thee" means under God's care, and "forever" means without end. His throne will be "established," that is, secure.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple, but God answers that He will build him a "house," a dynasty. The promise includes Solomon, although many Christians see it fully fulfilled in Jesus, a descendant of David. Jews understand it in other ways.

Today we can trust that God keeps his promises even when we fail. If you feel insecure today, remember that his faithfulness does not depend on your perfection. Rest in his word and respond with gratitude, as David did.
exp.10:13:
The text says that the next morning David wrote a letter to Joab, his general, and sent it with Uriah himself. The phrase "por mano de" means that Uriah was the messenger who carried it.

The passage follows the story of David, Bathsheba, and Uriah. David had sinned with Bathsheba, who was pregnant. He wanted Uriah to sleep with his wife to cover it up, but Uriah did not go home, not even when he was drunk. So David moved to a worse plan. Without knowing it, Uriah was carrying his own death sentence, as the following verses show.

For today: a hidden sin often leads to another, more serious one. If you have failed, do not cover it up with lies or manipulation. Confess to God and seek help in time, as David later did (Psalm 51).
exp.2:12:
David agrees to make a covenant with Abner, the commander of Ish-bosheth's army. But he sets a condition: Abner will not be allowed to appear before him unless he first brings Michal, Saul's daughter. The verse's note about the old form "Á" and "Michâl" is removed here, since the reader's verse does not contain those words.

David speaks as king of Judah at Hebron. Abner, who had been supporting the reign of Ish-bosheth, offers to switch sides to David and unite Israel. Michal had been David's wife, but Saul had given her to another man. Scholars often see here both a legitimate claim and a political move, since being Saul's son-in-law strengthened his right to the throne. We cannot be certain which motive weighed more.

For today: important agreements call for clear and honest conditions. But it is also wise to examine our motives, so that what is right is not mixed with self-interest, and to think about how our decisions affect other people.
exp.17:11:
This man answers Joab that he would not harm Absalom even for a thousand pieces of silver, which was a very large sum of money. He refers to Absalom as "the king's son," and recalls that everyone heard David's order to Joab, Abishai, and Ittai: "Beware that none touch the young man Absalom." Your reader will find the word "shekels" in the verse, and shekels were silver coins.

The speaker is a soldier of David who found Absalom hanging from a tree during the battle against the rebels. Joab, the commander of the army, rebukes him for not killing Absalom. The soldier refuses out of respect for the king's command. Joab, however, later kills Absalom anyway.

For today: this soldier teaches us to remain faithful to what is right even when we are offered a great reward or when someone in power pressures us. Obeying God and acting with integrity is worth more than any reward.
exp.18:27:
Mephibosheth tells King David that his whole family deserved death before him, yet David seated him at his own table among those who ate with the king. So he feels he has no right to keep complaining. The guests are the people invited to eat at the king's table, and the phrase "deserved death" means that he deserved to die.

He speaks as Saul's grandson when David returns to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Ziba, his servant, had accused him of disloyalty, and Mephibosheth says that Ziba deceived him. The Bible does not fully make clear who was telling the truth. What stands out is his humility and his gratitude toward David, who had earlier shown him kindness.

For today: when we remember that we have received favors we did not deserve, such as forgiveness and God's care, it is easier to live with gratitude and let go of our complaints. We might ask ourselves today: what am I complaining about, and what kindness of God am I forgetting?
exp.11:27:
