Here Joab tells David to gather the rest of the army, set up camp in front of the city of Rabbah, and take it himself. The reason is that if Joab takes it, the city would carry his name and not the king's.

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. He was besieging Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and had already taken the part of the city that supplied its water, which left Rabbah nearly defenseless. Joab could have claimed the credit, but he preferred that the final victory belong to David, who was the king. Some see here sincere loyalty; others, also a political gesture. The text does not make this clear.

For today: learn not to always seek applause. Do your work well and, when possible, let others receive the recognition. In the end, all true glory belongs to God.
exp.11:13:
This verse says that David's sin, committed in that way, gave occasion for God's enemies to speak evil of Him. For that reason, the newborn child would die without remedy. The words "deed," "blaspheme," and "surely" appear in the verse your reader sees, so their meaning is clear from that verse.

The prophet Nathan, sent by God, speaks. David had taken Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah killed. David confessed, and God forgave his sin: he would not die. But forgiveness did not remove all the consequences. Some understand that the child's death shows how serious the sin of a king was; the text does not explain more details.

For today: God truly forgives those who repent, but our actions can affect others and the way God is seen by those who watch us. Let us live with humility, confess quickly, and take care of our witness.
exp.18:28:
King David cuts short the conversation with Mephibosheth. He asks why he should keep talking about it and announces his decision: Mephibosheth and Ziba will share the land.

David speaks after returning to Jerusalem following Absalom's rebellion. Ziba, a servant of Saul, had accused Mephibosheth of disloyalty, and David had given him all of Mephibosheth's land (2 Samuel 16). Now Mephibosheth says Ziba deceived him. We do not know for certain whether David fully believed him; some see in this decision a hasty arrangement or a political compromise. Mephibosheth replies that Ziba may keep everything, since what matters is that the king has returned in peace.

Today we can learn to value people more than possessions. It is also wise to listen calmly and seek the truth before deciding, so that we do not commit injustice.
exp.2:31:
This verse tells us that Abner was buried in Hebron. King David wept aloud beside his grave, and all the people wept with him. The phrase "lifted up his voice" means that he wept openly, without hiding his grief.

Abner was the commander of Saul's army. Joab and his brother Abishai had killed him to avenge the death of their brother Asahel. David had not ordered that crime, and with this public mourning he wanted to show that he had no part in it. Some believe he also sought to calm the people and keep peace among the tribes. The text says nothing more about his motives.

When someone dies unjustly, we should not stay silent or indifferent. To mourn sincerely and to reject violence and revenge is also a way of defending justice and peace.
exp.22:29:
This verse names two more of David's mighty men. Benaiah was from Pirathon, a town in the territory of Ephraim. Hiddai came from the brooks of Gaash, that is, from a valley or stream near Mount Gaash. These are only names and places of origin.

It is part of the list of David's thirty, the outstanding warriors who accompanied David (2 Samuel 23:8-39). The list appears after David's last words. The text simply records them and does not explain why each one is included. This Benaiah of Pirathon should not be confused with Benaiah son of Jehoiada, mentioned earlier. The names in this list are written somewhat differently in 1 Chronicles 11.

God takes notice of people who seem ordinary. These men came from small towns, and we know almost nothing of their stories, yet they were recorded. Your faithful service, even if no one applauds it, does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.22:13:
This verse says that David was in the stronghold, a protected place, while the Philistines, his enemies, had a garrison in Bethlehem. "Garrison" means a group of soldiers that occupies and guards a place. Bethlehem was David's hometown, so seeing his enemies there was painful.

Here the narrator describes the situation before telling the story of David's three mighty men. It is not known with certainty whether the "stronghold" is the cave of Adullam or some other refuge, and scholars interpret it in different ways. What matters is that David was living under pressure, and his longing for water from his homeland arises in that difficult moment.

For today: even when you are in a time of pressure or waiting, God sustains you. And when someone serves you with love and sacrifice, value it with humility and gratitude, as David did when he offered that gesture to God.
exp.14:24:
Here King David tells the priest Zadok to carry the ark of God back into the city of Jerusalem. David says that if the Lord looks on him with favor, the Lord will one day bring him back and let him see the ark again, along with the place where God dwells.

David is fleeing Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. The Levites had brought out the ark to accompany him, but David does not want to use it as a good-luck charm or to tie God to his cause. He prefers to leave his future in God's hands.

For today: when we go through a crisis, let us not try to manipulate God to get what we want. We can ask him sincerely and, at the same time, trust that his will is good, even when we do not yet see the outcome.
exp.0:7:
This verse is part of the account of a young man who comes to David after the battle of Gilboa. It says that Saul asked him who he was, and he answered that he was an Amalekite. The word "Amalekite" means that he belonged to the people of Amalek.

The one speaking is this young man, who arrives at David's camp with the news of Saul's death. His account is hard to confirm: 1 Samuel 31 tells of Saul's death in a different way, and many think the young man exaggerated or made up his part to win David's favor. Others believe something else may have happened. The Bible does not settle the question completely.

For today: let us not seek advantage through half-truths or by taking advantage of another's misfortune. God sees the heart, and honesty is worth more than any reward we hope to gain through deceit.
exp.10:26:
After the time of mourning for Bathsheba's husband was over, David had her brought to his palace. She became his wife and gave birth to a son. But what David had done was evil in the eyes of God. "Displeased" means that it did not please God; it grieved him deeply. The verse says the son was born to David, and the verse of the word "gave birth" is the same as the plain sense of "bore him a son."

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book. David had taken Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and then had Uriah killed in battle to cover up his sin. People could see an ordinary marriage, but the narrator shows us what God thought. Later, in chapter 12, God sends the prophet Nathan to confront him.

For today: even if we manage to hide a fault or make it look good, God sees everything. It is better to acknowledge sin quickly and come to Him with humility, for He offers forgiveness to those who repent.
exp.18:25:
Mefiboset explains to King David why he did not go with him when David fled from Jerusalem. He says that his servant deceived him. According to him, he had ordered that a donkey be saddled for him so he could ride it and go with the king, because he is lame.

David was fleeing from Absalom's rebellion. Now he returns in victory, and Mefiboset, Saul's grandson, comes out to meet him showing signs of mourning. His servant Ziba had said earlier that Mefiboset hoped to keep the kingdom for himself (2 Samuel 16:3). Who is telling the truth is not certain: David divides the lands between the two of them and does not fully settle the matter.

For today: before judging someone by what others say, let us listen to both sides. And if we are slandered, let us trust that God knows the heart, even when no one else sees it.
exp.6:5:
God reminds David that, since he brought Israel out of Egypt, he has never lived in a house of stone or wood. He always moved about in a tent and a tabernacle, that is, in the portable sanctuary that traveled with the people. The word "dwelt" here means "lived." God wants to show that he was not tied to a building.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Nathan. David was living in a palace of cedar and wanted to build a temple for God. His desire was good, but God makes clear that he had never asked for it and that he is the one who takes the initiative. He will soon remind David how he took him from tending sheep to make him a leader.

Today we can serve God with good intentions, but it is wise to remember that he does not depend on our works to be with us. Before we rush to do something for God, let us first listen to what he wants, and serve with humility, grateful for what he has already done for us.
exp.0:13:
Here David asks the young Amalekite how he was not afraid to lift his hand against King Saul. The word "anointed" refers to someone set apart by God with oil to be king. "Lord" is the name of God.

David speaks after receiving the news of Saul's death. That young man said he had killed him, hoping for a reward. But David, who had spared Saul's life even when Saul was pursuing him, does not celebrate the news: he grieves and fasts. For David, the king was still someone placed by God. (The young man's account differs from 1 Samuel 31, where Saul takes his own life; we do not know whether the young man lied or exaggerated.)

For today: respect what God values, even when someone has harmed you. Do not rejoice at the fall of others or seek advantage from it.
exp.1:18:
He says that Asahel pursued Abner without turning aside even a little. The phrase we must avoid is the one meaning neither to the right nor to the left, so in plain terms it means he did not turn to the right hand or to the left. Asahel was going after him in a straight line, determined.

This happens after a fierce battle between David's men and those of Israel, who were defeated. Asahel, brother of Joab and Abishai, was very swift. The narrator tells us that he went straight after Abner, the commander of the enemy army. Later Abner warns him to stop, but Asahel does not heed him. The text does not explain his reasons; we may suppose ambition or bravery, but that is only an interpretation.

Persistence is good, but we need to ask where we are going. Before pursuing a goal with determination, it is wise to pray, to listen to counsel, and to know whether God is guiding us. Sometimes stopping in time is wisdom.
exp.18:36:
Barzilai asks King David to let him return home so that he may die in his own city and be buried beside his father and mother. In his place he offers Chimham, his servant, to go with the king and receive his favor. The phrase "do to him what shall seem good unto thee" means: treat him however you think best.

Barzilai, a man of eighty years and very wealthy, had provided food and shelter for David and his people when they were fleeing from Absalom. Now David wants to reward him by taking him to Jerusalem. Barzilai, because of his age, humbly declines. It is not known with certainty who Chimham was; many think he was Barzilai's son, but the text does not say so.

For today: we can recognize our limits and the stages of life. Barzilai did not cling to honors or comforts, but preferred to be in his own home and to bless someone younger. We can do the same: serve with generosity, accept with gratitude what no longer belongs to us, and make way for others.
exp.14:17:
This verse describes David leaving Jerusalem. All his servants go at his side, along with the Cherethites and the Pelethites, who were guards or soldiers loyal to him. Six hundred men from Gath also go before the king; they had come on foot from that Philistine city.

The narrator recounts the moment when David flees Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. David leaves with his people to avoid a battle in the city. It is a time of humiliation and pain. The following verses show that the leader of these men from Gath is Ittai, a foreigner, to whom David gives freedom to return. This shows his considerate treatment of those who serve him.

For today: loyalty is tested in difficult times. We can ask ourselves whether we stand with others when they go through a crisis, and also whether, like David, we treat with respect and kindness those who follow us.
exp.19:18:
A woman from the city of Abel comes before Joab and tells him that she and her people are peaceable and faithful in Israel. She accuses him of trying to destroy a city that is important, one that is called "a mother in Israel," that is, a city with standing and with many families under its care. Then she asks him why he wants to swallow up "the inheritance of the Lord," that is, the people and the land that belong to God.

A woman whom the text calls wise is speaking. Joab was pursuing the rebel Sheba, and he had laid siege to the city where Sheba had taken refuge. She tries to stop the violence through dialogue. In the end, the city hands over Sheba and a massacre is avoided.

For today: before reacting harshly, it is worth taking the time to speak calmly and to look for a way out that protects the innocent. A wise word can prevent a great deal of harm.
exp.11:28:
It says that David gathered all the people together, meaning the army that was not yet in the battle, and went to attack the city of Rabbah, capital of the Ammonites. He fought against it and took it.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Joab, the commander of the army, had already taken the main part of the city, known as the city of waters. But he asked David to come himself, so that the final victory would be credited to the king and not to Joab. This happens after David's sin with Bathsheba, and the war was still going on at that time.

Today we can learn from Joab's attitude: doing our work well without seeking all the recognition. It is also good to give credit to whom it is due, working together as a team with humility.
exp.12:20:
This verse says that King David became very angry when he learned what had happened.

The narrator tells us that Amnon, David's son, had abused his half-sister Tamar. David hears of it and is outraged, but the text does not say that he did anything about it. Some ancient manuscripts, such as the Greek version and the Qumran scrolls, add that he did not want to grieve Amnon because he was his firstborn. That phrase does not appear in the traditional Hebrew text, so it is mentioned with caution. Absalom, Tamar's full brother, keeps a silent hatred.

For today: feeling anger at injustice is right, but it is not enough. God calls us to act with wisdom and courage to protect the one who was harmed, to listen to them, and to seek justice, without staying silent.
exp.21:29:
It says that David, with God's help, can defeat enemy armies and get over walls that seemed impossible to cross. "I can run through a troop" means defeating forces; "I leap over a wall" speaks of crossing strong defenses. The strength does not come from him alone, but from you and from my God.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, when God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. It comes from saying that God is his lamp and his light in the darkness. Then he affirms that God's way is perfect and that He is a shield for those who wait on Him.

For today: when you face a problem that looks like an enormous wall, do not trust only in your own strength. Pray, seek God's guidance, and take the next step in faith, remembering that He is with you and sustains you.
exp.23:21:
Araunah tells David to take whatever he wishes and offer the sacrifice. He points to the oxen for the burnt offering, which was an offering burned completely for God. He also offers the threshing tools and the yokes of the oxen to be used as wood for the fire on the altar.

Araunah, the owner of the threshing floor, the place where grain was threshed, speaks here. David had sinned by counting the people, and a plague came. Now he goes up to buy the threshing floor to build an altar and ask that the dying stop. Araunah, with respect, wants to give everything for free. In the next verse, David refuses.

For today: Araunah's generosity is beautiful, but David reminds us that sincere worship costs us something. We can ask ourselves what we give to God with real effort: time, attention, money, or service, and not just what we have left over.
exp.7:16:
This verse names three men in David's government. Zadok and Ahimelech were priests, that is, those in charge of worship and of offering the sacrifices. Seraiah was the scribe, the one who kept the records and wrote the documents of the kingdom. Some scholars note that the name "Ahimelech son of Abiathar" could appear in another form in other passages, where Abiathar is called the son of Ahimelech, and there is no single certain explanation for this.

The text is the narrator's account of how David organized his kingdom, now firmly established. After his victories, the list shows an orderly government, with those responsible for war, justice, worship, and administration.

For today: God values order and the service of each person in their place. Whether you care for others, teach, keep records, or serve quietly, your task matters. Faithfully carry out what has been entrusted to you.
exp.5:6:
God became angry with Uzzah and struck him down right there for his reckless and disrespectful act. Uzzah died beside the ark. The word for the anger that burned against him denotes a fierce, intense anger, and the act itself was carried out without the proper reverence due to God.

The narrator tells us that David was bringing the ark to Jerusalem amid music and celebration. The oxen pulling the cart stumbled, and Uzzah reached out and touched the ark. The Law said that the ark was to be carried with poles, and that no one should touch it (Numbers 4:15). Here it had been transported on a cart. Many think Uzzah wanted to help, but the text does not explain every detail.

Good intentions do not replace obedience. Let us draw near to God with love, but also with reverence, seeking to do things as He directs.
exp.10:4:
What it says: Bathsheba became pregnant after she had been with David. She sent word to the king with a short message: "I am with child." "Conceived" means that she became pregnant, and "sent and told" means that she sent word to him.

Context: The speaker is Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, a soldier who was away at war. David, as king, had her brought to him and he lay with her. The text reports the event in few words and does not say what she felt. Because the king had so much power, many believe she could not refuse, although the Bible does not make this clear. This notice puts David face to face with the consequences of his sin, and it leads him to try to hide it.

For today: A hidden sin does not disappear; sooner or later its consequences come to light. It is better to confess in time and ask God for forgiveness, rather than cover up one wrong with more wrongs.
exp.0:3:
Here David urgently asks what happened in the battle, and the messenger answers with three hard pieces of news: Israel's army fled, many soldiers died, and King Saul and his son Jonathan also died.

David was in Ziklag, waiting for news of Israel's war against the Philistines. The man speaking has come from the battlefield, with torn clothes and dirt on his head, signs of mourning. Later it becomes clear that his account includes details that do not match 1 Samuel 31, so his version is doubtful.

When difficult news arrives, it is wise to ask calmly and seek the truth before reacting. We can also ask God for wisdom to listen, to feel the pain honestly, and not to be carried away by the first thing we hear.
exp.21:28:
This verse says that God is David's lamp. A "lamp" is a light that guides a person through the dark, and "darkness" refers to difficult, confusing, or dangerous times. David declares that the Lord himself gives him light when everything looks dark.

David speaks near the end of his life, in a song of thanksgiving because God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. Shortly before, he says that God is just toward the humble and firm toward the proud. Then David speaks of the victories God gave him. This same song also appears in Psalm 18.

For today: when you do not know which path to take, do not despair. Pray, read the Bible, and trust that God will show you the next step, even if you cannot yet see the whole way.
exp.22:18:
It speaks of Abishai. It says he was the most outstanding (the word for "outstanding" here means standing out above others) among a group of three, and that he was their leader. Yet even so, he did not reach the level of the first three, David's most famous heroes.

The narrator of Second Samuel lists David's mighty warriors and their deeds. Abishai, brother of Joab, raised his spear against three hundred men. Scholars disagree about how to understand the two groups of "three": most likely they are two different trios, but the text does not fully clarify this.

Today: you can give your best and be recognized, and still not be "the first." The Bible records Abishai with honor all the same. Serve with devotion without comparing yourself, trusting that God values your faithfulness, not your place on the list.
exp.21:37:
It says that David will pursue his enemies and destroy them completely, and that he will not stop the pursuit until he has finished them off. Some of the words are old: the phrase that means "I will break them" means that he will destroy or crush them, and the word that means "finish off" means that he will put an end to them, that he will eliminate them.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving to God, when the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. The verses around it show that David does not rely on himself: God gave him a shield, strength, and firm steps. It is the language of war, typical of a king in his time, and the victory is credited to God.

For today: let us not take this as permission to hate people. We can apply it to our struggles against sin, resentment, or bad habits: with the strength of God, we should not stop halfway, but persevere until we win.
exp.22:1:
Here David says that the Spirit of God spoke through him, and that the words he uttered were not his alone, but God himself placed his message in his mouth. The name of God is the LORD, and "tongue" refers to the way he spoke.

These are David's "last words," that is, one of his final messages, spoken when he was already old. He was a king, but also a poet and singer, called "the sweet psalmist of Israel." Before speaking of the righteous ruler, he wants to make clear that what he will say comes from God. Many of his psalms reflect that same conviction.

For today: when you speak with others, ask God to let his words guide yours. Before you counsel, correct, or encourage, pray and seek his Word, so that what you say builds up and reflects his truth.
exp.18:4:
Joab enters the house of King David and tells him, firmly, that today he has put to shame all his servants. They had just saved the king's life, along with the lives of his sons and daughters, and the lives of his wives and concubines. The word "concubines" refers to secondary wives within the king's household, which was common in that time.

Joab is the commander of David's army. He speaks this way because the army won the battle against Absalom, the rebellious son, but David keeps weeping over him. The soldiers enter the city as if they had lost. Joab fears the kingdom will fall apart, so he confronts the king harshly.

For today: the grief is real and needs its time, but it should not make us forget those who stand beside us and have helped us. Even in mourning we can give thanks and care for those who accompany us.
exp.23:23:
David tells Araunah that he does not want to take the land for free. He insists on paying for it, because he would not offer sacrifices to God that cost him nothing. He buys the threshing floor (the place where grain was separated from the chaff) and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. A shekel was a unit of weight used as money.

David speaks after having sinned by counting the people. A plague was falling on Israel, and the prophet Gad had told him to build an altar on that threshing floor. Araunah, generously, offers him everything. But David wants to worship with a sacrifice of his own. In 1 Chronicles 21:25 another figure appears, and scholars explain it in different ways.

For today: God does not seek cheap gifts, but a willing heart. Ask yourself what you give to God that truly costs you: time, forgiveness, generosity, or obedience.
exp.19:15:
A wise woman called out from inside the city of Abel. She urgently asked that she be heard and that Joab be called to come and speak with her.

Joab, commander of David's army, was pursuing Sheba, who had rebelled against the king and taken refuge in Abel. Joab and his men laid siege to the city and began to tear down its wall. Then this woman, whom the Bible calls wise, speaks up to prevent the destruction of her people. She takes the initiative and asks for a conversation before there is more violence.

For today: when there is a conflict, before letting everything be destroyed, seek to speak calmly and wisely. A well-spoken word, at the right time, can protect many people and open the way to peace.
exp.16:24:
Absalom put Amasa in charge of the army in place of Joab. The text explains who Amasa was: the son of Ithra, a man of Israel who went in to Abigail, meaning he took her as his wife. She was the sister of Zeruiah, the mother of Joab. So Amasa and Joab were cousins.

The narrator of the book explains this appointment while Absalom prepares for war against his father David. Joab remained loyal to David, so Absalom needed a new military leader, and he chose a relative. Some manuscripts and other passages give different details about Ithra's background, so not everything is clear.

For today: power and family ties can give us positions, but they do not guarantee wisdom or success. Before deciding something important, let us seek God's guidance and not only our own convenience.
exp.21:50:
This verse says that God gives great victories to his king and is faithful to his anointed one. The phrase about multiplying salvations means that he multiplies the rescues and deliverances he gives. The phrase about showing mercy means that he acts with kindness and loyalty. His offspring means his descendants. The words "for evermore" show that this kindness has no end.

David speaks at the end of a song of thanksgiving. He composed it when God delivered him from his enemies, including Saul. David speaks of himself in the third person, as "the anointed," that is, chosen by God. The promise about his descendants recalls God's covenant with him. Many Christians see its final fulfillment in Jesus Christ, a descendant of David.

For today: when God has helped you, do not keep it to yourself in silence. Write down one concrete help you received today and give thanks for it in prayer. Trust that his faithfulness remains firm.
exp.17:10:
Joab challenges the soldier who had told him: if you saw Absalom hanging from the tree, why didn't you strike him down and kill him right there? Joab says he would have given him ten shekels of silver (an amount of money in weighed coins) and a girdle, which was a soldier's belt, as a reward.

It is Joab, the commander of David's army, who speaks. Absalom had rebelled against his father, the king. But David had ordered that the young man be treated with care. Joab wants to end the rebellion and, according to the text, does not hold back because of the king's order. The soldier refuses to obey him.

For today: having good reasons is not enough to justify a wrong act. Before following someone who pressures us or offers us a reward, it is wise to ask ourselves whether we are being faithful to what is just and to what God asks of us.
exp.21:33:
He says God gives David light and steady feet, "like a deer's feet," that is, like the feet of a deer that runs and leaps over hard ground without falling. He also says God sets him on "my high places," that is, on high and secure ground, far from danger.

David, now an older man, speaks in a song of thanksgiving because the Lord delivered him from Saul and from all his enemies (2 Samuel 22:1). He looks back and recognizes that his victories and his stability did not come from his own strength alone, but from the Lord. The "high places" can be understood as secure places on the battlefield, or also as his position as king; interpreters see it both ways.

Today, when you go through difficult roads, ask God for firmness with every step. And when things go well, remember to thank Him.
exp.1:6:
What it says: David encourages the men of Jabesh-gilead to be strong and courageous. The phrase "let your hands be strengthened" is an old expression that means: "be encouraged, don't lose heart." He also tells them that, after Saul's death, the people of Judah anointed him as king. "Your master" refers to Saul.

Context: David speaks through messengers. He wants to thank the men of Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul with respect. At the same time, he lets them know about his new reign in Judah, perhaps seeking their support. Later Abner set Ish-bosheth up as king over the rest of Israel, so the country was divided. David's motives may have been both gratitude and politics.

For today: Recognizing and thanking others for the good they do, even someone difficult, is a form of mercy. We can also encourage those living through uncertain times, telling them in concrete words that they are not alone.
exp.13:25:
It says that Absalom cut his hair once a year, because it was heavy and bothered him. When he weighed it, it came to about two hundred shekels "by the king's weight." A shekel was an ancient unit of weight, and "the king's weight" was probably an official measure of the king, though it is not known exactly. For that reason, the modern equivalent is uncertain, but it was a very abundant head of hair.

The narrator of the book describes Absalom, son of David, while he lives in Jerusalem without being able to see the king. First his beauty is highlighted, and then his children are mentioned. The text seems to show how much people admired his appearance. But it also lets us see that, although he looked perfect on the outside, there was an unresolved conflict with his father.

For today: let us not confuse a good image with a healthy heart. Let us ask God to help us seek reconciliation in our relationships, rather than caring only for what others see of us.
exp.7:5:
It says that David placed garrisons, that is, groups of soldiers stationed in place, in the region of Syria whose capital was Damascus. The Syrians were made subject to David as servants and had to pay him tribute, which was a kind of tax imposed on a conquered people. Then the text sums up: "And the Lord preserved David whithersoever he went," that is, the Lord protected him and sustained him wherever he went.

The passage is a historical account, not a speech. The narrator tells how David extended his kingdom after defeating Hadadezer and the Syrians of Damascus who came to help him. By saying that the Lord preserved him, the author implies that his victories were not only military strength, but that God was sustaining him.

For today: we can thank God for his care in every place and stage of life, whether it is a new job, a move, or a difficult challenge. His protection does not depend on where we are, and that encourages us to trust in him.
exp.14:31:
The account says that David came to the top of the mountain, where he used to worship God, and there Hushai met him. Hushai was a man from the region of the Archites. Hushai came with his coat torn and earth on his head, old signs of mourning and deep grief.

The narrator tells us that David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled against him. David goes along weeping, and he even learns that his counselor Ahithophel has joined the conspiracy. Hushai arrives loyal and grieving, and David will see in him an answer to his prayer against the counsel of Ahithophel.

Even in the midst of sorrow and betrayal, David stops to worship. When everything falls apart, we can turn to God in prayer, and He can send us help in unexpected ways.
exp.20:20:
This giant challenged and insulted Israel, and Jonathan, David's nephew, killed him. "Challenged" means that he mocked the people and provoked them to fight. Jonathan was the son of Shimea (also called Shimeah), David's brother.

The narrator of 2 Samuel summarizes Israel's last wars against the Philistines. He concludes by saying that four descendants of the giant of Gath fell by the hand of David and his servants. The text shows that the victory was not the work of a single hero, but of a whole team. Some scholars see difficulties when comparing the names with other passages, such as 1 Chronicles 20.

Today: you do not have to face your "giants" alone. God often gives us victory through family and brothers and sisters in the faith. Ask for help, and help others too.
exp.1:4:
David sent messengers to the people of Jabesh-gilead to bless them. He tells them that God should bless them because they showed kindness and loyalty by burying Saul, whom David calls "your lord."

David had just been anointed king over Judah, in Hebron, and he learns what the people of Jabesh did. Saul had been his persecutor, but David recognizes the value of honoring a fallen king. According to 1 Samuel 31, these men recovered the bodies of Saul and his sons. Perhaps David was also seeking their support, although the text does not say this directly.

Today we can learn to recognize and be grateful for the good that others do, even when it involves someone with whom we have had conflicts. A gesture of respect and gratitude can open doors to peace.
exp.0:5:
Here the young man answers David's question and tells how he came upon Saul. He says that he happened by chance upon mount Gilboa and saw Saul leaning on his spear, while the enemy chariots and horsemen came closer behind him. The young man who speaks is an Amalekite who arrived at David's camp with the news of Israel's defeat. David asks him how he knows that Saul and Jonathan died. His account presents Saul wounded and pursued. Later he says he killed him, but 1 Samuel 31 tells that Saul threw himself upon his own sword. For this reason many believe this young man invented part of his story to win David's favor. The Bible does not state this with complete clarity.

Today, before believing a piece of news or taking advantage of it, it is wise to ask how we know it and what interests the person telling it has. The truth matters more than convenience.
exp.2:27:
In this verse, David, on hearing that Abner had been killed, declared that neither he nor his kingdom bore any guilt for that shed blood. The phrase "I am innocent" conveys the same claim, and "before God" points to the same meaning. "Forever" shows that David wanted his innocence to be clear to everyone.

David speaks as king of Judah. Abner, commander of Saul's army, had just made a peace agreement with him. Joab, commander of David's army, killed him in secret, partly to avenge the death of his brother Asahel. David did not know this and feared that people would think he had ordered it, which would have ruined the peace.

For today: when others do something wrong in our name or near us, silence is not enough. It is wise to clearly reject injustice, to ask God to guide us, and to keep our witness honest.
exp.2:35:
What it says: All the people noticed how David had honored Abner, and they approved of it. The phrase "pleased their eyes" is an old-fashioned way of saying it pleased them. Whatever the king did seemed right to everyone.

Context: It is the narrator who speaks. Abner, commander of Saul's army, had been killed by Joab, and David mourned him publicly, fasted, and composed a lament. In this way he showed that he had no part in that death. The people, who could have suspected David, saw his sincere grief and accepted it. The verses that follow confirm this: they understood that the king had not caused that death.

For today: Our conduct speaks louder than our defenses. When we act with integrity, humility, and compassion, even in difficult moments, we naturally gain trust. Let us strive to live openly and sincerely.
exp.2:34:
It says that the people came to David to encourage him to eat something while it was still daylight. David made a solemn vow: that God would punish him if he tasted bread or anything else before the sun went down. The phrase "So do God to me, and more also" was a formula of swearing an oath.

Joab had killed Abner, the commander of Saul's army, who had been coming to make a covenant with David. David wept publicly and fasted to show his grief. In this way he made it clear before all Israel that he had not ordered that death, as the following verse says.

For today: when there is injustice, it is not enough to say that we disagree. Our conduct must also show sincerity, humility, and respect for life. We must take care that our actions match our words.
exp.16:0:
Here Ahithophel proposes a military plan to Absalom. He asks to choose twelve thousand men and set out that same night to pursue David. The verse says "Ahithophel said unto Absalom" and "pursue after David this night," so the names in the verse are the ones your reader will see.

Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David, and David had fled from Jerusalem. Ahithophel was a highly respected counselor, and here he gives his advice for ending the rebellion quickly. According to the verses that follow, he wanted to attack David while David was tired and weak. Later, Hushai offers a different counsel, and Absalom prefers it. The text says that the Lord determined to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel (2 Samuel 17:14).

For today: a plan may seem very wise and quick, but it guarantees nothing if it goes against what God allows. Before acting, it is good to pray, seek advice, and look for God's will.
exp.14:0:
He says that, after what had happened, Absalom got chariots and horses for himself, along with fifty men to run ahead of him. The phrase "got for himself" in the earlier wording means he obtained or procured them. The fifty men were like an escort that announced his coming and made him look important.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not one of the characters. Absalom was the son of King David. He had returned to Jerusalem after being exiled for killing his brother Amnon. This display of power seems to be the start of his plan to win over the people, and the verses that follow show how he gradually won the heart of Israel. Many see it as preparation for taking the throne from his father, though here the text only describes the events.

Today we can ask ourselves what we seek when we present ourselves before others. It is worth examining whether we serve with humility or whether we use our image and influence to make ourselves look great.
exp.22:19:
This verse presents Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, a brave man from Kabzeel, a town in the south of Judah. He is described as a valiant man, strong and courageous, and as one who had done many great deeds. He killed two lion-like men of Moab, or two warriors of Moab, depending on how the Hebrew is translated, since that wording is not entirely clear. He also went down into a pit and killed a lion in the midst of a pit in a time of snow, a difficult and slippery moment.

This passage is part of the list of David's mighty men at the end of the book. The narrator names the men who served the king with courage. Benaiah stands out as someone highly respected, although he did not become one of the first three.

For today: courage often shows itself in uncomfortable situations and without applause. We can ask God for strength to do what is right when it is hard, without expecting recognition.
exp.20:15:
During another battle against the Philistines, the verse says, a warrior named Ishbi-benob tried to kill David. He was a descendant of "the sons of the giant" (probably a family line of very tall and strong men). His spear had a bronze tip weighing about three hundred shekels, that is, close to three and a half kilograms. He also carried a new sword. "Girded" means that he wore it at his waist.

Here the book's narrator speaks. He tells that David, already an older man, went out to fight and grew weary. At that moment he was left vulnerable. The Bible does not explain in detail where this line of giants came from; it only shows that they were fearsome enemies. Soon Abishai rescued David, and his men decided that he would no longer go out to battle.

No one can carry everything alone, not even a strong leader. Recognizing our weariness and letting others help us is not weakness but wisdom. God often cares for us through people close to us.
exp.22:8:
This verse introduces Eleazar, son of Dodo, of the Ahohite family, as one of the most outstanding of David's three mighty men. He was with David when they stood against the Philistines, who had gathered to fight. At that moment, the men of Israel had withdrawn or gone up, leaving Eleazar almost alone at the front.

The writer of Samuel lists David's mighty men as a tribute to those who served him. The text that follows shows that Eleazar fought until his hand grew weary and stuck to his sword. It makes clear that the true source of the victory was God, and that the LORD brought about a great salvation. Commentators do not agree on the details of how Israel withdrew, but they do agree that Eleazar resisted with courage.

For today: sometimes we are called to stand firm even when others pull back. Let us do so with faithfulness and honest weariness, remembering that the final victory comes from God.
exp.18:32:
It says that King David invites Barzillai to cross the Jordan with him and to live in Jerusalem. David promises to look after him and to feed him at his own table, that is, at the king's own table with him. The word "Jerusalem" is the older spelling of Jerusalem, and the phrase "said unto" means "said to."

David is speaking as he returns to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. Barzillai, an elderly wealthy man from Gilead, had supported him with food when David was in Mahanaim. David wants to thank him for his kindness and to honor him. Barzillai, however, humbly answers that because of his age he would no longer enjoy the court, and he does not want to be a burden.

For today: let us learn to thank generously those who have helped us. Also, like Barzillai, let us be simple and realistic about the stages of our lives, without envying honors we do not need.
exp.6:18:
David tells God that what he had already given him seemed like a lot, but now God goes further and makes him a promise for the future of his family. "House" here means descendants or dynasty. "Servant" is how David refers to himself, with humility. The last question is hard to translate. It may mean that God does not treat David the way a man would, or that this promise reaches to all of humanity. Scholars understand it in several ways.

David speaks in prayer, after the prophet Nathan brought him God's promise: his kingdom and his family would endure. David sits before the Lord, amazed that God has chosen him.

For today: when God blesses you, respond as David did, with humility and gratitude, recognizing that everything comes from his grace and not from your merits.
exp.6:2:
Nathan tells King David to do all that is in his heart, because the Lord is with him. "Go" is an old way of saying "go ahead, do it." "Is with thee" means "is with you."

David had just been given rest from his enemies. Living in a house of cedar, he was troubled that the ark of God was still kept in a tent. Nathan, the prophet, answered right away by encouraging his good desire. But that same night God spoke to Nathan and corrected the answer: it would not be David who built the temple. Nathan spoke with good intentions, but without first consulting God.

For today: a good desire is not always God's plan or his timing. Before we act, and before we give advice, let us pray and seek God's guidance, and be willing to be corrected.
exp.16:2:
Here Ahitophel says that if only King David is killed, he will bring the people back to Absalom, the way a bride returns to her husband. The word "bring back" comes from the verse's wording of "bring back," and the verse uses "a" in the sense of "to." The phrase "the man whom thou seekest" shows that David is the only one Absalom wants to eliminate. In this way, he says, all the people will be at peace.

Ahitophel, once David's counselor, now supports Absalom's rebellion. He proposes a quick, surprise attack while David is exhausted. His plan sounds logical, and everyone likes it. However, Absalom decides to also listen to Hushai, who was in fact loyal to David. What follows shows that God would work through that second counsel.

For today: a piece of advice can sound wise and still not be good. Before following a plan, let us ask God for discernment and compare what we hear with his Word, not only with what suits us.
exp.2:23:
Joab comes before King David and confronts him with a sharp question: "What have you done?" He tells the king that Abner had come to him, and asks why he let him go. Some older wording needs explaining: where the text uses the word "díjole," the verse you're reading has "said," and where it uses "habíase venido," it has "came," and where it uses "fuése," it has "gone."

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. Abner, commander of Saul's army, had come to Hebron to make an agreement with David and unite Israel, and David had sent him away in peace. Joab had just returned from a raid. He distrusts Abner, and the Bible also reminds us that Abner had killed Asahel, Joab's brother. So there may be personal reasons behind his words, along with his concern for the kingdom.

Before we accuse or act against someone, it is wise to examine our own hearts. Joab says he is protecting the king, but perhaps resentment is what moves him. Let us ask God for sincerity, so that we can tell the difference between a just concern and a vengeance wearing a disguise.
exp.5:7:
This verse tells us that David was saddened, or grieved, because God had struck Uzzah. That is why they called that place Perez-uzzah, which means "breach upon Uzzah" or "outbreak against Uzzah," and why it was still called that when the account was written.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David was bringing the ark of God to Jerusalem, but they were carrying it on a cart, and not as God had directed, by carrying it with poles. Uzzah touched it, and God judged him. Some understand that David was also angry; others, that he was hurt. The text says that he was saddened, and then he felt fear.

For today: God is loving, but he is also holy. Let us draw near to him with reverence and obedience, not only with good intentions.
exp.15:10:
Here David tells Abishai and his servants that his own son, Absalom, born from him, is seeking his life. So is it any surprise that a Benjamite, Shimei, curses him? David asks them to let him alone, because the Lord has bidden him.

David flees from Jerusalem because Absalom rebelled against him. On the way, Shimei, from the family of Saul, insults him and throws stones at him. Abishai wants to kill him, but David stops him. His words about God can be understood in several ways: he probably recognizes that God allows this humiliation, without saying that God approves of Shimei's wickedness.

For today: when we are criticized or treated badly, there is no need to respond with anger right away. We can pause, examine our hearts, and place our pain in God's hands, trusting that he sees.
exp.9:1:
Here David decides to show kindness to Hanun, the new king of Ammon, because his father Nahash had died. The phrase "show kindness" means acting with goodness and loyalty. "To comfort him" means to offer condolences. David sends his servants with that message of support, and they arrive in the land of Ammon.

The text does not explain how Nahash helped David. It only says that David wants to return that favor. That is why he sends an official delegation, as was customary between kings. What follows shows that Hanun's advisers suspected bad intentions, and the king humiliated the messengers.

For today: practice gratitude through concrete actions. If someone helped you, look for ways to honor them or their family in their grief. And even when others misread your good intentions, keep acting with kindness and without malice.
exp.4:13:
This verse begins a list of the sons who were born to David in Jerusalem. The first four names are Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. The phrase "were born unto him" means that these were his sons, and "Jerusalem" is the city we now spell Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not David. After David was recognized as king over all Israel and set up his capital in Jerusalem, the text mentions his growing family. The list shows the expansion of his kingdom, though it also reveals that he took more wives, something the Bible later shows with painful consequences. Solomon would later be the king who followed David.

For today: God cares for people, not just for great events. Every name matters. Value your family, pray for it, and do not neglect it for your goals or responsibilities.
exp.20:0:
This verse tells that in David's time there was a famine that lasted three years in a row. David sought God to learn the cause, and God answered that the trouble came from Saul and from his household, which carried a guilt of blood, because Saul had killed the Gibeonites. Asking the Lord for guidance means David inquired of God, looking for his direction.

The narrator explains in the following verses that the Gibeonites were not Israelites. Israel had made them a covenant of peace (Joshua 9). Saul had attacked them, and God took that injustice seriously. The Bible does not say here when this happened, so we do not know more details.

For today: when there are problems, it is good to ask God with humility, and to be willing to acknowledge and repair injustices, even past ones, and to keep what we have promised.
exp.6:21:
This verse is a song of praise. David says that God is great because there is no one like him, and that there is no other God besides him. He affirms this based on what Israel had heard for generations about God's works. The phrase "you have made yourself great" means that God shows himself to be great and worthy of honor by what he does.

David speaks in prayer, sitting before the Lord. God had just promised him, through the prophet Nathan, that his family would reign for a long time. David had wanted to build a temple, but God promised him something more: to establish his house, that is, his descendants. David responds with amazement and gratitude, remembering how God had rescued Israel from Egypt.

For today: before asking for anything, take a moment to remember what God has already done in your life and in the history of his people. Thanking him and acknowledging his greatness helps you trust him more.
exp.20:5:
The Gibeonites ask that seven descendants of Saul be handed over to them to be executed by hanging before the Lord, in Gibeah, Saul's city, which they call "the chosen one of the Lord." David answers: "I will give them."

There was a famine in the land, and the text explains that Saul had mistreated and killed Gibeonites, despite Israel's ancient oath to them. David asks how the wrong can be made right, and they ask for this kind of justice. The text does not say that God commanded this method, and it is a difficult passage that is interpreted in several ways.

Today we learn that injustices and broken promises matter to God and leave consequences. If we have harmed someone, it is good to acknowledge it and seek to make amends with humility, without hiding it.
exp.3:11:
It says that David ordered his young soldiers to execute the two men who had killed Ish-bosheth. Then they cut off their hands and feet and hanged them up beside the pool at Hebron, in full view of everyone. Ish-bosheth's head, by contrast, was buried with honor in the tomb of Abner.

Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, ruled over part of Israel. Two of his captains murdered him while he slept and brought his head to David, expecting a reward. David, who had previously punished the man who announced Saul's death, condemned them for killing an innocent man. Their punishment was public and very severe, which was common in that era.

For today: God is not pleased to achieve good ends through unjust means. Let us seek justice without taking advantage of another's wrong, and honor the truth even when no one rewards us for it.
exp.21:40:
This verse says that God caused David to see his enemies flee and turn their backs on him. The phrase "giving me the necks" means that they showed him the back of their necks, that is, that they retreated defeated. In this way David was able to destroy those who hated him. The victory is presented as a gift from God.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, written when the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. It is a poem of praise, and it also appears in Psalm 18. The imagery of war is strong and typical of its time. David insists that the triumph was not his own but God's, who strengthened him.

For today: when you overcome a difficulty, do not take all the credit for yourself. Pause to thank God. And in the face of your struggles, remember that He can give you strength and a way through, not in order to hate people, but to overcome evil with His help.
exp.21:31:
This verse asks two questions to make a point: there is no other God like the Lord, and no one is as strong as our God. The word "save" here means "except."

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. He has just said that God gives him victory and that his word is pure and protects those who trust in him. Here David acknowledges that his strength was not his own, but came from God.

For today: when you feel weak or face a great problem, do not rely only on your own abilities. Before you act, take a moment to tell God, "You are my strength," and ask him for wisdom and courage for the next step.
exp.11:16:
It says that the elders of David's house came to him to lift him up from the ground, where he was lying. But David would not get up or eat food with them. "Elders of his house" refers to the older men of his family or his court whom he trusted. "Bread" means food in general.

The narrator recounts what happened after David's sin with Bathsheba and against Uriah. Nathan confronted him, and the child of the two of them fell ill. David, in grief and repentance, fasted and pleaded with God for the child's life. The elders did not want to see him suffer so much, but he kept crying out to God.

When pain crushes us, there is no single right way to react, but we can do what David did: bring our anguish to God with sincerity. And if someone is suffering, walking alongside them with tenderness is worth more than hurrying them to feel better.
exp.9:9:
This verse tells us that Joab, commander of Israel's army, placed the rest of his soldiers under the command of his brother Abishai. He charged him with arranging them in battle formation to face the Ammonites.

Joab is the one acting here, and the text narrates it. The Ammonites had hired Syrian troops, and Joab found himself surrounded: enemies in front of him and behind him. So he divided his forces. He took the best soldiers to face the Syrians, while Abishai was left in charge of the rest against Ammon. Afterward they agreed to help each other.

For today: when we face pressure from several sides, we do not have to carry everything alone. Joab organized, shared out responsibilities, and trusted his brother. We can do the same with family, church, or work: ask for help, offer support, and do our part with effort, leaving the outcome in God's hands.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that David ruled in Hebron for seven years and a half. During that time he reigned only over the tribe of Judah, his own house.

The narrator of the book, who keeps track of the time, is the one speaking. Meanwhile, Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, ruled over the rest of Israel. The book does not explain why there is a difference in the years: some think Ish-bosheth took time to be established, or that there were years of war and transition. This is a point that is not entirely clear. What we can see is that the kingdom was divided and that conflict would soon come.

For today: God keeps his promises, but often does so with patience. David was anointed, yet he waited years to reign over all of Israel. If you are waiting, remain faithful where you are.
exp.0:8:
He asks the young man to stand over him, that is, to come close and kill him. He says that anguish has seized him, that is, severe pain and distress, but that "my life is yet whole in me," meaning that he is still alive.

The one speaking is a young Amalekite who comes before David after the battle in which Saul died. He tells how the king died and presents his crown and armband, hoping for a reward. His account does not match 1 Samuel 31, where Saul falls on his own sword. Many believe he lied to gain David's favor, although the text does not state this directly.

Today it reminds us that we should not take advantage of others' pain or shape the truth to gain an advantage. God values honesty and compassion.
exp.20:16:
Abishai, nephew of David and son of Zeruiah, came to help him just when a Philistine giant was about to kill him. Abishai struck down the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men bound themselves to him with an oath: he would never again go out with them to battle, so that he would not put out the light of Israel. The light stands as a picture of the king's life and guidance, which gave light and hope to the people.

The ones speaking are the group of soldiers loyal to David. David was already older, had grown weary in the fighting, and had been in mortal danger. His men understood that losing the king could leave the whole people in darkness, and so they decided to protect him.

For today: God helps us through other people. Let us acknowledge our limits, accept the support of others, and also care for those who serve as a light for others.
exp.4:7:
David says that whoever goes up through the "gutter" (probably a water channel or tunnel; it is not known for certain) will strike the Jebusites. He calls those who mocked him "the lame and the blind," and says that his soul "hates" them, meaning he detests them. From this came a saying about the blind and the lame not entering the house.

David is the new king and attacks Jerusalem. The Jebusites, confident in their walls, mocked him, saying that even the blind and the lame could stop him. David responds with anger. Scholars debate the exact meaning of the saying. What is clear is that David takes the stronghold, and that "the LORD was with him."

For today: do not lose heart at mockery or at obstacles that seem impossible. Trust in God, act with courage, and remember that Jesus did welcome the blind and the lame with compassion.
exp.0:24:
This verse is a lament. David expresses his grief because strong and brave men died in the middle of battle. He mentions Jonathan in a special way, saying that he was slain on the heights, that is, on the hills or high places where he fell. The "mighty" are the warriors, and "fallen" means that they died.

David speaks in a funeral song. Saul and his son Jonathan had just died fighting against the Philistines. Although Saul had pursued him, David does not celebrate his death, but mourns the king and, above all, his friend Jonathan, with whom he shared a very deep friendship.

For today: when someone dies or we feel the pain of a loss, we can grieve honestly, without hiding our sorrow. We can also honor the good that was in other people, even if the relationship was difficult, and thank God for faithful friends.
exp.15:8:
Abishai, one of David's warriors, is outraged when he sees Shimei insulting the king. He calls him a "dead dog," an expression of contempt meaning someone of no worth or power. He asks permission to go over and take off his head. The phrase about taking off the head simply means that he would take off Shimei's head. "Let me go over" means he asks for permission to cross over to where Shimei is.

David is fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled against him. Shimei, a man from the family of Saul, takes advantage of the moment to curse him and throw in his face the blood of that house. Abishai reacts violently to defend David, but David stops him and decides to bear the insult with humility, leaving everything in God's hands.

When someone attacks us, our quick reaction is usually to take revenge. David teaches us to stop, to listen for whether there is some truth in the criticism, and to trust that God is the one who brings justice.
exp.6:16:
This verse says that the prophet Nathan told David everything God had said to him, leaving nothing out and adding nothing. The phrase "according to" is the key idea here, meaning that Nathan's words matched exactly what he had been given, and "vision" refers to the message Nathan received from God.

God had just promised David that his house and his kingdom would be made secure forever. David wanted to build a temple for God, but God answered through Nathan that He Himself would build a house for David, meaning a line of descendants. Many Christians see in this promise a sign that points to Jesus, a descendant of David.

Today we can learn from Nathan's faithfulness: when we share what God says in His Word, we should do so with honesty, without changing it to please others or to make it fit our own tastes.
exp.6:25:
This verse is part of a prayer. David asks that God's name be honored forever, and that people will recognize that the Lord of hosts, that is, the God of all power, is truly God over Israel. He also asks that his family remain firm before God.

David speaks after God, through the prophet Nathan, promised him a lasting line and kingdom. David does not begin by asking for honor for himself, but responds with humility and asks God to fulfill what he has already said. Many Christians see in this promise a foreshadowing of Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when you ask something of God, try to make your greatest desire that his name be honored. Trust his promises and pray based on what he has already said in his Word.
exp.17:1:
This verse says that David divided his army into three groups. He placed one group under Joab, another under Abishai, Joab's brother, and another under Ittai, a man from Gath. The verse's quoted word about "consigned" is rewritten here: it means that David handed them over to these men, putting them in charge. Then David announced that he himself would also go out with them into battle.

David is fleeing from his son Absalom, who rebelled against him. He is in Mahanaim, on the other side of the Jordan, and is preparing for battle. Ittai was a foreigner and had been loyal to David. As is seen later, the people do not let the king go, because his life was too valuable. David accepts their counsel.

For today: a good leader shares responsibilities and trusts others, but is also willing to share the risk. Moreover, he knows how to listen with humility when wise people give him advice different from his own.
exp.11:5:
David says the rich man must return the little ewe lamb multiplied by four. The word "tantos," meaning "times," would mean paying four times its value. And he gives the reason: the man did a cruel thing and had no pity, that is, he felt no compassion for the poor man.

Here David speaks as king and judge. The prophet Nathan had told him a story about a rich man who took away a poor man's only little ewe lamb. David did not know the story was about himself, because of his sin with Bathsheba and against Uriah. The law of Moses required paying four sheep for a stolen and slaughtered sheep (Exodus 22:1). Without knowing it, David pronounced his own sentence.

For today: it is easy to see clearly the sin of others and to soften our own. Let us ask God for a humble heart that examines itself first and acts with mercy.
exp.23:3:
This verse says that King David insisted on his order, even though Joab and the army commanders did not agree. The word "Notwithstanding" in the verse means "nevertheless," and the phrase "prevailed against" means that the king's order won out. So Joab and the commanders left the king's presence to take the count, that is, to number the people of Israel.

David is the one giving the orders, and Joab, his general, had already asked him respectfully why he wanted to count the people. Joab seemed to see a danger. The text does not explain all the reasons, but later the account shows that this census displeased God (v. 10).

For today: when we have authority or influence, let us listen to the wise advice of others. Not everything we are able to do is wise to do. Let us ask God for humility to stop and examine our intentions.
exp.12:36:
But Absalom fled and went to Talmai, son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son every day.

It is not entirely clear whether David was mourning for Amnon, who was dead, or for Absalom, who was far away. Many think it was for both.

The account tells that Absalom had his brother Amnon killed because of what Amnon had done to Tamar, Absalom's sister. Then he fled to Geshur, the land of his maternal grandfather. The narrator shows David's grief as a father and as a king, in a family wounded by sin and violence.

When a family is broken, the pain is real and it is not always resolved quickly. Bring your sadness to God and seek reconciliation with patience, without letting revenge make the decision.
exp.3:3:
This verse tells that Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son who was five years old and lame in his feet. When the news came that Saul and Jonathan had died, his nurse picked him up and fled in fear. In her hurry, the boy fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.

The narrator pauses the story of the murder of Ish-bosheth, another son of Saul, to introduce Mephibosheth. With Saul and Jonathan dead, the house of Saul was losing its power, and a young heir was in danger. Later, David will show him kindness for the sake of Jonathan.

For today: sometimes our lives are marked by accidents or tragedies we did not choose. But God does not define us by those wounds. You can trust that He cares for the vulnerable and can bring kindness, even after pain.
exp.21:13:
This verse says that God made his voice heard like thunder coming from the heavens. The word "thundered" means it sounded like thunder, and "the most High" is a name for God that stresses he is above all things. "Uttered his voice" means he spoke with force, so that everyone could hear him.

David, now older, speaks in a song of gratitude. He writes it after God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. He uses images of storm, fire, and trembling to describe God's power when he comes to deliver his servant. These are poetic images, not necessarily a literal account of an event.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems or fear, remember that God is neither far away nor silent. You can cry out to him with confidence, believing that he has the power to act on your behalf. And when he helps you, do not forget to give him thanks, as David did.
exp.21:32:
This verse says that God is the one who gives me strength and power to keep going, and that he himself clears the obstacles from my path. The word "strength" here refers to power or force. The phrase "strengthens me" means he fortifies or secures me. The phrase "makes my way perfect" can be understood as removing hindrances, or, as some other translations render it, making the way secure and sound.

King David is the speaker. This song of thanksgiving was written when God delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul, as the opening of the chapter explains. David looks back and recognizes that he did not triumph by his own ability, but because God sustained and guided him in the midst of battles and dangers.

For today: when you face a difficult task, do not rely on your own strength alone. Before taking the step, ask God for strength and direction, and then thank him for every advance, large or small.
exp.3:5:
Two brothers entered Ish-bosheth's house disguised as wheat merchants, as if they were going to do some business. The word for their disguise refers to clothing or costume, so the verse's "as though they would have fetched wheat" describes exactly that. They wounded him in the belly, near the ribs, and then fled. The Hebrew text of this verse is difficult, and some translations read it a little differently.

The narrator of the book tells how Ish-bosheth, son of Saul and David's rival, was treacherously murdered while taking an afternoon nap. Rechab and Baanah were his captains. They killed their own king, believing David would reward them. But later David punished them for this instead of rewarding them.

For today: do not use deceit or violence to achieve what seems good or convenient. God does not need our tricks, and gaining something through wickedness rarely ends well.
exp.3:8:
David answers Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite. Before giving his reply, David makes a solemn oath: "As the Lord liveth", that is, "as surely as God lives." He then states that the Lord has redeemed or rescued his soul from all adversity, meaning that the Lord has delivered him from every danger and trouble.

David is speaking as king in Hebron. The two brothers had just murdered Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, while he was sleeping, and they brought his head to David expecting a reward. They presented the killing as the work of God. David, on the other hand, recalls that God had looked after him without any need for betrayal or unjust violence.

For today: when God has sustained you through difficult moments, you do not need to achieve your goals through deception or injustice. Trust that He can carry out His plans in a clean and righteous way.
exp.1:1:
This verse tells that David went up to Hebron, as God had directed him. He was accompanied by his two wives: Ahinoam, from Jezreel, and Abigail, who had previously been Nabal's wife, from Carmel. "Went up" is used because Hebron was located in higher ground.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not David. Saul had died, and David did not move on his own initiative, but first asked God where to go. By naming the wives, the account shows that David was not going alone, but with his family. Afterward, in Hebron, the people of Judah anointed him as king.

For today: before making an important decision, ask God in prayer and seek his direction. And remember that your decisions also affect your family, so move forward with them in mind.
exp.20:14:
This verse says that the Philistines went to war against Israel again. David went down with his servants to face them, and in the middle of the battle David grew weary. The word "waxed" in the verse means "grew", and "servants" here means his fighting men, his soldiers.

The narrator tells this after the story of the famine and how the bones of Saul were buried. God had already been moved to act on behalf of the land. But the war with the Philistines was still going on. David was no longer the young man who defeated Goliath, and his weariness sets up what follows: a giant nearly kills him, and his men protect him. Some think David was older; the text does not give his exact age.

Even strong leaders grow tired and need help. You do not have to carry everything alone. Accept the support of others and rest in time, trusting that God sustains your life.
exp.21:49:
David says he will give thanks to God publicly, even before the nations that are not Israel. "I will give thanks" here does not mean admitting sins, but recognizing and declaring with praise who God is. "Among the heathen" refers to the foreign nations. David also says he will sing praises to the name of the Lord.

David speaks, already in his old age, in a song of gratitude because God rescued him from his enemies, among them Saul. This same song appears almost word for word in Psalm 18. After telling how God rescued him and gave him victory, David responds with praise. According to the New Testament, Paul quotes this verse in Romans 15:9 to speak of the nations also praising God.

When God helps you through a difficulty, do not keep your thankfulness to yourself. Tell someone about it this week and praise him with a song or a prayer aloud.
exp.13:5:
This verse tells a story that the woman presents to King David. She says she had two sons, who fought in the field, and since there was no one nearby to separate them, one struck the other and killed him.

The woman is from Tekoa. Joab sent her and taught her what to say, so that David would see her situation as a parallel to his own: Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and was living in exile. The story was not real but a prepared account meant to move the king's heart.

For today: God invites us to look at family conflicts with mercy and truth. Before we judge harshly, let us ask whether we seek justice with compassion, and whether we are willing to help reconcile what is broken.
exp.15:1:
King David asks Ziba what he means by all he has brought. Ziba explains that the donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for those who grow faint in the wilderness, that is, in the open, empty countryside.

David is fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Ziba, servant of Mephibosheth, arrives with supplies just when David is in trouble. Then he accuses his master of wanting the throne, and David believes him and gives him everything. The Bible later shows that Ziba may have been lying, although the text lets us see this only with some caution.

For today: helping someone who is suffering is beautiful, but we must make sure our generosity is sincere. And when we hear accusations against others, it is wise to wait and find out before we judge.
exp.0:22:
This verse says that Saul and Jonathan were loved and dear while they lived, and that not even death separated them. They were swifter than eagles and stronger than lions. The words about being swift and separated are explained as meaning quick, and divided, respectively.

David speaks in a song of mourning, sometimes called "the song of the bow." He has just learned that Saul and Jonathan died in battle against the Philistines on Mount Gilboa. Although Saul had pursued him to kill him, David does not rejoice: he honors both of them and weeps openly. Some think that "were not divided" refers only to dying together in battle, although their relationship as father and son was not always harmonious.

Today we can learn to remember the good in people, even in those who hurt us. In the face of a loss, instead of holding on to resentment, we can thank God for what was valuable in them and honor with respect the one who has passed away.
exp.14:3:
Absalom says that he would like to be made judge in the land, so that everyone who has a suit or a matter needing settlement would come to him, and he would do them justice. "Suit" is a legal dispute, and "matter" is an issue that needs to be settled.

Absalom, the son of King David, would stand each morning beside the gate of the city, where cases were heard. He would speak with the people who came to see the king, telling them that their cause was just and that no one would listen to them. In this way he criticized his father and won sympathy. The text says he "stole the hearts" of Israel, and this prepares the way for his rebellion.

Let us take care not to be carried away by fine words and by one who seeks to be admired. Let us ask God for sincerity to serve others without hidden motives.
exp.0:12:
David asked the young man who brought him the news of Saul's death: "Where are you from?" The young man answered that he was the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite.

David and his men had just wept, torn their clothes, and fasted for Saul, Jonathan, and the people of God. This young man claimed he had killed Saul, believing he would receive a reward. David asks about his origin because he wants to understand who he is and what he was doing there. That he was a foreigner and an Amalekite, a longtime enemy of Israel, highlights that he had no excuse for laying a hand on the Lord's anointed. The Bible presents this young man's account in a way that some scholars see as true and others see as exaggerated.

For today: respect the authority God allows, and do not rejoice at the fall of others, even if it was to your advantage. Weep with those who suffer, and do not seek advantage from their pain.
exp.22:22:
This verse speaks of Benaiah. It says he was more honourable than the thirty, a group of David's outstanding warriors, but that he did not reach the level of the first three. The verse that followed was about old spellings and quoted words; here the source-language terms are simply translated: "the thirty" refers to the group of warriors, "the first three" refers to the top three among them, and the word for "set" in the verse is the one in "And David set him over his guard."

These words are part of the "last words of David," a list of his brave men. The text wants to acknowledge and remember those who served the king with courage. Benaiah is presented as someone of great worth, though not the first of them all. Scholars understand the exact sense of the phrase "over his guard" in different ways.

For today: you do not need to be number one to be valuable. God sees the faithfulness and courage of those who serve steadily. Do your part with bravery and honesty, without comparing yourself too much to others, and trust that your service will be remembered.
exp.14:35:
He says that the sons of the two priests, Ahimaaz (son of Zadok) and Jonathan (son of Abiathar), are with them in Jerusalem. David explains to Hushai that through these young men they will send him word of everything they hear.

David speaks with Hushai, his faithful friend. Absalom, David's son, had rebelled, and David was fleeing Jerusalem. Hushai was to return to the city, pretend loyalty to Absalom, and help defeat the counsel of Ahithophel. The priests and their sons would be the secret channel for passing along information. The Bible here shows David's plan, and later the account says that God determined to defeat Ahithophel's counsel.

For today: in difficult times, let us not act alone. Let us pray and seek faithful and trustworthy people who will help us with wisdom, truth, and good counsel.
exp.10:9:
