Some people told David that Uriah had not gone home. Then David asked him why he had not gone down to rest, since he had just come back from a long journey.

David wants to hide his sin with Bathsheba, who is pregnant. Her husband Uriah was at war, and David called him back so he would sleep with his wife and it would seem the child was his. But Uriah did not go home; he stayed with the king's servants. David, surprised, asks him to account for himself, without admitting his real reason.

Today, this scene reminds us that covering one mistake with more deceit only makes it worse. While David pretended to show interest, Uriah showed loyalty and self-sacrifice. If we have failed, the best thing is to come to God with sincerity and repent, as David later did in Psalm 51.
exp.13:17:
In this passage, King David, after listening to the woman, asks her to be completely honest and not to hold anything back from what he is going to ask her. She replies that the king may speak.

Here David speaks with a woman from Tekoa. She had told a sad story about her sons, but Joab, the commander of the army, had sent her and told her what to say. David suspects there is something behind all of that, and that is why he asks for frankness. The following scene confirms that Joab planned the account to lead the king to be reconciled with his son Absalom.

For today: truth told simply helps to resolve problems. When we seek advice or correct something, it is good to speak with honesty and listen with humility, without hiding what is important.
exp.18:19:
Shimei admits before King David that he has sinned. He says he has come "the first of all the house of Joseph," that is, before the other tribes of the north, to go down to the Jordan and meet the king. "Servant" is a humble way of addressing him.

Shimei is the man who had cursed and insulted David when the king was fleeing from Jerusalem because of Absalom's rebellion. Now David returns as king, and Shimei, fearing punishment, comes forward humbly and asks for forgiveness. Some think he also hoped to protect himself with this gesture, and the text does not say whether his repentance was sincere. Even so, David spares his life.

Acknowledging our sin simply and without excuses is the first step in asking for forgiveness. God invites us to return to him, and we too can show mercy to those who have offended us.
exp.20:11:
This verse tells how David went to collect the bones of King Saul and of his son Jonathan. The men of Jabesh-gilead had taken them away secretly, from the street of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them after defeating Saul on Mount Gilboa.

This happens after a three-year famine in Israel. David sought God and understood that Saul had done harm to the Gibeonites. The sons of Rizpah had been executed, and she had cared for them with great grief and steadfastness. When David learned of this, he acted to give everyone a proper burial.

For today: God values the dignity and the memory of people. We can honor those who have died and humbly repair the wounds of the past, rather than ignoring them.
exp.20:13:
This verse tells how the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan were buried with honor in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, in the tomb of Kish, Saul's father. "They buried" means they laid them to rest, and "God was moved" means that God was appeased and showed favor toward the land. Everything was done as King David had commanded, and afterward God answered the prayers made for the land.

The narrator is the author of the book, who recounts events from David's reign. Before this there had been three years of famine, and David sought God. The cause was a wrong that Saul had committed against the Gibeonites, whom he had mistreated. David addressed that matter and also gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan, which the Philistines had exposed.

For today: God cares about justice and about making right what was done wrongly. If there is something we can correct or restore, it is good to do so with humility and honor.
exp.21:36:
It says that God gave David a wide and firm path to walk on, so that his feet would not slip nor his knees give way. "You enlarged my steps" means that God opened up a safe space for him to place his feet. The image is of someone who moves forward with steadiness, never wavering.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. Before this verse he acknowledges that God trained him for battle and protected him like a shield. Afterward he speaks of pursuing his enemies. David credits God for his firmness, not his own strength.

For today: when you face a hard season and feel your strength failing, ask God for steadiness instead of trusting only in yourself. Give thanks for the times he held you up without your noticing.
exp.11:20:
David's servants are astonished at his behavior. While the child was alive, David fasted and wept; but when he died, he rose up and ate. The words "you rose up" are a rendering of the phrase that appears in the verse, and "bread" here means food in general.

The servants speak. The child was the son born from David's relationship with Bathsheba, and he was sick as a consequence of David's sin. While he lived, David pleaded with God for his life. When the child died, David worshiped in the house of the LORD and then ate again. The servants expected more mourning, not less; that is why they ask.

For today: there is a time to plead with God with all your heart, and another time to accept his answer with humility. When sorrow comes, we can worship, rest in God, and move forward, without ceasing to feel sadness.
exp.16:7:
Hushai tells Absalom that David and his men are very brave warriors, and that right now they are full of anger and grief, like a bear that has lost her cubs. He also reminds him that David is a man of war with a great deal of experience, and that he will not spend the night together with the common people in the camp.

Hushai, David's friend, speaks here while pretending to take Absalom's side. His real purpose was to defeat Ahithophel's advice, which proposed attacking David at once. Hushai wanted to buy time so that David could organize his forces and cross the Jordan. The text presents this as part of God's protection over David.

Today we can learn that wisdom and good counsel matter a great deal. Before deciding something important, it is wise to think carefully, listen closely, and pray, because a hasty decision can turn out to be very costly.
exp.10:23:
Here the messenger tells David how the battle at Rabbah went. He says that the enemy's archers were shooting arrows from the wall and that some of the king's soldiers died. At the end he adds, almost in passing, that Uriah the Hittite also died. The "shooters" are the archers, and "thy servants" are David's soldiers.

The messenger repeats Joab's report. Joab had ordered Uriah to go to a dangerous place, as David had requested in a letter, and that is why other soldiers were lost. Joab knew the king might become angry at the approach to the wall, so he mentioned Uriah's death to calm him. David, however, responds coldly.

For today: a hidden sin never stays small; it drags others along and leaves victims. If we have failed, the best thing is to confess early and seek God's forgiveness, not to cover it up.
exp.12:7:
She went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took flour, kneaded it, and made small cakes (little fried cakes or rolls) in front of him, and prepared them so they were ready to eat.

The narrator recounts a key moment in a painful story. Amnon, the son of David, pretended to be sick so that he could be alone with Tamar, his half-sister. David, not knowing what Amnon was plotting, sent her to care for him. Tamar acts with obedience and goodwill, not imagining the deception. What follows is a serious abuse against her.

For today: the Bible does not hide evil or wickedness that disguises itself as need. We should look after the vulnerable, pay close attention when something seems wrong, and protect those who serve in good faith, so they are not left exposed to people who could harm them.
exp.22:7:
Here begins the list of David's mightiest men. The verse speaks of a warrior who was the chief among them and who struck down eight hundred men in a single battle. The text is part of the history of Israel, which honors the heroes of David's kingdom.

There are doubts about the exact name and the number. In 1 Chronicles 11:11 the name appears as "Jashobeam" and the number as three hundred slain. There may have been an error in copying, or these may be separate accounts. No one knows for certain. After speaking of the wicked, the text shows those who served faithfully.

Today we can value and thank those who serve with courage and steadfastness, often without many people noticing. We can also ask God for the courage to faithfully do what is ours to do, knowing that He sees and remembers our service.
exp.7:1:
It says David defeated the Moabites and made them lie down on the ground. Then he measured them with a cord: two portions of the line were for being put to death, and one full portion was for remaining alive. The survivors became David's servants and paid him tribute, that is, compulsory taxes. The word "smote" means defeated, and "measured them" is the same as "measured them with a line."

It is a historical account, not a speech. It tells how David extended his kingdom after defeating the Philistines. The passage does not explain why he treated Moab this way, and scholars do not agree on the details. Some think it refers to prisoners of war in a very violent era.

For today: this passage reminds us that the Bible honestly recounts the harshness of human history. It invites us to be thankful for the mercy of Christ and to seek peace, treating with compassion even those who have been our adversaries.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that Abner is going to take the kingdom away from the house of Saul and establish David's throne over all the people. "Translate" means to move something from one place to another. "Confirm" means to make something firm and secure. "From Dan even to Beer-sheba" was a way of naming the whole territory, from north to south.

Abner, commander of Saul's army, speaks very angrily. Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, had rebuked him over a matter involving a woman named Rizpah. Abner feels insulted after having been loyal, and he decides to switch sides. He says that God had sworn to give the kingdom to David. His motive mixes personal anger with the recognition of what God had promised.

For today: God carries out his plans even when people act from mixed motives. Let us ask God to cleanse our intentions, so that we obey his will with a sincere heart and not out of pride or anger.
exp.19:4:
This verse says that Amasa went out to gather the men of Judah, as the king had commanded him, but he took longer than the three days David had set for him. The word "tarried" in the verse means he delayed or was late. The verse does not give the reason for the delay.

The one telling the story is the narrator. David had just returned to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion, and Amasa was the commander David had put in place of Joab. Another uprising had broken out, the revolt of Sheba, and quick action was needed. Amasa's delay caused David to send others after Sheba. The Bible does not say why it took so long; some think he had difficulty winning the trust of Judah, but that is only one possibility.

For today: when you are given something important, carry it out on time, or let the right person know if you will be late. Responsibility and honesty in small things care for others and show faithfulness.
exp.21:5:
He says that David felt surrounded by pain and mortal danger. "Hell" here translates the Hebrew word "Sheol," which in this context means the place of the dead, the grave. The "snares of death" are like hunters' traps, and "prevented" means that they confronted him by surprise, when he did not expect it.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and describes how close he came to dying. This same song appears, nearly word for word, in Psalm 18. It is poetic language, with strong images to express a real anguish.

For today: when you feel trapped or caught off guard by a trial, do what David did: cry out to God with honesty. He hears those who seek him, even in the darkest moments.
exp.11:18:
This verse tells of the moment David realizes that his son has died. Seeing that his servants were whispering among themselves, he understood what had happened. He asked them directly, "Is the child dead?" and they answered, "He is dead." The word "servants" refers to his attendants or the household staff who worked for him.

The child was the son of David and Bathsheba, who became ill as a consequence of David's sin. For seven days, David fasted and pleaded with God for the child's life, lying on the ground. His servants were afraid to give him the news, thinking it might harm him. Here the narrator describes how David came to know it without being told.

For today: when painful news arrives, it is better to face the truth honestly than to hide it. David asked plainly and then worshiped God. We can bring our pain to God and go on trusting in Him.
exp.8:12:
It says that Mephibosheth stayed to live in Jerusalem, because he had a fixed place at King David's table. It also makes clear that he was lame in both feet. "Dwelt" means "lived," and "continually" shows that this was something constant, not a one-day invitation.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He closes the story in which David seeks out someone from Saul's family to show kindness, because of the promise he made to Jonathan, his friend. Mephibosheth was Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson. David gave him back the lands and treated him like a son of the king. Mentioning his lameness underlines that he had nothing to offer.

For today: God welcomes us by grace, not for what we are worth. We can imitate that kindness by inviting into our table, our church, or our life someone who feels small or rejected.
exp.20:6:
This verse says that King David did not hand over Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, to be put to death. The word "spared" means that he protected him and kept him safe. The reason was the oath made before the Lord between David and Jonathan. Be careful: this Mephibosheth is different from another man with the same name, the son of Rizpah, who was indeed handed over.

There was famine in Israel, and David sought God. The Gibeonites, whom Saul had mistreated, asked for seven of Saul's descendants. David chose others, but he took care of Mephibosheth because of the promise he had made to his friend. How to understand this ancient justice is a matter of debate among scholars.

For today: keep our word, especially promises made before God, even when years pass or circumstances change. Our faithfulness can bless and protect others.
exp.17:14:
It says that ten young men who carried the weapons of Joab surrounded Absalom, who was already wounded, and struck him until he died. The words "young men" and "armour-bearers" are the terms the verse above uses, so they are used here as well.

The narrator tells the end of Absalom's rebellion against his father, King David. Absalom had been caught hanging from a tree in the forest. David had asked that he be treated gently, but Joab, the commander of the army, chose to disregard that order. Some see in this a political decision to end the war; the Bible does not explain all of his reasons.

Today we see that pride and rebellion lead to a sad end. We also learn to value obedience and mercy: Joab ignored David's request. Let us ask God for humility to honor those in authority and to be reconciled before it is too late.
exp.7:8:
This verse says that Toi, king of Hamath, heard that David had defeated all the army of Hadadezer. The word "smitten" means that David had beaten him in battle. The verse is left unfinished, and the idea continues in the next one.

The narrator recounts David's victories over neighboring kingdoms. Hamath was north of Israel, and Toi was an enemy of Hadadezer. So when he learned of the defeat, he sent his son Joram with gifts and greetings of peace. In this way Toi acknowledged David's power and sought his friendship. David dedicated those gifts to the LORD.

For today: David did not keep the gifts or the fame for himself, but dedicated them to God. When we receive achievements, blessings, or recognition, we can do the same: thank God and put what we have at his service, rather than boasting.
exp.0:0:
This verse says that Saul had already died. David had just come back from defeating the Amalekites, and he stayed two days in Ziklag, his home town. The word "came to pass" is a way of saying "happened," and "defeat" here means that David beat them in battle.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who picks up the account from 1 Samuel. David did not yet know what had happened on Mount Gilboa. In the meantime, he had recovered the families whom the Amalekites had taken from Ziklag (1 Samuel 30). This verse marks a pause before he receives the news of the king's death.

For today: sometimes there is a time of waiting between a victory and the next change in life. We can use those quiet days to rest, to give thanks to God, and to trust that He directs what is coming, even when we do not yet know it.
exp.7:3:
David captured a thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers from the enemy army. He "hamstrung" the horses of the chariots, that is, he cut the tendons of their legs so they could neither run nor serve in war. He left only a hundred chariots.

The narrator of the book recounts David's victories over Hadadezer, king of Zobah. God had commanded that the king of Israel not multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16). For this reason many think David kept only a few chariots out of obedience, though the text does not explain this. The figures in this passage differ slightly from 1 Chronicles 18:4.

For today: do not put your trust in what you have, whether money, strength, or resources. Use what God gives you with wisdom, and trust that He cares for you, as He cared for David.
exp.19:10:
One of Joab's young soldiers stood beside Amasa's body and called out to the troops: "Whoever is for Joab and is on David's side, let him follow Joab!" Here "young soldiers" means servants or fighters under his command. "Stood beside" means he stopped and remained by the body.

Joab had just treacherously killed Amasa, his rival, by pretending to greet him as a friend. David had appointed Amasa commander of the army in place of Joab, and now Sheba, who had rebelled, had to be pursued. The soldiers were stopping by the body, and this young man wanted them to keep moving. His words mix loyalty to Joab with loyalty to the king, even though Joab had just committed a crime.

Today, loyalty to a person must not blind us to injustice. Let us be faithful to God first, and not excuse wrongdoing out of affection or the pressure of the group.
exp.14:16:
This verse says that King David left Jerusalem together with all the people who accompanied him, and that they stopped in a place away from the city, at its outermost edge. The verse's description of the group stopping in a place "far off" is explained here as a place at a distance, or the last house of the city, as some translations render it.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled and took the support of many in Israel. The narrator tells us that the king leaves with his family and his servants. They stop to organize the march and to see who will go with him. There the loyalty of people such as the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and the men of Gath appears.

For today: when a crisis forces you to leave what is familiar, pause for a moment to see who walks with you, and be grateful for their loyalty. Take care of faithful relationships, and trust God while you walk through uncertainty.
exp.21:7:
When God answered the cry of his servant, all of creation was shaken. The earth moved and trembled, and even the foundations of heaven, that is, the firmest supports of the universe, were stirred. The reason is that God was angry: his wrath rose against what threatened his son. This is poetic language, not a literal description.

David sings this psalm when God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He had felt that death surrounded him, he cried out to the LORD, and God heard him from his temple. Here David uses images of earthquake and storm to show how powerful that help was.

For today: when you feel surrounded by anguish, cry out to God. He hears you and is not indifferent to your pain. Perhaps you will not see the earth tremble, but you can trust that the God who moves the heavens is concerned for you and acts in his own time.
exp.2:20:
Abner tells David that he will set out to gather all of Israel to the king, who is David, so that they may make a covenant with him. In this way David would reign over everyone, as he desired.

Abner had been commander of Saul's army and had supported Saul's house. After fighting with Ish-bosheth, he turned to David. He had already spoken with the leaders of Israel and of Benjamin. David received him with a feast and let him go in peace, a sign of good will. What follows shows that Joab was not present and that the story would become complicated.

For today: when seeking peace with someone, it is wise to go about it calmly and with good will, as David did. Even so, one must act with wisdom, because not everyone responds the same way to reconciliation.
exp.23:17:
That same day the prophet Gad came to David and gave him a clear instruction: go up and build an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah, a Jebusite man. A threshing floor was a flat piece of ground where grain was beaten to separate it from the husks.

David had just acknowledged his sin in taking the census of the people, and the angel had stopped his hand at that threshing floor. Gad, who was a prophet and was with David, passed on God's direction to him. The altar would serve for offering sacrifices and seeking forgiveness. Many understand that this place was later connected with Jerusalem and the temple, although the text here does not say so.

For today: when we recognize our faults, God shows us a way to return to Him. Respond with humility and obedience, without delay.
exp.23:11:
God tells the prophet Gad to say to David: "I offer you three things; choose one of them, and that I will do to you." The words "Go, and say" are a command to carry a message. "Offer" means that God sets before David three options of punishment, and the king must choose one.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Gad. David had ordered the people to be counted, and then his conscience accused him. He acknowledged his sin and asked for forgiveness, but the consequences came all the same. The Bible does not explain in detail why counting the people was so serious; some believe David trusted in his military strength instead of trusting in God.

For today: when we fail, it is good to confess quickly, as David did. God's forgiveness is real, but some consequences may remain. Even so, we can place our lives in the hands of a compassionate God, not in the hands of fear or of other people.
exp.15:17:
Hushai answers Absalom with carefully chosen words: "No, I will be of the one whom the Lord, and this people, and all the men of Israel choose, and with him I will abide." The verse below is translated into plain English.

Hushai is a friend of David, and David sent him to Jerusalem to defeat Absalom's counsel, since Absalom had rebelled. Absalom suspects his loyalty. Hushai does not clearly say whom God has chosen, so his words sound like support for Absalom, though they can be understood in another way. Commentators debate how much cunning and how much real loyalty to David is present here.

For today: our most important loyalty is to what God has chosen, not to what is fashionable. But truth is not defended by deception. Let us ask God for wisdom to be faithful and honest in our words.
exp.2:36:
This verse says that on that day all the people and all Israel realized that King David had not been the one who ordered Abner, son of Ner, to be killed. The phrase "it was not of the king" means that Abner's death was neither David's idea nor his command.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Joab, the commander of David's army, had killed Abner, and many could suspect David. But David wept publicly, fasted, and honored Abner at his burial. Through those actions, the people saw that he was sincere. The text does not say David accomplished this with words, but through his conduct.

For today: when someone doubts you, the best answer is usually to live with integrity and humility, not only to defend yourself with words. God sees the heart, and over time your actions speak.
exp.11:17:
The verse tells us that the child of David and Bathsheba died on the seventh day. The servants were afraid to give him the news. They thought: if, while the child was alive, David would not listen to us, what would he not do now that the child is dead?

Here the servants speak among themselves. David had sinned with Bathsheba, and the prophet Nathan had announced that the child would die. David fasted and pleaded with God for seven days, hoping that God would show mercy. The servants saw his grief was so deep that they feared making it worse. Shortly afterward, David worshiped God.

For today: when we have to give bad news to someone who is suffering, let us do it with tenderness and without fear of the truth. And when we ourselves suffer, we can cry out to God with sincerity and then, after that, accept his will and keep worshiping him.
exp.17:8:
As Absalom was fleeing on his mule, he came upon David's servants. Passing under a great oak with thick branches, his head became caught in the tree. The mule kept going, and Absalom was left hanging, suspended in the air. The tree is described as a large, sturdy oak; the Hebrew text speaks of a strong tree, and some think of an oak or a terebinth.

The narrator is telling the story. Absalom had rebelled against his father David, and his army had just been defeated in the forest of Ephraim. The text does not explain how he became caught; some suppose it was by his head or his hair, but the verse says only "his head."

For today: whoever turns away from authority and from the love of their family out of pride or ambition will, sooner or later, be caught by their own decisions. Today we can ask God for humility and seek reconciliation before pride leaves us with no way out.
exp.18:37:
Here the king David accepts Barzillai's proposal. He says that Chimham will cross the Jordan with him and promises to treat him however Barzillai thinks best. Moreover, he grants him anything else he asks. The phrase "as seems good to you" means "as you prefer."

Barzillai was a wealthy old man from Gilead who had helped David with supplies when he was fleeing from Absalom. Now David was returning to Jerusalem and wanted to reward him. Barzillai, because of his age, turned down the honor and offered Chimham in his place. The Bible does not make clear who Chimham was; some think he was his son, but the text does not say so.

For today: gratitude is shown through deeds. And, like Barzillai, we can learn to bless others by generously sharing the honors we receive, without clinging to them.
exp.13:32:
This verse tells how Joab went to King David and reported what Absalom had said. Then David called for his son, and Absalom came and bowed himself down to the ground before the king. Then the king kissed him. The phrase about bowing himself on his face to the ground means that he prostrated himself as a sign of respect, and the kiss shows that David was receiving him back.

Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and fled to Geshur. After returning to Jerusalem, David would not see him for two years. Absalom even had Joab's fields set on fire so that Joab would come to see him. After Joab interceded, father and son met. The Bible does not detail what each of them felt, and the account later shows that Absalom would rebel.

For today: reconciliation begins with a concrete step, but a kiss is not enough if the heart is still unhealed. Let us seek forgiveness with sincerity and truth.
exp.14:26:
David speaks here to Zadok the priest and asks him, "Art not thou a seer?" Then he tells him to return in peace to Jerusalem, together with his two sons, Ahimaaz and Jonathan. The word "seer" refers to someone who perceives or sees what God wants to reveal. Some think David is also asking him to be his eyes in the city.

David is fleeing Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Zadok and Abiathar had gone out with the ark of God, but David decides that it should return to the city. He does not want to use the ark as a charm; he places his future in God's hands. Moreover, those priests and their sons could send him news.

For today: in moments of crisis, entrust your situation to God with humility, without manipulating things. At the same time, act with wisdom, relying on faithful people.
exp.11:23:
Here it says that David comforted Bathsheba, his wife, who was also grieving the death of their son. Later they had another son, and he named him Solomon. The text affirms that the Lord loved him.

The phrase "went in unto her" refers to their marriage relationship, and the verse says he "lay with her" in the sense of being intimate with her. "She bare a son" means that she gave birth.

The narrator tells what happened after David and Bathsheba's first son died, a child born after the sin of both of them. David stopped fasting and accepted what had happened. Then the account shows that God did not abandon them. The name Solomon is related to a Hebrew word meaning "peace," though some explain it in other ways.

For today: when someone suffers a loss, we can accompany them with tenderness and patience. We can also trust that God, in his mercy, can bring new hope after pain and repentance.
exp.16:17:
It says that a young man saw Jonathan and Ahimaaz and told Absalom. Even so, the two hurried away and came to the house of a man in Bahurim. That man had a well in his courtyard, and they hid inside it. The word "lad" means young person, and "nevertheless" means "even so."

This is part of Absalom's rebellion against his father David. Jonathan and Ahimaaz were secretly carrying a warning to David, sent by Hushai, so that he would cross the Jordan. The narrator tells how they came close to being caught, but they were protected.

God often cares for his work through simple and brave people, like this family who hid the messengers. Today we can ask ourselves: what can I offer, even if it seems small, to help others with faithfulness and courage when it is needed?
exp.1:3:
To anoint meant pouring oil on someone to mark him as chosen for an office. Then they told David that the men of Jabesh-gilead had buried Saul.

This is a historical account. Saul had died in battle, and David, who had already been anointed in private years earlier by Samuel, now receives public recognition from his own tribe. The news about the men of Jabesh-gilead leads David to respond with gratitude, as is seen later. His reign over all Israel would come later.

For today: David did not rush to take all the power, but accepted what God opened up for him step by step. He also valued an act of kindness toward someone who had died. We can learn to wait for God's timing and to recognize with gratitude the good that others do.
exp.13:30:
This verse tells how Joab, the commander of David's army, got up and went to Absalom's house. He confronted him angrily: "Why have your servants set my field on fire?" The word "fields" refers to his crops, and "set on fire" means they had set them alight.

Joab speaks here, annoyed because Absalom had burned his barley. Absalom had returned to Jerusalem after years in exile, but King David still would not receive him. Absalom wanted Joab to plead on his behalf and, since Joab was not coming, he turned to pressure. Commentators see here a man who is impatient and manipulative, though his pain at being kept apart from his father seems genuine.

For today: the desire to be reconciled is good, but the methods matter. Forcing others or harming them to get what we want usually makes everything worse. Let us seek peace with patience, honest dialogue and respect.
exp.21:46:
He says that the Lord lives, and David praises him with strength. He calls God "my rock," that is, a firm place where he is safe. Since the verse reads "blessed be my rock," the phrase here can be rendered as the rock that holds him up. "Exalted be the God of the rock of my salvation" means that God be lifted up and honored. "The rock of my salvation" means the firm place from which my rescue comes. David wants everyone to recognize the greatness of God.

David, the king of Israel, speaks in a song of thanksgiving near the end of his life. He wrote it when the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from Saul, as the beginning of the chapter indicates. The verses before it tell how foreigners submitted to him in fear. David does not claim the victory for himself; he gives it to God.

For today: when you get through a difficulty, don't stop at relief alone. Take a moment to thank God out loud, acknowledging that he was your firm refuge.
exp.21:22:
David says that he always kept all of God's laws before him. His "commands" are God's instructions, and his "decrees" are his righteous rules or standards. Some words here are used in older ways, meaning to pay close and careful attention to something. That is why he says he will not turn away from them.

David speaks this at the end of his life, in a song of thanks because God rescued him from Saul and from all his enemies. When he speaks of "my righteousness," he is not claiming to be perfect, since the Bible records his serious sins. Many understand that he is speaking of his general faithfulness to God and his desire to obey him. Others see here a contrast with his enemies.

For today: keep God's Word in view. Read a passage each day and put one concrete teaching into practice, so that obedience becomes a habit and not something occasional.
exp.18:21:
Here David rebukes Abishai and Joab, the sons of Zeruiah, because they want to kill Shimei. "Adversaries" means people who oppose you, and "know" means "I know." David asks whether anyone should die today in Israel, and he declares that today he is king over Israel once again and wants to begin with peace.

Shimei had cursed David when David was fleeing from his son Absalom. Now David returns to Jerusalem, and Shimei, frightened, asks David for forgiveness. Abishai asks for Shimei's death because he cursed the Lord's anointed. David decides to use his authority to forgive, although the Bible later shows that this story had other chapters.

For today: when we have power or reason to repay evil with evil, we can choose mercy. Forgiving does not erase what happened, but it opens the way to peace and reflects the heart of God.
exp.19:25:
A quick note on the text: the passage I was given for 2 Samuel 20:26 comes out empty. In the verse, the text reads: "And Ira also the Jairite was a chief ruler about David." What I was given as earlier context belongs to verse 25 and part of verse 24.

The verse says that Ira, from the family of Jair, was a chief ruler close to David. The word "chief ruler" here can be understood as adviser, official, or trusted officer. Some translations say "priest," and scholars do not agree on his exact office.

This verse closes the list of the main officials of David's kingdom. It is not about a single character speaking; it is the narrator recording who helped the king govern, after the rebellion of Sheba had come to an end.

For today: God uses little-known people, like Ira, to sustain important things. Serve faithfully where you are, even when few notice.
exp.16:8:
Husai tells Absalom that David is surely hidden in some cave or some other place. If some of Absalom's soldiers fall in the first attack, whoever hears it will spread the word that Absalom's army has been overthrown. "Whosoever heareth it will say" means "whoever hears it will say," and "overthrown" means defeated in battle.

Husai speaks as David's friend, though he pretends to be loyal to Absalom. His true purpose was to defeat Ahithophel's counsel, which proposed pursuing David at once. Husai wanted to buy time so that David could organize himself. Many understand that God used this to accomplish his purpose, as the text says shortly after.

For today: A well-considered word can change the course of a situation. Before acting in haste, it is wise to pause, weigh the consequences, and ask God for wisdom to speak and to decide.
exp.1:13:
Abner proposes to Joab that some young soldiers arise and "play" before them, that is, that they put on a kind of combat or contest in front of them. "Young men" here means young warriors. Joab agrees and says: "Let them arise."

The speakers are the leaders of two rival armies. Abner serves Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, and Joab serves David. They meet beside the pool of Gibeon, in the midst of a division among the tribes. The Hebrew word can suggest a game or a tournament, but what follows shows that it ended in a slaughter. The text does not say with certainty what Abner intended.

Today, this invites us to be careful with provocations that look like games but stir up pride and violence. Let us seek peace and think before challenging others.
exp.16:26:
This verse tells that when David arrived at Mahanaim, three men came out to meet him: Shobi, from the Ammonite city of Rabbah; Machir, from Lo-debar; and Barzillai, a man of Gilead who lived in Rogelim. The verse of the original wording is not included here, since the phrase is not part of this verse. The verse goes on in the next one, where it says what they brought him.

The passage has no speaker; it is the narrator telling the story. David was fleeing from his son Absalom, who had rebelled and taken the throne from him. David was tired, with little support, in a faraway land. These three men, from different places, arrived just when he needed them most.

Today, when someone goes through a hard time, we do not need to wait for them to ask for help. We can notice who is worn out and offer something concrete: food, company, or simply our time. God often cares for his people through generous people.
exp.21:12:
This verse says that, before the brightness of God's presence, burning coals were kindled. It is a poetic image: the light that comes from God is so intense that it seems to set things on fire. The burning coals are glowing embers, pieces of charcoal at red-hot heat.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when God delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. To describe how God came to his aid, he uses the language of a storm: clouds, thunder, lightning and fire. This is not a literal description, but a way of expressing the power and holiness of God, and that He does hear the one who cries out to Him.

For today: when you find yourself surrounded by problems that overwhelm you, remember that God is greater than they are. Cry out to Him with confidence, and also with reverence, because His presence is holy and powerful.
exp.13:0:
Joab, son of Zeruiah and commander of David's army, noticed that the king missed Absalom and that his heart was inclined toward him. The word "noticed" here is the same as "saw" or "understood." Some translations take the king's heart as being set on Absalom in the sense of a longing to see him; others see it as a leaning toward reconciliation.

Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and fled into exile. David longed for him, but did not act. Joab, a practical and clever man, decided to step in with the story of a woman from Tekoa. Interpreters debate whether he did it out of sincere compassion, for political reasons, or for both.

For today: when a broken relationship hurts us, feeling is not enough; we must seek paths of truth and justice to bring healing. Let us ask God for wisdom to be reconciled without ignoring sin.
exp.3:7:
It says that Rechab and Baanah brought to David, at Hebron, the head of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul. They presented the killing as an act of justice from God against Saul's family, whom they call "your enemy." "Seed" means descendants, and "sought" means "looked for."

The two brothers are speaking; they had just killed Ish-bosheth while he slept. They expected a reward from David. They use God's name to justify their crime, but David had not asked them for anything like this, and in the next verse he firmly rejects them.

Today: let us be careful not to use God's name to cover personal interests or unjust acts. God does not need our tricks to carry out his plans. Before saying "God willed it so," it is worth asking whether what we did truly reflects his justice and his character.
exp.19:22:
This verse opens a list of David's chief officials. It says that Joab was placed in command of the whole army of Israel, and that Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, was in charge of the Cherethites and the Pelethites. These were, as is commonly understood, the king's personal guard, though scholars are not entirely certain of their origin.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator who summarizes how David's government was organized. This comes after the rebellion of Sheba, which ended when a wise woman of the city of Abel persuaded the people to hand over his head. With peace restored, the account shows the order of the kingdom, although Joab remained in charge despite his violent deeds.

For today: clear order and responsibilities help us care for people. Serve where God has placed you, with honesty, and remember that holding a position does not excuse doing wrong.
exp.14:6:
Absalom asks King David for permission to go to Hebron and fulfill a promise he made to God.

Many ancient texts say "four years" instead of "forty," so the number is uncertain.

Absalom is David's son, and he is winning the people's affection with flattery and embraces. Hebron was the place where David was crowned, and there Absalom would begin a rebellion. The text suggests that the vow was an excuse to disguise his plans, though it does not say so in those words.

Today: speaking about God does not make our intentions pure. Let us ask Him to examine our hearts, so that our faith is not a mask for ambition, but a sincere surrender.
exp.1:8:
This verse says that Abner, the commander of Saul's army, made Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, king. He set him up as king over Gilead, the Geshurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel. The word for "made him king" means "raised him up" or "proclaimed him."

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not one of the characters. Saul had died, and David was already king of Judah in Hebron. Abner, however, did not want to hand over power to David, so he put Ish-bosheth on the throne. Some think he did this out of loyalty to Saul's family, while others think he also wanted to keep his own influence. The text does not make this clear. In this way the people were divided.

For today: before supporting any leader, ask yourself whether they are seeking God's will or only human interests. Ask God for wisdom to act with humility and not out of pride.
exp.0:10:
David heard the news of Saul's death, took hold of his clothes and tore them. The men who were with him did the same. "Took hold" means grabbed firmly, and "tore" means ripped them apart.

A young Amalekite had just arrived at David's camp carrying Saul's crown and armlet (a bracelet). He said he had killed Saul at the request of the wounded king. His account differs from 1 Samuel 31, where Saul takes his own life; many believe the young man lied to win David's favor. Tearing one's clothes was a way of expressing deep grief in that culture. David wept even though Saul had pursued him.

For today: learn from David not to rejoice at the fall of someone who harmed you. Let your heart feel sorrow and seek God in those moments.
exp.13:31:
Absalom answers Joab that he had sent for him so that he could send him to the king with a message. He wanted Joab to ask: "Why have I come from Geshur? It would have been better for me to stay there." Absalom asks to see the king, and says that if there is guilt in him, the king should kill him. The phrase "let him kill me" is the verse's wording for the same request; the sentence about an old form is removed because it refers to a word not in your verse.

Absalom speaks after murdering his brother Amnon and fleeing to Geshur. He has already returned to Jerusalem, but David does not want to see him. Joab ignored his calls, so Absalom had Joab's fields set on fire to get his attention. That shows his impatience and his impulsive character.

For today: reconciliation needs truth and humility, not pressure or manipulation. Absalom wanted to be forgiven, but he used force. If there is a broken relationship, let us seek to speak with sincerity, acknowledge what is our responsibility, and trust that God will guide us.
exp.21:18:
It says that, when the day of his misfortune came, his enemies attacked him with force. But God was his support. "They prevented me" means "they came against me suddenly," and "calamity" is a time of disaster or distress. "Stay" is someone who holds you up so you do not fall.

David is the one speaking. This song of thanksgiving appears at the end of his life, after God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul, as the text indicates. David looks back and recognizes that God held him up in the most difficult moments, when his adversaries were stronger than he was.

For today: when a hard day comes, do not wait until you feel strong before you draw near to God. Say to Him simply, "Lord, hold me up." Then, like David, remember and give thanks for the times He has already held you up.
exp.10:14:
This verse tells what David wrote in the letter that Uriah himself carried to Joab. The order was to place Uriah at the front, where the fighting was fiercest, and then leave him alone, so that he would be struck down and die. The word "abandon" in that instruction means to pull back and give him no support.

The narrator explains that David had already sinned with Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, and she was pregnant. David tried to get Uriah to spend time with his wife to hide everything, but Uriah would not go home while his companions were in battle. So David decided to have him killed, using the war as a pretext.

For today: a hidden sin often leads to another, worse one. Instead of covering up our failings, it is wise to confess them to God soon and seek the forgiveness and help that He gives.
exp.11:12:
David said that he acknowledged his guilt before God in few words: "I have sinned against the Lord." Nathan answers him that God has already put away his sin, that is, forgiven it, and that he would not die. Here "put away" means taking away or passing over the guilt.

Nathan, a prophet of God, had confronted David over his adultery with Bathsheba and over having ordered the death of Uriah. God announced serious consequences. When David breaks down and confesses, forgiveness comes. However, the text shows that forgiveness does not erase all the consequences: the child would die.

If we have failed, it is not wise to hide it or make excuses for ourselves. We can confess it honestly to God, trusting in his forgiveness. And, although some consequences may remain, God does not abandon us.
exp.22:27:
This verse names two of King David's brave warriors: Zalmon, who came from Ahoh, and Maharai, who was from Netophah. In this list, each man's name is joined to his town or his family. In the Reina-Valera 1909 the names are written in an older form. Some modern versions write "Zalmon the Ahohite" and "Maharai the Netophathite."

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. He is closing the account of David's reign with the list of his thirty most outstanding warriors. We know almost nothing more about them, because the Bible records only their names. That shows that God and the people remembered their service.

For today: God sees and remembers faithful service, even when no one applauds it. Serve where you are, with steadiness and humility, without seeking fame.
exp.18:42:
The men of Israel tell the men of Judah that they have "ten parts" in the king, that is, ten of the twelve tribes, and so they have more claim on David. They complain that they were treated as unimportant, because they were the first to speak about bringing the king back. But the words of Judah were harsher and more forceful than those of Israel.

David was returning to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Judah escorted him first across the Jordan, and Israel felt ignored. Judah defended itself by saying that the king was their relative. The argument was about honor and pride, and it grew heated. This clash sets the stage for the rebellion of Sheba, which comes next.

For today: when we feel overlooked, it is easy to answer with harsh words. That quarrel between brothers shows how quickly pride divides. Before you make a complaint, ask yourself whether you are seeking justice or only honor, and speak with humility.
exp.22:11:
This verse tells how Shammah, one of David's mighty men, stood his ground in the middle of a field full of lentils and defended it. He struck down the Philistines, and the Lord brought about a great victory.

The phrase "a piece of ground" means a portion or plot of land. "Victory" here means deliverance or triumph. "Slew" means that he defeated them in battle.

The passage appears in a list of David's mighty men, near the end of Second Samuel. The narrator points out that the people had fled, but Shammah held his position. Although the field seemed like a small thing, he did not give it up, and the account credits the triumph to God, not only to the warrior.

For today: sometimes we are called to defend something that seems small, such as honesty, family, or faith, when others give up. We can stand firm with humility, trusting that God gives the victory.
exp.7:13:
It says that David placed garrisons, that is, groups of soldiers keeping watch, throughout the territory of Edom. The Edomites (called the Edomites in this version) were brought under subjection and served him. At the end, the text sums up that the Lord kept, that is, protected and sustained, David wherever he went.

This is the account of the book's narrator, who summarizes David's military victories over several neighboring peoples. It comes right after mentioning the defeat of the Edomites in the Valley of Salt. The author wants to show that the kingdom was established, and he credits the success not only to David's strength but to God's protection. Edom was a neighbor of Israel, and its subjection is understood as part of that advance.

For today: our efforts and plans matter, but true security comes from God. We can work responsibly and, at the same time, thank him for caring for us in every place we go, at home, at work, or on the road.
exp.9:16:
When David was told that the Syrians were gathering again, he brought all Israel together, crossed the Jordan River, and came to a place called Helam. There the Syrians lined up for battle against him and fought.

The phrase that is rendered as "word was brought" refers to someone who gave David the news. The Syrians are the same people as the Arameans.

This is a historical account, not a speech. The Syrians had been defeated before, but Hadadezer brought reinforcements from across the Euphrates River, led by his commander Shobach. David acts quickly and gathers the people to defend Israel. The chapter describes how this war, which began with the conflict involving the Ammonites, came to an end. Locating Helam precisely is difficult, because it is not known for certain where it was.

For today: when a problem arrives, do not let it grow or ignore it. David heard the warning and acted with resolve and in unity with his people. Face difficulties with prayer, good counsel, and responsible action, trusting that God sustains the one who does what is right.
exp.11:11:
He says that David sinned in secret, but God would make the consequences visible in broad daylight, before all the people. "Before the sun" means in full daylight, in plain view of everyone. "I will do this" refers to the punishment announced earlier: violence and dishonor within his own family.

The speaker is the prophet Nathan, sent by God to David. David had taken Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and had Uriah killed to cover up his sin. Nathan tells him that God saw everything. Later, the story of his family shows serious conflicts, and many see this as part of these consequences.

For today: what is hidden is not hidden from God. Instead of covering up a wrong, it is better to confess it soon, as David did, and trust in God's forgiveness, even though some consequences may remain.
exp.21:27:
He says that God rescues the humble people, that is, those who recognize their need for Him. But His eyes are on the proud, the arrogant, to bring them down, that is, to humble them and pull them down from their haughtiness.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, which also appears in Psalm 18. He sings it when God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. Earlier he said that God deals with each person according to their heart: kindly with the good, and with the wicked, He shows Himself as one who will not be deceived. This verse continues that idea. Then David says that God is his lamp and gives him strength.

Today we can examine our hearts honestly. If we have done wrong, it is better to admit it and ask forgiveness than to defend ourselves with pride. God draws near to whoever trusts in Him with humility.
exp.14:4:
The verse tells us that when anyone came near to him to bow down, he would not let them bow. He would put out his hand, take hold of them, and kiss them, as though they were his equal. The phrase "came near to bow down" refers to that gesture of respect before someone in authority.

Absalon was the son of King David. He would stand at the entrance of the city, where lawsuits were settled, and speak with the people who came to ask the king for justice. Through these close gestures and his words, he sought to win the affection of the people. The text says that in this way he "stole away" the heart of Israel, that is, he won it by deceit, since his real aim was to take the throne from his father.

Today we can learn to tell the difference between sincere kindness and kindness used to get something. Let us examine our own motives when we treat others well, and ask God for an honest heart.
exp.18:3:
David, with his face covered, cried out in a loud voice and with great grief for his son Absalom. He repeats "my son" again and again, like someone who cannot find comfort. Covering the face was a sign of deep mourning and sorrow.

It is the narrator who describes David. Absalom had rebelled against his father and was killed in battle by Joab. David's army had won, but the king wept so much that the victory turned into mourning. Afterward Joab rebukes him, because the soldiers who risked their lives felt ashamed.

For today: a father's grief is real and should not be despised, but we must also care for those who stand beside us. When we suffer, let us ask God for comfort and wisdom so that we do not neglect others, nor stop thanking those who have served us faithfully.
exp.13:16:
The woman says she hopes the king's answer will bring "comfort," that is, peace and relief. She praises him by saying he is "like an angel of God" because he knows how to discern good from evil when he hears a case. She ends with a blessing: that the Lord, her God, will be with him.

It was a woman from Tekoa, sent by Joab, who pretended to be a widow with a family problem. Her story aims to make David reflect on his own son Absalom, who was exiled. Her compliments are part of a strategy, and afterward the king discovers that Joab was behind it.

Today we can learn to listen carefully and with discernment before we judge. We should also be cautious with flattery: it can be sincere, but sometimes it seeks to influence us. Let us ask God for wisdom to distinguish good from evil.
exp.22:24:
This verse names two warriors from David's group of thirty mighty men: Shammah and Elika, both from a place called Harod. Harod was probably a town or a spring near where Gideon camped, though scholars do not fully agree on this. In 1 Chronicles 11:27 the name Shammoth appears, so some believe there are variations in the names across the lists.

Here the narrator of Samuel gathers the list of brave men who stood with David in his battles. It is a record of honor, written to remember those who served the king faithfully, even though their names are not famous.

God remembers ordinary people who serve with faithfulness. Perhaps no one applauds what you do in your family, your work, or your church, but your effort does not go unnoticed. Serve with steadiness, knowing that God sees and values every act of loyalty.
exp.1:25:
Abner calls out to Joab with three questions: Will the sword keep devouring forever? Don't you know that in the end it will only bring bitterness? How long will it be before you tell your people to stop chasing their own brothers? Abner shouted, which means he called out loudly, and in the end means at last.

Abner was the commander of Saul's army, and Joab was the commander of David's army. After a very bloody battle between the two forces, Abner was fleeing and Joab was pursuing him. As evening was falling, Abner asked that they stop, because both sides belonged to the same people. Joab answered him and then blew the horn to call off the pursuit.

Today, when a conflict with someone close to us drags on, it is worth asking where it is leading us. We can be the ones who say enough before bitterness grows, seeking peace and not merely winning the argument.
exp.22:0:
Now these are the last words of David. This verse presents David's final message, the last thing he wants to leave behind. David describes himself with four traits: he is the son of Jesse, a man whom God raised up to a high place, the anointed one of the God of Jacob, and the sweet singer of Israel's songs, that is, the gentle psalmist of the psalms.

The speaker is King David, now an old man. He mentions that he is the son of Jesse, recalling his humble beginnings as a shepherd. He presents himself as one chosen by God, not by his own merit. What follows in the verses after this is an inspired word about how a just ruler should govern. Some scholars think these are not literally his last words in life, but rather his last recorded poem or prophetic message.

For today: if God has given you some place, whether in the home, at work, or in the church, remember that it comes from His grace. Use it with humility, justice, and gratitude.
exp.2:24:
Joab tells David that Abner did not come with good intentions. In his view, Abner came to deceive him, to find out his comings and goings, and to learn everything he was planning. "Your going out and your coming in" means everything you do from day to day, and "deceive you" means to make you believe something false.

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. Abner had come to offer that all Israel would join David, and David sent him away in peace. Joab may have had sincere suspicions, but he also had a personal motive: Abner had killed his brother Asahel. That is why the text then shows Joab killing Abner in secret. Some see political concern here; others see plain revenge.

For today: when we accuse someone, let us examine our hearts. Sometimes suspicion dresses itself up as caution, yet it hides resentment. Let us ask God for wisdom and a clean heart before we judge.
exp.6:3:
That very night, God spoke to Nathan. The word "happened" and the phrase "the word of the Lord came" mean that God gave him a direct message. "Jehovah" is the name of the Lord.

David, now settled in his cedar palace, was troubled that the ark of God was still kept in a tent. Nathan, without consulting God, answered him encouragingly: "Do whatever is in your heart." His intention was good, but he spoke on his own. Now God sets the course right and speaks to him again, for He has His own plan and His own timing.

For today: good desires are not enough; we must pray and wait for God's direction before acting. Even good advice from a respected leader should be brought before the Lord.
exp.0:14:
David ordered one of his young soldiers to come near and strike down the Amalekite, and the man struck him so that he died. The verse of "young men" is that they were the young soldiers who served David.

David speaks here after receiving the news of Saul's death. This foreign Amalekite claimed to have killed him, perhaps hoping for a reward. Another account of Saul's death appears in 1 Samuel 31, where Saul takes his own life; for this reason many believe the man was lying, though this cannot be stated with certainty. David judges him by his own words.

For today: David respected the authority that God had placed over him, even when Saul was his enemy. We can learn not to rejoice in the fall of someone who has harmed us, nor to take advantage of another's misfortune, and to take seriously the weight of our words.
exp.4:16:
This verse says that when the Philistines learned that David had been anointed king over all Israel, they went out, all of them, to look for him. David heard about it and went down to the stronghold, which here is a protected place, probably a refuge in the mountainous area. It is not certain exactly what it was, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

The narrator describes what follows David's coronation in Hebron over all the tribes. While David reigned only over Judah, the Philistines did not see him as a great threat. Now that Israel was united under a single king, they saw him as a danger and reacted at once.

When God gives us a responsibility or an advance, opposition sometimes comes with it too. David did not act on impulse: he took refuge and, according to the passage that follows, sought God's counsel before fighting. Before you decide, ask God in prayer.
exp.19:6:
This verse says that an army went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba, son of Bichri. Joab's men went, along with the Cherethites and Pelethites (David's personal guard, as it is commonly understood), and all the mighty men. The phrase that describes them going after him means following behind him, pursuing.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Sheba had led a rebellion against David, and the king feared it would be worse than Absalom's. Amasa had been slow to gather Judah, so David sent Abishai. Joab and his men went with him, and soon Joab would act violently against Amasa.

For today: when a problem arises, it is not wise to put off what is urgent. Delay, pride, or rivalry can do harm. Let us act responsibly and with a clean heart.
exp.22:26:
This verse names two warriors from David's army: Abiezer, from the town of Anathoth, and Mebunnai, from Hushah. "From Anathoth" and "from Hushah" indicate their place of origin. They are only names, with no details about their deeds.

The narrator of the book of Samuel presents the list of the thirty, David's most outstanding warriors. Anathoth was a town in the tribe of Benjamin, near Jerusalem. In 1 Chronicles 11:29 a warrior from Hushah named Sibbecai appears, and some think he could be the same person under another name, but this is not certain.

God remembers those who serve, even though almost no one knows them. Today, your faithful and quiet work in your family, your church, or your job also counts. You do not need applause to be valuable in God's work.
exp.13:28:
Absalom sent for Joab, asking him to speak to King David on his behalf. But Joab would not come. Absalom sent again a second time, and Joab again refused.

Absalom had returned to Jerusalem, but David did not want to see him. He had been without seeing the king for two years, because he had killed his brother Amnon. Joab, the commander of the army, had helped bring him back. Now Absalom wanted to be received by the king again. The text does not explain why Joab did not come; it could have been caution, or a wish to avoid more conflict with David.

For today: when we seek reconciliation, pressure and impatience can do more harm. Absalom ignored Joab's silence and ended up resorting to violence. Let us rather seek peace with humility, patience, and prayer.
exp.19:13:
The verse says that Sheba, the son of Bichri, went through all the tribes of Israel until he reached the city of Abel of Beth-maachah, and all the Berites. There the people gathered together and went after him. It is likely that "Berites" is the name of a place or of a group of people, and scholars are not entirely sure of its exact meaning.

Sheba had led a rebellion against King David. Meanwhile, Joab, the commander of the army, had killed Amasa and pursued Sheba to stop the revolt. This verse shows the rebel's route before they caught up with him.

For today: words of anger and division can spread quickly. Before following someone, let us ask whether they lead us toward peace or toward a break.
exp.21:15:
It says that the bottom of the sea was laid bare and the very foundations of the earth were uncovered, when God rebuked with force. "The channels of the sea" are the currents or depths of the sea. "The foundations of the world" are the base of the earth. "The blast of the breath of his nostrils" is a poetic image of God's anger, like a powerful gust of wind.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving at the end of his life, after God had delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He uses images of storm, thunder, and earthquake to describe how great God's power is in rescuing him. It is poetic language, not necessarily a literal account of a physical event.

For today: when your troubles feel like deep waters that threaten to swallow you, remember that God is more powerful than any force. You can pray with confidence and give him thanks, knowing that he cares for you.
exp.21:10:
He rode upon a cherub and flew, and he was seen upon the wings of the wind. A cherub is a heavenly being that in the Bible accompanies the presence of God. The sentence about "seen" in the source has been rewritten here: the phrase "was seen" matches the verse your reader sees. It is poetic language: it describes God acting with speed and power.

David speaks here, at the end of his life, in a song of gratitude. He dedicates it to God because God delivered him from Saul and from all his enemies. David uses images of storm, fire and trembling to show that God heard his cry and came to rescue him. It is not a literal description, but a way of expressing that God intervened with great power.

For today: when you feel alone or cornered, remember that God is not distant or indifferent. Cry out to Him with confidence and wait for His help, even if it does not arrive the way you imagine. He knows when and how to act.
exp.11:0:
It says that God sent the prophet Nathan to speak with King David. Nathan begins to tell him a story: in a certain city there lived two men, one rich and the other poor.

Before this moment, David had committed adultery with Bathsheba and had ordered the death of her husband Uriah. Nathan speaks on God's behalf. Instead of accusing him directly, he uses a parable, that is, a story that carries a lesson. In this way David could judge the case honestly, without becoming defensive.

For today: it is sometimes easy to see injustice in others and not in ourselves. We can ask God to show us our faults with humility, and to receive with gratitude those who correct us with love and truth.
exp.3:10:
David is outraged by a serious crime: two men killed an innocent man, in his own house and while he was sleeping. David asks, with force, whether he should not hold them accountable for that blood. Holding them accountable for that death means making them answerable for it, and removing them from the earth means putting them to death. Young soldiers are what is meant here.

David speaks to Rechab and Baanah, who murdered Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, and brought his head to him expecting a reward. David had already punished another man who claimed to have killed Saul. He wants to make it clear that he does not rejoice in the violence or profit from it. What follows, the execution and the mutilation of the bodies, was a harsh practice of that time; the text reports it without asking us to imitate it.

Today: let us not seek to gain advantage through unjust means, nor expect applause for doing wrong. God values justice and innocent life. Let us trust in Him and act with integrity.
exp.17:23:
David sat between the two gates, probably the inner gate and the outer gate of Mahanaim. The watchman, the guard who keeps watch from a high place, climbed up to the flat roof over the gate. He looked far into the distance and saw a man running alone.

This is part of the account of the battle against Absalom, David's rebellious son. Ahimaaz insisted on bringing the news to the king, though Joab did not want him to. David is not narrating anything here. The text describes the scene while he waits anxiously to learn how his army fared and, above all, how his son fared.

For today: waiting for difficult news is distressing. We can learn to bring that waiting to God in prayer, without letting fear control us, and to be attentive to others when they wait anxiously.
exp.12:1:
He says that Amnon was so distressed over Tamar, his half-sister, that he even fell sick. She was a virgin, and for that reason it seemed hard to him to do anything to her, that is, to bring about what he desired. What Amnon calls love is in fact an obsessive desire, which he himself sees as something he seeks to obtain.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. He tells how a tragedy begins within David's family. Tamar was David's daughter and Absalom's sister. After this desire will come a deception and a terrible abuse. The text does not justify Amnon; it shows how unchecked desire can lead to evil.

For today: when a desire takes control of you and steals your peace, do not feed it or look for advice that justifies it. Bring it to God and to a wise person, and learn always to respect the dignity of others.
exp.1:27:
Joab sounds the horn, which was a military signal, and all his men come to a halt. They no longer chase the soldiers of Israel who were following Abner, and the battle ends for that day.

After a hard fight between the men of David (Judah) and those of Ishbosheth (Israel), Abner called out to Joab to stop killing his own brothers. Joab agreed and gave the order to stop. It was a ceasefire, although the conflict between the two houses continued afterward. The passage shows the sadness of a war between brothers.

Today, knowing when to stop in time is a kind of wisdom. When an argument within the family, the church, or the workplace only leaves wounds, it is wise to listen to the one who asks for peace and to stop. Let us ask God for humility to hold back before bitterness grows.
exp.10:5:
This verse tells how David sends a message to Joab, his commander, asking him to send Uriah the Hittite to him. Joab obeys and sends him to the king. The word "Hittite" in the verse is the one that names Uriah's people, a man of foreign origin who lived in Israel. The word "sent" in the verse means "sent him."

David speaks here after learning that Bathsheba is pregnant from having been with him. Uriah, her husband, was at war. David calls him back to try to hide what he has done, by having Uriah spend time with his wife. Joab only carries out the order, without knowing, according to the text, the reason behind it.

For today: when we commit a wrong, the temptation is to cover it with another deception, and that makes everything worse. It is better to confess soon and seek God's forgiveness sincerely.
exp.12:8:
Tamar took the pan from the pan and set the fried cakes before Amnon, but he refused to eat. Then he commanded, "Have everyone leave me," and everyone went out.

Amnon, David's son, was pretending to be sick. Tamar, his half-sister, had come at her father's request to look after him. By refusing to eat and sending the others out, Amnon was left alone with her. The text does not say so here, but what follows shows that this was part of a plan to harm her.

For today: when someone insists on being alone with you in a strange way, or pressures you to be, do not ignore it. God cares for the vulnerable, and we too must protect them, believe them, and speak up in time.
exp.17:22:
Ahimaaz insists on running with the news, even though Joab had already told him it was not worth it. Joab gives in and says to him, "Run." Ahimaaz takes the way of the plain, which was longer but easier and faster, and he outruns Cushi. "Whatever happens" means "come what may."

Absalom, David's son, had rebelled and has just died in battle. Joab first sent Cushi with the message. Ahimaaz, son of the priest Zadok, wanted to carry the news too. Joab hesitated because the message would be painful for David. The Bible does not fully explain Ahimaaz's reasons; some think it was eagerness.

Haste and good spirits are not enough; we also need to know what message we are carrying and how to deliver it with wisdom and love. Before speaking or acting in a hurry, let us ask God for discernment.
exp.13:24:
This verse says that in all Israel there was no one so admired for his beauty as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, he had no flaw. The phrase about being greatly praised means that he was very highly admired.

The narrator of the book pauses to describe Absalom. Joab had just brought him back to Jerusalem, but King David did not want to see him. This description sets up what follows: a very attractive and popular man who would later rebel against his father. The Bible does not say that his beauty was wrong, but it also does not show that it reflected a good heart.

Today we can remember that appearance draws attention, but it does not reveal character. God looks at the heart. Let us ask him to help us value people, and ourselves, for humility, honesty and love, and not only for what can be seen on the outside.
exp.22:38:
The verse names Uriah the Hittite as the last name on the list of David's mighty men. The total is given at the end as thirty and seven in all. The word "Hittite" means he came from the Hittite people, that is, he was a foreigner. The number thirty-seven is understood as the thirty well-known men plus some others, such as the three chief warriors, although scholars explain this in different ways.

The writer closes a list of the loyal men who fought alongside David. Uriah is the same husband of Bathsheba, whom David had put to death (2 Samuel 11). Placing him at the end of the list shows, sadly, how serious that sin was. He was a faithful soldier.

For today: value the simple and faithful people around you, regardless of their origin. And remember that our decisions can hurt those who trust us. Ask God for an upright and humble heart.
exp.9:12:
This verse tells us that Joab, the commander of Israel's army, advanced with his soldiers to fight against the Syrians, and they ran away. The Syrians are the Arameans.

The context is a war against the Ammonites, who had hired the Syrians as allies. Joab found himself surrounded and divided his troops: he would face the Syrians, and his brother Abishai would face the Ammonites. Before the battle he encouraged everyone with words of courage and confidence that God would decide the outcome. After that, the Syrians fled.

For today: do your part with diligence, work as a team, and leave the outcome in God's hands. We must be brave, remembering that He has the final word.
exp.7:2:
It says David defeated Hadadezer, king of Zobah, an Aramean kingdom north of Israel. "Smote" means defeated, and "border" means territory or boundary lines. The text speaks of extending that border to the river Euphrates, but it is not clear whether "he" refers to David or to Hadadezer. Some believe it was David expanding his kingdom, others that it was the king of Zobah.

The narrator of the book recounts David's victories over several neighboring peoples. He shows how the kingdom of Israel grew stronger. Many connect this with God's promise to give land to Israel, which named the Euphrates as its limit.

Today we can learn to trust that God keeps his promises in his own time. It is also worth reviewing our goals: growing is not wrong, but we should ask God for direction and not depend only on our own strength.
exp.13:15:
This verse says that the woman trusts the king will listen to her and rescue her from the one who wants to destroy her and her son. It explains that the word for "destroy" in the original means to wipe out or eliminate, and that "the inheritance of God" refers to the land and people of Israel, where they had their place.

A woman from Tekoa speaks, sent by Joab with an invented story about two sons, one of whom killed the other. With that story she seeks to make David reflect on his son Absalom, who was banished for having killed Amnon. She asks that her son not be cut off from the family, and so she prepares the way for David to see his own situation.

For today: God teaches us to seek paths of restoration, not only of punishment. Before shutting the door on someone, ask yourself whether there is a fair and loving way to reconcile.
exp.10:6:
It says that when Uriah came before David, the king asked him questions about how Joab was doing, how the army was doing, and how the war was going. The words "how they fare" here mean well-being, that is, "how are they doing." "The people" refers to the soldiers. Everything sounds like an ordinary conversation between a king and a soldier.

The narrator tells us that David had already gotten Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, pregnant, and now he is trying to hide it. That is why he has Uriah called back from the front. The questions seem kind, but they are a smokescreen: David wants Uriah to go home to his house so that everyone will believe the child is his.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, when we try to cover up a mistake, we use kind words that hide bad intentions. God sees the heart. It is better to confess in time than to pretend everything is normal and make the damage worse.
exp.13:22:
So Joab got up and went to Geshur, the place where Absalom had been living since he fled. There he took Absalom and brought him back to Jerusalem.

Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and had been in exile for three years. Joab, the commander of David's army, arranged for a wise woman from Tekoa to prepare a story that would persuade the king to let him come back. David agreed, though with reservations, as seen in the fact that he would not see him. Commentators debate what Joab's true motives were.

For today: returning to the house is not the same as being reconciled. If a relationship is broken, it is not enough to stay at a distance; it takes sincere forgiveness, honest conversation, and truth. Let us ask God for the courage to take that step.
exp.3:6:
