They say that the two brothers entered the house of Ish-bosheth while he was resting on his bed, in his bedchamber. They struck him, killed him, and cut off his head. Then they took his head and walked all night along the road through the plain, that is, along the road through the field or the valley of the Jordan. "Bedchamber" is simply his sleeping room.

The narrator tells how Rechab and Baanah, captains of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, murdered him treacherously. They hoped to win David's favor by bringing him the head. But the account goes on to show that David did not reward them; instead he condemned the crime (verses 9 to 12).

For today: God is not pleased when we seek gain by unjust means, even when it seems they serve a good cause. David rejected that path. We can ask God to help us wait for his timing and to act with honesty, never betraying anyone to come out ahead.
exp.21:35:
He says that God gave David a shield that comes from his salvation, meaning a protection that springs from God's saving help. "Salvation" here means rescue or deliverance, not good physical health. Gentleness is kindness and a warm, considerate way of treating someone.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that appears near the end of his life, after God rescued him from Saul and his other enemies. Earlier he mentions his swift feet and his hands trained for battle. Now he acknowledges that his strength and his victories did not come from himself, but from God's protection and kindness.

For today: when something goes well for you, do not think only of your own effort. Take a moment to thank God for his care, and trust that his goodness also sustains you in what you still face.
exp.11:3:
He says that a visitor came to the house of a rich man. The rich man had many sheep and cattle, but he did not want to prepare any of his own to feed the traveler. Instead, he took the poor man's one little ewe lamb and cooked it for his guest. The words that describe cooking and preparing the meal simply mean preparing food. The traveler is the one who came to visit.

The one speaking is the prophet Nathan, sent by God to King David. Nathan tells this story as a parable. David had taken Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and had arranged for Uriah to be killed. Nathan does not accuse him directly, but uses the story so that David can see his own sin.

Today we might ask ourselves: do I judge the faults of others harshly, but am I soft on my own? Let us ask God for humility to hear correction, and let us take care of what others have, without abusing our power or advantage.
exp.5:9:
This verse says that David decided not to bring the ark of the Lord to the city of David, which was Jerusalem. Instead, he left it in the house of Obed-edom, a man from Gath. The word "Gittite" means a native of Gath. The phrase "unto him" means bringing it along with him.

It is part of the narrator's account. David had just seen Uzzah die for touching the ark, and he felt sorrow and fear before the holiness of God. So he stopped. Later, when he saw that God blessed the household of Obed-edom, David resumed the move with joy. Some think Obed-edom was a Levite; the text does not make this clear.

Today we can learn that drawing near to God calls for reverence and humility. If we feel confused or afraid, we can pause, seek God, and return to obeying Him as He directs.
exp.10:7:
He says David tells Uriah to go down to his house and wash his feet, that is, to rest after the journey. When Uriah leaves the palace, the king sends after him a portion of royal food, a gift from the king's table. The phrase "go down" is "go down," and the words that follow say it was sent after him.

David speaks after having made Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, pregnant while Uriah was at war. He calls him back from the front with an excuse. Many understand that the real purpose was for Uriah to sleep with his wife, so that the pregnancy would seem to be his. The text does not say this directly here, but the context strongly suggests it.

For today: a kind gesture can hide a crooked intention. If we have done something wrong, let us not cover it with appearances; it is better to confess to God and seek the truth with humility, as David did afterward in Psalm 51.
exp.19:17:
Here the wise woman says that in ancient times there was a saying: "They shall surely ask counsel at Abel." With that, the matter was settled. The verse you are reading uses "spake" and "wont," which correspond to the word for "said" and the phrase for "used to," so no separate explanation of the old wording is needed here.

Joab had laid siege to the city of Abel of Beth-maacah, because Sheba, who had rebelled against David, had taken refuge there. The woman speaks to stop the destruction. She appeals to Abel's reputation as a place of good counsel and peace. Some believe the saying shows that people sought wisdom there; the text gives no further details about its origin.

For today: A wise word spoken with respect can prevent great harm. Before acting in anger, let us learn to listen and to talk things through, as Joab did, and always seek peace.
exp.4:8:
David settled down to live in the stronghold he had just captured in Jerusalem. He gave it the name "City of David" and began building all around it, from Millo inward. Millo seems to have been an area of earthworks or fill, though its exact nature is not known.

The passage is a historical narrative. David was already king over all Israel and needed a central, well-defended capital. The Jebusites had considered the city impregnable. By taking it and strengthening it, David made it the political and, later, religious center of the nation. The next verse says that God was with him.

For today: David did not only win a battle; he also committed himself to building and caring for what he had won. We can learn not to be satisfied with an achievement, but to build steadily on what God entrusts to us: family, work, the church, and to do so depending on Him.
exp.12:33:
This verse says that Absalom fled right away after killing his brother Amnon. Meanwhile, the young man who was keeping watch from the tower (the watchman's post was a lookout) lifted up his eyes and saw many people coming along the road behind him, on the side of the hill. The word "young man" means a youth, and "behind him" means behind him.

Here the narrator tells the story. Amnon had abused Tamar, Absalom's sister, and Absalom ordered that Amnon be killed at a feast. First came the rumor that all the king's sons had been killed, but Jonadab said that only Amnon had died. The watchman saw the king's sons returning, and so what Jonadab had said was confirmed.

For today: unaddressed pain and revenge only bring more pain. When someone suffers an injustice, it is wise to seek justice and healing without taking matters into one's own hands. And before repeating alarming news, it is good to verify it first.
exp.13:21:
Joab falls to the ground with his face toward the earth, and shows respect to the king. He blesses him, that is, he wishes him well and gives him honor. Then he says that now he knows David regards him with favor, because the king has granted his request. The phrase about finding favor in the king's eyes means being looked upon kindly and receiving a benefit. The phrase about bowing down means that he bent low out of respect.

Joab, the commander of David's army, speaks. He had arranged for the woman from Tekoa to tell the king a story and move him to allow Absalom to return, since Absalom had been sent away for killing his brother Amnon. David agrees, though afterward he keeps Absalom at a distance from his presence. Joab rejoices because he has achieved what he was seeking.

For today: reconciliation requires truth and wisdom, not just good intentions. Before trying to settle a conflict, let us ask God to guide us to act with honesty, patience, and love.
exp.13:20:
Here King David tells Joab that he will do what was asked of him: bring back his son Absalom. The word "young man" means a young person, and "bring again" means to bring him back to Jerusalem.

David speaks with Joab, the commander of his army. Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and fled to Geshur, where he had lived in exile for years. Joab wanted him to return, so he sent a woman from Tekoa with an invented story to move the king's heart. David discovered that Joab was behind it, yet he still gave in. Scholars do not agree on whether this was David's wisdom, his tenderness, or his weakness.

For today: forgiving and seeking reconciliation is good, but it is wise to do so with truth and repentance, not only out of emotion. Let us ask God for wisdom to join love and justice in our relationships.
exp.1:29:
This verse tells what happened after the battle. Joab stopped chasing Abner, came back, and gathered the whole army to count the losses. On David's side, nineteen men were missing, besides Asahel. "Servants" here means David's soldiers, and "were missing" means they had died.

The narrator of the book describes the end of a civil war between David's followers, in Judah, and those of Abner, who supported the house of Saul. Asahel, Joab's brother, had pursued Abner, and Abner killed him. That is why his name appears separately, since his death would have consequences later on.

For today: fights between brothers leave real losses and people who do not come back. Before feeding a conflict, think about the human cost. Seek peace and reconciliation while there is still time.
exp.18:16:
This verse says that a thousand men of the tribe of Benjamin were accompanying Shimei. Ziba, the servant of the house of Saul, also came, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants. All of them crossed the Jordan River before the king arrived.

This is the account of David's return to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. The men of Benjamin, the tribe of Saul, wanted to show loyalty to the king. Shimei and Ziba had earlier acted in questionable ways toward David, so their haste to arrive seems to be seeking the king's favor. Their true intentions are not stated here, and the text does not explain them.

For today: when we have failed or offended someone, it is good to approach them with humility and sincerity, not only with outward gestures. God looks at the heart, and true reconciliation begins with honest repentance.
exp.16:18:
This verse tells how the woman of the house took a cloth and spread it over the mouth of the well where Jonathan and Ahimaaz were hiding. Then she scattered threshed grain on top of it, that is, grain already separated from the chaff, as if she were drying it out.

"And the thing was not known" means that no one discovered the matter.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David was fleeing from his son Absalom, and these two young men were carrying a secret message to warn him of Ahithophel's plan. They were seen and took refuge in Bahurim. The woman protected them with cleverness, and the pursuers left without finding them.

For today: God often uses simple people who are little known to accomplish his purposes. An act of courage and quiet help, such as protecting or supporting someone in danger, can have great value before God, even though no one notices it.
exp.21:8:
This verse describes God with images of powerful fire: smoke rises from his nostrils, and fire comes from his mouth and devours, so much that even coals are set ablaze. It is poetic language. The word "devour" means that it burns up and destroys everything it touches. The phrase "was angry" shows his anger against evil.

David, already an old man, speaks in a song of thanksgiving because God rescued him from Saul and from his enemies. He was in distress, he cried out, and God answered. These images are not a literal scene, but a way of saying that God acted with strength to deliver his servant. Scholars understand these figures as poetry about divine intervention.

For today: when you feel that no one is listening, cry out to God. He is not indifferent to injustice or to your pain. Trust that his anger against evil is part of his love for his own people.
exp.3:9:
Here David recalls something that had already happened. A man brought him the news that Saul had died, thinking he was bringing good news. David had him seized and put to death at Ziklag, as the price for that report. Seized here means that he took him into custody.

David speaks to Rechab and Baanah, who had just murdered Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, hoping for a reward. David reminds them that he did not reward the one who came to him announcing Saul's death. If that was punished in this way, then all the more would he punish those who killed an innocent man in his own bed.

Today we learn that the end does not justify the means. God is not pleased when we seek gain through wickedness, even when we call it "help." Let us ask him to guide us to act with justice and honesty.
exp.14:36:
This verse says that Hushai, David's friend, came into the city of Jerusalem, and that at nearly the same time Absalom also came into it. The word "friend" here indicates a close counselor who was loyal to the king. The narrator simply reports their arrivals.

David was fleeing Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled against him. Before leaving, David asked Hushai to return and pretend to serve Absalom, in order to frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel and send word through the priests Zadok and Abiathar. The narrator thus marks the moment when David's plan is set in motion: Hushai is already inside, just as Absalom takes the city.

For today: when we go through difficult situations, God may have loyal people placed in the right spot. We can pray with confidence and also be, for others, faithful friends who serve with courage and wisdom when they are most needed.
exp.21:44:
This verse says that people from other nations, the foreigners, drew near to David either in fear or with feigned submission. The verse you have says "Strangers shall submit themselves unto me," so the "strangers" here are the foreigners. The text describes them as ready to bow to him as soon as they hear of him, so their obedience is described as immediate, with no need for David to press them. Some readers understand that this obedience was sincere, and others that it was forced, and the text leaves room for both ideas.

David sings this hymn of gratitude at the end of his life, after God delivered him from Saul and from his enemies. He acknowledges that God made him king and gave him victory over peoples he did not even know. The verse notes that the wording "as soon as they hear" means that, as soon as they heard about him, they were already obeying him.

For today: when a responsibility or an achievement comes your way, do not credit it only to your own effort. Give thanks to God, as David did, and use your influence with humility and justice.
exp.9:17:
The Syrians (Arameans) fled before Israel. David defeated the men of seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen (soldiers on horseback). He also struck Shobach, the captain of their army, and he died there.

The narrator tells of the war that began when the Ammonites humiliated David's messengers. They hired the Syrians, and David went out to face them. In 1 Chronicles 19:18 the numbers are different, and this is explained in several ways: copying errors, or different ways of counting. What is clear is the total defeat of the Syrians.

For today: when a conflict grows out of pride or out of backing a mistaken cause, it ends up costing a high price. Let us seek peace in time, and not ally ourselves with someone who persists in doing wrong.
exp.17:3:
David accepts the counsel of his people. He tells them, "Whatever seems best to you, I will do." Then he stands beside the gate of the city while all the soldiers go out in groups of a hundred and of a thousand.

David is fleeing from his son Absalom, who rebelled against him and tried to take away his kingdom. The army is divided into three parts, and David wanted to go into battle with them. The men stop him, because if he is killed, everything would be lost. He yields and stays at the gate, and from there he watches his troops march out. Later he will ask that they deal gently with Absalom.

For today: knowing how to listen to good advice is a sign of humility. Even when we are leaders, we do not always have to impose our own desire. Let us ask God for wisdom to accept the help of others.
exp.10:12:
This verse tells how David invited Uriah to eat and drink with him, and made him drink until he was drunk. Even so, Uriah went out in the evening and slept on his bed among the king's servants, without going home.

David had sent for Uriah from the front of the war so that he would go home and sleep with his wife Bathsheba, in order to hide the fact that she was pregnant by David. Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refused. Then David tried another way out through the wine, but that did not work either. The text does not say that David planned every detail of this, but his intention is clear: to cover up his sin.

For today: when we fail, the answer is not to hide the mistake with more deception, because that only makes it bigger. It is to confess in time and seek God's forgiveness.
exp.15:19:
Here Absalom asks Ahithophel for advice and says to him, "Give counsel among you what we shall do." That is, he asks what the next step should be. The phrase here is rendered with the wording of the verse, so it is translated directly.

Absalom had rebelled against his father David and had taken Jerusalem. Ahithophel, who had once been David's counselor, now stands on Absalom's side. Hushai had just offered his loyalty, although the Bible shows that he was in fact loyal to David. Ahithophel will give an evil and shameful piece of advice, which will make reconciliation between Absalom and David impossible.

For today: asking for advice is wise, but it matters a great deal whom we ask. Let us seek voices that draw us closer to God, to truth, and to peace, not voices that feed our pride or our bad decisions.
exp.20:9:
Rizpah took a sack of coarse cloth, the kind worn in mourning, and spread it out for herself on the rock. She stayed there from the start of the barley harvest until the rain fell from heaven. She watched over the bodies of her two sons and the five others who had been hanged. She did not let the birds of the air touch them by day, or the wild animals by night.

The account is told by the narrator of Samuel. There was famine in David's time, and the Gibeonites asked for justice because of the violence Saul had done against them. David handed over seven of Saul's descendants. Leaving a body without burial was a great dishonor. Rizpah, grieved, protects her own. The text does not explain everything, and this episode has been much debated.

For today: faithful love can show itself in quiet perseverance. Staying close to someone who suffers, without abandoning them, is a real way of honoring their dignity. God also sees such acts.
exp.1:2:
This verse tells us that David did not go to Hebron alone. He also brought the men who had stayed with him during his years of flight, each one with his family. They settled in the towns around Hebron.

This is the narrator's account, following the death of Saul. David asked God what to do and obeyed his answer: go up to Hebron, in the territory of Judah. Those men had been loyal to him while he was being hunted. Soon after, the men of Judah anointed him king over their tribe. Hebron thus became the center of a new beginning.

For today: when God opens a new stage for us, we do not live it alone. Let us care for and thank those who walked with us in hard times, and seek God's guidance before taking each step.
exp.13:13:
It says that we all must die, like water spilled on the ground that can never be gathered up again. But God does not take pleasure in taking people's lives; rather, he looks for ways so that the one who has gone away from him is not kept apart forever.

A wise woman from Tekoa speaks, sent by Joab, according to the account. She tells King David a story about his son to lead him to think about Absalom, who was banished for having killed his brother Amnon. She suggests that David should seek a way to bring him back.

For today: God seeks the return of the one who has gone away. If someone has turned away from you or from God, do not give up; pray and look for a path of reconciliation, with wisdom and patience.
exp.11:26:
Joab sends word to David that he has already fought against Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and has taken "the city of waters." The verse notes that the words "sent" and "messengers" are clear, and that the word translated "fought" is the same as "struggled." The "city of waters" was probably the part of Rabbah that controlled the water supply, and it can also be understood as the royal quarter. Scholars explain this in different ways.

Joab, David's general, is the one speaking. Israel was at war with the Ammonites, and David had stayed behind in Jerusalem. Joab had nearly conquered the city already, but he wants David to come and complete the victory, so that the honor belongs to the king and not to Joab. This comes right after David's sin and the word of Nathan.

For today: learn not to take credit that belongs to others. When you accomplish something, acknowledge those who gave you the opportunity, and work with humility and loyalty, without seeking your own fame.
exp.1:19:
Abner turned his head back and asks Asahel whether it really is him, the one who has been chasing him. Asahel answers with a simple "Yes." The phrase "looked behind him" means that Abner turned around to see who was following him so closely.

We are in the war between the army of Judah, under David, and the army of Israel, under Abner, after the death of Saul. Asahel, brother of Joab, was very swift and ran after Abner without turning aside. Abner speaks to him, and the verses that follow show that he wanted to avoid killing him and wanted him to stop.

For today: sometimes we rush after something with such eagerness that we do not listen to warnings. Being quick and brave is not enough; wisdom is needed to know when to stop. Let us ask God for discernment before we follow a path.
exp.17:26:
What it says: The watchman standing in the tower recognizes the first runner by the way he runs. He says it looks like Ahimaaz, the son of Zadok. King David replies that Ahimaaz is a good man and that he surely brings good news.

Context: David is waiting for news of the battle against his son Absalom, who had rebelled. The watchman speaks from the wall, and David, anxious, interprets what he hears. He expects good news because of Ahimaaz's character. But what truly worries him is his son, and Ahimaaz's answer will be evasive. The Bible does not say why, but the text shows that the news is painful.

For today: It is easy to expect the news we want simply because we trust the one who brings it. Let us learn to wait with humility, asking God for strength to receive the truth, whatever it may be.
exp.13:23:
In this verse, King David decides that his son Absalom may return to Jerusalem, but he does not want to see him. "Let him turn to his own house" means that he is to live in his own home. "Let him not see my face" means that he will not be able to come before the king. Absalom obeys and spends a period of time without seeing his father.

It is David who speaks. Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and fled to Geshur. Joab, the commander of the army, managed to get David to allow his return. But David did not receive him fully: there was a return, but not a reconciliation. The Bible does not explain all of David's reasons; they could be grief, doubt or indecision.

For today: a partial forgiveness leaves open wounds. If there is a broken relationship in your family, seek with prayer and humility a true reconciliation, with truth, justice and love, not merely a peace that only looks like peace.
exp.10:20:
Here Joab gives instructions to a messenger. If David became angry because the soldiers went so close to the city wall, the messenger was to remind him about Abimelech, who died in Thebez when a woman dropped a piece of a millstone on him from the wall. After that he was to add: "Thy servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also."

Joab speaks after David, wanting to hide his sin with Bathsheba, ordered that Uriah be placed at the front of the battle. Joab carries out that order and prepares the report to soften the king's anger. The sentence about Uriah reveals what really mattered.

For today: when an unjust decision is hidden behind good explanations, the death of a person remains serious. Let us be honest, acknowledge our faults in time, and not let others pay for them.
exp.18:23:
It says that Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, went down to meet King David. He had deliberately left himself unkempt: he had not washed his feet, had not trimmed his beard, and had not washed his clothes. This was from the day David left Jerusalem until he returned safe and sound. Having feet that were washed and a beard that was trimmed were normal signs of personal care.

Context: The narrator tells of David's return after Absalom's rebellion. This follows his pardon of Shimei. Mephibosheth was lame and had been treated with kindness by David. His servant Ziba had accused him of disloyalty. Here his appearance seems to be a sign of mourning for David, although he himself will explain this in the next verse. The text does not fully resolve who was telling the truth.

For today: When someone is falsely accused, sincerity and humility speak louder. And whoever judges should listen calmly, without rushing to conclusions.
exp.1:22:
He says that Asahel would not stop chasing Abner, and Abner struck him with the back end of his spear (the metal tip at the bottom, used to plant the spear in the ground). The blow was so hard that it went clear through him, and Asahel died right there. Those who were passing by stopped, probably out of sorrow and shock at seeing his body.

This is part of the war between the army of Judah, with David, and the army of Israel, with Abner, who supported the house of Saul. Asahel, brother of Joab, was chasing Abner. Abner warned him twice to turn aside, because he did not want to kill him or get into trouble with Joab.

For today: when a wise person gives us a clear warning, it is wise to listen. Stubbornness and pride can lead us to lose more than we imagine.
exp.6:6:
God reminds David that, throughout all the time he walked with Israel, he never asked any of the leaders: "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?" To "shepherd" means to care for and guide, like a shepherd with his sheep. "House of cedars" refers to a luxurious palace built of fine wood.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple, but God answers that he had never asked for one, since he had accompanied his people while they lived in a tent. Some see here a call to humility; others see God himself deciding the timing and the form. Then he promises to build David's house, that is, his descendants.

For today: our good intentions do not replace God's guidance. Before doing something great for him, ask him what he desires, and remember that he always acts first on your behalf.
exp.5:11:
It was reported to King David that the Lord had blessed the household of Obed-edom and everything that belonged to him, because of the ark of God. So David went and brought the ark of God up from the house of Obed-edom into the city of David with joy. The word "aviso" in the source phrase simply means "word" or "message," that is, he was told. "City of David" is Jerusalem. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence among his people.

The narrator describes what happened after David became frightened. Shortly before, Uzzah died when he touched the ark while it was being carried (2 Samuel 6:6-9). David left it for three months at the house of Obed-edom. On learning that blessing was found there, he understood that drawing near to God was possible, and he resumed moving the ark. The Bible does not describe how that blessing appeared.

For today: God deserves respect, but he also wants to bless those who receive him. We can draw near to him with reverence and joy, making room for his presence in our homes.
exp.10:22:
This verse gives the messenger's report to David about the battle. It says that the men of Rabbah were stronger and came out into the field against the Israelites, but that the Israelites managed to push them back as far as the entrance of the city gate. The word "prevailed" in the verse means that they gained the upper hand.

The messenger speaks following Joab's instructions. Joab had been reckless in approaching the wall, and he feared David's anger. Moreover, that attack cost the life of Uriah, whom David had ordered killed to hide his sin. The messenger gives the details of the battle first, as Joab had instructed him.

For today: when we have done something wrong, it is easy to hide it behind well-arranged words. God prefers that we live in truth and confess in time, for He forgives those who repent with sincerity.
exp.15:0:
David had just gone a little past the top of the hill (the Mount of Olives, on his flight), and there Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, came out to meet him. He had a pair of donkeys with their saddles on, loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred cakes of dried figs, and a bottle of wine. A "bottle of wine" is a skin, a leather bag for holding wine.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Ziba, who had been a servant of Saul's household, appears with provisions just when David is weary and in need. Afterward he accuses Mephibosheth of treason. We cannot be certain whether Ziba was telling the truth or was seeking his own gain; the later account leaves doubts.

Today we can be thankful for timely help, but it is also wise to discern. Before believing what someone says about another, especially when it benefits the one speaking, it is wise to investigate, to pray, and not to judge in a hurry.
exp.18:34:
Barzillai tells King David that he is already eighty years old and feels that his age has taken away his strength and his senses. He says that he can no longer discern between good and evil, that is, he can no longer taste what he eats or drinks, nor enjoy the voices of singing men and singing women. So he asks why he should be a burden to the king.

Barzillai was a wealthy man from Gilead who had helped David with food and supplies while David was fleeing from his son Absalom. Now David wants to reward him by taking him to live with him in Jerusalem. Barzillai is grateful, but he humbly declines the offer and suggests that Chimham, probably a young man from his household, go in his place, although the text gives no further details.

For today: let us learn to recognize our stages of life with humility and gratitude. We can serve with generosity without demanding rewards, and we can also help others receive opportunities that we no longer need ourselves.
exp.18:40:
Here the men of Israel (the northern tribes) go to King David and complain with irritation. They protest that the men of Judah, "our brethren," took the king away in secret, so to speak, and helped him cross the Jordan River with his household and his men, without including them. The phrase "stolen thee away" does not appear here, but it is understood that they felt left out.

After Absalom's rebellion, David returns to Jerusalem. Judah was quick to receive him, and Israel felt ignored at a moment of honor. It is the people of Israel speaking, wounded in their pride. This tension shows divisions that would later grow within the kingdom.

For today: when there is reconciliation, let us take care that no one feels excluded. Before complaining in anger, it is wise to speak with humility and seek peace, for wounded pride can break what God wants to heal.
exp.1:5:
David wishes the men of Jabesh-gilead that the Lord will deal with them in kindness and faithfulness. He also promises that he himself will repay them with good, because they cared for the body of King Saul. The words "kindness and truth" speak of loyal love and of a faithfulness that stays firm. "I will requite you" means that he will treat them with favor.

David speaks as a king just anointed over Judah in Hebron. The men of Jabesh had buried Saul with honor, and David sends messengers to thank them. He may also have been seeking their friendship, since he later encourages them to be brave and tells them that Judah has anointed him. The Bible says nothing more about his intentions, so it is best not to claim more than the text states.

Today we can notice those who do acts of kindness that no one sees or that bring them no benefit. We should thank them with sincere words and, if possible, with a concrete gesture. In this way we reflect the kindness and faithfulness of God.
exp.18:15:
This verse tells us that Shimei, son of Gera, of the tribe of Benjamin and from the town of Bahurim, hurried down to meet David. The phrase "hasted and came down" means that he moved quickly. He came along with the men of Judah to welcome the king who was returning.

The narrator describes David's return after Absalom's rebellion. Shimei was the same man who had earlier cursed and thrown stones at David as he fled (2 Samuel 16). Now, seeing that the king was coming back with power, he rushes to show himself a friend. The Bible does not say how sincere his heart was; the text only shows his speed, and then he falls down and asks for forgiveness.

We can ask for forgiveness truly and in time when we have failed. But we also learn to examine our motives: are we seeking reconciliation out of love and repentance, or only out of convenience? God looks at the heart.
exp.18:35:
Barzillai tells King David that he will go only a little further with him, as far as the Jordan River. "Servant" is a humble way of speaking about himself. "Reward" means a payment or a prize. He asks plainly why the king would want to give him such a great prize for something so small.

Barzillai was a wealthy man from Gilead who had supplied David and his people with food when they were fleeing from David's son Absalom. Now David is returning as king and offers to let Barzillai live with him in Jerusalem. Barzillai, who is eighty years old, humbly declines because he feels too old. He asks that his young Chimham go in his place.

For today: we can serve with generosity without expecting honors. It is also wise to recognize our stages and limits, and to open the way for younger people with gratitude and peace.
exp.0:23:
This verse calls the women of Israel to weep for King Saul. It reminds them that, during his reign, he gave them clothing of scarlet (a bright red cloth, very valuable) and gold ornaments for their garments. It speaks of a time of abundance and celebration.

David speaks in a song of mourning for the death of Saul and Jonathan in battle. Although Saul had pursued him, David does not rejoice at his death. He highlights the good the people received during that reign and honors the fallen king. Scholars see here a tone of public tribute.

For today: even when someone has done us harm, we can recognize the good they did and avoid rejoicing in their fall. Honoring with truth and respect is also a way of loving.
exp.11:24:
This verse says that God sent a message through the prophet Nathan, and that because of this the child also received the name Jedidiah. This name means "beloved of the Lord." The phrase "because of the Lord" can be taken to mean "out of love for the Lord" or "because the Lord willed it"; some understand it as a sign that God accepted him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David had sinned grievously with Bathsheba and lost the first child. After that sorrow, Solomon is born. God sends Nathan, the same prophet who had earlier confronted David, now with a sign of grace. The Bible does not explain in detail how the message was delivered.

For today: God can restore and bless after repentance and sorrow. If you have failed, return to Him with sincerity, trust in His forgiveness, and walk with hope.
exp.10:1:
It says that one evening David got up from his bed and went for a walk on the flat roof of his palace. From there he saw a woman bathing, and the Bible says she was very beautiful. The verse opens with "it came to pass," which means "it happened," and the word "saw" is spelled in an older way.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book, not David. He points out that it was the season when kings went out to war, but David stayed in Jerusalem while Joab and the army fought. The text does not say this in so many words, but it shows that David was not where he should have been, and that prepares the sin that follows.

For today: many falls begin with carelessness, not with a great evil. Looking was not the greatest sin; what was serious came afterward, when he let desire take charge. When something tempts you, move away quickly, busy yourself with what is rightly yours to do, and ask God for strength.
exp.17:30:
This verse tells how Cushi came before David with news he thought was good. Cushi says that the Lord has taken up the king's cause and freed him from all who rose against him. Notice that he does not yet mention Absalom.

Cushi is a messenger sent by Joab after the battle against Absalom's army. David was waiting to learn whether his son was alive. Cushi presents the victory as the work of God, but David asks about Absalom, and the answer breaks him. Here the Bible shows David as a king, but also as a wounded father.

For today: a victory can come mixed with pain. We can thank God for what is good and, at the same time, be sensitive to someone who is suffering, without rushing to celebrate.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that Mephibosheth had a young son named Micha. It also says that all of Ziba's household, that is, his sons and his servants, were placed at the service of Mephibosheth. Servants are those who work for another person, and to dwell means to live in a place.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David, because of his covenant of friendship with Jonathan, sought someone from the house of Saul to show kindness to. He found Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, and returned to him the lands of his family. Ziba and his household were to work those lands. Micha is mentioned because Jonathan's family would continue. Later Micha will have descendants (1 Chronicles 8:35).

For today: keep the promises you have made, even when time has passed. Think of someone to whom you can show kindness without expecting anything in return, as God does with us.
exp.18:22:
Here David tells Shimei, "Thou shalt not die," and confirms it with an oath. The word "sware" means that he made a solemn promise, before God.

David returns to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Shimei had cursed him as he fled (2 Samuel 16), and now he comes to ask for forgiveness. Abishai, who wanted to defend the king, asked that Shimei be put to death for cursing the Lord's anointed. David rejected this and chose to show mercy on the day of his return. Later, before his death, David gave his son Solomon instructions about Shimei (1 Kings 2), and readers debate how to understand that.

Today we can learn that forgiveness opens the door to peace. When someone has offended us and repents, we can respond with grace instead of revenge, and keep the word we have given.
exp.11:10:
God says he will bring punishment on David through a disaster that will come from his own household. His wives will be taken before his eyes and given to "your neighbor," that is, to someone close to him. That man will lie with them "in the sight of this sun," meaning in public, in broad daylight. "Lie with" means to have sexual relations.

The prophet Nathan speaks, sent by God, after David abused Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah killed. David did this in secret, but God responds with a punishment visible to everyone. Later, the Bible tells of his son Absalom doing something similar (2 Samuel 16:22). Afterward David acknowledges his sin and receives forgiveness, though the consequences remain.

For today: God forgives the one who truly repents, but our decisions can leave marks. For that reason it is wise to act with integrity, even when no one sees us.
exp.8:7:
Mephibosheth bows again before David and says, "What is your servant, that you should look upon a dead dog like me?" It is a very humble way of speaking. "Look upon" here means to notice someone with favor and care. Calling oneself a "dead dog" was calling oneself worthless, someone not deserving of attention.

He speaks as Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan and grandson of King Saul. David has just promised him kindness for the sake of Jonathan, his friend, and restored to him his family's lands. Mephibosheth was lame in his feet (2 Samuel 9:3, 4:4), and came from a fallen family. His reaction shows astonishment, not pride.

For today: God treats us with grace that we have not earned. We can receive his kindness with humility and gratitude, and share that same kindness with those who seem to have nothing to offer.
exp.4:17:
This verse says that the Philistines came in large groups and spread out across the valley of Rephaim, an area near Jerusalem. The word spread out in the verse means that they scattered over the land and took possession of it.

The account is told by the narrator of the book. David had just been anointed king over all Israel, and the Philistines, who had previously tolerated him, now saw him as a threat and came up to attack him. David withdrew to the stronghold. Scholars debate exactly which stronghold that was. What matters next is that David did not act on impulse but sought the Lord's counsel.

For today: when a great problem comes, before reacting, ask God in prayer and seek his guidance in the Bible. He can give you clear direction.
exp.14:13:
David says to all his servants in Jerusalem that they must get up and flee, because they will not be able to escape from Absalom if they stay. He asks them to hurry, for if Absalom catches up with them, he will bring disaster upon them and strike down the people of the city. "Make speed" means "hurry," and "with the edge of the sword" means "with the sword," that is, with death and violence.

David is speaking here as the king of Israel. His son Absalom had plotted against him and was winning the hearts of the people. When David learns that Israel is going after Absalom, he decides to leave the city. It seems he wants to spare Jerusalem from fighting within its walls, and also to save his own people.

For today: sometimes acting wisely means withdrawing rather than fighting out of pride. When a conflict could hurt others, thinking first about their well-being can be an act of humility and love.
exp.6:8:
It says that God was with David in all his ways. The verse notes that one word in the older wording means "cut off" or "eliminated," and God removed David's enemies from his path. God also gave him a great name, that is, fame and respect, like that of the most important men in the world.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple, but God reminds him that it was He who took him from tending sheep and made him king. Before speaking about what David would do for God, God shows what He had already done for David. Then He promises him a house, meaning a lasting family and kingdom.

For today: before we worry about what we must do for God, let us remember what He has already done for us. Looking back and giving thanks gives us humility and confidence for the future.
exp.19:3:
King David says to Amasa: "Assemble me the men of Judah within three days, and be thou here present." The words used in the older wording for "assemble" and "be present" are simply "assemble me" and "be here present" in the verse above. "Men" here means men able to go to war.

David speaks as king, after the rebellion of Absalom. Now Sheba, son of Bichri, is stirring up Israel against him. David gives this task to Amasa, who had been commander of Absalom's army and to whom David had promised a place of command (2 Samuel 19:13). In this way he was seeking to win the people back. The text does not explain why Amasa was later slow.

For today: when we receive a responsibility, timing matters. Carrying out what has been entrusted to us on time shows faithfulness and prevents bigger problems.
exp.10:19:
This verse is part of the instructions Joab gives to a messenger. He tells him that if King David becomes angry and asks why the soldiers went so near the city walls, the messenger should remind him that people inside the city usually shoot things down at attackers from above. The word "shoot" in the verse means throw or fire things, as arrows or stones.

Joab speaks after having attacked the city of Rabbah. Earlier, David had ordered him to put Uriah at the front of the battle so that he would die, and Joab carried out the order. Now he prepares the message to anticipate the king's reaction. In the end, the news of Uriah's death was meant to calm David.

For today: when an unjust decision leads us to hide the truth or to prepare excuses, it is better to stop and change course. God prefers a sincere and repentant heart over explanations, however well put together.
exp.16:6:
Hushai tells Absalom that the counsel Ahithophel has just given him is not good, at least at this time. The words "at this time" show that Hushai is not attacking Ahithophel in general, but is saying that this particular plan is a mistake. The phrase "said unto" is an old way of writing "said to."

Hushai speaks because Absalom, who had rebelled against his father David, asked for his opinion. Ahithophel had proposed pursuing David at once. Hushai was a friend of David and, according to the account, was there to thwart Ahithophel's advice. That is why he speaks with great cunning, though the text does not say everything he was thinking.

For today: before deciding something important, listen to more than one opinion, and ask whether the counsel is wise, not just whether it sounds convincing. And ask God for discernment.
exp.4:20:
This verse says that the Philistines, fleeing in defeat, left their idols there, that is, the images of their gods. David and his men burned them. The word "idols" refers to figures that people worshiped or trusted for their protection. Other translations say that David and his men carried them off, as appears in the Hebrew text of other passages; here the Hebrew tradition and the ancient version differ a little.

It is part of the historical account of when David was already king of Israel. The Philistines came up to attack him, and David first inquired of God. After the victory at Baal-perazim, it is clear that the idols could not save those who carried them. Burning them shows that David trusted only in the LORD.

For today: ask yourself what things you have relied on for "protection" instead of trusting God. Consult the Lord first in prayer and, if anything has taken his place in your heart, let it go with resolve.
exp.23:6:
This verse describes the last stage of the route that Joab and the commanders took while counting the people. They reached the stronghold of Tyre and the cities of the Hivites and the Canaanites. Then they went out toward the south of Judah, as far as Beersheba. The phrase about the south is explained here: the route went from north to south, so they finished covering the land from north to south.

The narrator describes the census that King David ordered Joab, his military chief, to carry out. Joab traveled through the whole country, and the journey lasted almost ten months. Earlier, Joab had warned David not to do it, but the king insisted. The text says David acted out of pride or confidence in his own strength, and afterward he acknowledged that he had sinned (v. 10). Some scholars see here a sign of his lack of trust in God.

For today: it is easy to measure our security by numbers, such as money, achievements, or approval. Today you can remember that your confidence rests in God, not in what you have.
exp.17:18:
Ahimaaz, the son of the priest Zadok, asks Joab for permission to run and bring the news to King David. He wants to tell him that the Lord has avenged him of his enemies. The phrase about the Lord having avenged him means that God brought him justice, and the word "news" here simply means tidings.

Ahimaaz speaks as a young messenger who is loyal to David. Absalom's rebellion has just ended with his death. Ahimaaz sees the victory as the work of God and wants to make it known. But Joab knows that David will grieve over the death of his son, and for that reason he holds Ahimaaz back. His zeal was sincere, though perhaps he did not take into account the king's pain.

For today: when we want to share something good, let us do it eagerly, but also with sensitivity. Good news needs the right moment and the right words, thinking about how the one who hears it will feel.
exp.15:2:
Here King David asks about Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, and Ziba, his servant, answers that he stayed behind in Jerusalem. According to Ziba, Mephibosheth thinks the people of Israel will give him back his grandfather's kingdom today. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and "the son of your master" refers to Mephibosheth.

David flees Jerusalem because of the rebellion of his son Absalom. Ziba arrives with supplies and, very conveniently, accuses his master of treason. The Bible does not confirm in this passage whether it is true. Later, Mephibosheth gives a different version (2 Samuel 19), so Ziba may have been lying to keep the property. David decides quickly, without listening to Mephibosheth.

For today: before believing an accusation against someone, especially when the person making it stands to gain, it is wise to stop, ask questions, and listen to both sides. Being fair requires patience, even when we are tired or under pressure.
exp.17:5:
The verse tells us that David's soldiers went out into the open country to fight against the army of Israel, which was following Absalom. The battle took place in the forest of Ephraim.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Absalom, David's son, had rebelled against his father to take away his throne. David, although he was the king, does not go to the battle; he stays near the gate and asks his commanders to deal gently with Absalom. His grief as a father shows through in the middle of the war. Where that forest was located exactly is not known for certain.

For today: even when someone has hurt us, we can seek justice without losing compassion. David reminds us that love can remain alive in the midst of conflict, and that we should ask God for wisdom to act with firmness and with mercy.
exp.17:20:
Joab tells Cushi to go and report to King David what he has seen. Cushi bows low before Joab as a sign of respect, and then runs off.

The phrase "bowed himself" simply means that he bent down in respect.

"Cushi" can be understood as a man from Cush, that is, an Ethiopian or Nubian, and he was probably a servant of Joab.

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. Absalom, the king's son, had rebelled and has just died. Joab knows the news will deeply grieve David, so he does not want Ahimaaz to carry it, since Ahimaaz had brought a message of victory. He chooses Cushi, who had seen what happened. The Bible does not explain all of Joab's reasons, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: Some news must be given with honesty and with care. Before speaking in painful moments, let us think about who should say it, how, and with how much compassion.
exp.0:2:
David asks a man who has just arrived, "Where have you come from?" The man answers, "I have escaped," meaning that he has got away from the camp of Israel.

David is speaking because he is at Ziklag, waiting for news after defeating the Amalekites. The man arrives with torn clothes and dirt on his head, signs of mourning and grief in that culture. Later he will say that Saul and Jonathan died. As the story goes on, we will see that his account of how Saul died includes details the Bible does not confirm, so it is wise to read it carefully.

For today: when strong news arrives, ask calmly and listen closely before you react. David asked for facts and then asked more questions. Doing the same helps us be prudent and keeps us from being carried away by rumors.
exp.22:20:
He defeated an Egyptian who was a very tall man and was carrying a spear. Benaiah did not have a weapon like his: he went down to face him with only a staff. He took the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with that same spear. "Defeated" here means "killed" or "overcame," and "brave man" means a man of courage.

This passage is part of "the last words of David," where the account lists his mighty men. The narrator wants to show the deeds of Benaiah, who was famous among the thirty, though he did not reach the first three. David placed him on his council, that is, he gave him trust and responsibility. The text does not explain every detail of the fight.

For today: courage does not depend on having the best tools, but on acting with faith, determination and wisdom in the face of what we confront. God can use the little we have, and He also calls us to be faithful in difficult times.
exp.17:6:
This verse tells us that the army of Israel, the one that followed Absalom, was defeated by David's men. There was a very great slaughter that day: twenty thousand dead. "Servants of David" refers to his loyal soldiers. "Slaughter" in the verse refers to a great number of deaths in battle.

The narrator describes the battle in the forest of Ephraim, when Absalom rebelled against his father David. Shortly before, David had asked his captains to deal gently with his son. Even so, the fighting was fierce. The text says the forest devoured more people than the sword did, though it does not explain in detail how. The figure of twenty thousand may be understood literally or as an approximate number.

For today: decisions of rebellion and pride leave deep wounds that reach many people. Before following a path of division, it is wise to stop, seek God, and consider the harm we might cause to others.
exp.21:1:
Here David says that the Lord is his rock, his fortress, and his deliverer. These are three images: the rock speaks of a firm place where one does not fall; the fortress, of a secure place against attack; and the deliverer, of someone who rescues.

David sings these words on the day God delivered him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, who pursued him for years. It is a song of thanksgiving that looks back and acknowledges that God sustained him through real dangers. This same song appears, with small differences, in Psalm 18.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, remember how God has helped you before and make it known to him in prayer. Putting his faithfulness into words strengthens trust, and you can run to him as to a firm refuge.
exp.16:1:
Here Ahithophel proposes attacking David by surprise. "Weary and weak handed" means without strength, discouraged. "Come upon him" means to fall on him suddenly. His plan is to frighten David so that the people who are with him will flee, and so strike down only the king.

Ahithophel had been David's counselor, but he joined the rebellion of Absalom, the king's son. David was fleeing from Jerusalem, exhausted and saddened by the betrayal of his son. Ahithophel takes advantage of that moment of weakness and proposes acting that very night, before David can regroup.

For today: a piece of advice can sound very logical and still be unjust or harmful. Before following an idea, it is good to ask whether it is right before God, not only whether it is convenient. And if you are weary today, remember that God cares for the weak.
exp.3:4:
This verse tells how Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon from the town of Beeroth, went to the house of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul. They arrived at the hottest time of the day, when he was resting in his room.

The author of the book tells the events as a narrator. Ish-bosheth was ruling over Israel after Saul's death, and David was ruling over Judah. These two brothers were captains serving Ish-bosheth, and they were planning to kill him, most likely to win David's favor. The narrator makes it clear that this was a betrayal, and later David punishes the murderers.

For today: let us not justify wrongdoing with the excuse that it suits us. God does not need our schemes or our disloyalty to carry out his plans. Let us seek to move forward with integrity, even when it seems slower.
exp.23:1:
Here the king David orders Joab, the commander of his army, to go through the whole land, from Dan in the north to Beer-sheba in the south, and to count the people. David wants to know how many people there are in Israel. The phrase "go through" means to travel across the whole area, and the order is given to several people at once, so it is a command for a group to carry out.

Before this verse, the text says that God was angry with Israel and that David was moved to take the census. The text does not explain the reason for the anger. Joab objects, but the king insists. Many readers understand that the problem was David's trust in the number of soldiers rather than in God, although the passage does not say this in those words.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: in numbers, money or resources, or in God. It is also wise to listen to those who warn us with good judgment, as Joab did.
exp.12:37:
He says that Absalom escaped after killing his brother Amnon and went to Geshur, a region northeast of Israel. He stayed there three years. The words "fled" and "went" show that he moved away in order to hide.

The account is told by the narrator of the book. Amnon had dishonored Tamar, Absalom's sister, and Absalom took revenge by killing him. Then he took refuge with his maternal grandfather, King Talmai, since his mother was that king's daughter. Meanwhile, David was grieving the loss of one son and the absence of the other.

For today: revenge and wounds left unhealed can separate families for years. If there is conflict in your home, do not wait for three years to pass; seek to speak with humility, to ask for forgiveness or to forgive, and let God guide the reconciliation.
exp.22:10:
After him, the verse says, another of David's mighty men was Shammah, son of Agee, from a place called Harar (the text says "Ararite," which probably indicates his origin). The Philistines had gathered together in a troop, and there was a piece of ground full of lentils, and the people had fled. A "piece of ground" means a plot of field, and "fled" means they ran away.

This passage is part of the list of David's mighty men, at the end of the book of 2 Samuel. The account has no direct speaker; it is the narrator who recalls the deeds of these men. The purpose is to show that, even when the people gave way out of fear, God worked through people who did not turn back. The next verse makes clear that it was the Lord who gave the victory.

For today: sometimes everyone around you gives in to something that seems small or worthless, like a field of lentils. Ask God for the courage to stand firm in what is right, trusting that the victory comes from Him.
exp.6:23:
This verse says that God made Israel his own people, in a way that is firm and lasting. It also says that the Lord himself became their God. The first phrase, "you have confirmed," means that you affirmed it and established it with certainty. The second phrase, "you became their God," means that you took them as your people.

David speaks this prayer after the prophet Nathan delivered God's promise about his house and his descendants. David feels humble and thankful. He remembers how God rescued Israel from Egypt and chose them. His prayer rests on what God has already done and promised.

For today: when you doubt whether God sustains you, remember that his faithfulness does not depend on your strength but on his character and his promises. Pray as David did: give thanks for what God has already done, and trust in what he has promised.
exp.11:15:
In this verse we are told that David, when the son he had with Bathsheba fell ill, sought God with all his heart. "Pleaded" means he begged or asked earnestly and persistently. The verse says he went apart from the people and shut himself away alone. He fasted, took no food, and spent the night lying on the ground, showing grief and humility.

The narrator of the book describes what happened after the prophet Nathan confronted David about his sin with Bathsheba and against Uriah. Nathan told him that the child would die. David did not defend himself or grow angry; he cried out to God, hoping that He would have mercy. The Bible does not fully explain why God acted this way, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: when we fail or suffer, we can come to God with sincerity and humility, without excuses, trusting that He hears us, even though He does not always answer as we wish.
exp.11:9:
God tells David that the sword will never leave his family. The reason is that David "despised" him, that is, he gave no weight to God and showed him no respect, and he took Uriah the Hittite's wife to make her his own. "Sword" speaks of violence and death within his household.

The one speaking is the prophet Nathan, sent by the LORD. David had taken Bathsheba and then ordered her husband Uriah killed in battle to hide his sin. God reminds him of everything he had given him, and that is why his wrong was so serious. The consequences he announces are seen afterward in the history of David's family.

For today: sin leaves its marks, even though God forgives. If we have failed, we can come to God with sincerity, hiding nothing, and accept his correction. And if today we have everything, let us remember to thank him and not treat his word lightly.
exp.14:25:
This verse says that David places himself in God's hands. If God were to say to him, "I have no delight in you," David answers, "Here I am," that is, "I am ready." Let God do with him whatever seems good to Him. The verse's word "if he thus say" is an old way of saying "if he says," and "seemeth good" means "seems good."

David speaks with the priest Zadok while he flees from Jerusalem, because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. The Levites had carried God's ark out to accompany him, but David asks that it be brought back to the city. He does not want to use the ark as if it were a charm that would secure God's favor. He prefers to trust in the Lord's will, whatever it may be.

For today: when you go through a crisis, you can pray with humility and entrust the outcome to God. Trusting does not mean doing nothing, but acting wisely and accepting with peace whatever He decides.
exp.9:11:
Joab encourages his brother Abishai to be brave. "Be of good courage" means keep up your spirit and strength. He says they should fight firmly for their people and for the cities of God, and that the Lord should do what seems good to Him.

The one speaking is Joab, the commander of David's army. Israel was surrounded: the Ammonites on one side and the Syrians who supported them on the other. Joab divided the troops and promised mutual help. Then he did his part with courage, and he left the outcome to God. The text tells how the Syrians fled and then the Ammonites as well.

For today: do what is yours to do with dedication and courage, without waiting for others to do it, and lean on those around you. Then leave the result in God's hands with humility, trusting that He works for good.
exp.21:45:
This verse says that foreigners, or people who were not part of the nation of Israel, lost their strength and were filled with fear. "Fade away" means they grew weak from dread. "Close places" refers to hidden places or strongholds where they took cover. Some translations understand it as meaning they came out of their hiding places trembling.

David, now an older man, speaks in a song of thanksgiving to God for rescuing him from Saul and his enemies. He acknowledges that his victory and his kingdom came not by his own strength alone, but by the help of the Lord, whom he calls his rock.

For today: when problems or people make you feel intimidated, remember that God is your firmest refuge. Instead of relying only on your own resources, pray and give thanks for the times He has sustained you, and walk with courage and humility.
exp.23:5:
This verse follows the route of Joab and the commanders as they travelled through the land to count the people. After crossing the Jordan and reaching Aroer, they passed on to Gilead and to the lowlands mentioned in the text. Then they came to Dan-jaan and to the area around Sidon, in the north. The name in the lowlands is a difficult one: the Hebrew text is uncertain, and some scholars interpret it in other ways.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David had ordered the census, and Joab carried it out even though he thought it was a bad idea. The journey through so many regions shows that the order was carried out in full detail, from the east to the north, and that it took almost ten months.

For today: when a decision springs from pride or from distrust of God, it can move forward with great order and effort and still be a mistake. Before planning in detail, it is wise to ask ourselves whether what we are doing honours God and trusts in Him.
exp.12:3:
Jonadab, Amnon's friend, noticed that the prince looked thinner and weaker every day. He asked him directly what was wrong. Amnon answered that he loved Tamar, his brother Absalom's sister.

The speaker is Jonadab, described as a very crafty man and Amnon's cousin. Amnon was suffering over Tamar, who was in fact his half-sister. What he calls love here is a desire that later leads to a serious abuse. Jonadab does not restrain him; instead he gives him a deceitful plan. The account shows how a wrong desire and bad advice can bring down a family.

For today: when a desire consumes you, tell it to someone wise and faithful, not to someone who will only give you clever advice. Seek out the one who draws you close to God and to what is right.
exp.22:28:
This verse continues a list of names. It mentions Heleb, son of Baanah, from the town of Netophah, and Ittai, son of Ribai, from Gibeah, a town in the tribe of Benjamin. They are two more among David's mighty men.

The text is told by the book's narrator, not by David. After the king's final words, the account lists the warriors who supported him. It is a record of honor: although their deeds are not told here, their names were kept. That Ittai was from Benjamin, the tribe of Saul, shows that David had support from different places, though the text does not explain more.

For today: God notices those who serve without being famous. Do your part faithfully, even when no one applauds it. And value those who serve beside you.
exp.5:1:
David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale of Judah, to bring up from there the ark of God. The ark was a sacred chest over which the name of the Lord of hosts was called, the One who dwells between the cherubim, that is, figures of angels that were on the lid of the ark.

The narrator tells what David did as king. He had just gathered thirty thousand chosen men. He wanted to bring the ark, the symbol of God's presence, to the center of his kingdom. Baale of Judah is usually identified with Kiriath-jearim, although the text does not explain this here.

For today: David sought to make God the center of his nation's life. We can ask ourselves whether, in our homes and our decisions, we give God first place. But we must also seek Him with reverence and obedience, as He directs, not only with good intentions.
exp.8:0:
Here David asks a question: is there anyone left from the family of King Saul to whom he can show kindness? "Kindness" here means faithful, loyal treatment, not just forgiveness. And he would do it for Jonathan's sake, that is, in honor of his friend.

David is speaking as the king of Israel now. Saul, his predecessor, had died, and Jonathan, Saul's son, had made a covenant of friendship with David. Normally, a new king might see the family of the previous king as a threat, but David looks for someone to bless. The following text shows that he does so because of the promise he made to Jonathan.

For today: keep your promises and show kindness without expecting anything in return. Ask yourself: whom can I bless today, even if they cannot repay me?
exp.21:30:
This verse says that God's way, that is, his manner of acting, is perfect, without error or wickedness. His word has been tested like metal refined in the fire until it is clean and proven. And God is a shield to those who trust in him, which here means relying on him and taking refuge in him.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that appears at the end of his life, after God had delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and recognizes that God was faithful in the midst of danger. This same song appears, with small variations, in Psalm 18.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God is trustworthy and his word is sure. Read it calmly and take refuge in him, even if you cannot yet see the answer.
exp.21:21:
David says he took care to follow the way the Lord set before him, that is, his manner of life and his commands. The word "kept" here means that he obeyed them and watched over them carefully. "Have not wickedly departed" means that he did not turn away from God in a rebellious or malicious way.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, near the end of his life, after the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He does not claim he never failed; the Bible shows his serious sins. Here he speaks of the general direction of his life: he sought God and, when he fell, he returned to Him. Many understand this to refer to his underlying faithfulness, not to total perfection.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our direction is toward God. We do not need to be perfect, but we should return to Him promptly when we stray, with humility and sincerity.
exp.16:13:
What it says: Absalom and all the men of Israel decided that the counsel of Hushai the Archite was better than that of Ahithophel. The text explains that the Lord had determined to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, in order to bring evil upon Absalom. The word "defeat" here means to make it fail or leave it without effect.

Context: Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David. Ahithophel proposed pursuing David at once, but Hushai, who was secretly loyal to David, advised waiting and gathering all of Israel. His plan gave David time to escape. The narrator tells us that behind that decision was the hand of God.

For today: When things seem to go wrong or the plans of others seem stronger, we can trust that God is still at work. Let us pray and do what is right, resting in the knowledge that He governs even what we cannot see.
exp.2:5:
This verse says that while the conflict continued between the supporters of Saul and those of David, Abner was growing stronger, or gaining more influence, within the house of Saul. "Made himself strong" here does not refer only to working hard, but to asserting his power and his position.

It is the narrator who speaks. After the list of the sons born to David in Hebron, we are reminded that the kingdom was still divided. Abner, commander of Saul's army, was supporting Ish-bosheth, Saul's son. What follows shows that his power would soon clash with the king he was supporting.

For today: power and influence can grow without our noticing, and they can also turn the heart. Let us ask God for humility, to use whatever position we have with integrity and to serve others, not to exalt ourselves.
exp.10:11:
David asked Uriah to stay in Jerusalem one more day, and said that the next day he would send him back to the war. Uriah obeyed and stayed that day and the next.

David speaks with Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers. David had taken Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, and she was pregnant. To cover up his sin, he wanted Uriah to sleep with his wife so that it would appear the child was his. But Uriah, out of loyalty to his companions in battle, refused to enjoy his own house. So David extends his stay, hoping he would change his mind.

For today: when we hide a sin, we tend to invent more plans and even deceptions. It is better to confess in time and ask God for forgiveness, who forgives the sincere heart.
exp.22:16:
Here David says that he cannot drink the water that his three mighty men brought him. They risked their lives to get it, so David compares it to their blood. The phrase "Be it far from me" is an old way of saying the same thing as "I would never do such a thing." Then he poured it out before God as an offering, and the text stresses that these three mighty men performed this deed.

David speaks during a time of war against the Philistines. He had a passing longing for water from his town, Bethlehem, which at that moment was held by the enemy. Out of loyalty, his soldiers broke through the enemy lines to bring it to him. David understood that something so precious was not for his own pleasure, but to honor God.

For today: value the sacrifice of those who serve you, and do not use others to satisfy your whims. When someone gives themselves for you, respond with gratitude and with reverence toward God.
exp.4:19:
It says that David came to Baal-perazim and there defeated the Philistines. He recognized that it was God who gave them the victory, and he compared the victory to water that bursts through a wall and rushes out. The verse says "smote," which means struck down or defeated, and "broken forth," which is like breaking open a gap. For this reason he named the place Baal-perazim, which is usually understood to mean "the Lord of the breach" or "the one who bursts through."

The speaker is the narrator, and then David. The Philistines had invaded the valley of Rephaim, near Jerusalem, shortly after David was made king over all Israel. Before fighting, David consulted God and received a clear promise of victory. His response shows gratitude, not pride.

For today: before making important decisions, seek God's direction in prayer and in His Word. And when something goes well, give Him thanks instead of claiming the credit for yourself alone.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that David, now settled in Jerusalem after leaving Hebron, took more wives and concubines, and that he had more sons and daughters. Concubines were women of a lower rank than a wife, but they were part of the king's household.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not David. Just before this, the text says that God had confirmed him as king and that his kingdom was growing. Then his sons born in Jerusalem are listed, including Solomon. The text only reports the facts; it neither approves nor condemns them. However, the Law asked that the king not multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17), and this set the stage for family problems later on.

For today: when God blesses us with success or power, we should take care with our decisions and obey his Word. Blessings do not protect us from mistakes.
exp.19:16:
This verse records a short exchange. Joab comes near the wall, and the wise woman asks him whether he really is Joab. Joab answers, "I am he." She asks him to hear her words, and he agrees: "I do hear." Words that need a note: "handmaid" is the woman herself, spoken with humility; "hear" means listen.

Joab, David's commander, was pursuing the rebel Sheba, and he had the city of Abel under siege. They were about to bring down the wall. A wise woman, who spoke for the people of the city, asked to speak with him to seek a peaceful way out and prevent destruction.

For today: before acting harshly, it is worth stopping to listen. Joab could have continued the attack, but he listened. Listening calmly can prevent great harm and open the way to peace.
exp.14:10:
This verse says that two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom because he had invited them. They went with simple hearts, meaning with good faith and no bad intentions, and they knew nothing, that is, they did not realize that Absalom was preparing a rebellion against his father David.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Absalom asked the king for permission to go to Hebron, saying he was going to fulfill a vow by means of a sacrifice. In reality he planned to proclaim himself king. He invited respected people to give his plan an appearance of legitimacy, and they were used without realizing it.

For today: good intentions are not enough; it is wise to ask where we are being led before following someone or supporting a cause. Let us ask God for wisdom, inform ourselves well, and think about who is inviting us and for what purpose, so that we do not lend our name to something we do not understand.
exp.19:19:
Joab answers with force: "Never, never!" He says that he does not want to destroy or overthrow the city. The phrase "may that never happen to me" is an old way of saying: "May God keep me from that!" And "overthrow" means to ruin or tear down.

Joab, commander of David's army, was pursuing Sheba, who had rebelled against the king. Sheba took refuge in the city of Abel, and Joab besieged it. A wise woman called to him from the wall, and Joab made clear that his aim was not to level the city, but to capture the rebel. In this way a massacre was avoided.

For today: before reacting harshly, it is wise to listen and to clarify what we truly seek. Often a calm conversation prevents greater harm and makes it possible to solve the problem without hurting the innocent.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul who was ruling over Israel, fell silent before Abner. He did not know what to answer him. The phrase "could not answer a word" means that he did not say even one single word, and "feared him" means that he was afraid of him.

Abner was the commander of the army and Ish-bosheth's main support. He had become angry because Ish-bosheth accused him of something related to one of Saul's concubines. Abner answered with force and swore to help David. The king stayed silent because he depended on Abner's power.

For today: when fear makes us silent in the face of what is unjust, it is wise to ask God for courage and wisdom. We should also take care that our leadership does not depend only on the power of other people, but on acting with integrity.
exp.14:5:
This verse says that Absalom kept up his habit with every Israelite who came before the king to ask for justice. Through those friendly gestures and words, he was winning the people over, that is, gaining their loyalty little by little.

The narrator describes how Absalom, son of King David, was preparing a rebellion. He would stand by the road, listen to those who came with their disputes, agree with them, and tell them that the king would not give them a hearing. He showed them closeness, embraced them, and kissed them. In this way he gained their goodwill while weakening their trust in David. The passage suggests that his affection was a strategy for gaining power.

For today: let us be wary of anyone who flatters us only to gain something. And let us examine our own dealings with others, so that our kindness is sincere and not a tool for using people.
exp.20:7:
