Here it says that David took seven descendants of Saul. Two were sons of Rizpah, a woman of Saul's household: Armoni and Mephibosheth (not the son of Jonathan). The other five were sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, raised by her. "Brought up" means "raised" or "cared for as a child".

The context is a famine lasting three years. God connected it with Saul's violence against the Gibeonites, with whom Israel had made a covenant. The Gibeonites asked for justice, and David, the king, agreed. He spared Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, because of his promise. Some manuscripts name Michal here while others name Merab, and this difference is explained in several ways.

Today: Unjust decisions leave wounds that reach other people, even years later. Keeping one's given word and repairing the harm with humility, rather than ignoring it, honors God and protects others.
exp.7:7:
This verse tells us that David took a great quantity of bronze from Betah and Berothai, two cities that belonged to Hadadezer. The word "brass" here refers to bronze or copper. "Exceeding much" means an abundant amount.

The narrator of the book recounts David's victories over the neighboring kings. After defeating Hadadezer, David receives spoils and tribute. The text emphasizes that "the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went." Later, in 1 Chronicles 18:8, it is said that this bronze was used for the temple, although it is not mentioned here. It is not known with certainty where those cities were located exactly.

For today: everything we have, whether much or little, comes from the protecting hand of God. We can ask ourselves how we use our resources, and whether we put them at the service of something greater than ourselves.
exp.4:9:
David kept growing stronger and greater, and the Lord God of hosts was with him. The phrase about David growing and increasing refers to his power, his kingdom and his influence advancing little by little. The title of God as Lord God of hosts presents him as the Lord of all power. The phrase about God being with David means that God accompanied him and supported him.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David had just taken Jerusalem, which had been a fortress of the Jebusites, and he made it his capital. The text explains the cause of his growth: it was not only his skill, but the presence of God. Shortly afterward, Hiram, king of Tyre, sent him help, and David understood that God had confirmed him as king.

For today: if you are moving forward in your work, your family, or your service, do not forget that the true support is God. Seek his company first, and thank him for every achievement.
exp.6:10:
This verse says that God gave his people rest from the time he set judges over Israel, and that now he will also give David rest from all his enemies. Then God announces to him that he himself will make a house for him, that is, a family and a dynasty, not a building.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple for the Lord, but God answers that it will be he who establishes David's house. He reminds David that he has always been with him and promises stability for Israel. This promise is known as the Davidic covenant, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: before doing great things for God, remember what he has already done for you. Rest in his faithfulness and serve with gratitude, not with anxiety.
exp.11:1:
This verse says that the rich man in the story had a great many sheep and cattle. He owned large flocks and herds, so he lacked nothing. The phrase prepares the contrast with the poor man, who had only one little ewe lamb.

Here the prophet Nathan speaks, sent by God to David. David had committed adultery with Bathsheba and had had her husband Uriah killed. Nathan does not accuse him to his face, but tells a parable so that David himself will recognize his sin. The rich man represents David, who had many wives and yet took another man's wife.

For today: when we have much, it is easy to want more at the expense of others. Let us ask God for a grateful and honest heart, one that cares for what others have instead of taking it away.
exp.5:19:
David returned home to bless his household, after the great celebration when he brought the ark into Jerusalem. There Michal, his wife, met him with mockery. She told him the king had made himself look very impressive, but she said it with sarcasm. "Stripped himself" probably means he took off his royal robes and was left in light linen clothing, not necessarily without anything on at all. A "clown" is a crude man who acts out foolish antics.

Michal, the daughter of King Saul, speaks. She looked with contempt as David danced with all his strength before the Lord. To her, a king should keep his dignity. David answers that he was worshiping God, who chose him.

Today, let us not allow the fear of other people's opinions to keep us from worshiping God with sincerity and joy. And let us take care not to despise the devotion of others simply because it is expressed differently from our own.
exp.14:22:
This verse tells us that all the people of the region were weeping loudly as King David and his followers left Jerusalem. They crossed the brook Kidron, a stream east of the city, and continued along the road that leads to the wilderness. A brook like this is a stream that flows strongly, especially in times of rain.

The narrator describes David's flight. His son Absalom had rebelled against him, and David left the city with his servants and his loyal followers, such as Ittai. Later, David asks that the ark be brought back to Jerusalem and leaves his future in God's hands.

For today: when we go through times of loss or betrayal, we can weep honestly and, at the same time, keep trusting. David did not cling to what he had, but placed his situation in God's hands.
exp.12:2:
This verse introduces a new character: Jonadab, Amnon's friend. He was the son of Shimeah, who was David's brother, so he was Amnon's cousin. The King James Version calls him "a very subtil man," and that word here means clever and crafty.

The narrator tells the story of Amnon, David's son, who desired his half-sister Tamar and suffered because of it. At that moment Jonadab appears, sees his sorrow, and in the verses that follow gives him a deceptive piece of advice that leads to a grave sin. The text does not say that God approved of this; the Bible shows it as a tragedy within David's family.

For today: let us be careful about whom we listen to. A clever friend is not always a good counselor. Let us seek voices that bring us closer to God and to what is right, not voices that feed our wrong desires.
exp.7:11:
This verse closes the list of what David dedicated to the LORD: the silver and gold taken from the Syrians, Moabites, Ammonites, Philistines and Amalekites, and also the plunder he won from Hadadezer, king of Zobah. "Plunder" means what is taken from a defeated enemy.

The account is narrative, told by the author of the book, not by David. It recounts that, after several victories, David did not keep everything for himself. When Toi sent him gifts of silver, gold and bronze, David set them apart for the LORD along with the rest. The text shows that he recognized God as the one who gave him the victory, and it confirms this at the end: "The LORD preserved David wherever he went."

For today: when you receive achievements or possessions, acknowledge that they come from God. Set aside a part of them with gratitude, whether as an offering, your time, or help to others, instead of keeping it all for yourself.
exp.18:24:
This verse tells how King David returns to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Mephibosheth comes out to meet him, and David asks him a direct question: "Wherefore wentest not thou with me, Mephibosheth?"

David speaks with Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul. When David fled, Mephibosheth stayed in the city. He appears neglected, as if in mourning. His servant Ziba had accused him of treason (2 Samuel 16), and it is not easy to know for certain who was telling the truth. David wants to hear his side.

For today: before judging someone by appearances or by what others say, let us give them the chance to explain themselves. Listening with patience helps us seek justice and care for our relationships.
exp.8:6:
David tells Mefibosheth not to be afraid. He promises him kindness (the word here means gentle and generous treatment) for the sake of Jonathan, his father. He will also give back to him the lands of Saul, his grandfather (in that time "father" could refer to an ancestor), and invites him to eat at the king's table always.

David speaks as king now. Earlier he had made a covenant of friendship with Jonathan, and he wants to keep that promise to Jonathan's family. Mefibosheth was Jonathan's son, lived hidden in Lodebar, and had a disability in his feet. As Saul's grandson, he could fear that the new king would harm him. David, on the other hand, shows him a favor he did not deserve.

For today: just as David honored a promise and reached out to someone who had nothing to offer in return, we can keep our word and show kindness to those who cannot repay us. Many Christians see in this a reflection of God's grace.
exp.10:10:
Uriah answers David that the ark of the covenant, Israel and Judah are living in tents, and that Joab, his commander, and the servants are camped out in the open fields. For that reason, he cannot go home to eat, drink and be with his wife. He swears this with force: "as thou livest, and as thy soul liveth." The phrase "in the open fields" refers to the open country.

Uriah speaks, a Hittite soldier loyal to Israel. David had him return from the war expecting that he would spend the night with his wife Bathsheba, and so hide that she was pregnant by David. Uriah, knowing nothing, refuses that rest out of solidarity with his companions. His integrity contrasts with David's deception.

For today: true loyalty is shown in sacrifice. Let us ask God for an upright heart, and if we have failed, let us not cover up sin, but confess it with humility.
exp.10:24:
Here David tells the messenger to tell Joab, his commander, not to be troubled by the losses in the battle. He says the sword kills one as well as another, so Joab should press the attack against the city until he takes it, and encourage him.

David speaks with the messenger who brought the news from Rabbah. Earlier he had arranged for Uriah to be placed at the front so that he would die, and so hide his sin with Bathsheba. That is why his reply sounds calm, almost cold. The text goes on to say that this displeased the LORD.

For today: when we have done something wrong, it is tempting to use soft words to cover it. God sees what lies behind them. It is better to confess quickly, as David did later, and to seek his forgiveness.
exp.17:0:
This verse tells how David counted and organized the people who were with him. The verse of the word for "counted" is that it means he examined them or reviewed them. Then he appointed leaders: the commanders of a thousand soldiers and the leaders of a hundred. In this way he divided the army into groups with clear leaders.

The account is told by the author of the book of Samuel. David was fleeing from his son Absalom, who had rebelled and taken the kingdom. They were at Mahanaim, on the other side of the Jordan. Before the battle, David prepared the army in an orderly way, placing Joab, Abishai, and Ittai in charge of the troops.

For today: Before facing a great challenge, it is wise to pray and also to plan in an orderly way. God does not despise preparation; He shares out responsibilities, asks for help, and trusts that He guides the outcome.
exp.1:15:
Each young man grabbed his opponent by the head and drove his sword into his side, and all twenty-four fell down dead together. That is why the place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which means something like "the field of sharp edges" or "the field of swords"; the exact meaning of the name is debated. It was in Gibeon.

Abner, the commander of Ish-bosheth's army, proposed a contest of combat with twelve men from each side, and Joab, David's general, agreed. What seemed like a practice duel ended in a slaughter that ignited a larger battle. The text does not say who started it; it only shows how divided and violent Israel had become.

For today: what is treated lightly, like a game of pride or rivalry, can end in real harm. Before we pit ourselves against someone, let us ask God for humility and seek peace.
exp.17:19:
Joab tells Ahimaas that he will not be the messenger today. He may carry news another day, but not today, because the king's son has died.

Joab, the commander of David's army, had just killed Absalom, who had rebelled against his father. Ahimaas wanted to run and tell David about the victory. Joab knew that David, although he had won the battle, would suffer greatly over the death of his son. So he sent Cushi instead and tried to protect Ahimaas from receiving the force of the king's reaction. Interpreters explain Joab's reasons in different ways.

For today: not everything true is said in just any way. Before giving painful news, think about the moment, the person, and how to accompany it with care.
exp.14:8:
King David gave his son Absalom permission to go to Hebron. "Go in peace" was a common way of saying goodbye and giving a blessing. Absalom got up and went.

David speaks here with a father's confidence, believing that Absalom was going to fulfill a vow made to God. But the verses that follow show that Absalom had another plan: to prepare a rebellion and proclaim himself king in Hebron. As for the "forty years," some scholars think the original text meant four, because that is how it appears in other ancient versions. This is not certain.

Today we can learn that using religious words does not always show a sincere heart. It is wise to ask God for wisdom to discern, and to make sure that our own promises to Him are true and not a pretext for other purposes.
exp.20:4:
The Gibeonites answer King David. They speak of Saul, whom they describe as the man who destroyed them and devised a plan to wipe them out completely, leaving no one in any part of Israel's territory. "Devised" means that he planned something in secret, and "destroyed" means to tear something out by the root, to eliminate it entirely.

There is a famine in the land, and David seeks God, who explains that it is because of the blood Saul shed against the Gibeonites. They were a people with whom Israel had made a covenant (Joshua 9). The Bible does not recount the details of that slaughter here. David asks them how he can make amends for the wrong, and they explain their complaint.

For today: injustices of the past matter to God, even when time has passed. If we have harmed someone, it is good to acknowledge it with humility and seek to repair the damage, not to ignore it.
exp.21:11:
He says that God surrounded himself with darkness, as if it were tents or canopies around him. That darkness is made of dark waters, that is, clouds heavy with rain, and of thick clouds. "Pavilions" are tents or canopies. "As though" means "as if it were."

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, near the end of his life, after God delivered him from Saul and from all his enemies. He uses storm imagery to describe how God came to rescue him. It is poetic language, not a literal account of what could be seen.

For today: God is greater than we can see or understand. When your life feels dark or confusing, remember that God may be at work even among the clouds. Trust in Him and ask Him for help with sincerity.
exp.12:31:
Jonadab tells King David not to believe the rumor that Absalom had killed all his sons. According to him, only Amnon died. He explains that Absalom had decided this from the day Amnon forced himself on (raped) Tamar, his sister. The phrase "the young men, the king's sons" refers to the princes, and the phrase "by the appointment of Absalom" means it was a settled plan fixed in his mind.

Jonadab is David's nephew, and he was the cunning friend who had earlier advised Amnon on the scheme to get Tamar alone. David is shattered by the false news, and Jonadab speaks with apparent calm and confidence. The Bible does not explain how he knew this; it only shows that he was well informed about the matter. It is notable that he now speaks like someone who knows what happened.

For today: an injustice not addressed in time can grow until it becomes a tragedy. Let us seek justice and healing soon, and let us take care whom we receive counsel from.
exp.11:7:
God reminds David of everything he had given him: the house of Saul, his former master, and Saul's wives, who were placed into his keeping and authority. He also gave him the kingdom of Israel and Judah. And if that had been too little, God would have given him such and such things, meaning even more blessings.

Here God speaks through the prophet Nathan. He has just told David a parable about a rich man who stole the only little ewe lamb of a poor man. David became angry, and Nathan answered him: "You are the man." God shows his kindness so that David may see the seriousness of his sin with Bathsheba and Uriah.

For today: when we are tempted, let us remember how much God has given us. Gratitude helps us not to seek what is forbidden and to live with humility.
exp.0:15:
Here David tells the man who has just been condemned: "Thy blood be upon thy head" means that the guilt for his death rests on him himself, not on David. The man himself had declared, "I have slain the Lord's anointed." The word "anointed" refers to the king chosen by God.

David speaks after receiving news of Saul's death. A young Amalekite claimed to have killed him, hoping for a reward. According to 1 Samuel 31, Saul had taken his own life; so it is possible that the young man was lying or exaggerating. David did not reward him but judged him by his own words, since he respected Saul as the king set in place by God.

For today: our words carry weight and bind us. Let us speak with truth, without seeking advantage through lies, and respect what God considers sacred.
exp.17:7:
It says that the battle spread across the whole region, and that the forest caused more deaths than the sword did. The phrase "over the face of the land" means the surface or extent of the terrain. "Sword" here stands for the fighting itself. The verse does not say how the forest killed people; some think of swamps, ravines, wild animals, or people who got lost or fell while fleeing.

This is part of the account of Absalom's rebellion against his father David. The narrator describes the battle in the forest of Ephraim, east of the Jordan, between David's men and Absalom's followers. What follows is Absalom's death, when his head became caught in a tree.

For today: disasters do not always come from where we expect them. When life is thrown into disorder by conflict, even what seems harmless can harm us. That is why it is wise to seek peace, ask God for direction, and avoid unnecessary quarrels.
exp.6:14:
He says that God will never withdraw his mercy from David's son, even when he corrects him for doing wrong. With Saul it was different: God removed him from his place as king. "But" means "but," and "mercy" here is a faithful, steadfast love that does not abandon.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan to David. David wanted to build a temple, but God promises him something greater: to establish his dynasty forever. This promise is directed first to Solomon, who would build the temple, and Christians also see it fulfilled in Jesus, a descendant of David. Interpreters debate how some of the details apply, but the promise of faithfulness is clear.

God corrects his children without ceasing to love them. If you fail today, do not think that God has rejected you. His discipline seeks to restore you, not to destroy you. Return to him with confidence and humility.
exp.2:16:
Abner speaks to the elders of Israel, who were the leaders of the tribes. He reminds them that for a long time they had wanted David to be their king. The phrase "in times past" means "for a long time now," and "sought" means that they had been looking for him or desiring him.

Abner was the commander of the army of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, but he had become estranged from him and wanted to switch sides to David. He had already brought Michal back to David, and now he is preparing the ground among the leaders. We do not know with certainty all of his motives; the text shows both his personal interest and the recognition that God had promised the kingdom to David.

For today: sometimes we know what God wants, but we let time pass without obeying. Let us ask for the courage to act with sincerity and not only out of convenience.
exp.4:24:
David did exactly what God had commanded him. He defeated the Philistines, who fled, and pursued them from Geba all the way to Gezer. "Struck" here means that he defeated them in battle. Many versions read "Geba" and "Gezer," so the place names vary depending on the manuscript.

David was at war with the Philistines, who wanted to defeat him as soon as he became king over all Israel. Before fighting, David sought God's guidance, and God gave him a strategy: go around the enemy and wait for a sign, the sound of wind in the tops of the trees. Then God himself would go out ahead of him.

Today, before important decisions, seek God's guidance in prayer and in his Word. Then obey with patience, waiting for his timing even when his plan does not look like yours.
exp.12:4:
Jonadab advises Amnon to lie down and pretend to be sick. When King David comes to see him, Amnon should ask that his sister Tamar come, prepare food right there, and serve it to him from her own hand.

Jonadab is Amnon's cousin, and the text describes him as very crafty. Amnon had become fixated on Tamar, his half-sister. Jonadab does not encourage him to seek what is right; instead he proposes a deception so that Amnon can be alone with her. What follows in the account is a terrible tragedy of abuse and violence.

For today: let us be careful about whom we listen to. A crafty friend may offer advice that seems clever but leads us into wrongdoing. Let us seek counselors who love truth and justice, and ask God for wisdom to reject deception.
exp.12:24:
Here King David answers Absalom's invitation to the sheep-shearing feast. He tells Absalom that they should not all go, so that they will not be a burden to him. Absalom pressed him, but David would not go; even so, he blessed Absalom as he sent him off.

The speaker is David, Absalom's father. Two years have passed since Amnon dishonored Tamar, Absalom's sister, and David did not bring justice. The Bible does not yet say that Absalom is planning anything, but the story that follows shows that the invitation hid a plan for revenge. David did not know this.

Friendly appearances can often hide twisted intentions, and unresolved wounds can grow in silence. Today we can seek justice and reconciliation in good time, with honesty and prayer, rather than letting resentment ripen. It is also wise to ask for wisdom to discern.
exp.18:17:
This verse says that a boat crossed the Jordan River to carry the family of King David to the other side, and to do whatever he wished. The source's comment on its old wording (the phrase meaning "pleased him") is replaced here by the verse's own words: the verse says the boat was to do "what he thought good," so that is the phrase to note. When David had already crossed the Jordan, Shimei threw himself down before him, that is, bowed down to the ground as a sign of humility.

This is part of David's return to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. Earlier, Shimei had cursed and humiliated him while he was fleeing (2 Samuel 16). Now, with David victorious, Shimei arrives with a thousand men from Benjamin and asks for forgiveness. We do not know whether his repentance was sincere or for convenience; the text does not make this clear.

When we have wronged someone, it is best to acknowledge it soon and with humility. Asking for forgiveness without excuses opens the door to reconciliation, even though we cannot control how the other person will respond.
exp.4:21:
This verse says that the Philistines attacked again. The phrase that is rendered here as "came up yet again" carries the sense of returning, and the phrase about spreading out describes them deploying their forces across the valley of Rephaim, a valley near Jerusalem.

The narrator of the book speaks here. David had already defeated the Philistines at Baal-perazim and had burned their idols. Even so, they returned. What matters comes next: David did not trust in the earlier victory, but went back to inquire of the LORD, and God gave him a different strategy.

For today: a past victory does not excuse us from praying again. When a problem returns, do not face it with yesterday's formula out of habit. Ask God, listen for His guidance, and move forward with patience, trusting that He goes before you.
exp.22:23:
This verse opens the list of the "thirty," a group of brave soldiers of David. It names Asahel, brother of Joab, and Elhanan, son of Dodo, of Bethlehem. The word "thirty" and the spelling "Bethlehem" are the names as they appear in the verse above.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recording the names of the most distinguished men in David's army. After telling of the deeds of the first three and of Benaiah, the text lists the others. Asahel died young, in a battle against Abner (2 Samuel 2), so his name is kept as a memorial. Some scholars think the list gathers men from different periods of David's reign.

For today: God does not forget those who serve, even when their name is little known. Faithfully doing your part, without seeking applause, also has value before Him. Simple names were written down in the Bible.
exp.6:27:
He says that the Lord is the true God and that his words are firm, meaning sure and trustworthy. David recognizes that God made him a good promise. The old-fashioned spelling of "a" in this verse, and the phrase "this good" refers to that promise of blessing.

David is praying after the prophet Nathan told him that God would build him a "house," that is, a line of descendants and a dynasty. David wanted to build a temple, but God promised him something greater: that his family would endure. This prayer comes from gratitude and humility. Christians often see in this promise an announcement that points to Jesus, a descendant of David, although each tradition explains it with different nuances.

Today we can pray as David did: remember what God has promised in his Word and rest in the fact that he is faithful. When you doubt, repeat his promises in prayer and trust.
exp.1:11:
Abner, the son of Ner, went out from Mahanaim toward Gibeon. The servants of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, went with him. Here "servants" means the men in his service, probably soldiers.

The narrator describes a time when Israel was divided. Ish-bosheth ruled over Israel, and only Judah still followed David in Hebron. Abner was the commander of Saul's army and was supporting Ish-bosheth. His movement toward Gibeon sets up the meeting with Joab and David's men. The text does not say clearly what his exact purpose was; some think he was seeking to strengthen Ish-bosheth's power.

For today: when there are divisions, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are seeking God's will or only defending our own side. Let us ask him for wisdom to pursue peace.
exp.18:29:
Mephibosheth tells King David that Ziba may keep all the lands, not just half. For him, what matters most is that the king has come home safe and sound. "Let him take them" means "let him take them all," and "in peace" means without harm, in well-being. Here the quoted phrases are not in the verse, so the reader sees the verse's own wording: "let him take all" and "come again in peace unto his own house."

David was returning to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Mephibosheth, grandson of Saul and son of Jonathan, had been treated with kindness by David. Ziba had accused him of disloyalty, and Mephibosheth maintained that he had been deceived. David decided to divide the lands. Some think Mephibosheth spoke with sincerity and gratitude; others see resignation in the face of an unfair decision. The text does not make this entirely clear.

Today we can learn to value relationships and peace more than material gain. When something does not turn out the way we want, we can ask ourselves: what is truly most important? Being thankful for what we have received helps us let go of resentment.
exp.4:3:
This verse says that David was thirty years old when he began to be king, and that he reigned forty years in total. The phrase "began to reign" means that he started his reign, and the old spelling of the word "to" in that phrase is the same as the modern word "to" with a different accent mark.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not David. After years of conflict with the house of Saul, the elders of Israel come to Hebron and recognize David as king. The author summarizes the length of his reign: seven and a half years in Hebron over Judah, and thirty-three in Jerusalem over all Israel. The number forty is round, and the text presents it as a summary.

For today: God can bring a person to his purpose with patience. David waited for years from the time he was anointed until he reigned over everyone. Trust God's timing and be faithful while you wait.
exp.15:14:
This verse says that Absalom and all the people of Israel who followed him entered Jerusalem. Ahithophel came with them. "Absalom" is Absalom, "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and "Ahithophel" is Ahithophel, a highly respected counselor.

The narrator describes the moment when David flees the city because his son Absalom rebelled and seized power. While David moves forward tired and humiliated, Absalom enters as the new king. Ahithophel, once David's counselor, now stands on Absalom's side. Shortly afterward we will see that Hushai, David's friend, steps in to help him in secret.

For today: difficult situations can make it seem as if others are winning and God is silent. Even so, He keeps working. When you feel tired or betrayed, do not act out of bitterness; trust that God cares for you and still directs the story.

sum.22: Near the end of his life, David says that God spoke through him: a just ruler who fears God is like the morning light. He admits that his household is not perfect, yet God made an everlasting covenant with him. Then his mighty warriors are named, and David refuses to drink the water that his men risked their lives to get for him, and he pours it out to God.
sum.7: David won many battles against the Philistines, Moab, Syria, and Edom, and those peoples came under his control. The text repeats that Jehovah kept him safe wherever he went, and David dedicated the silver and gold of the defeated nations to God. He ruled with justice and organized his government with his officials.
sum.17: David sends his army out against the rebels and asks them to deal gently with his son Absalom. But Joab kills him when he is caught hanging from a tree, and David wins the battle. When the king receives the news, he does not celebrate; he weeps with grief for his son, and he wishes he had died in his place.
sum.18: David weeps so deeply for Absalom that his people are ashamed, until Joab confronts him and the king encourages his servants again. Then he returns to Jerusalem, forgives Shimei, listens to Mephibosheth, honors Barzilai, and Judah and Israel argue over who has the greater claim on him. We see a wounded kingdom seeking to be reconciled.
sum.14: Absalom slowly won the hearts of the people through deception, and he had himself proclaimed king in Hebron. David fled Jerusalem in tears, and his loyal followers went with him, including Ittai. David left the ark in the city, trusting in God's will. He also asked Hushai to return to Jerusalem so that he could thwart the counsel of Ahithophel.
sum.12: Amnon, son of David, deceives his sister Tamar and rapes her, and then he cruelly rejects her. Her brother Absalom holds a grudge and, two years later, has Amnon killed, and then he flees to Geshur. This chapter shows how unaddressed sin brings more pain and violence to a family.
sum.10: David stayed behind in Jerusalem while his army was fighting, and he abused his power by taking Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, who became pregnant. To cover up his sin, David tried to trick Uriah, and when that failed, he ordered that Uriah be left to die in battle. Afterward he married Bathsheba, but this displeased the LORD.
sum.9: David wanted to show kindness to Hanun, the new king of Ammon, so he sent messengers to comfort him over the death of his father. But Hanun grew suspicious, humiliated David's messengers, and prepared for war with the help of the Syrians. Joab and David defeated them, and the Syrians made peace with Israel.
sum.16: Absalom preferred the advice of Hushai to that of Ahithophel, because the Lord had determined to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel. Hushai secretly warned David, who crossed the Jordan safely, and Ahithophel took his own life. In Mahanaim, David received generous help.
sum.13: Joab, seeing that David longed for Absalom, sent for a wise woman from Tekoa to tell David a made-up story about two sons and a revenge killing, so that he would be moved to forgive. David agreed that Absalom could return, but he did not receive him for two years. After a dispute with Joab, Absalom finally got to see the king, and David kissed him.
sum.15: While David is fleeing from Absalom, Ziba brings provisions and accuses Mephibosheth, and David gives him everything that belonged to Mephibosheth. Shimei curses and throws stones at David, but David endures the insult and hopes that God will look upon his affliction. Meanwhile, Hushai pretends to be loyal to Absalom, and Ahithophel gives him shameful advice.
sum.0: David learns at Ziklag that Saul and Jonathan have died. The news comes from a young Amalekite man, who claims that he killed Saul at Saul's own request and brings Saul's crown to David. David and his men mourn and fast. David orders the young man put to death for having said that he killed the Lord's anointed. Afterward, David composes a lament that honors Saul and Jonathan.
sum.1: David, guided by God, goes up to Hebron, and there the men of Judah anoint him king. He thanks the people of Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul. Meanwhile, Abner makes Ish-bosheth king, and the rivalry ends in a cruel battle in which Asahel dies. The chapter shows that David seeks God's direction, and that division brings sorrow.
sum.3: When Abner dies, Ish-bosheth and all Israel are filled with fear. Two captains, Baanah and Rechab, kill Ish-bosheth while he sleeps and bring his head to David, expecting a reward. David condemns them for killing a righteous man in his own bed, orders them executed, and they bury Ish-bosheth's head in Abner's tomb.
sum.4: The tribes of Israel went to Hebron and anointed David as king over all the people. He captured Jerusalem, made it his city, and grew stronger because God was with him. Then he defeated the Philistines twice, always asking God for guidance and obeying it.
sum.6: David wanted to build a house for God, but God answered him through Nathan that He would instead build a house for David. He promised to establish the throne of David's descendants forever and to be a father to his son. David responded with humility, praising God and asking Him to keep the promise He had made.
sum.19: Sheba, a man from Benjamin, stirred up a rebellion, and almost all of Israel abandoned David, but Judah remained loyal to him. Joab treacherously killed Amasa and then pursued Sheba as far as the city of Abel. A wise woman persuaded her people to hand over Sheba's head, and in this way the city was spared from destruction.
sum.5: David wanted to bring the ark of God up to Jerusalem, but Uzzah died when he touched it. David then left the ark for three months at the house of Obed-edom, and God blessed Obed-edom. Later they brought the ark up with great joy, and David danced with all his strength. His wife Michal despised him for it, but David answered that his joy was for God.
sum.21: David sings a song of thanks to God for rescuing him from Saul and from all his enemies. He calls God his rock, his shield, and his savior, and he describes how God heard his cry and came down with power to save him. David praises God for being faithful to the humble and promises to sing to his name.
sum.8: David asks whether anyone is still left from the house of Saul so that he can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan. Ziba, a servant of Saul's household, tells him about Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, who is lame in both feet. David has him brought in, gives back to him all the land of Saul, and invites him to eat at the king's table regularly, just like one of the king's sons. Here we see a mercy that keeps its promise and gives honor to someone who feels unworthy.
sum.2: David grew stronger while the house of Saul grew weaker. Abner, offended by Ish-bosheth, switched sides to David and tried to unite Israel under him. But Joab killed him through deception to avenge the death of his brother Asahel. David publicly mourned him, fasted, and left the punishment in God's hands.
sum.20: There was a famine for three years, and God told David that it was because of the blood Saul had shed when he killed the Gibeonites. David handed over seven of Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites, and Rizpah kept watch over the bodies. David then buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan, and after that God was moved to show mercy to the land. Later, Israel defeated Philistine giants.
sum.11: God sends the prophet Nathan, who uses a parable to show David how serious his sin with Bathsheba and Uriah was. David admits, "I have sinned against the Lord," and God forgives him, but He announces painful consequences, including the death of the child. Later, Solomon is born, and Joab and David capture Rabbah.
sum.23: David ordered a census of the people, even though Joab warned him against it. Afterward David's conscience struck him, and he confessed his sin. God gave him a choice of punishment. David chose to fall into the hands of God, a plague came, and God stopped it. David bought the threshing floor of Araunah, built an altar there, and the plague ended.
